These walking snails—」 SKREEEEEK 「—will sincerely believe that I did all sorts of things wrong, anyway, and so by punishing me they are 'realiiizing juuustice.' Bleh!」 SKREEEEEK What on earth was making such a sound? To the Inspectorate members it was a total mystery. The sound of a living thing in agony? A noise produced by inanimate objects colliding, or being stirred together until they lost their shape? They could not even tell whether there was anything in the natural world to liken it to. 「…Haa. My Dissolution Force research is at a standstill, too—」 But Aurena's voice, which followed, cleanly swept away such trifling curiosities. 「—and here I am, just whining like this. I thought the Lucid lot might bring me something a little fresh.」 The Inspectorate members exchanged glances in disbelief. Yet everyone had heard the same thing. The Lucid? Had she joined hands with those branded a heretical cult by the sect that reigns as the continent's de facto bishopric? 「They helped me grasp the interaction between an operating biochemical system and Dissolution Force, but it's all far too rule-of-thumb—no good at all. Maybe I should pull out by now?」 Aurena yawned. Along with it, what sounded like the prelude to the recurring strange noise rose faintly, then subsided. 「Observations made by a test subject who knows it is a test subject are always distorted. I've been rubbing shoulders with the walking snails for a while now, so honestly I can't stomach playing nice with the plain snails outside the Society either, and… oh!」 Aurena yawned again. The sense of her rummaging through something, then bringing it before her to examine, followed presently. 「Still, I ought to wring this dry to the last and toss it… they said rifts… have opened nearby, too, a few of them?」 The sound of scratching her head. She began to mumble. 「Maybe I should just really go?… As if there's a better laboratory than there.」 "Aha! So that's where she's tucked her tail and fled!" said one of the Inspectorate members who had kept silent all the while.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main3_Content_2: "To flee, of all places, into a crucible of chaos where all order and continuity are severed—and she calls herself a scholar?" "If she walked into The Rapids on her own two feet, all the better." The other Inspectorate members began to add a word or two each. "Outsiders were harmed as well, so if this matter blows up, we won't be able to settle it ourselves. It'll give them outside a pretext to take issue with the neutrality of the Moonlight Sanctuary." "I do hope she never comes back." "Never comes back—is that all?" One of the members shouted in a sudden burst. "We ought to pray she meets a wretched end in The Rapids outright!" After that they examined the rest of the records in the quartz, but there was nothing of great significance. Whether it had not been procured for research in the first place, apart from the single recording containing that preposterous self-rationalization, only private—at times excessively private—content followed, one after another. Through all the records as they played, only one thing remained unchanging. "Where did the sage's brooch go? It's a valuable asset of the Society—we must recover it without fail." SKREEEEEK "I searched everywhere; it was nowhere to be found." "Hmph. Unbecoming of her tongue, she must have cherished it and carried it off with her when she bolted." SKREEEEEK "How are we to fathom the thoughts of such a lunatic? Dwelling on it only costs us." SKREEEE— The last record, no longer even speech, was cut off, and the laboratory sank into stillness. Anew, every Inspectorate member fell to brooding over his own curiosity. It had become a subject of no consequence now, but inwardly they wondered what that sound might have been. "Somewhere around here…." Meanwhile there was one Inspectorate member who had not yet lost his zeal. He was pulling the remaining books from the shelves and reshelving them, knocking on the walls, scrutinizing the joints of furniture large and small. He was searching for a secret passage Aurena might have slipped away through, or a hidden safe and the like. "…Hard to see in here, but there might be something… huh?" The tip of a glove, groping along the underside of a heavy desk fitted with drawers and the like, caught on something. When he yanked his hand back, startled, he felt a stiff resistance, as when one rubs skin against sandpaper. Had he pulled even a little harder, the tip of his glove would have been scraped clean away. "What is it?" "L-look at this." The member whose glove had been frayed beckoned his colleagues with a gesture. Then, joining forces, they flipped the desk over. What was revealed were marks. Marks where the underside of the tabletop, in a place no eye reached, had been gouged. Marks as though stabbed with an awl, scraped with a carving knife, dug out with a chisel, hollowed with a long blade, clawed and torn at with talons sunk in—they covered the underside of the desk without a gap. So relentless were the traces that the whole board had laid its snow-white inner flesh utterly bare. And there were others who, seeing that sight, gained some inspiration. "Here too!" And indeed it was so. There were similar marks elsewhere as well. They lifted the thick carpet covering the floor, and they were there too. They looked inside the empty drawers, and they were there too. They dragged out the furniture flush against the walls, and they were there too. As though a beast with talons and fangs bristling all over its body had run amok, every concealable surface in the laboratory had been clawed and dug at without exception. The deep furrows had, at times, stopped only barely short of the far side, leaving a gap thin as tissue paper. What had been carved out of them was, again, hidden away in every nook. Heaps of sawdust and thread-shaped slivers of wood, nails snapped in two at the middle… someone, looking at it, recalled the strange sound within the Resonant Quartz; someone else, looking at it, thought that the marks left where the furniture had been scraped resembled an enormous talon's grasp. And so, at the center of a laboratory whose every surface, on all six sides, had been slashed ragged, the Inspectorate members gulped. To think that the perpetrator of such a frenzy had vanished of her own accord and would not return—somehow, it set them at ease.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main3_Short: An emptied chamber, a forgotten quartz, and a voice convinced its own justification is flawless. What are the claw-marks beneath the desk hiding that even she could never say aloud?
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main4_Content_0:
That day, into the boundless, mysterious world called The Rapids, a single drop of foreign matter mingled in. To that foreign matter, which called itself Aurena, the first impression was wonder, and the experience that followed was bodily fatigue. Hauling every necessary item piled on her back as she moved was nothing but the repetitive labor she most loathed, without the slightest innovative facet to it. Back in her laboratory days, there had been any number of assistants whose bodies fairly burned with the wish to be of help.
The next thing she met after that experience, however, was an unceasing procession of enemies.
"What are these things?"
spat Aurena, who had unfastened her pack and was kneading her shoulders. Dream beasts—their very forms a chaotic, slapdash mess—approached, baring white teeth.
"Is this a spectacle? Get lost."
Heedless of her, the encirclement steadily tightened. Like minnows swarming to a brook where bait has been scattered… without even time to ponder such a simile, the tension turned to menace, and soon enough slid into the phase of a one-sided hunt. It was not that Aurena was without a plan, however. She straightened her back and steadied her breath. With both hands on her hips, she watched the beasts hurtling at her. Then she shrugged.
"If that's what you want."
And then the grasping hands wrought of gold revealed their full form.

They were not mere fingers, for the thing took on the complete shape of a hand; and they were not mere hands, for, of a hand's many aspects, the thing emphasized only those of suppressing, subduing, and destroying—that is, only the violent function of a "talon's grasp." Fingertips keen as a bird's beak, knuckles thick as the bursting thigh of a warhorse, sinews firm as a stump that had sunk its roots into a cliff—each twitch of them cast a golden afterglow. The majesty of that form could not be likened to any object such as some immense beast or machine. For nothing capable of producing power so precise and so mighty had yet been born or invented.
"Will you keep at it even now?"
The Golden Talons wheeled through the air in time with Aurena's gestures. A dazzling radiance overlaid a movement that seemed almost weightless, scarcely even substantial. Yet even before such a sight, the beasts did not shrink in the least.
If anything, they seemed all the more roused to hurl themselves at her.
"A perfect chance to test just how deftly I can wield Dissolution Force—"
A Talon snatched up one of the beasts. Aurena smirked.
"—you mean!"
Bone tearing through the muscle that wrapped it, muscle through the surrounding fat, fat through the outer skin—the beast spilled out, turned into a pulp with everything inverted. Watching it, Aurena twisted her expression. From disgust? Quite the opposite.

"What is this?"
For the dead beast's body soon, under some unknown influence, transformed wholesale into pale, bluish, viscous colloidal particles. Only after a similar pattern had repeated several times in the ensuing engagements could she retreat to the safe bulwark of inductive reasoning. In other words, she accepted the fact that this was what generally occurred.
"If I can't preserve the carcass—"
The interlaced Talons came crashing down. The beast that had been between them and the ground was flattened into a paste.
"—then I can't dissect it—"
The Talons began a circular motion at a constant angular velocity, like the blades of a windmill. As petals scatter on a bitter wind, the beasts too were flung this way and that, spitting blood.
"—and I can't research it, can I!"
A Talon cleaved the air. The body of the foremost beast fell, parted into several strands. To shake off the things snagged in the gaps of her hand—not her real hand, but the gaps of the Golden Talons—she clenched a fist. The pleasant recoil of sturdy bone-marrow and tough tendons being crushed was transmitted to her. Aurena laughed. Quite apart from its difficulty as a research subject, this act was a pleasure. There was even an impression of being beneficial. The beasts that simply charged in without a thought were truly convenient. They were an easy equation to handle—no, a single point (·) upon that equation. Watching one beast rampage and another follow after to rampage in turn, they were nothing but a single material point upon a linear function, from whose slope one could derive the entire rest of the graph and more. She laughed scornfully.
"Come, as many as you like."
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main4_Content_1:
*

"What a chaotic place this is."
It was after enough time had passed for that impression to fade. Even an equation whose next value could be predicted linearly without limit—if anything kept surging in endlessly, Aurena, for her part, grew sick of it.
"How many are left?"
It was after both of the Golden Talons had each made the carcass pile its ninth-and-one, or perhaps its ninety-ninth-and-one. Aurena stood on the tips of her toes to gauge the distant view stretching off into the distance, but could make out nothing. Whether night had come, all around was dim. And yet, for some reason, the sun hung at the zenith? She blinked. From the absurd, contradictory scene of sunlight pouring down brightly while night lay drawn beneath it, she felt not so much the intellectual pleasure of paradox as another, far more foul sensation. Narrowing her brow, she looked closer. A black horizon, and stretching on from it black hills and valleys and plains and… stretching on unbroken right up to where she stood, a tide of black beasts.
Aurena's lips pursed small.
"Me? Impossible."
"You were scared—you flinched, Aurena!"
Reproachful soliloquies began pouring out in disarray.
"You flinched, just now!"
"Impossible—from creatures this simple, this brutish, I…."
Having seen something, Aurena's face turned ashen. It was the upper body of a beast that a Talon had "dealt with" once and passed by. Even with its body cut in half, it was still alive. Wriggling a body slashed to look like a great cushion, it tried to inch its way closer. Toward her.
The gold Talon pressed its head down with a squelch and kneaded it together with the soil, but Aurena's complexion—and her heart, which had begun to pound—did not return to as they had been.
"This is supposed to be my field, too…."
Organic chemistry, physiology, and the like had been useful for tending the test subjects, who had not realized that they had volunteered, or had volunteered without knowing it. But here they were of no use at all. One could not expect anything to happen by injecting or depriving of something the monsters that, bearing bodies that were not bodies, had consigned their sanity to a hunger that could never be filled. So she had to keep fighting. For how long?
Until the black horizon regained its original hue?

*

"Uh—uh?"
Aurena wiped at something falling slantwise from one side of her jaw. Trickling down in droplets, wetting her bare skin with an iridescent sheen, it was drool.
"Did I… nod off?"
She opened both eyes wide. She had been dozing!
"How—how—how long?"
It was dusk. Using the mountainous heaps of carcasses and the bluish river-course as her fortress, she had been holed up. Roughened eyelids scraped across her eyeballs like wood shavings. Her throat burned. The small of her back was stiff. She was tired. Tired beyond measure. The mist that filled her head and every corner of her body now refused to clear. No matter how she repeated large, refreshing motions with the gold Talons, her condition did not improve. The battle was not yet over. There were beasts that had survived, a pack that had not yet abandoned its obsession with Aurena. All manner of pincers and talons and feelers squeezed out through the gaps in the terrain that had become her fortress. Gasping for ragged breath, she nonetheless drew herself rigidly into battle posture, and then—she happened to look at the two Golden Talons. There were flaws that would not heal. The products transmuted with Dissolution Force, failing to maintain their complete form? On the outside, this had never happened.
"Is that… a bite mark?"
There was no time. She had to find something to transmute into gold in their stead. Out of urgency, Aurena rummaged through her pack. She selected the items closest to disposable—those it would not matter to smash or break several of—and exposed them to the reaction equation. The small quantity of gold dust produced replenished the lacking portions of the two Talons.
"On the outside, this never happened."
Aurena murmured. This was a fact she had thought already codified. An axiom forming the very foundation of her logical system, and the premise of all her experimental designs.
"They'd fill in by themselves, little by little."
And so she could by no means brush it off as trivial.

*
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main4_Content_2:
It was now the dead of night. A moon small as a pinhole had risen in the sky. Glaring at the bare ground that cast no shadow, Aurena convulsed desperately. With every breath, the inside of her ribs ached as though being beaten with a cudgel. The limbs she had braced on all fours trembled uncontrollably. She had not the strength to lift a single finger, but at least, now, all around had fallen quiet. She had driven off every last beast that lunged at her. It was her victory. The victory of Dissolution Force. The brilliant achievement of the great sage Aurena.
"This time," that is.
"If it keeps on like this, wherever I go…."
A taste of blood rose in her throat. Gritting her teeth, Aurena spat out the sticky things pooling beneath her tongue, in her nose, on the roof of her mouth. They bore the kind of color and viscosity that might come only from an animal on the verge of death.
"If I patch the Talons by transmuting my experimental apparatus for battle—how long can I hold out?"
It was strange. Her head would not turn properly. Tiredness was a matter of course, but an inexplicable, vicious helplessness—the impression of deficiency—had grown stronger still. And what was more, the best stopgap she could devise was to transmute her fittings on the spot and graft them onto the Talons? Aurena scoffed at so naïve a fantasy. Had she not entered the dream world in the first place for analysis and research? To use the tools gathered for that purpose to grapple with beasts instead would be like wrenching out the stone propping up her own foot and hurling it at the enemy. Even if she survived for the moment that way, if she could not carry out valid research activity—if she failed to grasp the nature of dreams and drifted aimlessly to and fro—she would in any case, sooner or later, be overwhelmed by sheer numbers.
I could die in here.

Having conjured up that chilling possibility, Aurena realized anew that she had been holding her breath. In the stillness, the surrounding scenery and scents and sounds and temperatures and textures felt more vivid than ever. The unfamiliar forests and rivers and marshes and deserts and steep slopes and dense thickets that filled every direction all felt like monsters watching for nothing but a chance to kill her. A sage who had stolen the raw flesh of wisdom upon the chopping block where the butcher's blade comes down—the great rat Aurena—was scurrying for her life.
"No, no."
she wailed in a wholly hoarse voice.
"I can't die in a place like this… I'm different from the other snails!"
Unable to master her indignation, Aurena struck the bare ground with her fist. What she had transmuted as a weapon took the shape of a talon's grasp, but the hand she actually wielded was, in fact, so fine and soft. There was only one tiny, dear little callus on the knuckle that had braced her pen as she scribbled. As the result of those delicate, jade-like hands being swung about heedlessly, in defiance of a fury fit to turn her eyes inside out, but unable to vent it effectively—naturally, by the grace of so unpracticed a motion—a scrape was opened on Aurena's bare skin. A single drop of dark blood timidly poked out its head. As she watched it, a very strange inspiration occurred to her. Aurena turned the reaction equation of Dissolution Force over in her mind, and applied it directly to reality.
The blood exploded.
Not into flame and smoke and noise, but into a glittering radiance, and the foam that gushed it forth. Golden bubbles, round and broad as ripe fruit, or the crown of a bell, or the back of a human head with the flesh stripped away, came bubbling out in torrents. They collapsed when gripped in the hand, lost their shape and crumbled when kicked by the foot—but they had unmistakably become pure, weighty, dazzlingly shining gold. From a single drop of blood, enough poured forth to fill a cylindrical wooden bathtub to the brim!
{IMAGE}
"How did this happen?"
"How, indeed? You observed the whole process with your own eyes, and you still don't know?"
What stood in the transformation term of the reaction equation was blood. A single drop of her own blood. No other catalyst or peculiar condition that might have assisted the reaction was observed.
"How did this happen?"
"Either there's something special about me, or about my blood, or else…."
She was at once so absorbed in it that she lost all other interest. Even as she crawled on all fours, as though she had never been wrung dry and exhausted, the eyes of one confronting a new object of curiosity glittered with sharpness, not to be outdone by the overflowing golden foam. The most powerful yet most ambiguous clue to The Rapids and the dream world—to the function that real-world gold serves within them—was thus handed to her.
The interpretation was Aurena's to make.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main4_Short: From a single drop of her blood pours a tide of gold — radiant, heavy, impossible. What price hides behind a reaction she watched with her own eyes yet dares not interpret?
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main5_Content_0:
Though she thought of herself as a researcher by nature, Aurena had always considered writing to be a rather unfree undertaking. However long or short the writing, of whatever character, the impression did not change. The moment one draws the first stroke at some point upon the paper, which holds infinite possibility, the letter that emerges is predetermined. Depending on what part of speech that letter takes, the phrases and content that follow are all predetermined too. Depending on what grounds those phrases use to develop their thesis, the conclusion is predetermined as well. So the single free thing in writing is only the moment one draws the first stroke of the first letter of the first sentence of the first paragraph.
Exploring The Rapids was just the same.
The decision to enter had unmistakably been her own free will, but everything thereafter was an inexorable sequence of events. Wandering about, she would meet a hostile pack of creatures, and fight and win, or take cover midway. Then, wandering about, she would meet a hostile pack of creatures, and fight and win, or take cover midway. Then….
"I'm tired."
Diagnosing her own state objectively brought nothing to a clear resolution. It only turned her into an ordinary person who states the obvious in the obvious way as a matter of course. The great sage Aurena—obvious, of all things!
"It's not just that it's exhausting—this is something… something different."
Aurena drew her feathered arm before her eyes and examined it. The color had changed. Not from the root up, as when pigment drains away, but the reverse. It was changing from the very outermost tip of the feather. It was slowly being stained by something. By a sallow, golden hue with a lustrous metallic sheen. This, too, was a phenomenon she had never witnessed on the outside—even though she had verified the reaction equation of Dissolution Force far more, and far more often, than now.
When she removed her gloves and shoes, the same thing was happening. Her fingertips and toes were paling, little by little. Pale—but not the pallor of skin drained of blood; rather the color of pure silver and platinum. A continuous band of light hung trailing along her fingers and the back of her hand, along the curves of the soles of her feet. At first she had supposed they had merely been added onto her body. Like the golden horn ornament atop her head. But she, who had never wished for thimbles wrought of gold or dancing slippers shaped from pure silver, tried to scrape them off with a sharp awl. And then she shrieked and fainted. It hurt tremendously. As though raw flesh were being gouged with a blade.

"That, too, is something that didn't used to happen."
Things that didn't used to happen, things never witnessed—were there merely one or two? The fact she had suspected in that first day's battle had, within a few days, turned into certainty. Even amid the melee, she had seen it clearly. The dream beasts that pounced upon the sloughed-off fragments of the Golden Talons and devoured them in ravenous haste. Yet how was it that the beasts displaying such pica suffered no ill effect whatsoever, while Aurena's body—which had not touched a single mote of gold dust to its lips—was the one being gradually replaced by metallic elements? This soon expanded her thinking even to the situation in which she had had to transmute several pieces of her experimental apparatus into gold and graft them onto the Talons.
"The living things, and the inanimate things, within this place cannot be transmuted into gold."
"Are you certain?"
Grating on her own nerves with soliloquy was a talent in itself, at this point. Aurena drew out a gold Talon and scraped the boulder behind her. She liked the sight of the rough surface crumbling away, producing furrows of uniform width and depth and stone fragments small as beads. She was pleased by the sight of decomposing the boulder—a single, irregular, continuous, indecomposable object—into small, regular measured values. While she was at it, she applied the reaction equation of gold transmutation to those crushed stones, whose surface area had swelled, making them perfect for exposure to Dissolution Force.
Nothing happened.
"So of course it can't be replenished here, either."
Aurena muttered dispiritedly.
"On the outside there was only a difference of efficiency—everything was transmuted. Air, perhaps, or tiny particles, must have kept attaching themselves without my noticing…."
And so in the dream world she could not rely on it. She had to abandon the expectation that turning the faucet of the reaction equation would send infinite gold from an infinite source gushing out. What she could use was what she had brought in upon entering. Experimental apparatus, research notes, theoretical texts, garments… and her own body? Before she knew it, Aurena had wrapped both arms around her forearms and shoulders. Gooseflesh rose. How exactly she ought to interpret what she had seen back then—a single drop of blood swelling into a tremendous quantity of gold—was a still-contentious subject—no, in fact it was not. Wandering The Rapids all this while, she had already repeated several experiments.
It was a matter of whether Aurena could bear the conclusion that was drawn.

"…First experiment."
Her lips parted.
"Test with a finely shredded piece of cloth I brought, and a piece of a leaf from a woody plant native to this place."
She exposed both to the reaction equation. The piece from the outside was transmuted; the leaf was mute and unresponsive. This was closer to preliminary work for chewing over the most basic premise—dream objects are not transmuted into gold.
"Second: two finely shredded pieces of cloth."
Aurena said.
"On one I smear my own blood; on the other, the blood of a native creature of unidentifiable taxonomic lineage."
Gradually the experimental conditions grew more exacting. Even obtaining the bodily fluid of a dream creature was a string of trial and error. When alive they thrash about as though their feet were on fire, and once dead they quickly turn to bluish particles, with no way to reverse the process. Still, she succeeded in obtaining it. A few drops of intact blood.
"The transmutation ratio changed, but it was meaningless."
The cloth smeared with her blood spat out a golden vine that grew lush and vigorous. With no support to wind up and climb, it looked rather like someone's scalp flung onto the ground—but it was a valid result all the same. The cloth smeared with the dream creature's blood, on the other hand, was transmuted in exactly the same manner as cloth smeared with nothing.
"So blood was not the decisive variable."
The next experiment was to compare her own blood with that of others—those who had, precisely, come in from the outside. The Aurena of now smiled, recalling the Aurena of then, and the laborious work she had had to do.
"It was urgent, so it couldn't be helped… you should have kept better watch, that's what."
At any rate, a third type of experiment was conducted accordingly. A scrap of cloth smeared with Aurena's blood, and a scrap of cloth smeared with another's blood. Comparing the quantity of gold that poured out, she could now draw a clear inequality. The cloth smeared with nothing yielded the least, the one smeared with another's blood yielded more than that, and the one smeared directly with Aurena's own blood yielded the most.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main5_Content_1:
"So it's not the blood—is it that I alone am something special?"
the Aurena of then had thought. That hypothesis was intuitive, and even seductive—it would amount to one more layer of evidence attesting to the superiority between her and the rest of the snails. But before long she realized a grave error. The fact was that the states of the two bloods smeared onto the cloth scraps had not been strictly controlled. Her own blood, of course, having been freshly squeezed from a cut in her living flesh, bore a clear vermilion; the other had been collected and then stored for the experiment, and was on the verge of internal component separation. She had, of course, accounted for all that. The other's blood ultimately smeared onto the cloth had received all the organic-chemical treatment required to prevent coagulation and to eliminate the layers formed by differences in specific gravity. But what if, in that process, something had been missed?
The fourth experiment. This time three kinds of blood were needed, and all of them Aurena's.
One freshly squeezed; one deliberately left for a long time with no treatment whatsoever; and the last, after being left thus, treated so as to restore it to the same material properties as the original blood—at least, so it was regarded within the biochemical system that she knew. This result, too, came with a vivid inequality. The freshly squeezed blood, as ever, produced an explosion of gold, while the other two types of blood both showed only feeble reactions. So the initial hypothesis that her blood alone was special lost its force.
"What is different about these?"
the Aurena of then, and of now, thought. To find out, the tools she had gathered by her own hand were no longer enough. She needed equipment capable of realizing greater physical quantities, and measuring instruments with finer resolving power. Large-scale repeated experiments, too… all of them things unobtainable within this place. The thought that this might perhaps be a factor not to be overcome even by an improved experimental environment tormented her persistently. The systematic error whose cause she had failed, in the end, to find even on the outside; the plainly pseudoscientific character that Dissolution Force possessed… From the blood left to sit, something had vanished as time passed. Some primordial force that did not return even when the necessary treatment was applied.
Her own viewpoint, Aurena thought, was drawing ever nearer not to reductionist science but to holism—even, boundlessly, to pantheism. But once the focus tilted, there was no stopping it. Everything seemed to fall into place. Before and after the blood was transformed, some primordial property it had originally borne—something so primordial that it could not be accounted for within the system of knowledge Aurena knew—had vanished? Could one say that the difference between blood that interacted actively with other tissues within a single living system, and blood severed from it, was that the latter had lost its function and fitness within a living system—that is, that it had "died"?
If so, must one regard "the very fact that something is alive" as having been transmuted into gold?

"Meaning is not transmuted into matter. I cannot accept a conclusion like this."
the present-day Aurena shook her head.
"This is not the conclusion of an argument. It is unfalsifiable, metaphysical, a leaping non sequitur."
A gold Talon was digging up the bare ground. Aurena saw that the boulder she had been tormenting had vanished without a trace. Had it shot up into the sky, or sunk into the earth? No. It had merely been finely decomposed. If one could gather up all the uneven fine particles and split-off pebbles scattered in the process, the complete form and mass of the boulder could be reproduced. It must be so.
"But if it is not a boulder, but a living thing—"
she said.
"—then cutting it into pieces and joining them back together does not make Vitality Essence reappear."
She was at an impasse. At the dead end of dusk's logic, unfolding a map written in an unfamiliar tongue, the Traveler Aurena was stamping her feet impatiently.
"If the fact is the catalyst of the reaction… then have I, all this while, been turning 'the fact that I am alive' into gold, little by little?"
The upper half of her, slumped to the ground, swayed like a reed. Aurena, unable to hold herself up, toppled over at last. With every gasp of breath, her chest and lower belly swelled and shrank by turns.
"And when it's all used up, what happens?"
The thoughts in her head were drifting off to some far-distant place. The persistent mist, the vicious fatigue of unknown cause, ran rampant once more. No—there were any number of things that could be the cause. Of course she was exhausted, having researched so busily to become a Full Moon. Of course—she had just become a sage and was adapting to her surroundings. Of course—she was fleeing the Inspectorate. Of course—she was fighting battle after battle in an unfamiliar place called The Rapids.
That she was squandering "the fact that she is alive"—what nonsense!
"They're all just… matters of course…."
The bare ground was cold and hard, but it was a floor of sorts, and when she laid her back against it, all the strength drained absurdly from her whole body. Eyelids overwhelmed by drowsiness slowly fell shut. Her tongue grew ever looser.
"I didn't do… anything wrong…."
Aurena's mouth closed. Her breathing came even—yet somehow shallow and uneasy.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main5_Short: The gold creeps inward from the tips of her feathers, and every equation leads to a conclusion she cannot bear. With each transmutation, is she spending the very thing that makes her alive?
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main5_Title: Research Methods - Measurement and Statistical Analysis
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main6_Content_0:
A single impurity that refused to be decomposed was roaming The Rapids. The impurity that was Aurena and her thoughts—
having collided with the proposition that "the property of being alive" plays a certain role in the reaction procedure of Dissolution Force—a proposition that could not be hastily dismissed as either true or false—she was drifting, truly, without aim. No matter how many of The Rapids' places she saw and felt and learned, so long as she could not solve that problem in the end, Aurena could not escape the plight of wandering an infinite labyrinth with infinite entrances and exits.
"The hypothesis about Vitality Essence is undecided. I can't be certain."
Aurena said. Even if she could neither prove nor disprove the unprovability of the problem now gripping her, a compromise—a humiliating one—with reality was at least possible. For if, as she used Dissolution Force, the mist within her body and the vicious fatigue kept accumulating, then in the end, when a dangerous situation befell her, she would have no choice but to be helplessly overwhelmed. So one could say, roughly, that excessive use of Dissolution Force impairs Vitality Essence—or, to put it crudely, results in the loss of one's life.
"Have you even considered the possibility that this fatigue isn't an effect of Dissolution Force in the first place?"
"So you're saying the reaction equation is lying?"
As if it could! An equation does not lie. If it appears to, that is nothing but the researcher's own contrition at having failed to derive the equation sufficiently globally and consistently. It is merely in a form that cannot be seen with the eye or touched with the hand—some object must necessarily have reacted, and that is why the transmutation ratio differs between cloth smeared with blood and cloth that is not. Just as air or tiny particles were posited in the Dissolution Force procedure on the outside, some property held in common by Aurena and other living things had, without her noticing, been steadily added as a background value to every reaction pattern. Perhaps the multiple mean values that had formed among the experimental participants were for that same reason?
"So I have to take it that some component within my body, or some disposition, really is being continuously consumed."
Aurena absentmindedly touched the wound on the back of her hand. A scab had formed. The dried blood, however, was very smooth. As she kept stroking it, it even gave off a metallic sound.
She gazed down at the vein of gold that had shyly poked out its head at the center of the back of her hand.

"Is this why I'm being stained in this way, too?"
At first the ends of her body hair, terminal tissues like her nails, had been gradually replaced. Now that had progressed to expressing itself from within, by way of the wound. If some concept within the body is consumed, if an empty place is created, then it must be filled by something in its stead? Or perhaps it was a phenomenon prior to that. If every substance in reality holds the potential to transition into gold, then among them the organic-chemical systems of especially high efficiency, those in dynamic equilibrium, could be regarded as unstable substances liable to change at virtually any moment into gold, a more stable form. Her body, affected by her frequent use of Dissolution Force, absorbs the residual energy of this and turns to gold.
"Gold transmutation by Dissolution Force is a reversible reaction."
she said.
"I ought to be able to turn this back into my flesh and bone and blood again."
"But that's not working, is it?"
"So am I going to keep having more and more of me become gold and silver like this?"
Aurena pinched the golden patchwork that spread smoothly over one corner of her forearm. Once it had felt this and that, like real bare skin, but from some point on it had simply gone numb unless she deliberately prodded it. She looked at the hand she had used to pinch her forearm. Bringing together the golden palm—now grown beyond a thimble into something like a fingered glove—she pressed it precisely flush against the part stitched over like a golden patchwork quilt. The two gold-waters merged naturally, with a movement just like droplets of mercury. With one arm thus joined to the middle of the other forearm, Aurena suddenly closed her eyes. She felt the downy hair at the back of her head bristle up.
A very strange feeling came over her.
It was not merely that one hand covered the other arm; it was as though her body had originally been made in that shape. Just like this, with her eyes closed, perceiving herself in the configuration of one arm clinging to the other like the handle of a cup, she could move about, dodging this way and that so as not to touch walls or other obstacles. And yet, could this be called unexpected? If gold perfectly replaces the body's intricate, manifold tissues and the interactions among them, what reason was there that it could not replace the underlying motive force and, above all, one's very will itself?

"Then what happens?"
"Do the parts I can call myself all vanish, and only the thoughts I have now remain?"
Flustered, Aurena lost her footing where she stood. She barely braced herself against the floor with the arm that had become a cup handle. She was short of breath. Her head ached. Above all, it felt remote. It was a feeling similar to the day she had realized she might die a stranger's death wandering the dream world. And yet, on the other hand, it was far milder than then.
Rising to her feet, if anything, she grew numb to it quickly.
"Which exact part of the emotional statement that I cease to be myself is the problem?"
To contemplate with self-reference—that is, to decompose her own contingent, at times even invasive, emotions—was an interesting thing. The impressions that were unmistakably a viewpoint inherent in her, yet could not be called "a thought Aurena consciously had," were already familiar to her. They would be closer to the instincts of a living creature, or to an accumulated set of impulses.
"Come to think of it… mightn't there be advantages, too?"
Aurena imagined her body and the various subsets that composed it being replaced wholesale by gold and silver affected by Dissolution Force. She conjured up the material properties of a body thus turned inorganic. How many times, on the outside, had she imagined herself as a flame of obsession that had caught onto the paltry, expendable thing called a body? The time she had pulled an all-nighter for a full week and then, blinking awake, found herself sprawled on the laboratory floor with a great lump on her brow, was but one example. To maintain the flow of an experiment she would skip appointments, refuse meetings, miss meals as a matter of routine. Only when, on rare occasion, she became convinced that her stomach was right then carrying out a self-referential catabolism, would she cram down her throat some tough, sticky, intensely dust-flavored "lump"—a high-calorie special of Aurena's own, whose safety could be verified nowhere. And then, when the ailment flared up and the Society's herbalist drew her blood again and again, she would gnaw at her hapless fingernails, fretting over some dish she had left in the laboratory and the reagents within it.
"Maybe I could be freed from such things."
Once she had used the word, she could not ignore it. All the more so, having used a word like "freedom"—which even sounded factional—about her own body. Quite apart from that particular moment when, ashen-faced, she had had to seek out the herbalist, how often, in the midst of pure inquiry into the laws of the world, had she been forced to look away on account of her body's petty defects? Whenever something within her body was in excess or in deficit, she had to pay tribute dutifully each time, and if it was even briefly delayed, her head would ache, fever would come, her mouth would turn foul, her eyes would sting, her joints would ache, her back would grow stiff, her muscles would cramp… Thinking that far, Aurena suddenly pursed her lips and opened her eyes wide.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main6_Content_1:
"If things like that were gone, I could do nothing but experiment to my heart's content!"
she cried in a falsetto. She shuddered. Unable to contain her joy, she even bared the soles of her feet and bounded up and down like a child.
"Youngest Full Moon, they said, and all that. Now I'm beyond even that!"
Aurena was thinking of a mathematical equation in her head. Not a particular equation, but an arbitrary one, and the process by which it abstracts and comprehends reality. An equation laying out constants and variables, operators, and an equals sign ought, in itself, to be nothing more than the phenotype of some sequential procedure, with no purpose or desire of its own. To put into that equation—which is nothing in itself—values that bear isomorphism to reality, and to produce a result. Only in that process is the "meaning" of a mathematical equation born.
Where was the law that said she, freed from the body, could not become such an equation?
"Mere has-been geezers in the back room; mere snails who, far from envying my genius, hadn't even the wit to recognize it… now I'm becoming the sun!"
Aurena shrilled on in that high, thin voice. What is the sun? It does not wane. It does not age. Above all, it never grows hungry, never crawls into bed wracked with illness or fatigue. The ever-burning flame of the procedure of proof. That, indeed—at least as Aurena saw it—was the sun.
"If I become an infinite denominator and operate forever, then however large the numerator that is the truth of the world, I can drag it down to zero!"
The cup handle, pushed along by the fierce movement that followed her cheering, came loose at some point into two complete arms. The gold-waters that had elsewhere arisen or budded across her body sculpted valleys and ridges upon their surface like small ripples, then began to trail waves of the finest gold dust into the air. In the very heart of a dream world that stakes its life on gold—quite literally so—who could guarantee that this would not summon a train of unpleasant prying eyes?
Time passed for a while in that state.
Trembling the two fists she had thrust up in excitement, Aurena steadied the breath that came in pants from leaping about alone. Her heart pounded and her face grew hot. The flesh above her neck flushed red, giving off heat and the smell of sweat. Yet, swollen with anticipation all the same, she opened her eyes. And she met the sight she had long been awaiting.
"You've come?"
Aurena offered a glad greeting. To the black horizon that had welcomed her on the first day she set foot, uncomprehending, in The Rapids. Now, however, to a mere audience for her, who had arrived at the great moment of truth.

"Is that all it takes?"
Without withdrawing the broad smile spread across her face, she gripped a single transmuted object in her hand. A dagger curved like the hooked talon of a beast of prey. Perhaps because she had cobbled together the impression piecemeal in her head, the handle was far too short and the blade, conversely, far too long. Its thick body looked as though whatever it stabbed would, before spilling blood, writhe in agony and bite through its own tongue. Holding that object in a reverse grip—that is, with the blade pointed toward herself—Aurena kept on laughing. Until the curved part of the dagger had hidden itself entirely within her arm; and then until it had torn open every bit of the living flesh between, passing along the forearm and the bone.
"With just that, what can any of you do now?"
The pain was an instant, and the outflow of blood and bodily components briefer still. Aurena unfolded the reaction equation upon everything that had poured out like the delta of a river's lower reaches. Soon a vast forest—a Golden Forest, sinking dazzling roots and hanging, along its glittering trunks, countless vines and branches that likewise glittered—swallowed up the whole sky and horizon. Drawing forth the well-known Golden Talons besides, Aurena rummaged without reserve through the golden trees. And then she drew them out. What? Anything at all. Every kind of arms and destructive emblem rivaling the Talons. Double-edged swords circling in the air, burning chariot wheels, the wing-feathers of the monstrous birds of legend, the hammer of a blind giant, and a storm of living blades that gathered and scattered like an angry swarm of bees.
Amid the resounding clamor of the black horizon, in the Golden Forest that looked down upon them, a maiden in a pure-white dress and a crimson floral crown danced. It was the dance of a skeleton. The dance-movement of a skeleton shrouded in bones white as white could be, fitted with bloodstained fangs. Having stripped away the thriving flesh and let the anguished marrow drain off, leaving only the gauntest, most purposive framework standing bare—to her, who had wholly surrendered herself to the thirst for knowledge and burned her own body away to the last, death, it seemed, would no longer have any power.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main6_Short: She calls it not loss but liberation — a body of gold that never hungers, never tires, never fades. But once the self dissolves into the equation, who is left to become the golden sun?
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main7_Content_0: "Oh dear… the reaction isn't finished yet." Aurena clicked her tongue. She looked for another test tube to divide the solution into, but there were none to be found. She furrowed her brow. She rummaged again at the bottom of her pack, searching for some other test tube that might have rolled about as a shard of glass and… she remembered. The ones she had used, on a day that now felt like the distant past, to transmute and replenish the Golden Talons. Losing a few test tubes would be no trouble, after all. "Granted, I tossed them because they were the least useful." Aurena smacked her lips. Her eye fell on the silver brooch pinned to her chest. The memory rose of the day she had received that Full Moon brooch—a day that felt even further in the past than when she had fed the test tubes to the Golden Talons. At words like the Arcanum, the youngest sage, the Seven Spires… words that somehow felt now like child's play, she let out a snorting laugh. "Once I succeed in completely resetting the Dissolution Force system into its basic axioms and the propositions beneath them, I won't need toy-like honors like this." she went on, fingering the brooch. "This, of all things, is the most useless object." Aurena twisted the brooch off. Then she gazed at it absently. Compared to the gold she could transmute in an instant, it was utterly paltry. From wearing it continuously, it had even grown grimy and lost its luster. Better to convert it into transmuted gold and let it remain that way forever. It was the logical thing. Aurena gazed at the brooch, saying nothing. Aurena rolled the brooch between her fingers. Aurena gripped the brooch in her hand. Aurena pinned the brooch back on. "Something, something like this. Not even worth bothering to do anything with." She gave a snort. And yet, even so, she checked whether the brooch was properly fastened in its original place on her chest. "It's not that I mean to go back… that's right! To sneer at these fellows, I still need this." Snapping her fingers, Aurena laughed. She laughed—she did laugh, she had laughed, and yet… her gaze wavered uneasily. "What am I doing right now?" What does it precisely mean to have completely described the Dissolution Force system—to have developed it from the most essential set of axioms and the theorems and propositions arising therefrom? What becomes of Aurena once she has achieved it? A single brain that interprets one world and commands all its powers as its limbs—the sole entity able to extract meaning and purpose from an infinite string of characters. And, having risen to such a height, the best she can manage to do is to return to the organization she once belonged to and sneer at them to their faces? "This is an illogical act." Aurena said. "While I polish a single coefficient of my equation, the researchers I knew, and their sons and daughters, will die, and then their grandchildren will be off learning how to pretend they aren't snails—why should I care about such a thing?" Her hand fingered the brooch again, twisted it, but did not pull it off. "This is a habit." "No, it's illogical." "I've always worn it, so I just keep wearing it… there's nothing wrong with that." "You are performing an illogical act right now, Aurena." The voice of conscience—that hidebound discourse of self-censorship—had never been popular with her. What sustained her was, rather, the voice of reason and rationality, and above all of scientific methodology. "There's no reason to care this much about walking snails." "And yet here you are, imagining returning to those very walking snails to sneer at them, thinking how satisfying it would be." A Golden Talon had appeared at some point. Whimpering like a sick dog, it was raking up the nearby soil, the blackish wood grain, the hard boulders. "I shouldn't be flustered like this over something like this." Because that sound grated on her nerves as never before, Aurena scowled. "I'm going to become an infinite procedure of proof… I mustn't be held back by something as trifling as this." A certain conundrum that had stirred up the academic world in her days as a sage of the Arcanum suddenly crossed her mind—Can a system meant to prove an arbitrary object prove its own consistency? According to one analyst who had studied the theory, any formal system composed of finite symbols and producing proofs through reproducible, mechanical procedures executed by means of them….
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main7_Content_1:
{IMAGE}
"So here you were."
At the unfamiliar voice, Aurena lifted her head. There stood a woman. Lightly dressed overall, she trailed long cuffs and hems and moved gauzily, like a waterfall woven of some fiber. It did not look like attire one would choose in the heart of a dream—but come to think of it, was she herself not dressed the same way?
"I've been looking for you."
"Why?"
Aurena loathed the snails' time-worn custom of needlessly asking back about information already implied within a question. But now, actually facing such a frantic moment herself, she found it took a certain quick wit not to volley back the statement "For me?" in response to "I've been looking for you."
"Why have you been looking for me?"
"You leave traces of gold all over, so it seemed you'd soon be in danger. Above all—"
The woman—though, unknowing herself, Aurena already knew her name—looked around. As a result, she readily confirmed that, far from being in danger, Aurena was on the contrary, by way of the enormous Golden Talons, inflicting grave danger upon the structural totality of everything around her.
"—and it's an act that, if a commotion breaks out over the gold, drags the surrounding dream creatures into danger along with you."
"Ha! What do the creatures in here matter?"
Aurena scoffed loudly.

"Everything I've seen so far is nothing but constants added equally to both sides, and tautological propositions that justify themselves circularly. There wasn't a single one—not one head—worth caring for or cherishing."
"As for your original theories on others, I do hope I'll have no occasion to hear them, even later…."
Aurena flinched. For she had felt some energy converging—not Dissolution Force, but something different, yet closely bound up with the qualities of dreams. A rival, perhaps a pioneer of the provinces with no ties to the establishment? Whenever she met someone who clung to the hackneyed expression "Power of Dreams" instead of Dissolution Force—and each time, she felt a clear duty to spread this correct term far and wide—someone who could deftly wield it, who delighted in contact with those who came from the outside, and who sought people to lend strength to her plan… come to think of it, the story she'd heard about such a someone….
At this point Aurena realized who the woman was.
"Will you not ask who I am?"
"I've heard. You're the Guide, aren't you?"
she said, smiling.
"If I go around dropping gold, you go around dropping rumors. I heard, until my ears were sore, what you mean to do and why. My answer, of course, is—"
Polaris saw the Golden Talons, which had been destroying the terrain behind Aurena, rise into the air. The five fingers then lined up side by side, flanks together, and spread flat. A courteous yet resolute gesture.
"—not interested. I won't be joining your plan."
"Hardly a surprise."
Polaris said coldly.
"If you're so enlightened, then surely you also know what will become of your body if you linger here long?"
"You can see for yourself, I should think."
Aurena, as if at play, undulated her ten fingers—her real fingers, not the gold Talons—like one striking piano keys. Several of them had already undergone considerable "replacement," with solid masses of pure gold settled into place. Even setting aside the dream creatures, it was a sight to stir greed.
"Are you not even afraid of that?"
"Why would I be?"
"Are you, too, perhaps a fanatic?"
"Got someone in mind, have you?"
"Yes—someone who'd suit you well, I think."
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main7_Content_2: The question marks dutifully attached to the end of every clause were of the sort mainly used to recommend or request something of the other party—yet, for some reason, the atmosphere grew ever more strained. The insects in the grass around them sang a serenade hushed to the utmost, suppressing their presence with discretion. "I am not the kind of imbecile who stakes her life on an unfalsifiable, metaphysical existence. I merely… can tell apart my mood and what actually happens, according to logic and reason." Aurena pondered her words a moment. A snail has a level suited to a snail. The explanation, too, had to be pitched to that level. "You were born here, weren't you? So you know all about the dream world, how it works, and the role gold plays?" "…I do, yes?" "Then aren't you curious about what comes next?" At Aurena's words, Polaris tilted her head aslant. "By 'next,' you mean?" "Anything. It could be the next in 'sequence,' the next in 'turn'… facts don't line up in a fixed pattern like physical objects do. The point is that even when you think you know all there is to know, there may yet be a 'next' that has not been uncovered. And that's where the difference between you and me arises." She straightened her chest proudly as she spoke. "I knew none of those things. I found them all out only after coming in. The place where you, knowing from the start, simply settled and grew complacent—I reached it through deliberate effort. So I can keep pressing on, still curious about what lies beyond it—until I've interpreted every last thing about dreams." Aurena gazed at her gold-turned fingers with a warm look. The look seemed almost fond. "And for that, if it means escaping this wretched body of mine—forever lukewarm, then cold, staggering, then stiff—why should I fear that I'll cease to be myself?" "How very self-assured you are." Polaris said. She did not trouble to hide that it was not pure admiration alone. "I wonder how long that resolve will last." "It'll last forever." Aurena declared boldly. "Because I'm about to be reborn as a body that is no body—as the indomitable golden sun." "Is that so?" A taut gaze passed between the two. It was the Guide who broke the silence. "That resolve of yours, that firm conviction—what form did it take?—" It was a question whose meaning could not be grasped. "—what color is it? What scent does it give off? What sound does it make, what texture does it have?" "What are you trying to say?" "A thought that exists, in fact, nowhere—its taking shape and ripening is a matter of in here, of the abstract." Polaris went on, tapping her temple. "Once you are completely replaced by the Power of Dreams, those things will no longer remain an inviolable, intrinsic domain of their own. They'll be all too liable to undergo transformation and transmutation, and to mingle into this place." Polaris said. "And if, in the midst of that, you were suddenly to appear with that resolve gone—if all the thoughts and wills save that one resolve were assembled among themselves alone—would the you in that state have any confidence of noticing the wrongness?" "Of course." A shameful thing, but that reply just now was not a scholar's. It was closer to a retort that flew out reflexively. For the Guide's words, oddly, touched the very same misgiving Aurena had been entertaining just before—Can a system meant to prove an arbitrary object prove its own consistency? "…Yes, I can." Aurena said. This time with conviction. "And the grounds to support that?" "Because I would do it." she went on. "I might temporarily forget, or retreat, but in the end, if there's a motive, I'll get back there again. The me of that time will still be curious, will observe phenomena under controlled conditions, will hold the decisive variables advantageous and go on with the proof. And among those—" she pointed at the one listening. "—will be you too, Guide of Dreams." Polaris's eyebrow twitched with interest. "You intend to 'prove' me?" "Is that surprising?" Aurena shrugged. The Golden Talons moved along with her. "You may regard yourself as special, as the Guide, but to my eye you are no different at all from everything I've seen so far. Approximate you with a sum of polynomials containing a finite computational process, and… ah, my mistake." "There's no need to worry I won't understand." Polaris said. "It's enough that I know how very grand your aspirations are." For a while the two looked at each other in silence. A side-quarrel did follow briefly, but, as Aurena had pointed out and Polaris had never denied, the crux of this moment was, in the end, that the Guide of Dreams was seeking someone to side with her plan. Aurena had refused, and there the meeting had, in essence, ended. "Never something I wish for, but this will not be the last time, I think." "No." Aurena said. Her confident smile had not wilted in the least. "Next time we meet, you'd best be ready to be proven, every last bit of you, Guide of Dreams."
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main7_Short: A stranger arrives with a plan to fuse a whole world into one — and receives a courteous, unshakable refusal. Yet one question lingers and gnaws: would she even notice if a piece of her resolve quietly went missing?
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main8_Content_0: Aurena tidied the laboratory, humming a tune. Her assistant was away, but that was just as she wished. In fact, it was she who had sent him home, rather. She could not let others see her present state, after all. "Moon-dear?" At the youthful voice, she turned around without breaking off her humming. "What?" "When are we going to see the museum…?" It was a small child. A small child seated on a backless stool, both feet dangling and kicking at empty air, whose tousled mop of hair barely reached as high as Aurena's waist. Allowing the child—who would otherwise address her, a sage of the Arcanum, by the easy title of Full Moon—to shorten even that, by a contraction only a small child would apply, into "Moon-dear," had itself been a means of meeting the child at eye level and winning its affection. It had also made it easy to bring the child, obedient, all the way to a laboratory where no eyes watched. "What luck!" "Moon-dear?" Aurena hummed, blocking the only entrance there was. "If the Ethics Committee insists on obstructing me to the bitter end, then I'll just have to procure one myself. Now, the concentration…." Aurena pondered, looking at the aqueous solution. Glancing sidelong at the child, who was beginning to sense that something was off, she estimated by eye its body weight and likely reaction pattern. If the concentration was too high, the subject's usefulness would run out before any observation could be obtained; if too low, it would merely waste time to no purpose. "Moon-dear? …Moon-dear?" "What now?" At Aurena's irritable voice, the child shrank its shoulders. Then it brought both hands together between its knees and began to rub them. It looked toward the door it had come in by, but Aurena's body, fussing about as she arranged the experimental instruments, blocked squarely in front of it. "I just want to go home…." "You can't." Am I mad, to just let it go here? Aurena thought with a scoff. An outsider with no ties to the Society—one found by Aurena entirely by chance, wandering lost without so much as any official itinerary—such a run of luck was hardly something she would meekly let slip away. "Aren't we going to the museum?" "We can't." "Then what are we doing?" "Does that matter? In any case, you're not getting out of here." Aurena drew out leather straps, buckles, clasps, and the like, and began to measure the necessary lengths. "You're going nowhere. Not after I went to all the trouble of bringing you here." "I-I just want to go…." The child began to sniffle. Aurena thought how good it was that, as soon as she had been assigned a laboratory as a sage, she had paid out of her own pocket to line it with thick soundproofing. "Daddy…." "Don't cry so much." she said. "When you get worn out, the reaction pattern changes." "Daddyyy…." "And if the crying goes on, the bodily components become uneven, too." "Daddyyyy…." Aurena's hand suddenly stopped. She felt strange. Don't they usually call for their mother? she thought, and wished to convince herself that this alone was the source of the sense of wrongness. She had to shut her mouth and simply get on with the work. "So your daddy looks after you?" "N-no, sir." It was hard even to tell which orifice of the face—kneaded into a paste of tears and snot—the words spilled from. "Every day, he's busy, with research… please send me hooome…." Aurena looked at the teapot set on the bookshelf. Among the various degrees and plaques of merit, that teapot held, by her own reckoning, a rather incongruous object—brandy, and one giving off the scent of apples at that. It was, however, the only scent of family that Aurena could remember. At the very least, she remembered the memory that it was the scent of family. "If your father had seen this….” The people who had cared for her in childhood used to say it as a matter of habit. They also said that he had enjoyed drinking this thing called "brandy." Aurena remembered those words. She remembered that she had to remember those words. She understood the sentence "My biological father liked brandy" as a true proposition. She would pour it out and, now and then, smell it. And as she did, she would try. Each time, she would try, in case she might recall something. "Daddyyyy… I want to go hooome…." Aurena blinked and returned to reality. "Waaah…." The child was looking about. In search of an escape? That there was none, the child knew best of all. Then what was it searching for? And was it, what's more, pricking up its ears while holding back its sobs? Drawing in a great breath through its nose? Aurena recalled the moments she had spent smelling the brandy. Not merely smelling it, but trying to find something that could not be found. The child was doing the same. It was searching. But the child was not memory—it was experience. It was searching for what it had seen with its own eyes, the scent it always smelled, the sounds it always heard. Aurena clenched her teeth. She felt strange. "Go." Aurena gestured, having stepped aside from the open door. A breeze stirred the child's short trouser-hems. "Hk… hhk." "Get out, before I change my mind!" she shouted in a sudden burst. Then she seized the child's forearm and went to the threshold. Flinging the little thing—staggering, uncomprehending—out, she barred and locked the door. Whatever commotion might arise outside, now she could neither hear nor see it at all. Turning her back on it, she made to approach the desk, then halted her steps. She laid a hand on her chest and took a deep breath. She spent some time leaning her body against the door. "It was useless anyway, that's right." Aurena spat through teeth bared white. "With a sample size of one… the control of variables is a shambles, nothing can be done at all." If your father had seen this…. Some face, eyes brimming with tears, rose faintly to mind. Aurena realized she had absentmindedly been rubbing the brooch pinned to her chest. At once she sprang upright like a released spring. She peeled her body—her slack limbs—from the door she had leaned against. She stood by her own strength alone. "I don't need it, a thing like that. I don't need any of it." she huffed, fists clenched. "I don't need a single bit, not a single bit, not a single bit of it…." {IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Main8_Short: A child, a bolted door, and the faint scent of apples she has decided to call family. Why does she need none of it — and why can she still not erase it?
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Short0_Content: Aurena read the apprentice's mind perfectly—the desperate eagerness to impress her. There was no need to invoke her status as a sage. A single glance, a few honeyed words, and a calculated gesture. Simply offering the recognition and image the other party craved was more than enough. That she wielded not only her intellect but also the charm of her appearance as calculated tools was, to her, not a matter of shame but simply one of obvious efficiency. Before the signature was even dry, several dangerous experimental designs had already taken shape in her mind. What the other party actually wanted was hardly an important question to her.
ui.TravelerStory_Aurena_Short1_Content: Her mother died giving birth to her, and her father died researching dreams. Aurena grew up clutching those research notes. Born of two different bloodlines, she came to possess a distinct appearance unlike any other Anguillian. Her unusual looks, extraordinary intellect, and an anything-but-normal upbringing were the fundamental reasons Aurena struggled to connect with others. Scholarship and the books her father left behind were the first—and only—friends she ever learned to know.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main1_Content_0: “Now, where did we leave off last time?” There were hands that wove cloth. Old, wrinkled, rough-knuckled hands. And those same hands were the hands that told the stories. “Up to the part where the knight climbed all the way to the top of the tower and finally met someone!” There were hands that spread out and folded the woven cloth. Young, clumsy little hands. And those same hands were the hands that listened to the stories — though that was not all they were. “Yes, that's right… hmm.” Smacking the toothless, inward-curling lips, the hands that wove the story sorted out the next passage in their head. “And so our knight, who had met Princess Spark…” “But Grandma—” The listening hands suddenly cut in. “—you said he met someone, but you never said whether it was the one he was looking for, whether it was Princess Spark!” “Goodness, did I now?” The hands that wove the story smiled fondly. Released at last from the needle and thread they had held all that while, they came to rest stroking the little girl's hair. “Then who do you think it was?” “Mmmm, I think it was…” The listening hands pursed their cherry-red lips and held their silence a moment. Then the head snapped up. “That's it! I think the merchant they met in Bargain Town must have gotten there first!” “And why would that be?” “Because, because…” And so, to call the child merely a pair of listening hands would never have been a fair judgement. The two who traded stories were always like that. Sometimes the prepared tale would twist this way and that. The names and natures of the characters, the places, the endings would all be knotted up in some entirely different way. Sometimes the grandmother never got the chance to open her mouth at all. On the days the child took it upon herself to be the hands that wove the story, it was all one could do just to keep up with that ceaseless, chattering prattle. Even so, the old woman did nothing but smile fondly each time. From the very beginning she had understood this moment with the child not as teaching an already-decided story, but as a moment of making a story together. “And then, I think it went like this.” “Did the two of them already know each other before they met? Back when they fought in the cave…” “…it was different from what she'd imagined on her own, so she was surprised! That's why she lied about her quiver being empty…” With the trailing ends of her bandage streaming, the child eagerly imagined and filled in the empty parts of the story. Characters from utterly unrelated tales would meet; promises would be kept later on; bonds would deepen and new ones be forged. The little branches and root-hairs that strayed from the main stem of the story, the birds and insects that folded their wings to rest a while… all of these she imagined and tended with care, adding a richer narrative. To the story she had so fleshed out she gave a coat of five-coloured light, adorning it like a rainbow, like the crystal of some lovely metal. And then, long after the weaving itself was finished, time would have slipped away, until at last the old woman had to be the first to restrain the child and rise from her seat. For the child — who listened to and chewed over stories of places she could not go and could not see, and above all treasured beyond measure those moments she could make her own memories — it was an unwelcome thing. “Goodness, you little rascal.” The old woman said, as if at a loss. “You mustn't play tricks like this on your grandma… where are you?” The old woman's hands fumbled through the darkened room. “If I trip on something and fall, your grandma will be hurt very badly…” “Grandma, got you!” Feeling the child's frail little body fling itself into an embrace, she let out a sigh of relief. The hand, callused and dappled with liver spots, stroked and gently soothed the child's forearm, her shoulder, and then her cheek. When it rubbed the sulkily puffed-out cheek, the child's spite — swollen taut like a hedgehog with its quills bristling — came through plain as day. “Let's carry on with the rest tomorrow, all right?” “Hmph.” The child jutted out her lips in a pout, yet accepted that it could not be helped. After that the old woman lit a candle and made the room bright once more. I only have to wait until tomorrow. The child thought. When tomorrow's story ends, then the next day, and when that day's story ends too, then just until the day after. The child thought. On and on like this — no matter how many times it ends, there's always a next. It'll always be that way. The child thought. Because she did not want to think of the other case.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main1_Content_1:
*

“Grandma?”
The child took a handful of earth. Thanks to the villagers having tamped it down so carefully, the feel of it was peculiar. Just clenching and unclenching her fist around it seemed enough to call up a new story.
“Grandma… is it cold over there?”
The earth did not answer.
“I still have to finish the story about the old man who looked after the rabbits…”
The freshly heaped earth, the buds not yet sprouted, the stone the village mason had shown off his skill to carve neatly square, the nameless wildflowers the villagers had picked and laid all around — none of them spoke.
“And I even imagined names for all the rabbits.”

“…still, what can you do but take turns watching over her?”
A little way off there were village grown-ups watching the child. Composing their reddened eyes, covering with one hand the mouths twisted with pity, enduring it with folded arms, they agonised over what would have to be done next.
“Where might there be a household willing to take that child in so readily?”
“Everyone's busy enough just feeding their own kin.”
“Still, it's a mercy the child can't go wandering off on her own.”
And so a roof to keep off the rain and the dew — sometimes only an eave — was given to the child. Not enough to fill her belly, but now and then her stomach could be filled. The clothes were patched from leftover cloth, yet there were garments to cover her bare skin. She could go to the school at the edge of the village and learn her letters and pick up this and that useful skill. Just as the grandmother had told her many stories while she lived, the grown-ups said, at school you could learn many such stories. But the child had never thought of stories as something to be learned. A story was something to listen to, something to think over again, and something to make together.
Sadly, the school was far from such a place.

*

“They say she doesn't fit in with the other children.”
“Her hands aren't deft, so even when she tries to help with something it comes to nothing, I hear.”
“She kept so quiet that I went to see what she was doing, and she was just sitting there lost in a daydream.”
“She tries to draw or write something, but no matter how you look at it you can't make out what it is.”
Such were the eyes the grown-ups turned on the child after she had attended school a while. And the assessment of the children her own age was not so very different — leaving aside, of course, the cases of plain, unprovoked cruelty visited upon any newcomer from the start, like tugging at her worn bandage to tease her.
“What are you good at?”
The children asked the child, who only kept her mouth shut. In the world of children, that was everything. Being able to hold your breath a long time, being fast on your feet, being good at throwing stones, being good at finding pretty pinecones… among children, such things were one's talents and the shortcut to making friends.
“I'm… probably good at stories.”
“Then do one.”
There is no hesitation in children's actions. On the spot a stage is laid out, and the chance to prove one's claim is given. Curious-eyed spectators cluster close, one by one lending an ear. Sitting in their midst, the girl with her air of somehow mysterious power summons a silence almost like magic. Now all she has to do is tell them a story — the one she had shared with her grandmother and coloured in to make more perfect — and all will be well.
But the magic vanishes without a trace soon enough.
“That's not what that looks like!”
“That's not how that goes.”
“It's different from what you know.”
She did not like it. The child, glad to be a storyteller once more after so long — a storyteller with someone listening, to be precise — did not like that situation one bit.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main1_Content_2: “And how would you all know that?” At the storyteller's sharp retort, the listening children faltered and glanced at one another. Little children's actions are by nature unflinching. But faced with a question like that, they did hesitate, just a little. They had to think it over. Still, in the end they would answer. “Because we can see.” The child blankly felt the bandage over her eyes loosen and slip down. She reflexively reached to find her grandmother, then had to tie it back on herself. While the worn cloth was pulled taut and knotted, no one spoke. Some child sniffled. Someone scuffed the ground with the tip of their toe. A gentle breeze blew. “Let's go! She's boring.” She herself would have no sense of it, but mercifully someone took the lead at just the right moment and the silence was broken. “First one to the hill is the general!” “No, the second one is the general, and whoever gets there first is the prisoner!” “Oh, then I'll be the prisoner! Prisoner's the best!…” There were the voices of the children boisterously chattering away into the distance, but the voice of a storyteller who could no longer tell a story was nowhere to be found. There were children racing along, each watching over the other's shoulder, but she alone was the exception — she who had never even known the colour of the sky, nor the pain of looking at the sun with the naked eye, let alone one another. She is not, now, and is not there. She is nothing, and is nowhere. “The story of the cicada who rode the clouds…” The child quietly sat down and began to do something on the bare ground. Something that was neither a picture nor letters, a record of events and characters that had now become a story thoroughly her own alone. And then she dimly realised that she was doing something utterly useless. The child could not, in any case, read what she had made. The shapes scored into the earthen ground crumble the moment a palm is laid against them to “read” them. And the others, who could look at them without touching, could not make out what the child had carved. They had no interest. “So that's how it is. So that's how it is.” The child said evenly. As far as stories go, it was a clear ending. “No one is interested in my story.” That isn't so. A strange voice was heard. The child listened closely. “That's a voice I haven't heard before.” The child murmured softly. Because she wanted to make sure it wasn't something she had imagined. “Who are you?” I am a book. An empty book. “Your voice is strange… where are you speaking from?” If you want, I can come right there to you! There was no one there. There was no one who could see what was happening. And so no one could be startled. In the place the child turned toward, vaguely imagining some person, there was in truth a vast, formless Rift carved into the air. A sight that would make even someone ignorant of what lay beyond it, of what was happening now, scream on the spot — a tear that had ripped the empty air in two. And one who knew exactly what lay beyond it and what was happening would, on the contrary, be unable even to scream, and faint dead away. Because the child was so utterly ignorant of all of it, she stepped toward the “someone” who, to her mind, was speaking to her. She reached out a hand without a trace of fear.
