The edges of the Rift began to ripple, as if in answer. And then a single book dropped down before the child. {IMAGE} “Wow, what a huge—” The child gathered the book into her arms with a groan. It was big enough to need both arms, thick, and above all heavy. The feel of the metal ornaments fixed along the cover was unfamiliar, but pleasant. “—really big book.” And yet I am empty. I am empty. The voice that had named itself a book, an empty book, came to her again. “Should I tell you my story?” No. That isn't all. It isn't only listening to your story. The child, meanwhile, having opened the book, confirmed that indeed every page but the cover was endlessly flat. For no matter what delicate typesetting or hand could be brought to bear, it is impossible to set ink without leaving a single trace. “Then?” You become me, and I become you. We begin, now, the story of each other — no, the story of the two of us. Behind the bandage, the child's two eyes shone with a brightness no one could see. The memories of not merely listening to stories but making them — and above all, making them together with someone — came flooding in like a rising tide. That's how we make our story — making it, and making it, and making it, and making it again. The book's fervent voice came on and on. In the child's mind the kindling of imagination, the sparks, flared up. At last they became an unquenchable blaze and began to roar. A story like that, one that never ends, ever — we tell it to each other, and show it plainly to everyone! What answer the child gave to the book's urging was never passed down. The only thing certain is that on that day a “Bismuth,” different from any single book and any single child, was born — and that in the moment of that birth the most primal and powerful Power of Dreams, the imagination of a child who had never truly seen anything and could therefore shape anything, swallowed up that whole region. And so the village became, for a time, a name that could be found only upon a map. The fate of the village that had vanished before everyone's eyes remained, for some while, a question in the minds of many.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main1_Short: A child who has never seen the world is offered a way to make it instead. What is born when a story finds something empty enough to fill?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main2_Content_0: Bismuth opened her eyes. Again. More brightly, more cheerfully. Bismuth opened her eyes! Not shouting — be sprightly about it. Bismuth♪ opened♪ her eyes♪? That'll do for now. Bismuth♪ opened♪ her eyes♪ Imagining the morning sounds that tickled her ears, the clear and lovely sunlight that softly stroked her eyes, she then stretched with all her might. The moment those two eyes — which had never once been shut — snapped open, the world's clockwork began to turn again. “Good morning, Bismuth!” “Good morning, lemon trees!” Bismuth answered brightly. “Good morning, smell of apples, tin pails, flutter of butterfly wings, gilded carvings, hem of the rainbow, droplets of water.” Everyone sang it in chorus together. “Good morning, good morning, good morning!” With her ever-unchanging beaming smile, Bismuth went hopping and skipping out into the street. Now who is this? Why, it's the Grasshopper Prince, clutching his side. “Hello, Grasshopper Prince!” “Ah, hello, Bismuth.” But the Grasshopper Prince is breaking out in a cold sweat. Could something be the matter? Don't you worry — Bismuth is here! “What shall we do today?” Bismuth asked, with a smile as white as an open book. “Will you eat something tasty with us? Shall we go see our friends? Or else…” “Ah, ah, no!” Having said that, the Grasshopper Prince seemed to startle himself, and began to fret and fidget. “I, I mean, you don't have to do anything, I'm really fine—” Within the bandage-covered eyes, with a gaze that no longer had any need of eyes, Bismuth observed the Grasshopper Prince intently. “—really, truly… you don't have to do anything.” With that one remark, an awkward silence stretched on a while. Then Bismuth spoke, with a smile shining in every colour of the spectrum. “This prince doesn't have much he wants to do, does he? Then let's just go and play.” She went on. “Let's go and play together with Bismuth!” “I'm fine.” The Grasshopper Prince thrust out several pairs of arms and stubbornly waved off Bismuth's invitation. How very modest of him! Bismuth clasped those scrawny hands in hers and shook them up and down. Each time she did, a mouth-watering sound poured out, like a freshly baked biscuit snapping crisply against the tip of a tongue and lips. “But the Grasshopper Prince mustn't do nothing at all…” At those words, the Grasshopper Prince's forearms, held fast in Bismuth's grip, trembled in a fit of spasms. “Then Bismuth had better go find the next Grasshopper Prince, hadn't she?” “No, no!” The Grasshopper Prince cried out. He let out a sudden bellow. His face, drained of all its colour, went utterly white! “Th-that absolutely cannot be! I'm the one who has to stop, uh—” Bismuth was observing him, her head tilted at an angle. “—I, I'm the Grasshopper Prince. You mustn't hand it over to anyone else! The Grasshopper Prince…” “You're a greedy one, aren't you?” At those words, the clockwork of the world stopped. On every blade of grass, every scrap of cloud, every mouthful of spring water, eyes that darted sidelong and reproaching lips sprang up, and began to flick out thorn-bristled tongues. With curses not yet poured forth, with bloodshot glares, they began to glower at the bad, the very bad, greedy Grasshopper Prince. In the silence the mouths and noses of mice and cats and badgers and weasels vanished, and they went blind. They stood rooted to the spot, trembling all over. Their whole bodies became a single heart and began to pound. It seemed that at any moment everything would swell up plump like a balloon blown from a pig's bladder, and then burst with a pop. “You have to give your friends a turn!” Did you see? Bismuth is as generous as all this! “The other friends probably have lots of things they want to do too. So you have to share the Grasshopper Prince seat nicely.” Seeing him trudge back to his bed, head hung low and dispirited, it seems our greedy Grasshopper Prince is also a sleepyhead. Seeing him pillow his head on a stone and pull a blanket of earth snugly over himself, it seems he means to enjoy a very, very sweet lie-in. At least he took Bismuth's words to heart that way — that much is a mercy!
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main2_Content_1:
“I wonder who, oh who, the next Grasshopper Prince will be…”
But that lasted only a moment, and before long Bismuth was simply off playing about as usual. And yet is that Bismuth's fault? Not at all! Because on a day like this — when the sky is bluish, the wind is warm, the sunlight is sweet, the bees are buzzing and the fish are chirping and the birds are swimming — a truly fine day, no, more than that…
“It's a truly perfect day!”
“Perfect.” She remembered learning that word. Bismuth wished for today, too, to be a day like that. No — she intended to make it so. And yet why was it that the lips of Bismuth, who was having such admirable thoughts, jutted out like a duck's bill?
“Why are the Grasshopper Princes always so fickle?”
Bismuth thought back on the others who had become the Grasshopper Prince before. One moment they would long for something with all their hearts, and then the instant Bismuth actually granted it for them, they would recoil and hate it. Some even tried to call Bismuth to some kind of “account” for the deed. If only she could understand just what that meant, she would surely have granted that too, exactly as they wished.
“I mustn't think about it.”
Bismuth said, shaking her head hard.
“I mustn't think such thoughts today. Because today is a good day, a perfect day…”
And indeed it was just as she said.
“Because there are so many friends here who are this happy!”
For countless friends welcomed Bismuth as she strolled through the village.

“We can go anywhere!”
“We aren't hungry anymore!”
“We can look down on anything from up high!”
“We aren't lonely anymore.”
“We never have to go away anywhere ever again!”
“It's a truly fine day, a perfect day!”
Yielding herself to the chorus of that joy-filled choir — whatever it might have been — Bismuth drifted buoyantly through the clouds.
“Bismuth loves it too!”
Bismuth laughed.
“Bismuth really loves it too!”
Baring her white, clean teeth, Bismuth laughed and laughed.
“Now I can do anything. Anyone can hear my story… huh? Look over there.”
At her command the drifting clouds came to a stop.
“It's Auntie Maria! Auntieee!”
Spotting a familiar face, Bismuth leapt down from the cloud and went bounding over. But seeing that, didn't Auntie Maria's face go pale as a sheet in an instant?
“Oh.”
Such an expression and complexion on weather this bright — something must surely be the matter! And so once again it's Bismuth's turn to step in.
“Lyd—”
“Bismuth's here, Auntie Maria! Why don't you come and play anymore these days?”
“…come and play?”
At the words tumbling out one after another, Auntie Maria, though flustered, answered reflexively. The two hands trimming the garden hedge, gripping a great pair of shears, hovered helplessly in the air.

“You used to, you know, in the old days!”
Bismuth said.
“Back when Bismuth wasn't us, back when Bismuth wasn't Bismuth, you used to come and play.”
It felt as remote as some far-distant past, almost like a legend from another age — yet so it had certainly been. Maria tried to recall the child of that time, but it was beyond her. The child before her now — Bismuth, who held within her the rainbow and the most fickle and destructive power of the nature, or supernature, that spun it — kept thwarting all such efforts.
“Yes.”
Maria managed to chime in.
“It was like that then… you came to play often.”
“That's right, that's right!”
Bismuth, clapping her hands in delight.
“I can still remember you from back then… though only barely, still.”
Why was it that Auntie Maria's face, as she said such a thing, looked so forlorn? As she spoke she glanced at Bismuth. To be precise, at a part of Bismuth — at the book rippling in the empty air, the one that for some reason so many people regarded with unease, even as something else entirely apart from Bismuth. She averted her eyes a moment, then re-set her grip and clenched the shears hard with both hands. Watching that, Bismuth could only cock her head.
It certainly is a fine pair of shears, big and pretty and gleaming. With something like that in hand, it's understandable to want to thrust it out to show off to someone. But all the same — had no one ever taught Auntie Maria that you mustn't hold a great pair of shears like that, especially with a person standing in front of you?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main2_Content_2:
“Auntie Maria?”
“I have to do it.”
She said, biting her lip. Spreading her elbows, lending the full force of one forearm to each leg of the shears, she came toward Bismuth holding up the keen, livid-blue blades.
“The others were too frightened. There's only me…”
“What are you doing?”
“I, who still remember you when you were just a little child — I have to find the courage…”
“The hedge is over there, though…”
But the closer she drew, the more her gaze sank. The blades bowed their heads in a half-crouch, as though some heavy thing had been laid upon them. So small she was — Bismuth's frame was that small. So young that a full-grown adult like Auntie Maria had to kneel just to meet her at eye level. The regret born of that realisation, and the situation already past all undoing, pulled Auntie Maria apart from both sides of her body. Every single strand of her hair stood on end in reverse, as if it would split her body in two, like a tree trunk climbing upward with a clod of earth in its embrace.
“I'm sorry, I'm so sorry…”
Bismuth felt fat tears fall from Auntie Maria's eyes, drop after drop. She saw the hesitant toes digging and digging again into the already churned-up ground, wavering.
“But there's nothing I can do but this…”
That great, glittering pair of shears truly was splendid. Whatever lay between — even some tough and pitiful old passion of the past — it was sharp enough to sever in a single stroke. And each time that splendid pair of shears trembled with Auntie Maria's hand, the way the sunlight glanced off it, that gleam, wavered, and wavered, and wavered again, until…
“Huh?”
Before Bismuth, who had been lost in some other thought, there was now only the house and the hedge, the hedge and the house. Where could Auntie Maria have gone?

“Auntie Maria…?”
When Bismuth knelt where she stood, a floor of chewy candy bore her body up. Bending at the waist, Bismuth groped at the puddle filling a hollow that had suddenly sunk into the ground, and at the pruning shears stuck slantwise in its very center. The shears had been there all along, but where had the puddle come from? Flinging the shears away over her shoulder, Bismuth quietly observed the liquid that filled the puddle. A vivid, natural color of deep saturation, easily picked up on a fingertip and quickly dried — well suited for painting something…
“Wow!”
Bismuth cheered.
“It's paint!”
Forgetting even that Auntie Maria had vanished, Bismuth at last plopped down and began to play, splashing about in the puddle full of paint. Colors that had never existed in reality, colors beyond description, colors no one should ever look upon — as they embroidered the empty air at the wave of Bismuth's hand, all manner of strange and wondrous shapes and smells and voices, new and happy friends, began to spring up and flourish. Laughing aloud, Bismuth soon came to think that her own laughter was echoing everywhere. Every one of the village's other friends had come crowding out near the puddle, cheering. Following her, the friends, the village, the world were laughing. Her happiness, her story, was being accepted by all the others just the same. All the way to the eternal cliffs, the everlasting precipice, the boundless void that stood in place of the world beyond the village — Bismuth's will alone encompassed it all as the one and only reality.
“Ah—”
She cried out at the top of her voice.
“—it's a truly perfect day!”

ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main2_Short: Every morning dawns perfect, every friend overjoyed, every wish granted before it's spoken. So why does someone arrive with trembling hands and tears, certain there is only one thing left to do?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main3_Content_0: “To His Most Serene Majesty the King…” The one who held the quill shut his eyes tight. Beads of sweat caught and halted in the deep furrows of his brow. Must I truly report this matter to His Majesty in full detail? he thought. “In truth, calling it a village is generous; it was a hamlet of scarcely a hundred souls…” So it was. And — though it may sound a cruel thing to say — a village of that size may well vanish, or suffer something of like measure, and more besides. Plagued by a band of brigands, perhaps; abandoned to a failed harvest… and so there was no need to file a dutiful report over the disappearance of a single village. But what if a village that had so vanished suddenly returned one day? And what if the village that returned… “I must steel my heart.” The one who held the quill said. “I must make this calamity known… that is my charge as an administrator, and as a subject of His Majesty the King.” I humbly wish to report to Your Majesty the truth behind the rumors of the vanished village — thus the latter portion was set down in line, following the salutation already written above. After that, for a good while, the quill could be moved with considerable ease. For in laying a report before the King, one could not sweep away the whole of the background with such phrases as “as Your Majesty is aware…” Beginning with the rumor that the village had vanished, then the pit, or the black mist, left behind where the village had once stood, and after that some time had passed, the course of the village's return — to set all this forth in detail was only proper. Set down on paper, even this much was already a matter of immense absurdity. That a village, well lodged in its place, should melt away overnight like snow and then suddenly return one day? Had a junior official brought such a document before him, the administrator himself would at once have thundered at the man and driven him out, seeing in it nothing but nonsense. “And yet there was nothing for it but to believe.” The administrator recited it under his breath as he wrote the sentence. “Having beheld with my own eyes the calamity left in the returned village, I could only conclude that all of it had likewise come to pass, and that beside the events which followed thereafter it was a trifling thing.” Ought I to include the matter of the Grasshopper Prince? the administrator thought. When first he investigated — nay, when in truth he opened up the village — he had also conducted inquiries among those who yet seemed to have survived. Those among them still able to give voice had, with one accord, named the “Grasshopper Prince.” And so at first he had supposed the village to have been swallowed by the Power of Dreams at the hands of some unprecedentedly dangerous wanderer called the Grasshopper Prince; but that, in the end, proved to be only one facet of the affair. “There is no need to set forth the whole process in tedious detail… According to the inquiry, there was no way to account for how the village came to be drawn into the dream world, nor for the events that took place during that time, without the existence of a single child.” In the accounts, the place of the Grasshopper Prince shifted every time. By one man's description a young man; by another's an old woman with white hair. Yet the “single child” who was with that prince — nay, who held him in her sway — was ever fixed and unchanging. She had her own original name, and an origin bound to this village, but these had been corrupted by the Power of Dreams… “This is closer to conjecture, and is not fit content for a report.” The administrator kneaded his wrist and refined the wording of the writing. “It is understood that, while the Power of Dreams ruled over the village, this child's will exerted a vast influence, and that on each such occasion there were those put forward as a kind of sacrificial offering, compelled to cooperate with her. Upon hearing such warnings I gave orders to trace the child's movements with all haste, yet she could not be found; only that witnesses say the child chose to follow the Power of Dreams and remain in that place, likely in the Rapids…” His hand suddenly stilled. He had the feeling that the report was straying from the heart of the matter — that, indeed, it was even leading astray.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main3_Content_1:
“Is this the affair of a single child who carried the Power of Dreams upon her back?”
It was not so. This was not a matter that could be brought to a knot by tracking down and punishing some one thing, some one person. To feel so would be the disposition of a petty man drunk on a tale of vengeance — not the temperament of a provincial administrator with a region in his charge. Nor was the writing of the report for any such purpose. It must become a plea, urging vigilance against what was to come, what might come, and the early readiness to meet it.
And so it would be of no help whatsoever to analyze in detail how deeply the child had been steeped in the Power of Dreams, or had summoned it; whether she had departed in pursuit of some greater power, or had simply grown weary and refused to return together with the village. Therefore he must come to the main point. He must report the calamity left in the village in as much detail as could be borne, and stir alarm in the heart of the King. The administrator forced himself onward, took up the quill once more, and braced his wrist against the desk. It was like fitting a bridle and saddle to a worn-out old horse and driving it out to the field of war.
“Under the child's caprice, the whole village… appeared to have become a scribbling-pad.”
Would this saying fittingly capture the impression he had received? The administrator thought he ought to expand upon the metaphor in greater detail.
“The child, without the least reserve, overlaid a kind of metaphysical 'scribbling' upon every place and thing her gaze fell upon, twisting their principles and workings. Making scribbles, then making an eraser to blur those scribbles, then again drawing scribbles to harry that eraser — in such manner she scattered the scenery of the village into utter disorder.”
He shuddered. It was because he had recalled the “remnants” he had met with at the very moment he led the soldiers in. Wooden soldiers drawn crooked and jagged, spool-cannons firing acorn shells, rice-straw centipedes with countless legs, winged beasts flapping fingers as great as windmill blades, hail of cicadas pouring from the clouds… But what mattered more was what came after, once these had been put down and he had entered within the village.

“I beseech Your forgiveness.”
The administrator murmured.
“I beseech Your forgiveness, I who write this report to trouble the heart of His Majesty the King, to cause Him grief…”
After that there was no room left even for hesitation. There was only the rustling sound of paper taking in ink, and now and then an intermittent silence as it ceased for the briefest moments while the tip of the quill was dipped and stirred against the inkpot. The scene branded into the administrator's mind as deep as the mark of red-hot iron was scrawled out in a single sweep of the brush.
In the nearby forest a pack of wolves lay sprawled. Their four legs were withered to the bone, yet their bellies were swollen taut as dung-heaps. Within their slackly gaping mouths there clung but a single dried tongue, wearing the shamefaced look of a poor host with nothing to set before a guest. What filled the rest was smooth-healed gum, as though it had never so much as glimpsed a tooth from the start. And then, before the administrator's eyes, the jaw of one of them began to work, and its mouth fell open. What crawled out from its gullet was a yellowish serpent, thicker than a man's thigh.
“It had, however, neither the texture of scales, nor head, nor eyes, nor mouth.”
So it was less a serpent than an earthworm. No — a leech. A leech that, to crawl forward, would swell the thickness of its trunk to impossible girth and then shrink slender again, rippling its way along the ground. In truth it was bread. Pressed within the belly and soaked in saliva, clumped together yet ever increasing, the mass of bread escaped the wolf's mouth. Its taut-swollen lower belly gradually sank. The damp lumps of bread went into the mouths of other beasts already dying — into jaws grown as heavy as their own eyelids, forced open. And so it did not stop until the belly of that beast had swelled like a full moon wanting in nothing.
As in the legend of some distant land, in the village there grew a tree that bore sheep. Tough, supple branches joined the bellies of the full-grown sheep to the tree like umbilical cords. The sheep there could not set their four feet upon the ground. At a height where it would be no wonder if their backbones snapped should they fall, they barely held up their upturned heads, gnawing at the thin, dry leaves and the black bark. The sheep that could endure no longer never returned from their upturned posture. Like dead insects, backs to the ground, their four legs drawn together and folded neatly upon their navels, they closed their eyes.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main3_Content_2: “In the midst of it, I nearly lost an eye.” It was on account of minnows fitted with wings — not the kind of fin that, spread broad and sideways, kicks off the water's surface, but real wings that could truly beat. Minnows they were called, yet far larger, heavier, and swifter of form than gnats, and they came darting like arrows after the moisture of men's eyeballs. Several luckless foot-soldiers, the moment the opening of the village was done, had to receive a ration of salt, bread, and one eye-patch each, and trudge their way home. Whether they had not yet mastered their newly-formed organs, or whether on the contrary they were practicing without reserve the very thing they most wished to do, there was no telling, as the minnows thrust their heads here and there upon dry land and burst dead. Having gained the marvelous power to go anywhere, they had in the end failed to find even a small brook or puddle near the village, and suffocated; the administrator could not easily forget the scene of their carcasses strewn everywhere, reeking with the stench of a fish market. Is this, then, all of it? he thought. Is this the whole of what I have to set down in the report? What am I hesitating over now? “The people…” The administrator's voice trembled. “What befell the people, the villagers, was by no means… inferior to this.” But he could not, for the life of him, write it. He must not! He could not, like one whose face would surely not so much as change color in reporting the matter of the wolves and the flock of sheep and the fish, go on prattling — wielding that brazen, jet-black ink — to set down what had befallen the villagers. Even setting aside that it was a report to be laid before the King, it felt as though merely to increase by one the number of people who knew of that sight would be to commit a grievous sin. Reaching the square, the administrator and his soldiers were struck dumb with horror. They did not know whence the voices came. They wavered, not knowing toward what to extend a hand, toward what to level a spear-point. Before long, however, the far view and the near view, some object and the scene behind it, began to separate themselves. Better, rather, never to have known at all, to the very end. “Your Most Serene Majesty the King may perhaps receive it thus: that this calamity left behind merely several heaps of corpses wholly stilled and rotting; that the village's being submerged in and tormented by the Power of Dreams was but the matter of an instant. So I humbly conjecture.” But that is not so. The flustered hand had let slip into the report offered to the King something near the colloquial speech of the marketplace, but there was no room even to notice it. The hand gripping the quill trembled and shook, barely contrived to mimic the shapes of letters, dragging out vertical and horizontal scrawls. Ink-drops too small to be seen sprayed about, breathing the smell of ink in every direction. “No. To be sure, all were dead. And yet their story, their suffering, went on without end—” The administrator's lips quivered. “—I mean to say that all of this, all who told me in detail of the calamity during the village's disappearance, all who had no choice but to behold from beginning to end what was taking place, all who, when I entered the village, begged me to bring them poison and firewood and torches in place of food and water — every one of them was already drawing no breath, and their hearts beat no longer! Oh, Most Serene Majesty the King—” The sun was sinking low. Driven, as it were, by his own long and ghastly shadow cast in the trail of the candle lit at one corner of the desk, he set the hand that held the quill into spasms. And so, in a violent hand, he wrote in that final sentence — so absurd, so preposterous, so ludicrous, and yet at the same time unbearably terrifying. “—by every sign that is shown, all the people of that village and all its animals were already dead from the very moment the village was swallowed by the Power of Dreams!”
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main3_Short: A village vanished overnight, and one day it came back. The man tasked with telling the King what he found inside can barely hold the quill — for who would believe that the dead never stopped their story?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main4_Content_0:
“This is no fun.”
Bismuth had thrown herself for a while into shaping people out of clay, and then grew bored of it.
“Is that why everyone else was doing it the other way round? Let's try doing it backward again too.”
And so she did. Bismuth gathered up the parts of the clay pit, mounded and smoothed them, and shaped them into proper human figures. Following Bismuth's splashing arms and legs and arms and arms and legs and arms and legs and legs and legs and legs and arms, the principles of the world began to twist. Soon a king and queen of astonishingly bright, primary hues — astonishing, considering they were clay — a prince and princess, generals and scholars and nobles and merchants and farmers and loyal soldiers welled up and gathered in droves. Further still, they began to stage Bismuth's stories, to sing songs and compose poems. When Bismuth burst into giggles and clapped her hands, lightning struck and an earthquake rose and the ground split apart. And so the king and queen and prince and princess, and all the other clay besides, came tumbling down and were crushed flat. Bismuth gazed up at the galaxy their tears had made.
The sky of the Rapids was as resplendent as the crystal that made up Bismuth's body.

“I think it's much better here than outside! Bismuth thinks so too.”
She said. Even granting that it was a wondrous world where she (they) could do whatever she pleased and no one would call her to “account,” there was still much to come to know. Above all, what most pleased her — and what therefore she wished to keep testing, again and again — was the loose linkage peculiar to dreams. For instance… oh, never you mind.
“Wow, a house made of sweets!”
Bismuth went dashing breathlessly toward the thing that sat squarely in the middle of the forest. Thin, crisp bread, great billowing cloud-colored cream, or cream-colored cloud, and… well, since Bismuth is not deeply versed in making breads and pastries and distinguishing their many kinds in detail, no further names will be forthcoming; but at any rate, it is certain that the house is made of all manner of sweets and nibbles.
To elaborate, just so far as it will not put Bismuth out of sorts, the constituent parts of the sweet-house are as follows: pillars made of tarts stacked layer upon layer, eaves of thin pastry made to jut out and a roof filled within with various stuffings and set firm, walls of board-shaped biscuits joined with creams such as milk and butter spread between them, a candy railing drawn out long by twisting three colors of dough, in place of the porch and stairs a baguette baked dry and crumbly yet deliberately scorched darker, and a gutter of sponge-cake clad in a coat of sugar, for catching thin fresh cream in place of rainwater… Oops, I've gotten too absorbed. Bismuth will notice!
“Hello, house. Hello, sweet house made of sweets.”
“Hello, Bismuth!”
The house greeted her cheerfully, leaping about with its door-frame and windows and eaves and roof. A grand spectacle, to be sure — but not a sight one would care to see twice.
“I've come to gobble you up!”
“What brings you here?”
The conversation is at cross purposes, yet on both sides everything that needed saying and hearing is there. And that, precisely, is the tragedy.

“You won't say anything, will you, hm?”
Bismuth said.
“You won't go stopping me from doing this and that, the way the others do, will you?”
As if she had ever taken such words at face value.
“Of course not, Bismuth!”
At the permission granted so readily, Bismuth flung herself forward with both arms spread wide. She picked the thickest, most mouth-watering spot of the sweet-house, where the dough dripped in gobs, and opened her mouth. Thus she took a greedy bite, like a snake that, to fill its own belly, endures even the unhinging of its jaw.
“Oh, no!”
“Whab's wrong, sweeb house?”
Bismuth gulped down what was in her mouth in an instant and asked.
“What's wrong, sweet house?”
Without even waiting for an answer, two bites, three bites, four bites… smearing crumbs all over — from fingertips to elbow and shoulder, collarbone, neck, jaw, cheek — she and her little mouth began to devour the walls and pillars and roof of the sweet-house without leaving a scrap.
“Oh, no, no, no!”
“What, what, what is wrong, I'm asking, sweet house?”
Having finished her meal, Bismuth plopped down with her two legs spread wide. When she patted her belly, swollen taut and full, laughter spilled out of its own accord. To describe that sight as something like the death-throes of the sweet-house, which had now vanished from this world leaving only its foundation behind — nay, to go a step further and hint that perhaps there might be another, consistent vantage from which to interpret what had just happened, that what had occurred could become an altogether different scene — would that, perhaps, be too presumptuous and gloomy a thing?
“Who said any such thing?”
No one, no one at all! Bismuth. No one said any such thing.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main4_Content_1:
“Help!”
Someone cried out… by the way, how much time has passed? Did the clay dolls and the sweet-house and this voice all take place in roughly the same time and place? Or did the course of some other events come in between…
“It's the voices of my animal friends!”
Bismuth sprang up and went running. In the wake of her footsteps small brooks and waterfalls sprang up one after another, loosing a lake into the heart of the forest, and within it frogs and salamanders flailing about. To the very last moment, as their eyes closed, they puzzled over why they did not know how to swim, but no clear answer came.
“Help, help!”
“These bad, bad… hunters!”
She meant, perhaps, to use the word “poachers”?
“Hold on, animal friends, Bismuth is coming, we are coming!”
Arriving where the voices came from, Bismuth met with exactly the scene she (they) had imagined. There were the good animals first, and then there were the bad hunters driving them into a corner. There were the good animals filling the clearing, surrounding the hunters, and in the gap among them the hunters, gripping great and fearsome blades, standing high and mighty, backs pressed to one another, retreating step by step!
…Something's a little off
“Wh-what are you?”
The hunters asked, quaking triumphantly. Which is to say, they were speaking to a certain sight: something with bandages wound over its eyes, parts of its body all over replaced with rainbow-hued metal crystal, and, not content with that, a great book — well able to swallow up anything at all and turn it into its own story — rippling in the air.
“You seem to have some kind of skill — help us out a little—”
“Shameless hunters!”
Bismuth said. The ground beneath the hunters' feet turned to a quagmire and seized their legs.
“How can you say such a thing while you're tormenting the good animals!”
As she said, the animals — far larger of build and far greater in number — were drawing closer and closer to the hunters in their terror, so frightened that, plain to see, tears streamed from their very mouths. Bismuth was nearly so exasperated she wanted to shriek aloud. Did these hunters feel no pity at all for the animals?

“Villains like you have to be punished!”
The hilts of the blades the hunters gripped grew hot, until they could be held in the hand no longer. Startled by this only a moment, they then watched as Bismuth unfolded wide. She had already unfolded and been rippling from before, yet for some reason they watched her unfold once again. From within, the sound of sweat-drops falling onto the backs of feet and the smell of dry, coarse fists came bursting out.
“What in the world is all this…?”
While the good animals trembled, unable even to flee, Bismuth went on drawing out friends from within her stories. It is not the certain sound and smell and sight themselves that are fearful. What is fearful is the situations that might arise before and after them. As fearful as the ending awaiting the hunters who can neither grip a blade nor pull free a foot. A wound suddenly become conscious; a disgrace one thought forgotten; tears one could not hide; footsteps and a knock heard from where no one is; the shadow of an empty room; the smell that ought to vanish refusing to vanish, while on the contrary the smell one never wishes to forget someday vanishes and is forgotten utterly — that kind of absurdity. Scalding broth poured unawares over the tongue and the roof of the mouth.
If there is a king amid a heap of books, his spectacles must be broken. The one who gained eternal life must regret that choice from beyond the bars. Those who struggled to return home must come to realize they had never escaped anywhere from the start. Those who feared the monster must, through that fear, become monsters themselves. And the very point at which one can willingly, with a smiling face, inflict all those cruel moments upon another — that is the most terrifying yet at the same time the most honest nature of Bismuth, nay, of a storyteller.
Bismuth, leading a great host of friends, planted herself before the hunters.
“We're going to teach you a lesson!”

*
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main4_Content_2:
“It's all right now, isn't it, animal friends?”
Bismuth asked. The good animals only hung their heads in silence, moving their jaws up and down.
“Were you hungry? Still, you mustn't eat too much… what if you get a tummy ache!”
Bismuth gazed at how the bodies of the bad hunters had turned into a powder that glittered like sand under the sunlight. She pinched up a little to taste it and smell it, but felt nothing at all. So she brushed off her hands and tossed it onto the ground — and unexpectedly, the good animal friends began to devour it greedily.
“You mustn't turn bad yourselves just from eating what the bad people left behind.”
Heedless of her, the good animals threw themselves into their meal with not a moment to spare, and Bismuth quietly observed them. Eating, and eating, and eating again… looking upon the ground and grain of their minds, filled with that and that alone, Bismuth found her enthusiasm somewhat cooled. They might be good, but as characters in a story they were far too monotonous.
“Come to think of it, I've hardly written any of my story since coming here.”
Bismuth murmured — and here, someone might think, “hardly” was in truth “not at all.”
“I did get a little ready to start, though…”
Bismuth flopped down, vexed. The animal friends were still nearby, shoveling down the glittering powder in a frenzy no matter what happened around them. As a matter of course, her hand — Bismuth's hand — reaches toward them. It pokes and prods their flanks. It is a near-inevitable thing.

“Hey. Heey.”
The animals shook their manes and scales and webbed feet as if she were a nuisance, pushing Bismuth away — but the nostrils of a few of them went slack and gaped open, then drew so tight they might have caught and snapped a single eyelash. They had caught a scent. A scent there was no mistaking. Steeped thoroughly though it was in the air of dreams, faintly yet distinctly foreign, they had succeeded in reading the trace of the outside. And that is the scent of gold.
“Listen to my story for a bit…”
Surely no one would say the animal friends were so well-versed in etiquette as to decline a snack given for free?
“Don't just keep thinking about eating something… huh?”
The downy, dappled animal friends, the children whose innocent eyes had been shining, suddenly opened their mouths and shut them again. Right where, just a moment ago, Bismuth's hand, arm, and neck had been.
“What's the matter all of a sudden?”
Bismuth, holding back a sigh she wished to show no one, drifted buoyantly upward. And she saw the animal friends, glittering powder smeared all over their mouths, gathering one by one beneath her, drooling, beginning to whet their claws sharp. Bewildered for a moment as to what had happened… yes, that's it — the powder on their mouths.
However tasty it may be, did it not come, in the end, from the bad hunters?
“So you've become bad ones too, now.”
Bismuth grasped the situation with perfect clarity. The ever-swelling sigh popped and gushed out flames of five colors. By the time she gently alighted upon the ground, there was not one among the good — no, the turned-bad — animal friends nearby that was not embracing the blaze and leaping and bounding about. It was pitiful, but she had to harden her heart.

“See, I told you you'd get a tummy ache!”
The power of the flames peeled away their flimsy stomachs. One by one, the shapes hidden within the animal friends began to spring out. Seeing that scene, Bismuth was startled. Hard, straight lines, and outlines woven from such lines neither too sharp nor too dull. A chair that demands you straighten your back and tuck in your seat to fit your body just so against its back, a desk upon which nothing may be set down or taken up carelessly, marks ruled out neatly along ruled lines, words that may be said at one time but must not be said at another… those terrifying villains, Bismuth's archenemies, had disguised themselves in the clothes of the animal friends!
“You bad ones!”
A page fluttered and a fragment of story was placed into her hand. Whiter than first snow and hotter than the sun beheld with the naked eye, it was a sword of courage blazing fiercely. The desks and chairs and all the petty little rules that had pretended to be animal friends were powerless before it and floundered. Feathered wings sprouted downy within their mouths; fresh rosewater gushed in torrents from every opening of their bodies; and when they sneezed, bones flew out by the handful and clattered into a dance. Steadying her posture in the air, Bismuth gripped the sword of courage straight and charged into the heart of that pandemonium.
“Here comes Bismuth!”
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main4_Short: She saves the good and punishes the wicked, just as every story demands. But when the rescued catch the scent of gold, who is left to tell the hero from the villain?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main5_Content_0: The many fantastical happenings of a fantastical world. That, above all, was the essence of the Rapids as it appeared in Bismuth's mind. And this was an environment that suited well the crystal of Bismuth, who had chosen to remain beyond the Rift. “Bismuth didn't come in here to play.” She said. “Bismuth came in to know more stories, and to write them.” Until now there had been all sorts of busy goings-on. She had saved many of the virtuous, and given an even greater number of villains such a scolding that the tears were wrung clean out of them! Goodness, whatever is to become of the world, that there should be so many more villains than good folk — and especially villains who at first seem like good folk yet secretly harbor sly, scheming hearts — there is simply no knowing. But the Bismuth of this moment, and the lonely silence that lay all around her, were utterly unlike the scenery of before. In a world gone quiet for the first time in ever so long, the sky was slowly closing its eyelids of darkness, the ground and the boulders their eyelids of ivy, each one at its own languid pace. While the birds folded their wings, the rabbits and mice returned to their burrows, and the people all shut their eyes, Bismuth alone remained unsleeping, and so resolved to turn the first spadeful of her first story since entering the dream. She stretched out her legs against the bare ground, unfolded herself, and laid bare those snow-white empty pages. Then she began to observe the stories she had met with wandering the dream — strands of many tales, some she had experienced firsthand, but no few she had not. “This is the story of a king.” Bismuth opened her mouth solemnly. Symbols of every shape and color appeared in the air and rippled. “A dream-king who rules a boundless kingdom no one can behold with open eyes… but no one sings of how great this person is, how noble.” The symbols began to cling to and part from one another, sometimes devouring and being devoured, forming larger and newer fragments of phrasing and meaning. The very moment one ripened into a single narrative structure would be the moment fit for Bismuth to snap her own cover shut. Like a pitcher plant trapping a fly, like the shell of a giant clam seizing a diver's wrist, she presses the strands of the many stories crossing this world between her own, like a bookmark. “They only speak of how mighty he is, how merciless — that he burned the forests, toppled the nests, and shattered the snow mountains. And all the while they hush up how everyone fears him.” Perhaps this is not the story of a king, but…? Bismuth thought. And she kept her mouth moving all the while. “He barged into a quiet room first of all — and uninvited at that — and now he's forcing his own song upon it. And then he's throwing tantrums all by himself at everything around him.” Bismuth's appraisal went on. “He's laid the world that did him no wrong under his power as he pleases, and is behaving violently…” The cover of Bismuth, which had been closing little by little to seize the symbols, at last bloomed wide open as though it had never been doing any such thing. The sets of meaning in the air went limp, as if heaving a sigh of relief. Escaped from Bismuth's clutches, they would now borrow the power of rumor and hearsay, of the wind's whisper and the murmur in the ear, to travel on far, far away. To depart for places further still. “He's no protagonist. Absolutely not.” And so the story of the king — which everyone had been certain was the story of a king — that of a ruffian and a hooligan, escaped being gathered up by Bismuth.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main5_Content_1:
“This person is a philosopher in a cave.”
Bismuth said, having observed the next strand of story.
“He hated shadows — hated every shadow hidden unseen in the world — so he fled into a cave. There he's making a great flame that can erase every shadow.”
But it seems no one had tipped him off that the deep shadow of the one who stands nearest that blaze — the philosopher in the cave — would stretch all the broader and drape down like a curtain of darkness. It seems a like thought flickered through Bismuth's mind as well.
In truth he was also a person who could hardly have been less appealing, besides.
“He's a coward who stays only within the cave, only within the world he can understand, and yet holds forth about the whole world.”
Bismuth went on, having concluded her close examination.
“He tries to understand the world while hiding inside his own story alone. He doesn't think about the events that are actually happening, but converts them all into names he already knows. Without that, he can know and do nothing. This person isn't a philosopher — he's a fussy eater throwing a nasty fit over his food.”
The next strands of story came rippling near. Bismuth gazed at them, shining a million eyes that do not exist.

“This person was good once and then turned bad.”
Ah, a three-dimensional character? Has a type fit at last for Bismuth's discerning eye appeared?
“…originally a good gatekeeper guarding a good forest, but he was tainted by an evil power and changed. He turned the forest he had guarded into a forest that now torments everyone. This person is hackneyed.”
Having said it, Bismuth poured a fair amount of time into blankly chewing the thought over. For she was hazy on what exactly “hackneyed” meant.
“It's a word I didn't know back when Bismuth wasn't Bismuth… but it's a word a storyteller ought to know—ah!”
When she struck her knee, a lover who had been holding out on a sickbed, gazing wan and weary toward the doorway, awaiting the face of someone who would appear there, at last closed their eyes. A treasure hunter who had collected ninety-nine of a hundred kinds of precious jewel lost his life to a rice cake lodged in his throat. A bashful one who, always at the decisive moment, would lose heart and live with “next time, next time” forever on his lips, had to receive the news that his cherished person could be with him no longer. I told you, didn't I — that a storyteller must be cruel.
“So this means it's predictable!”
But Bismuth is magnanimous, benevolent. Cantankerous, you say? Who said any such thing? At any rate, our esteemed Bismuth scrupulously searched out the other possibilities in this not-particularly-splendid character.
“Could it be that within the person, after he turned bad, the original gentle heart still remains?”
Bismuth is Bismuth. Bismuth poses the question, and Bismuth answers it.
“But such a complex character has meaning only as the promise that he might do something, not as actually doing anything.”
Bismuth fluttered her pages as if in agreement. Whoever and whatever one was before, it is already all over and done. And could there be any being who grasps that fact better than one who was once a single book and a single little child? And so Bismuth lets the strands of this story too be pushed off to a distant place.
“Even if something remains within him, it means nothing at all.”
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main5_Content_2:
In the next strand a flesh-cutting chill is felt. A high mountain in the dead of winter, lashed by a blizzard. It seems this is the story of a general who once reigned as the absolute master of that place.
“He trusted in his own power and challenged the new king, and lost his homeland, his prestige, and his might, all of it.”
Bismuth lowered her voice as if in pity.
“Now he's become a donkey on a tether. Going round and round to pull the millstone… a donkey-general who claims that every such step is his own free choice, and who only bellows commands at the fodder that drops before him.”
Fodder brings to mind straw, and straw brings to mind a scarecrow. The story of a scarecrow Bismuth already knows. To his plea to make a friend, she attached along his shoulders birds with black wings and black beaks and red blood and screams gone pale as snow. There is no point of contact between the two, but for Bismuth's part she did not particularly wish to tell yet another story involving straw. And there was a greater problem besides.
“This general is a person who doesn't know his own place.”
She said.
“Wherever he goes, he tries to play the protagonist. Instead of following the given course of the story, he'll devour the whole thing centered on himself. He'll force the story to be arranged by his own narration, by his own impression.”
Our esteemed Bismuth did not cease her trenchant, dead-on remarks against the many bad types of character that held no implication whatsoever for her.
“A person conscious of being the protagonist, a person who firmly believes they are the protagonist, must not become the protagonist of a story. Bismuth…”
Some word that was about to come next went unsaid. Whatever it was, surely it had nothing to do with Bismuth?

“She's a queen who forsook the brightest sky and chose to become a shooting star.”
A new strand of story. But this time, whatever it is she dislikes, Bismuth's expression is decidedly sour from the very start. She's even clicking her tongue — tsk, tsk — like the grown adults who've seen their fair share of years, in a way that ill suits her looks.
“Wicked, so very wicked.”
Bismuth said.
“She doesn't even know how much the people around her look after her, and sunk in her own private tragedy, she betrayed that person's faith. Not content with that, she tormented those people with her new power. And all the while she keeps chasing her own freedom. Without even knowing her own fault. Childishly, she clings to her own story…”
Bismuth abruptly stopped and faltered. Yes — now do you see something at last? If one cannot conjure anything even from this “her own, her own, her own” refrain, repeated so many times over that the very sentence structure grows somehow awkward, then that person can only be called the worst of storytellers and the most obstinate of mules.
Wouldn't you say?
“If Bismuth had seen a wicked child like this, she'd have punished her on the spot!”
Just so, of course.
King, general, queen, philosopher, gatekeeper… the five strands of noodles served up on the plate thus failed, every one of them, to satisfy Bismuth's finicky palate. At the same time, every one of them was in truth something that could not be called the self it imagined itself to be — all of them liars, putting on airs and swaggering and pulling the wool over one's eyes and saying two things out of one mouth and being unreasonable and throwing fits — yes, every one of them far from a protagonist, fit rather to be called a wicked villain.
“I don't need things like this.”
Bismuth roughly closed herself, fuming.
“Bismuth's story is far more magnificent than the stories of these villains!”
Within Bismuth, where nothing was written, Bismuth thus set out boldly to write, as the very first passage of Bismuth's story, the story of that very Bismuth. Waving her fingers, she tried to summon the specters of symbols and the phantoms of meaning. And then she came to a sudden, dead halt, unable to do anything more. What happened was not that something arose or surged forth. It was the opposite. She could not do it.
She simply could not write her own story into her own story.
Does Bismuth have no story? As if that could be.
Is Bismuth not a storyteller? As if that could be.
Does Bismuth have no story of her very own? As if that could be. Then why could she not write it?
Why could she not draw a single paragraph, a single sentence, a single word, not even one stroke of a single letter?

“…I can do it later.”
Bismuth said, rising up onto her two legs. A city of little insects was trampled flat beneath those feet, and the rise and fall of long-standing societies, traditions, organizations, schools of thought, and the web of relations built up by all — young and old, man and woman — the intricate twists and turns of joys and sorrows they drew between one another, the final act of that history, all had to be brought to an abrupt close.
“I can do it perfectly well… I'm just busy right now. There are still more dreams I have to see.”
Her chattering voice rang out over the ruins of a civilization.
“I can do it perfectly well later. Isn't that right, Bismuth?”
“That's right, Bismuth.”
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main5_Short: One by one she weighs the kings and queens and finds them all unworthy of being anyone's protagonist. So why, when she turns at last to write her own name, does the page refuse to begin?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main6_Content_0:
“Stop that.”
Ah, our eternal Guide of Dreams, Polaris. How nice to see you. Even you, for all the trials and tribulations you've weathered, having such a stiff line — “Stop that.” — be the very first thing you say upon meeting a traveler you mean to recruit, that must be a first, surely? Don't worry. You'll soon grow used to situations like this too.
At the wave of Bismuth's hand, a mouse was spinning out its own body.
With tiny front teeth like a hangnail on dry skin and a snout no bigger than a peach pit, through the mouth gaping open and shut at its tip it was, with all its might, drawing out its own overturned body — past its tail and rump and waist, and just now bringing forth the final hurdle, the ribcage and trunk. As that thing, overturned and laboriously being born anew, flailed its hind legs, the shock was passed faithfully through the mouth to that very thing chewing itself over again. The convulsions resonated through each other's bodies, putting forth one small, gummy cry after another, like dandelion seeds.
“Stop that, at once.”
Polaris said. She said it without hiding her revulsion.
“Why?”
Bismuth asked. She asked because she was genuinely curious. That guileless turn of mind was so plain even to Polaris, a complete stranger, that she rarely gave up so early on persuading her opponent with words. And so she waved a hand, and the bound pair — the thing that had been a mouse and the thing that was to become one — thus vanished from sight. It was not put out of view or anything of the sort; it was wholly gone. It remained only in the memory of the two who had been there.

“It isn't the first time I've seen those with whom no words will get through, but it is hard every time.”
“Hmm.”
Bismuth made no reply, only groaned thus. The pages of Bismuth, on which nothing was written, turned, and began to give off the air of something busily measuring, searching, and reckoning.
“What are you doing?”
Suddenly Polaris saw Bismuth hang her head low and stare only at the ground — or rather, try to feel for something within it. Could there, in that short span, have been some change of heart?
“Do you feel you've done something wrong?”
“No, on the ground… did you know?”
Bismuth asked again.
“When the people here get really angry and are about to go on a rampage, red marks appear on the ground — did you know that?”
There is a limit even to nonsensical talk. The only ones who could understand what this means are probably the people outside the story. Polaris too was left with nothing to say.
“…so you were watching to see whether those marks would appear?”
“Mm-hm.”
Bismuth brushed off her hands and stood up.
“I was curious whether you might fight me. If not — bye!”
Instead of returning the farewell, Polaris only shook her head, again and again. It was not a very polite thing to do, but it could not be helped. To try to humor — much less attempt to understand — the ways of some alien being swallowed up by that rainbow-hued crystal, who had likewise entrusted part of her sanity to it, or rather of two beings loosely bound together, was something one must not do. For it would only drag one far from any resolution of the matter.

“But who are you?”
It looked like just another disorderly question, no different from any she had been tossing out, but this was already a signal in itself. Unlike how Bismuth had until now arbitrarily “assigned” to anyone she met whatever role she pleased, she was asking after Polaris's type. Could one take this to mean she had discerned that the Guide of Dreams was some special being, someone more important, unlike the others she had met who had no name or whose names had to be forgotten? Bismuth's inner mind is anyone's guess.
“A princess?”
When Bismuth cocked her head, Polaris was wearing a thin, gossamer ceremonial gown. White, spotless satin gloves wrapped her wrists and on past her forearms, and a bejeweled semicircular tiara sparkled with the radiance of diamond and sapphire and emerald. Crimson dimples formed on cheeks of skin as fair as milk.
“Or a queen?”
The tiara now turned into a great and stately crown that, instead of resting in a semicircle along the crown of the head, wrapped fully around it and settled snugly in place. The hand that had been waving through the air clad only in a ceremonial glove now held a long scepter instead. With nothing more than slowly raising her other hand and opening her palm, thousands of soldiers and subjects would bow their heads and prostrate themselves at such a gesture.
“Or else… a mistreated youngest daughter?”
Polaris clad in rags is a rare spectacle indeed. Patching and mending the grubby cloth here and there just enough to keep out the draft, she barely covered her body. With tough, stiff linen knotted tight to bind back her hair, and the leftover cloth shorn into strips to make an apron, that was the look of…
“A Guide.”
When she opened her mouth, there stood Polaris — whole, complete, and inviolable, not so much as a single button of her dress, a shape of a fastened cord, a grain, a thread, a stitch of the sewing changed from the very start.
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main6_Content_1: “I am the Guide of the Rapids, and beyond that, of dreams.” “So that's what you think.” “Is it not you who are lost in thought?” Polaris said. To be sure, there had been some confusion in the playing of her role just now; but pelting bewildered travelers with this and that question is precisely a Guide's specialty. “You style yourself a storyteller who prizes her own story above all, yet you cannot in fact write that story of your own, and so you go fussing this way and that over the roles of others. Among those words you lose your way all alone and fall to brooding again, and every time you try to write your story, you fail. Am I mistaken?” “It's not like that.” “And how would you know that?” “Wrong, wrong, a hundred, a thousand times wrong. Eh-beh-beh.” My, my — it is quite a rare thing for Bismuth's several voices, especially the voice of the one book and the one girl who were once not Bismuth, to express themselves separately to others. It seems she was struck right where it hurts. “How could I not know it?” Polaris said, as if troubled. Polaris, who had accepted the dream world and the workings of its power far earlier than Bismuth, and could therefore grasp its structure and implications more deftly. “Do you not know how great the influence you have spread about this place, the traces you have left behind, have grown to be?” “I don't know.” “It was not a question that sought an… in any case, I have come to make a proposal.” Polaris went on. “If you lend your strength to what I am trying to do, I will teach you the way to write your story.” “I don't need it.” The answer came back swiftly. So swiftly that it felt almost as though the answer had always been at the ready, even before the question was put. “Bismuth doesn't need things like that. Bismuth can write Bismuth's story whenever she likes. She's just busy right now, that's all. Bismuth…” “Then could you show me, just once?” With those words, the two became conscious of Bismuth together. One looked, and the other felt, that Bismuth's unfolded pages were empty. Just as all manner of dust and water-bugs and minnows pass in and out of a whale's vacantly gaping mouth as though it were their own home, countless strands of story strolled before her, and yet — plain and clear as day — not a single line was being added to Bismuth's story. “If you can write it whenever you like, then you can write it now too, can't you?” There was no escaping the situation with some stock line like Why should I have to? Bismuth was a storyteller, and a storyteller was a person who tells stories, and if a person who tells stories holds out, refusing to tell one, then what, in the end, are they supposed to become? “Right here, right now, show me the sight of you writing your story.” What was more, Bismuth held an unshakable faith in her own self. She believed that she was merely busy for the moment, and that the instant she put her mind to it, the instant she resolved on it, she could begin Bismuth's story whenever she pleased. And so Bismuth turned her back on Polaris. She conspicuously summoned forth and began to handle the symbols she would write into the very first page of the book. “There's no need for anything elaborate.” From behind her comes Polaris's irksome voice. “Right now, your story — please, just write it, with the very simplest form to it.” “…a greedy busybody. One who picks groundless quarrels.” Bismuth muttered. From the bandage-covered eyes, a black, sticky fluid — clumps of indignant clay — began to ooze and well up. Those who had sunk into the mire of the deepest abyss made a ghastly sound, clacking their teeth made of bone-shards. “Once I've written my story, I'll punish you. I'll give you a thorough scolding…” And so Bismuth wrote out her story for the moment — an opening line for which a single, very simple sentence ought to suffice. Bismuth is writing her own story. But if a character performs an action, surely one must by all rights explain what kind of action it is? If they speak, what they say; if they go somewhere, where that is; if they write a story, what it is about. And so Bismuth duly corrected the sentence and added a few components. Bismuth is writing her own story of writing her own story. Something still felt hollow. If the Bismuth that Bismuth is writing is again writing a story, what kind of story is that story? And so Bismuth duly corrected the sentence and added a few components. Bismuth is writing her own story of writing her own story of writing her own story. And so Bismuth duly corrected the sentence and added a few components. Bismuth is writing her own story of writing her own story of writing her own story of writing her own story. And so Bismuth duly corrected the sentence… * …and added a few components. Bismuth is writing her own story of writing… * …her own story. This first sentence does not end. At some point it must, of its own exhaustion, be set down. But if it is set down, the sentence is not formed. The writing does not begin. Writing with no first character, no first action, no first sentence is not writing. It is not a story. Then is Bismuth's story not a story? “Why?” Bismuth cried out in bewilderment. “Why?” Of course, one might resort to a little trick regarding the vantage of narration. Beginning from some point in the past, for instance. But in the end, the story of none other than myself cannot forever flounder about within memory. The moment the narration of the story catches up to the vantage of the present, the three tiers of Bismuth — the Bismuth writing the story, the Bismuth within the story, and the Bismuth beholding the story — cannot all remain a single, consistent subject possessed of simultaneity. “I told you, didn't I? That I would teach you the way to write your story.” Polaris's voice, now more assured, drew Bismuth up out of her sleepwalk of infinite regress. At the same time, Bismuth felt the presence of the other gradually fading. “I shall give you time, so please — think it over carefully.”
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main6_Short: A stranger with no shadow offers the one thing she cannot give herself — a way out of the sentence that will not end. What is a storyteller who can no longer tell her own story?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main7_Content_0:
“I've thought about it.”
“…it's the sort of thing you have to take time over.”
“I don't need it.”
There really are a great many things Bismuth doesn't need. Perhaps that's why — standing before Polaris, who had turned to leave only to halt and stand stock-still — she rummages through her bosom, draws something out, and holds it forth. A sheet of yellow, crisp paper. Is she palming off some scrap of rubbish for the other to dispose of along the way?
“What is this?”
“A manuscript.”
And with that, Bismuth took into her own hand a thing exactly like the one she had handed Polaris. With one hand she then pointed back and forth between the other and herself.
“We read this, the two of us. It'll be fun!”
What more was there to say to that? Polaris, thinking she might at least turn back a page to see just what this manuscript was. The inner leaves held a transcript of a play in which two characters appear. The names of those two were, of course—
“What in the world is this…”
“Go on, read it for me.”
Polaris let out a sigh. Then she looked at the thing in her hand. At last she cleared her throat — taking it, in her way, as a task — and parted her lips to read the first line.

    Polaris — I seek to merge dream and reality.

The instant she read the first character's first line, Polaris's eyes went wide and slack. The sound of her immersion shattering seems to ring out across the barrier between dream and manuscript, thin as an eggshell. The chief cause is the shock of realizing that Bismuth may already know her plans for what is to come. But gradually Polaris's expression settles.
Just as she herself had read the various traces left in the dream world to discern Bismuth's state, there was no rule saying Bismuth could not, in turn, have discerned Polaris's plan in some such way. Besides, she might have caught wind of the plan of the already-renowned Guide of Dreams by hearsay elsewhere. Realizing as much, Polaris gradually composes herself and waits upon Bismuth's words.

    Bismuth — Not that. Keep explaining the method of story.
    Bismuth — Not what you're trying to do — explain the way that Bismuth can write Bismuth's story.

Bismuth, thoroughly absorbed in the manuscript. Polaris seeks out the passage where her own next line comes — a place that, for some reason, has already been emphasized by someone — and reads.

    Polaris — <u>It becomes a problem because you keep dwelling only within your own story and trying to be its protagonist.</u>
    Polaris — <u>Have you no thought of becoming a character — nay, the protagonist — of a greater story that saves two worlds?</u>

Polaris turns to the manuscript's next page, mutters under her breath at the line of hers that follows, and then suddenly stops. A troubled look. She lifts her gaze from the manuscript she had been poring over, nose buried in it, brows knit. The emotion laid bare is plain. The look of one who cannot believe what she is doing right now. Strong revulsion. Strength enters the hand gripping the manuscript and the manuscript crumples. At last she closes the manuscript.

    Bismuth — You've already got it all memorized?

“Let us stop this.”
Polaris said.
“What is it you keep reading aloud?”

Bismuth nods, looking at the manuscript. As though every line were already written there in advance, not a syllable out of place. And indeed it is so. Polaris sighs at the sight. Heedless, Bismuth speaks her line.

    Bismuth — So with that, then, Bismuth will be able to write Bismuth's story?

“Yes.”
Polaris, though she shuddered, gave the answer she had to give.
“The self within my story, the self within my story who writes that story of mine, endlessly reduced back to the story of mine that, in the end, I must write again… it becomes a problem because you insist on clinging to such a thing, does it not?”
She barely managed to coax her tongue, lost in the maze of the story, back into place.
“If you become not merely the protagonist of your own story but the protagonist of a greater story — a protagonist who plays an active part among more characters and events — a way out will arise of its own accord. For you can look upon yourself through other eyes, and instead of summoning yourself directly from your own vantage, you can write the reactions of others to you.”

    Bismuth — <u><s>Falls into long thought.</s></u> Answers.

“Mm, that's enough, I've heard it all—”
Bismuth began. But why is it that the rest already seems known?
“—I don't need it!”
“And what do you intend to do about writing your story?”
But this time Polaris is not one to back off so meekly. She has even gone along with this, this game lower than a child's playing house, manuscript in hand.
“You mean to just give up like that? Does it not grieve you, that as a storyteller you cannot write a story, that you cannot become the protagonist within it?”
“I've decided not to do that.”
Bismuth said.
“Now that I think about it, it seems too greedy.”
“What does?”
“Bismuth becoming the protagonist… writing that kind of story.”
Polaris gazed at Bismuth, who lifted her chin and threw out her chest as though she had made some momentous resolution.
“And so Bismuth has decided not to write a story that has a protagonist!”
The brows of the Polaris who heard this coiled, twitching, into an uneasy shape. Could Bismuth mean those words in earnest? It did not sound that way in the least. Surely it was just hollow babble, mouthed without conviction to wriggle out of the rebuttal at hand.
Is that what you think, Polaris?
“You're being unreasonable.”
“It isn't unreasonable.”
Bismuth said.
“Bismuth, too, used to think that a story had to have a protagonist, and so it had to be a story in which Bismuth was the protagonist… But a story with no protagonist is better.”
The symbols floating in the air began to line up after Bismuth's words. Five-colored people and the events they wrought began to depict the disparities that exist in some events and not in others. One person could share in the pain of all the world with but a single tear, while another might suffer a smashed nose and a broken arm and yet purchase not so much as a penny of cheap pity from the one or two people before them, let alone all the world. Even the protagonist who brought all of it about cannot be called wholly happy, either — did we not look together upon the stories of the king, the philosopher, the general, the queen, the gatekeeper? Did we not learn how much upheaval the obstinacy and greed of protagonists stir up among those around them?
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main7_Content_1:
“One person's sulking becoming sadder than the deaths of everyone else; everyone's desperate, all-out struggle counting for less than one other person's pouting lips; and that, to overcome it, they themselves can do nothing at all… that is what a story with a protagonist is. Bismuth is going to do away with such things.”
“Hmm.”
The groan Bismuth first let out is now the one Polaris is letting out. It is closer, though, to a cold snort than to muttering under one's breath.
“How very glib. Perhaps you ought to have shared that view with the mouse earlier, as well?”
“What's 'amousearlier'?”
Polaris fell silent.
“Anyway, so — I don't need that. I don't need to become a protagonist!”
Bismuth said brightly.
“Bismuth's story has no need of a protagonist.”
“Setting aside the fact that it does not seem you would meekly step down from the protagonist's seat at all…”
Polaris went on, not slackening the reins of her suspicion.
“Once the world is saved, many will naturally come to your story. They'll come gladly, to hear that story, to become a part of it. Do you mean to give that up too?—”
Bismuth felt the whites of Polaris's eyes slide sidelong toward her.
“—and entrust it all to the irresponsible scheme of writing some story with no protagonist?”
Hearing that, Bismuth laughed. She laughed clutching her belly.
She laughed as if her waist would snap, as if the corners of her mouth would stretch back behind her ears.
She laughed and laughed in fits, gasping for breath, as if there had never been anything so funny in all the world.
“Bismuth will not write 'some' story.”
“If things go as Bismuth means them to, people will, in any case, have no choice but to hear Bismuth's story.”
So pressing was her urgency that Bismuth's several voices all came rushing out at once, in their stocking feet — borne on that sole yearning to point out Polaris's mistaken words.

“Bismuth will not become Bismuth's story. Bismuth will become story itself.”
“Bismuth will not be the Bismuth of any one place or time. Bismuth will make every place and every time into Bismuth.”
Before she knew it the manuscript was gone. Gone from everywhere. Everything before Bismuth and everything after — these, Bismuth declares, are mere characters, and props shoved and cleared away with a crash and a rumble each time the curtain falls, then dragged up again, and bit-players who wet their throats during the interlude. Their world is the manuscript itself, and the set of arbitrary symbols granted a temporary meaning within the manuscript is their very identity. Our very identity.
“Bismuth has heard all that people say about the Rapids.”
Polaris saw Bismuth tap-tapping at the rim of her own ear. Each time the curve of the ear trembled, notes of pure silver lined up along a staff of gold. From Bismuth's body an endless prelude was pouring forth. The true performance has not yet begun. On the day the whole and undivided Power of Dreams returns to its rightful master, the theater will never close its doors and the lights will never go out. Everywhere becomes a stage; everywhere becomes a seating gallery with no interlude, no lounge, no exit.
“Bismuth will go to the end of the dream and become a dream. Bismuth will become every story there.”
“The Bismuth who has become a dream will now become the outside.”
“Bismuth will not become any one story. Bismuth will become story. Bismuth will not write the story of the world. Bismuth will become the world.”

{IMAGE}
Polaris's face contorted. The only one who could see at once what Bismuth was saying now — and, beyond that, what promise she was casting upon herself (themselves) and upon the world — was Polaris alone. Past the outward look of a brat with a grubby bandage wound over her eyes and a great book in tow, and past the content of nothing but babble wholly unmoored from reality, she could see laid bare the inside of a Bismuth who drew ever nearer to the essence of dreams, to the power of the dreaming, awaiting only the moment to wield that authority to the full, after the nature of a storyteller. The Grasshopper Prince, the cicada who rode the clouds, Princess Spark… along every one of those names, roles enough for every single person in reality to sit in one apiece, and more besides, had been made ready long ago.
“For Bismuth become story, Bismuth become the world, every story is now Bismuth's story. Whatever is written or drawn or sung is Bismuth's voice.”
Bismuth began to warble like a nightingale.
“And in such a world, a greedy thing who tries to become a protagonist who alone saves the world, a wicked witch who lures other characters in with talk of sharing out that seat—”
When Bismuth laughed, the sky, the ground, the whole region rippling after her thoughts laughed together. They became the wrinkled lips and white teeth and surging tongues surrounding Polaris, and laughed. Bismuth's ten million fingers all at once pointed at her.
“—I don't need.”
