ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main8_Content_0:
A village that has become part of a dream. Once there were other people, and beyond the village's bounds there were other villages, the lord's castle, the rivers and mountain ranges drawn on maps. In that same place now only a boundless precipice yawns open. Now, there, there is Bismuth. There is Bismuth and her friends, Bismuth and her Grasshopper Prince.
“Now you're the new Grasshopper Prince!”
Bismuth said. Wearing a pretty crown woven of blades of grass and wildflowers, the prince looked around himself in bewilderment. The village looked different. Very different. Different enough that he did not want to open his closed eyes again.
“The Grasshopper Prince…?”
“It's the seat for making stories together with Bismuth — here!”
Bismuth held out her hand. From every line and whorl of her palm and fingerprints hung glistening beads of sweat — no, husks of story. Each time she swung the flail and brought it down, thwack, thwack, the well-ripened grains of story scattered, shimmering.
“What do you want to do?”
Bismuth asked. The all-colored light she gave off was enough to hurt the eyes.
“What's your wish? What do you want to see, what story do you want to tell? Just say the word! Of course — whatever it may be!”
“You'll grant whatever I say?”

Slowly, the Grasshopper Prince realized that, even before he could ask his question, Bismuth had already answered it. So that meant she would grant it. Whatever it might be. The prince gazed quietly down at Bismuth — no, at the child who called herself Bismuth. Her real name… at least the name people had called her by, the Grasshopper Prince still remembered.
“Is there nothing you want for yourself? Lyd—”
“Bismuth is doing plenty of what she wants to do right now.”
With a smile thin as a closely-pared fingernail, Bismuth laughed.
“Shaping the stories of Grasshopper Princes like this — that's what Bismuth wants to do.”
“I don't mean doing for others what they want done instead.”
When the prince shook his head, the crown set upon it rang with the sound of lily-of-the-valley, tinkling and chiming.
“Isn't there something you yourself want to do, apart from that?”
“No, there isn't.”
Bismuth does not hesitate. She does not deliberate. Every answer is decided even before the question is put. Rather, only a question so decided can be put at all. That, by all rights, is the catechism of a storyteller. But a storyteller, too, can sometimes fall silent.
Like the Bismuth after she gave that answer.

“If there's nothing you want to do, then was there nothing you wanted to do?”
At the Grasshopper Prince's question, the silent Bismuth thought. Something seemed about to surface. Not others, not some other story, but “something you yourself had wanted to do.”
“Honey…”
The clouds in the sky shifted shape with the sound of wind. Honeycombs, hanging in clusters like ripe bunches of bananas, swayed as though they might snap at any moment, unable to bear the weight of the rich honey. The long-trailing waterfall of honey plunged down into the village, and the instant its sticky sweetness embraced everyone's eyes and noses and mouths and ears, this too, in the end, was no different at all from the countless stories Bismuth had presented before…
“…milk with honey in it — that was my favorite!”
“Then do just that.”
Bismuth was holding a small earthenware cup. Inside it was exactly what she had said: a luxurious drink made by dipping a knitted cloth thoroughly in honey, lifting it out, and stirring it into the milk just so, letting the sweetness soak into every corner of it. At the smell of it, gooseflesh rose along Bismuth's forearms.
“What about you, Grasshopper Prince?”
“This is enough for me.”
The prince said.
“It's enough that you got to do what you wanted to do… I'll make this my Grasshopper Prince.”
And so, pillowing his head on a stone and pulling a blanket of earth over himself, the prince closed his eyes. Now all that remains is Bismuth, holding the milk with honey.

{IMAGE}
Have you ever seen a little child holding a cup with their very favorite thing inside it? Seen the graceful, the most elegant motion of the hand — the index through ring finger curled around the handle, the thumb and little finger each extended to brace the rim and the bottom of the cup?
If there is even a moment to spare for that.
There is only both hands brought together to grip the very middle of the cup hard enough to crush it. And then to bring it to the mouth and tip it until its bottom faces the sky. While a white milk-mustache is etched onto the upper lip, the peculiar tartness not wholly strained out of the honey, together with a faint floral scent, spreads all around — and that sight, though it lasts but an instant, is for the child who drank it a memory etched forever.
The cup, its bottom now bared, Bismuth sent back to the story before the story. Then she licked clean every trace left around her mouth, not leaving a drop. It was a taste that drew a smile of its own accord. Patting her belly, swollen taut and full, she sat down where she was. She stretched. She yawned. And then her head began to nod, and nod again. Even breathing followed. At last Bismuth drew Bismuth over herself. Pages warm as a cotton quilt wrapped snugly around the child with the bandage wound about her face.
After that, for a long while, and forever after, nothing happened in the village.
No birdsong came falling down, no clapping of hands filled the sky, no bodiless legs went scurrying across the middle of the village in search of a new owner. There was only everyone's belly rising and falling alike, following the soft, even sound of Bismuth's breathing. Only the lips of the soundly sleeping Bismuth stirring, murmuring babble in her sleep.
Bismuth and all her friends — sleep well!
ui.TravelerStory_Bismuth_Main8_Short: Asked at last what she ever wanted for herself, she remembers something small and warm and entirely her own. When the storyteller lies down to rest, what does the world she dreamed become?

Yet even that final page is never truly completed.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main1_Content_0:
The cold seizes, the cold lulls to sleep, the cold shall wake the eyes anew. An apostate stirred awake in the back of a remote cell. When he braced a hand against the floor, the smooth, hairless skin peculiar to toothed-whale beastfolk crept and bristled. It was the work of the frost that had stained the cell on every side. A sight to make the body shudder on its own.
And this — though the bottomless cold was pouring, in truth, out of the apostate himself.
“…It hurts.”
He said it in a low, heavy voice. He drew the hand back from the floor as if to clutch his head, but at once the Stocks and Shackles, bound joint by joint, yanked savagely at his limbs. Thick as his hide was, mountainous as his bulk was, it made no difference. He wanted to tuck both hands under his arms like a child and shiver. He wanted to bury his face against his chest and grieve.
“…I'm cold. It hurts.”
If this counted as pain, how bitter must it have been for all those who had been forced to close their eyes? Still more for those who had to be slaughtered by an Enforcer of the Lucid Sect — mercilessly, and, in truth, innocent? The thought came to him in the end: that he had no right to it. Cetus — once the harshest lesson the Lucid Sect had to teach, now fallen to a test subject and an apostate — clenched his teeth.
He had likely worn much the same expression the day he first grasped the truth of the Sect.

When the Rapids opened all across the continent and it was proven, after all, that the dream-world truly existed, he was awed that his faith had taken a shape outsiders could understand — and at the same time sank into deep worry. If the savage dream-beasts were ever loosed into reality, the innocent would suffer terribly. As Enforcers, he and his comrades pooled their resolve and put a petition before the Dream Judges: that rather than seize the moment to spread the Sect's influence, they should first rein in the believers so none of them acted rashly; and that rather than lecture the people caught up in a calamity they could not comprehend, they should first help them in every way, in body and in means.
“The time has not yet come.”
But those were the words that came from the mouth of the Grand Dream Mage — the foremost authority of the Lucid Sect, the one said to receive the oracles of the almighty Primus directly. Cetus and the Enforcers with him could not defy that one's word. They could not so much as harbor a doubt. It was not that doubt was profane, or rude — it was simply impossible. So they waited.
They waited in silence until the world had suffered enough.
The more people came to fear the power of dreams — the more there were who painfully turned over the memory of family and friends struck down by dream-beasts — the more flocked to the Sect. People who once would have driven Lucid's missionaries off with a beating now raced one another to the meeting halls. They begged to be taken in, swearing they would gladly offer wealth heaped like mountains and an unshakable devotion. The Sect, in its mercy, took them in and cared for them.
Having watched, all the while, the power of dreams spread unchecked.
Having left untouched the places where passages into the Rapids were likely to open.
Having sent the Enforcers out against the outsiders who had gathered, in the early days, to set things right — charging them with 'the sin of defying Primus's will,' 'the sin of recklessly disturbing the dream-world,' and the like.
Cetus's heart began to waver.

“Let us return to a pure faith.”
That was the second course he and the other Enforcers chose. In truth, though, it was a retreat — a flight more regressed than the attempt before it.
“Let us pray to Primus. That his true oracle might at last descend upon us…”
The Sect spoke lies. That much was certain. But where did the lie begin? That the Grand Dream Mage received Primus's oracles directly — was that the lie? That the believers of old could converse with Primus freely, at will — was that the lie? Kneeling with his head bowed could not shake such questions loose. However devout, it amounted to nothing but an abuse he inflicted on his own mind. And so, inevitably, a third course appeared.
Once persuading the leadership and clinging to faith had both been denied him, the only road left was to do what he himself could do, and to hope it might change the world little by little. Soon a strange spectacle unfolded all across the continent: Enforcers of the Lucid Sect coming into conflict with missionaries of the Lucid Sect. Word spread of a handful of Enforcers who would gladly offer protection from the dream-beasts even to places that flew a different banner and raised a different symbol of faith. They naively believed their sincerity would one day be accepted — but the moment such reform-dreamers become the worst thorn in the eye is not when they are childish or shortsighted.
It is when they break their very bones in earnest to right the wrongs of the organization they themselves belong to.

“Apostate Cetus, hear this.”
The Usher reading the proclamation — the one granted the authority to draw his own map of dreams — clucked his tongue, as if genuinely sorry.
“Now that the dream-world has at last revealed itself before the unbelievers, in so grave and critical an hour, to have beguiled fellow Enforcers and organized seditious activity…”
He would have liked to say that every one of those words was still vivid to him — but it was not so. He would have liked to claim that before the loyalist Enforcers who came to take him, he had bellowed some heart-kindling speech about what was right and what was wrong — but that was not how it went. Emptily, Cetus stood still and accepted every charge and every fetter, and let them be clapped on. Had he flared up and thrashed about, it would at least have felt like relief. It is an easy thing to brand the Sect as corrupt beyond saving and set to force. But then what does that make him — him who, until that very day, had obediently done the bidding of those 'corrupt beyond saving'?
Had all the apostates and unbelievers and criminals who, in his days as an Enforcer, had knelt before him — who had twisted their words back and forth, who had lost their heads — truly carried sin enough to deserve it?
“…I'm cold.”
The present Cetus — fallen from the Lucid Sect's most promising Enforcer to nothing more than a beast of penance — bit his tongue. Even in the spit that spilled from his mouth, grains of ice crunched and crackled. He believed that coming to bear this cold had itself been part of the penance he offered of himself. He wanted to believe it.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main1_Content_1:
There were many ways the Sect spent the lives of those it had judged undesirable. The experiments that injected the power of dreams were only one of them. Though the lives of the test subjects destroyed in the process were, of course, only ever given once.
Locked in his cell, Cetus asked to become, willingly, a vessel for that power of dreams. Dragged in by force, deceived, framed for crimes they never committed — in place of those who would be ground to pulp by the power of dreams for such reasons, he resolved to endure, for a time, every procedure that was required. This served the Sect as well. It gave them a story to hold up to the world: the penance of a wayward apostate.
On the day he first exposed his whole body to the power of dreams — endlessly gathered, filtered, and warped — Cetus regretted his rash choice more than a thousand times over. That alien force hauled his body this way and that, dug through it, then trampled it to a sodden mass and flung it aside like a toy it had lost interest in. When that had repeated enough times, some pattern of response, some force found nowhere in reality, came to dwell in his flesh forever. The cold he could not shake off was the most pronounced of those forces. His body adapted in a strange way: the flashes of agony, sharp as living flesh being carved away, faded, and in their place there remained only a chronic suffering, like a chill that would not pass.
“This, at least, is how I'll do my penance.”
The great bulk sprawled carelessly across the cell floor spoke.
“Be experimented on, be watched for how I heal and adapt, be experimented on again… and then one day, when I can't take any more—”
The tongue, standing at a cliff's edge, stopped. In his mind he was staring down into a bottomless chasm. A final full stop set by self-sacrifice through death. But would that be penance done properly? Could the death of one man wash away the weight of sin he had piled up as an Enforcer until now?
“And yet it's the only penance I can offer.”
Cetus said. From between teeth white as salt, a blizzard whiter still came pouring out.
“Even if it falls hopelessly short, there's nothing else for it…”
His black, glistening skin — were it not for the frost clinging along its surface — could not have been told apart from the darkness behind closed eyes. When Cetus shut his mouth, a silence that was, quite literally, like death settled over the place.
But it seemed someone was still thinking of him.

“Get up!”
The voice was not pressing him or barking an order — it was calling to him. Calling in a frantic rush, as if afraid of being overheard. Cetus opened his eyes and jerked his head up before he knew it. It was a fellow Enforcer, a familiar face. Behind him, he could see the cell door standing ajar.
“How did you get in here…?”
“There's no time to talk, brother.”
He strode over and went to lift Cetus up, then winced. There were any number of reasons. The stench inside the cell; the cold that gripped Cetus's body and would not let go; the enormous frame slumped limp, its will to live gone, clad in Stocks and Shackles bound with magic too intricate to undo on the spot… Cetus stared blankly into his comrade's eyes.
“What is it you want me to do…?”
“Oh for — damn it! Just keep quiet and follow me!”
Cetus's eyes went round. The man before him was mild by nature, and Enforcers could hardly use coarse language in ordinary times anyway, so that such words came out of him at all was hard to imagine.
“Do I have to spell it all out? We're doing this to get you out, brother! And it's not just me in on it—”
“Why would you do such a thing?”
“Don't you worry about us!”
From the end of the corridor, another fellow Enforcer — who for some reason had taken the seat where a guard should have been sitting — came over.
“We'll just say you smashed everything to pieces with that monstrous body of yours and broke out!”
“I — I have no right to—”
Held up by several Enforcers, he finally began to move. Limping, but one step, then another, he left the cell he had believed he would never walk out of on his own — and soon the whole detention block behind him. He knew the layout from here by heart. A few more doors, a few more corridors, and he would be outside.
Free.

“I have to make my penance—”
“You think we're doing all this so you can swan off and gad about having fun?”
Another Enforcer snapped at him sullenly. When he threw back a lay believer's robe — part of the disguise he must have worn to get in — the first thing to greet Cetus was a pair of sulky, jutting lips.
“You close your eyes here and it's over — penance, all of it, just finished. Nothing changes, ever, and that's the end.”
“You won't even leave a headstone behind.”
“Who's going to remember an apostate's name? Even we scattered to the winds the moment they locked you up, and only just managed to gather again.”
The Enforcers pressed in around Cetus, all but dragging his great bulk along as they added word after word.
“So if you've got any sense, knock each of us out cold right now, one good blow apiece—”
A brief silence fell. Every gaze passed, one by one, over Cetus's brutish fists, shaped like frozen siege-hammers.
“…go easy, just make it look real. Then smash up a few doors and walls, get out, and — whatever, lie low and help people, or preach the true faith, just do something.”
“Live — and prove that you, that we, weren't wrong…”
Carrying out an escape at that broken, halting pace while trading such talk was hardly a good way to make the time fly — but it was, at least, the only way. Through doors and corridors, corridors and doors, doors and doors and corridors and corridors — each as dangerous as the last, each seeming to hide an ambush, every one of them setting the hair on his neck on end — until at last they came upon the place that led outside.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main1_Content_2: “Oh, here — take this.” He hadn't even known there was still anything like a pocket left in his clothes, but a crumpled, folded note settled neatly into it. “What is this…?” “There's somewhere you can lie low for a while once you're out, and so on. Be careful!” That rough hand patting Cetus's shoulder, which stood about level with the top of the man's head. Meanwhile the last door drew nearer and nearer. Open it, and beyond lay a wide courtyard. There was nowhere to hide there, and the surroundings were strewn with watchtowers and other tall structures — but once past it, the forest grew thick and dense at once, making it the ideal place to disappear into. There were several seeds of the tragedy. They were spent from hauling Cetus along. So they had no spare moment to think. Up to now the escape plan had slotted together without a hitch, so they had let their guard down. With no danger immediately in sight, they had set their minds at ease. Cetus, though, was different. His instincts, far keener than a human's, sent up a warning — accurate, but at the same time too late. “So you've come at last?” The owner of that languid voice was the Usher — the very one who had ordered Cetus's arrest. Archers under his direct command packed the watchtowers; warriors gripping swords and axes filled the courtyard wall to wall. In the midst of a procession of torches blazing fiercely enough to make one forget the night sky, the Usher shrugged and gestured at his subordinates. “If you hadn't come, I was worried I'd be the only villain — the one who'd disturbed the rest of all these dear brothers and sisters.” He made a gesture, and what would happen was plain as day. With no reason at all to draw it out over any passage of time. Cetus watched the comrades who had helped him be made into beehives. So many arrow-fletchings rained down in driving sheets that it looked as if someone had swung a feather pillow open and started a game with it. Arrows, arrowheads — punched out through their backs, torn clean through flesh, halted inside against bone or thick muscle, bent or snapped along the way — arrows and arrowheads. Beyond counting. It was too quick even to be horrified, even to mourn. Cetus, not a single wound on his body, gazed blankly up at the Usher. The warriors closed in on him by degrees. He saw now that more of them held throwing-spears and tough snares than swords and axes. So I'm still of use, then. Cetus thought. Whereas the fellow Enforcers, who already held no trace of the warmth of life… At this he could not hold back a hollow laugh. There was one more thing he decided not to hold back. Cetus raised both arms in threat. Two, four, more than eight thick, massive forearms answered him and shot up in a flash. The warriors ringing him and the archers in the towers, however, showed no reaction at all. In truth, they had not even noticed that he had raised his arms. For those arms were not his body to begin with — they were unseen arms, arms that were not there. And Cetus realized, all at once, that the cold which never left his side had been under his command from the very start. The raised arms came smashing down in an instant. {IMAGE} The cold seizes — a wave of ice spread out in a fan and cast dozens of living statues. The cold lulls to sleep — before a single bowstring could be loosed, a blizzard came howling in. The archers, their feet treading empty air and the backs of their heads and spines braced against the wall behind them, lost consciousness in an instant. The cold shall wake the eyes anew — Cetus faced the disabled men, his eyes blazing fierce. Now all he needed was a single step, a single swing of his fist. After that, everything that had to happen would unfold as it should. He had only to give himself over to the fury racing through his whole body and rampage at whatever came. So that was what he meant to do… had the note not flickered, just then, into his mind — the note his comrade, no, his 'friend,' now gone, had tucked into his pocket. Go out and show them you were right Such mirror-reversed writing — the ink, not yet dry, scrawled on impulse after the main message had been written out, had bled through to the back of the paper. Cetus fell into thought for a moment. Then he saw it: the dazzling wave that had reached out from his own body was devouring not only the enemies but his friends' corpses too, whatever it touched. He hastily drew the cold back and shut it away inside himself. He could not tell whether the alien sensation gnawing into his very bones was his own cold, which he could never grow used to, or guilt. Perhaps he did not wish to tell the two apart. “The Usher… turned tail and fled, did he.” Cetus, his friends' corpses slung across his shoulders, growled. And he moved with care. He took pains not to accidentally shatter the warriors trapped in the ice, their eyes alone left blinking and wide. He crossed the courtyard like that and was about to leave outright when he stopped short, turned, and faced the ruin he had left behind. For a very long time, in silence — letting the blood that ran from his friends' bodies trail down his brow and jaw like a long tattoo, until it froze over white. “I am no longer an Enforcer of Lucid.” He opened his mouth. “The life I lived to inflict pain on others is over. From now on I will set things right, and save, and make amends.” Cetus packed the cold, straining to spread again, deep down inside his own body, and clenched his teeth. He was cold, and it hurt. But it was the right thing. “Never — never again must this happen.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main1_Short: He turns his back on everything he believed — yet the cold he was made to carry will not let him go. Whose hand was it that left the door open?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main2_Content_0:
He had been raised in the Sect from childhood. The first word he learned was 'Primus'; the first phrase he ever spoke was 'the almighty dream-god Primus.' Attach any matching predicate to it, and it became, just so, a complete sentence. He had bolted from that Sect. An apostate who had forsaken his faith, he was now a fugitive from prison as well. There was no place that would call such a Cetus its own. But there was everywhere to go. Like fire leaping from one thing to the next, the power of dreams ran rampant everywhere. Whether or not the beasts that condensed from that force crossed over, it was enough to torment the people nearby. Cetus wandered such places. He sought out the people who suffered from the power of dreams, and helped them.
The village where he was staying now was one of the places he had come upon that way.
“Hold the line. Keep holding.”
Cetus's resolute voice swept through the villagers. They strained until their faces went crimson, makeshift spears thrust out before them. The moment you noticed a cool air soothing your beaded sweat, brushing your cheek — that was no time to let your guard down. It meant that the stern drillmaster who, for whatever reason, always carried fine frost-crystals around him — Cetus — was standing right beside you.
“Always be conscious of putting your whole body's weight into it,”
Cetus said. With each step he took, the great Shackles clanked like bells forged from a mountain range.
“Put the strain only into your forearms, your wrists, your shoulders, and you'll lose the stance in no time… Third row.”
Not just the third row, but the people in front of and behind them — in fact the whole formation — startled as though a switch had touched their backsides. The entire line flinched and folded in on itself like one great flower. They might have grown somewhat used to the look of him — a toothed-whale beastfolk of a size you'd be hard pressed to see anywhere, and clad in those grim Stocks you wanted to ask about but never truly wanted the answer to — but that low, overbearing voice chilled them to the core every time they heard it.

“Hold the formation. You must not forget—”
The words that came after were already branded, like a red-hot iron, into the villagers' minds: break the formation and you die. Lower your spear-point and you die. Turn your back and flee, and you die the hardest, surest death of all. Hold the formation for dear life, never break from the line, and then build the stamina and the staying power to endure — only then does even a sliver of a chance to live appear.
“—that all of you…”
Cetus's gaze, sweeping over the whole formation again and again, suddenly stopped at one spot. Sensing something off about a particular someone in the front row, he scanned to either side and behind, searching for the someone who was supposed to be there.
“De— … Front row, number three.”
He had started to call a familiar name, then corrected himself. Referring by number to people whose names he'd exchanged over his whole stay felt thoroughly awkward, but it was not a choice Cetus relished either. These people would have to take up arms and fight — not after the autumn harvest was in, not after the child they loved more than their own eyes had grown up. It could be next week. It could be tomorrow. To drill into them, in so short a time, the discipline to stand against the dream-beasts, there was no other way.
“And fourth row, number six. Why have you switched places?”
“'Cause that fellow said he was scared.”
The farmer who had taken the front-row spot in his stead answered with a shrug.
“I'm all right with it, see. Ever since I was a boy folk've told me my nerve's something special.”
Cetus fell briefly into thought. But it would not do. What a soldier needs is not some unmeasurable variable like a thicker nerve than the next man's, but experience and skill. There was a reason the formation was arranged the way it was. Put plainly, the man now standing in the front line in his friend's place was someone who should never have been put in the front line at all.
“I can't allow it. Both of you, return to your proper places.”
The words sounded too harsh even to Cetus himself. Watching the two of them deflate a little pricked his conscience. And was it not true, after all? He was no general — not even a military strategist. What expertise had a man who'd spent his whole life as an Enforcer in the Sect suddenly contrived, that he should appoint himself drillmaster among farmers? And yet, inwardly, he knew. He was coming to realize, little by little, that the disciplines he had labored to learn and master during his time in the Lucid Sect had in fact been far from any path of pure faith — that they were closer to military training.
Take, for instance, the knack of marshaling believers into ranks. Form them up in columns, not rows; thicken the files, not the lines. Above all, station the seasoned ones chiefly at the very front and rear of each lateral line, and fill the space between with the unskilled. In his Sect days he'd simply followed it, assuming that was just doctrine — but teaching the villagers how to fight, treating the believer as a foot soldier and the rank as a battle formation, he understood it far better. It was meant to keep raw soldiers from taking fright and breaking from the line. A formation that made veterans into walls at the front and back. You could not call that bad in itself. It was a means of protecting oneself on the battlefield.
But what reason was there for the Sect, in times of peace, to keep up such teachings at all?
As if they had known early on that the world would fall into chaos as the rifts into the Rapids began to open, one by one. As if, perhaps, it was the very thing they had longed for. As if they had set their minds on putting forward a private army readied in advance, on a vast scale, to bring the chaos swiftly under control and swell the Sect's reach.
…He was in the middle of a drill. This was no time to sink into self-reproach.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main2_Content_1: “We'll rest a moment.” At Cetus's word the villagers set down what they held, one by one, and breathed relief. As they all flopped down on their backsides, little mirage-like shimmers spread out in every direction at once — the shape made by sweat that had poured down like waterfalls, soaking their chins, their necks, their collars. Cetus watched them with something like pride, yet he did not let his guard slack. Looking at the truth of the long things the weary people had let go of — the 'makeshift spears' — he had all the more reason not to. Only a few were fit to serve as proper weapons; the rest were farm tools rigged up in haste, with blades driven into their ends. Until the dream-beasts began to plague it, that was the sort of village it had been. A place far from any royal seat or noble house's crest. They simply tilled and dug what they were given, and lived. If, of all places, a rift into dreams had opened near a spot that only now and then drove off the odd bandit or vagrant who wandered through, they could only be helpless before the mighty dream-beasts. Leaving aside, of course, whether 'of all places' was truly the right way to put it. “Have any of Lucid's missionaries come again since that day?” Cetus asked the people savoring their honey-sweet rest. No, none, haven't seen hide nor hair of them… and so on — scattered but trustworthy answers came back. The truth was, that was the very reason Cetus had decided to stay a while when he first set foot in the village. “Those people mean to tame you.” Back then the people were more taken with Cetus's appearance than with his name or his ideas. A mountainous toothed-whale beastfolk, clapped in fetters and Shackles as though he'd committed some heinous crime. And on top of that, the fiery tirades he'd suddenly spring to his feet and pour out, even when they'd said something perfectly ordinary by their own reckoning. Not exactly a first impression that made you want to share a meal with him. “But isn't the Sect the very place that handles the power of dreams?” the villagers had asked back, at the time. “They said it would affect us before long, and that's just what happened.” “Footprints we'd never seen before appeared — strange claws tore up all the fences and the ground.” “Even now we ought to go and ask them to protect us—” “Their words are riddled through with lies. You mustn't be taken in.” After that, Cetus made his appeal by showing them his strength — not only the strength of bone and flesh, but how to use the 'power' he had honed since escaping the Sect. He insisted, again and again, that he would help with all his might at the front, that he would train them, that there was a path by which the people could defend their own village and owe nothing to anyone. He explained the harms of the Lucid Sect in detail, too… It was never enough, but ironically, from that day on, whenever a similar question loomed he would cut himself short or change the subject entirely. The more he spoke in detail of the Sect's true designs, the more Cetus knew — the last question that must never be asked, the one risen to the back of their throats, showing in their eyes, dangling from the tip of their tongues. “How do you know the Lucid Sect's doings so well?” “I was once one of them.” How fine it would be if the explanation could end so harmlessly! He had not been a mere member. He was not the hammer that was swung but the hand that gripped it; not the cleat on the stamping hoof but the craftsman who had driven that cleat in and tended it with care. Many of the things Cetus only now understood were, when he thought about it, practices that had not changed in the slightest from long ago. To claim that the pure Sect's corruption had begun the moment the rifts were observed would be the conduct of the most brazen-faced creature the world had ever seen. As its most zealous Enforcer, however, he had not known the smallest part of it. You could not even say he had tried to know. And so the most naked answer to that question not yet voiced — how do you know the Sect's doings so well? — would have to be this: “I rolled up my sleeves and took an active part in that wickedness, and only now, to make belated amends, I am trading on your safety.” Sooner would he drive the cold into his own heart, his eyes, his tongue, and make the icicles it formed his gravestone. “Rest is over.” At his resolute voice the people grumbled even as they set themselves to rights. Here and there were some who had already gotten to their feet, stretching their arms and legs to loosen up. Cetus took great pains to keep a contented look from showing on his face. It owed something to how well his persuasion had taken — but at bottom it was because the villagers had themselves come to share the cause. “This is not a question of whether what you must believe in is Lucid or not.” the Cetus of the past had appealed to them. “There's no reason to hold out your hand first — not to Lucid, not to any other sect. Dream-creatures, for all that, are only a pack of beasts. You can win with your own strength. You can protect yourselves. Only then will the Sect, or any other power, not look down on you.” After training them, he went out onto the field himself and led the company. The more they swept the packs of dream-beasts near the village, the more their results piled up. Even among those whose legs had at first trembled like an insect's beating wings, there gradually emerged people who would boldly take the vanguard, and then appoint themselves drillmasters. The territory where the dream-beasts had run wild was severed and isolated further and further, until it dwindled to lines and dots on a map. Now all that remained was a single dot — what had to be called their last stronghold. I do hope this operation is the last one. Cetus thought. He couldn't let even that thought be tainted by the cold lurking in his mind. There was nothing to lose in picturing a future after things had gone well. Then he could leave this place with no regrets… or — perhaps? For the briefest instant, he pictured a different future. Settling down here for good. To settle among the people he had taught until now, the people he had formed ties with — to have, no longer a 'place to stay,' but 'my home'; to find some work to call my trade; and so to begin making my friends and my comrades, building a life like that. “We'll begin the drill again…” As his words and his actions began to drift apart, the control binding the cold loosened along with them. Cetus shuddered at a cold that stiffened the back of his neck. A strange feeling came over him. A Cetus settled in some village; a Cetus making friends; a Cetus surrounded by people who knew him and cared for him, turning experience into memory and the present into remembrance, little by little, until he became a member of that village. Could such a thing be possible? he thought. Would these people accept me? Ah — but the real question had not yet been asked. Could I accept such a self?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main2_Short: He teaches strangers to stand and fight, and still won't call their fires his own. If they would have him — could he ever have himself?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main3_Content_0: People never see the leaves turn. They never see the flowers bloom. Only when the autumn color has already faded, when the blossom has already opened, do they notice it all at once. Even so, can anyone conclude that the turning of a leaf, the unfurling of a bud, is a thing bound to happen anyway, and therefore a thing not worth minding? Without all the laborious changes working inside them, no leaf would ever have reddened, no flower would ever have opened in the first place. So it was with the villagers' efforts as, under Cetus's command, they gradually drove out the dream-beasts. One side were beasts, after all; the other, humans armed with strategy and weapons. Seen over a long enough span, which side would seize victory was plain enough. Even so, there was no holding back the villagers' overflowing joy. “This one's the last of them!” So declared someone who had kicked the slack jaw of a spent beast to make sure. The people cheered as one. The arms they raised were a riot of hardened scars, wounds not yet healed, and gashes still streaming fresh, uncrusted blood. From the spear-hafts in their grip rose the smell of grime and sweat; from their fists, the scent of wood-grain dripping with resin. Tongues even rougher and more cracked than their lips, gone bone-dry with tension, scraped over them again and again. But it was over. They had finished the last one. Now the village was freed from the dream-beasts! “Well fought, General!” “It's all thanks to our General.” “Hurrah! Hurrah!” Hands of encouragement fell busily onto Cetus's forearm — for no person of greater build could possibly exist. At first he had repaid each gesture of the goodwill that thronged about him like clouds, carefully, one by one, but before long he could only answer with a smile and a nod. So lavishly was the villagers' affection pouring over him. And yet he himself was caught in a worry that did not suit so joyous an occasion. They still depend on me. Cetus thought. This had been what one might call the last stronghold where the dream-beasts had huddled together. A place like that could not be toppled so simply. There had been several dangerous moments, and each time he had thrown aside drilled tactics and everything else, because he could do nothing but save the people first. The smaller beasts were dealt with helplessly before the wall of leveled spears, but there always appeared, without fail, the especially large one, the especially savage one, the especially swift one. And each such time, in the end, it fell to Cetus to step forward. He wielded the shackles bound to his limbs like a shield in tests of strength, and whenever he saw an opening, he whipped the chains around to lash the monster down. He froze the ground so that the soles pressing on it slipped, or froze fast and could not lift away again. When he ran a spear of ice, sharp as a razor, through a beast's trunk, the hot blood flowed steaming, then turned then and there into a crackling scarlet icicle. And once the breath was severed, the wave of ice — shifting its shape like rolling water — would rise again at the beckon of Cetus's hand and eye, becoming a monster with ten thousand tongues and a hundred thousand teeth that swept across the field. Many owed their lives to it, but Cetus, for his part, could not feel the satisfaction purely. I cannot look after these people for the rest of their lives. he thought. When I am gone, they will have to manage everything among themselves. Will they be able to? Perhaps he had set too arrogant a goal from the very start. Perhaps the villagers had merely played along to his tune, thinking that in the end there was nothing for it but to hold out their hands to the Lucid Sect or somewhere like it and pass under its rule. So in the end it all came full circle. The imagining of that day, when he had pictured a different future, rose again in Cetus's mind on this day all the same. Just settle down here, and everything is solved. Not some village, but my village; not some people, but my people — and the worry of leaving would vanish too. Cetus believed that this was what he wanted. He reckoned the villagers wanted it just as much, and that even if that were a step ahead of the evidence, they would at least not refuse if he made his wish known. Paradoxically, it was for that very reason — because no one would raise an objection when he decided to stay and build a life here again — that he had to think it through all the more fiercely. Into the eyes of such a Cetus came the sight of people gathered in twos and threes, talking among themselves. “What do we do about this place?” “Well… should we smoke it out with wet firewood?” It was before a small cave that opened inward at the place where the beasts had swarmed. “Shouldn't we go in and search every corner? If they slip out somewhere else and breed, it'll be a disaster.” “What's it like in there? Any other way out?” “I saw it as a kid — it's not deep, just a rock tunnel that runs straight back. No other openings.” “Good! Then we won't even need to smoke them out, will we?” someone said. “Just block it up and stand guard, and they'll all starve to death inside. Pick off the ones that crawl out half-dead.” To a man who happened to need time to think alone and quietly, it sounded made to order. “I'll go in and have a look.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main3_Content_1: Cetus half-guessed in advance that he would find nothing inside anyway. And even if he did find something, a beast in dire condition — met in a narrow, damp cave where his cold would prove most formidable, no less — would be no great threat. The darkness that filled every side was a problem only for humans. So it would be a time of the iron chains striking the polished limestone floor, of heavy footfalls echoing off the cave walls, of sinking into his thoughts as he listened quietly to his own breath and the beat of his heart. The thing he had not for an instant imagined he would find — yet which, on reflection, must of course have been there — that was what he came upon and could not unsee. “…I see.” Cetus let the words slip, unable to hide his bewilderment. “This would have been here… of course.” A dry laugh came on its own. He felt caught off guard. It was a fact he had known in his head since his days as a Sect Enforcer, but he had failed to connect it to what stood before him. He looked up at the crescent moon hanging in the air with a resentful gaze. A bluish flaw in space, appearing out of nothing and tearing open a place where there was nothing. Through a boundary that rippled like water churned with mud, it could spit out, suck in, and mingle the things within and without it at any moment — that conductor of infinite chaos, that helpless jester, the Rift opening onto the dream-world. The thing itself said nothing, but its meaning was plain. However weak a wave may be, the moment it breaks, every sandcastle is one day brought down. {IMAGE} “If I do not close this, none of it means anything.” Cetus saw the Rift shudder, as if in reply to his words. It is a strange way to put it, but it seemed to respond not to the content but to the voice — more precisely, to a part of himself. He wrapped his arms around his body, thinking a cold wind had suddenly risen, but not a single thread of his clothing, not a single grain of dirt on the ground, had left its place. The cold wind was coming not from outside the cave but from his own body. The cold was flowing out, slowly, against his will. It was trying to return. It longed, just the same, for the dream-world that reached out its arms in search of its own lost piece. If I go in, can I close this Rift? The thought that rose was rambling, yet inevitable. “General? Are you in there?” “You're all right, aren't you? We're coming in too.” The stir of people carried from the mouth of the cave. What silences such voices is not a rag or a cover over the mouth, but a part of oneself. The moment you close your own lips, the moment you press your own tongue flat against your gums, the voice will never come out. Closing the Rift to the dream-world must be the same. The moment you fit into it a piece of some shared nature — a power of dreams equal to its own, even if it was forced upon you — the gap, once filled, would vanish without a trace. Was it for this moment that I gained such a power? It was the moment the pain Cetus had inflicted on himself in the Lucid Sect's cells finally found its meaning. “So here you are.” True enough, it was a cave “not very deep,” just as they had said. Cetus watched the torches the villagers had carried in pour out their fierce brilliance. The hue of the Rift wavering over his shoulder, though frailer than that, was far more cunning. Rather than spend its strength against the deep color of the flame, it flattened itself, drawing a dim shadow at a glance. And yet it lay in wait, watching for its next chance — for the next dream-beasts to come bursting through, for the next moment to loose an alien power of dreams. If one were to say that the shape of the torn crescent hung in the air had, for an instant, turned into someone's venomous grin hauled up to the very ears — was that mere delusion on Cetus's part? Or was the Rift, the dream-world, truly laughing at him? Was it sending a chill mockery, a hollow show of comfort, because it knew his one remaining choice? Meanwhile, the villagers who had seen the strange sight unfurled at his back stopped in their tracks, one after another. “Wh-what is that?” “It's where the beasts came from. I haven't time to explain at length.” Cetus studied the faces of those who had come to find him. If he was the General, these would be something like his adjutants. They were people who had, more or less, learned in their bones the knack of handling weapons and of commanding others with a strong voice. For a long time — no, for a while — no, for the time being — they would manage well enough on their own. Because he did not mean to part from them forever. Because it would never come to that. Was that not so? “I must go inside this.” “What?” “While I am gone, you must carry out well what you have learned until now.” Cetus paused a moment. He wanted to give the villagers, not himself, time to chew over the weight of those words. “Do not slacken your training, do not lower your guard. Even without me, keep grinding your weapons as you have, keep posting sentries, and you must choose a 'General' to lead you.” “Wh-what do you mean, all of a sudden?” “It is all necessary.” Cetus stopped speaking with a heavy heart. This silence was for himself, not for those who listened. Then he went on. “Whether it is the Lucid Sect or any sect, you must never bow your heads carelessly to those who readily promise protection while wanting your 'goodwill' in return…. You have already done it. Trust one another.” He heard the boisterous laughter carrying faintly from outside. And here he looked straight into the eyes of people struck dumb, as if a bolt from the blue had hit them out of a clear sky. He nodded firmly. “For a while, you will be enough on your own, without me.” “What exactly do you mean to do, going in there?” It was a question that struck to the heart. It was not easy to answer, and Cetus alone might never be able to. But if there was a certain thing kept treasured deep in an inner pocket — a thing carried even as the worn clothes were patched and mended again and again — then he could answer it well enough. Cetus drew his five fingers, like rods of iron, together and clenched them tight. Its edges all frayed and faded, yet still vivid — that one line. Go out and show them you were right “I am going to settle a reckoning.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main3_Short: The last beast falls, and in the dark a wound in the world waits to undo it all. When he steps through, with whom does he mean to settle the score?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main4_Content_0:
It was a touch absurd, given that he had belonged to the Lucid Sect — which lost all composure at the mere mention of the dream-world — but this was in fact his first time entering it in person. The work of a Sect Enforcer was to punish those who had strayed and to seize those who roamed loose, which made it all the more so. He had crisscrossed every corner of the real continent in pursuit of deserters, building a wealth of firsthand knowledge there, while of the dream-world he had remained, shamefully, a mere bookworm. And so this was the Rapids, raw and unfiltered, met all at once and unexpectedly. It was not an emotion suited to the situation, but he felt a little thrilled. As he exchanged farewells with the villagers and took the last step across the Rift, he was even buoyant with anticipation.
It took less than a quarter-hour for that expectation to be shattered to pieces.
He had not, of course, expected a freshly groomed clean dirt road, crowds lining both sides clapping fit to bring the world down, a bright garland of flowers slipped over his neck. But neither was he in any way braced to be greeted by the host of vicious monsters that flew at him the instant they laid eyes on him. The geography peculiar to the Rapids played its part too — as though someone's muttering in a spring dream had been stitched together at random into avenues and forks, corners, alleys and stone walls. Just when it seemed to climb, it plunged; just when it seemed to run straight, his body tilted to one side. Just when he trusted it to be an instant, the four seasons would streak past before his eyes — no, an impossible way to put it, but the wreckage of a time that had once had five seasons would flash by like an arrow.

“What in the world makes you so—”
Cetus took a defensive stance, clucking his tongue. Even knowing they were beasts without reason, he could not hold back the complaint.
“—so set on flying at me with murder in your eyes!”
The shackles and stocks, the chains, then the shoulders and elbows. Cetus's body, planted firm as rock, met the beast that had not slowed at all head-on. It would not have been strange if invisible sparks had burst, smack, in midair. Yet despite an impact that should have snapped its neck in one blow and left it dead with its tongue lolling out, the beast curled its spine round like a small worm and clung to Cetus with its whole body, refusing to let go.
The claws on its limbs, the fangs in its snout, the long curved tail that lashed and coiled pliant as a razor — all of them threw Cetus's wits into utter disarray, as if each were a separate living creature. He felt as though he had lost his mind dwelling only on the deep pomegranate-colored juice that would spill out if they tore and split his bare flesh. Cetus watched a beast with a snout long as a horse's head — but bearing, in place of teeth, a great mass of saw-edges sharp enough to make the eyes ache — bite down on the broad part of his stocks and wind its body around him.
“I did not come here to grapple with the likes of you!”
Cetus wrapped his arms around the spine of the beast that had him to itself and crushed it until his elbows nearly touched. The beast's clutched body was, in an instant, mashed thick as a cloth wrung to squeeze out some draught. Even with the very middle of its waist pulped to tatters, the beast still raised its head to look at him. Howling at pain beyond imagining, it thrust that hideous maw at him all the same. The two spread jaws called to mind a gardener's shears with their bright blue edges honed keen. The only difference was that what would fall once the pruning was done was not a crookedly grown branch, but Cetus's neck.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main4_Content_1: “Hah!” It was the sound of Cetus loosing a battle-cry. It was the sound of tearing the limp-limbed beast from his body and dashing it down with all his strength — flinging it far, far off, somewhere it could not even dream of returning from. The thing, thrashing and flailing as it kicked at the air, slammed cleanly into the place where its kin were swarming. The uproar that spread out from that point — all the trembling and squawking and snarling and flapping and hissing and bounding — only raised the mood of the welcome ceremony surrounding him another notch. Cetus was not one to stand by and watch. When he swept his arm, the cold spread out like the beating of wings. Then a great crown of ice rose, jagged, to enclose him. The reactions of the beasts driven back were a sight, each in its own way. One bit at the ice and tried to hold; one threw its weight in blindly from behind; one led with nothing but its body, ignorant, and ended up limping with an icicle lodged in it…. Something bumped against Cetus's foot as he shifted his stance. He looked down and saw the head of some nameless beast. Long after it had been parted from its body, the thing was still blinking its two eyes and working its maw open and shut. Heedless of the dream-matter bodily fluid pouring out of its gaping neck, it was simply engrossed in idle gnawing, fierce enough to crack and shatter its own teeth. Its bloodshot eyes, of course, stayed fixed to the very end on its prey — on Cetus's body. It was hollowing enough to bring the gooseflesh out all over him. “Is this truly the dream-world I was told of?” After driving off the beasts and falling back, Cetus said, aghast. “Where in such a preposterous world is the power to grant wishes supposed to be preserved?” When he had fought the dream-beasts in reality, he had vaguely believed they must be brutes second to none in ferocity. He had taken it that such creatures came rushing out, jostling each other, to threaten the world outside. Once inside, it was the opposite. The biosphere the dream-beasts formed made even the law of the jungle in reality look refined by comparison. The relatively normal ones, the ones that could only be pushed out of it, were the very ones driven into reality. The place bore a workmanship extremely warped and absurd — beyond the level of merely baring teeth and taking wounds to fill the belly. How could a cruel world be a proper place at all, where every creature lived in dread with a long lit fuse strapped to its waist, where the moment it failed to swallow up something of reality, it crumbled at once into dream-matter? “How did this world come to be in such a state?” All at once the farewell he had given the villagers as he left them behind came to mind. It had at the same time been the moment he declared his own resolve. What did he mean to do inside, they had asked. He had answered like this: “I am going to settle a reckoning.” It had seemed to make sense at the time, but it was rather absurd. About what, in private with whom, was he going “to settle a reckoning”?… When his thoughts reached that far, a certain word came to him. Not just a word, but a name. The name he had taken pains to turn away from all the more since leaving the Sect hung about with a whole string of pious prayers and verses and hymn-refrains, like sparks scattering around it. “…Primus.” Speaking it after so long left a bitter aftertaste. Cetus sank down, all but landing on his backside. The implements hanging from him hindered his concentration, but before long he was able to sink into thought. It cannot be that everything the Sect taught is a lie — it was a thought he had had before, but inside this place he grew all the more conscious of it.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main4_Content_2:
“The dream-world is chaotic beyond measure, true, but there is plainly a direction to it.”
Cetus chewed over what he had seen and felt since crossing the Rift. There were, for instance, a few rules distinguishing the shallower from the deeper places of the dream. In some places you could not catch so much as a glimpse of a beast no matter what you did, while others were otherwise, and the tendency for stronger beasts to leap out the deeper you went was distinct. Above all, the periodic waves of black beasts that made it impossible to retrace one's path were the very product of the regularity the dream-world held within it.
“This direction itself must be the dream's self-correcting work, or the will of Primus that yet remains.”
Even if it were not, hope remained, Cetus thought. For at the least it was proof that this world could be tamed before order. Even if Primus were a being somewhat different from what he had been taught in the Sect, what would there be to gain by leaving his own world abandoned like this?
“These side effects can be solved by meeting in person.”
he said, nodding to himself.
“It cannot be a thing He wishes either, so by explaining it earnestly, all of it can be set right. So it is right to go 'to settle a reckoning.'”
For whose ears was he muttering such things to himself in the dead of night — no, in the literal midst of a dream? … In the midst of having his whole body pulled this way and that by the implements, having plopped down childlike on the ground and brooded until his backside went cold, was the only thing he had come away with a peace of mind he had cobbled together all by himself? Cetus drove his two clenched fists down onto the bare ground. Regrettably, it did nothing to make him feel any better, and only threw into sharper relief how very much like a child he was now behaving.
“……A child, is it.”
Outside, in his days as a Lucid Enforcer, there had been times he had to spend with snot-nosed urchins the Sect had not taken in. He could not very well stand stiff as a post when children gazed up at him with eyes full of some wanting, or fretted and whined, so there had been one tale he had dug up by asking around among his subordinates. A belief that exists only among children. Cetus knew of something close to a collective faith, not to be dismissed entirely as a fairy tale. A story that on a certain particular night of the year, some hunchbacked grandfather went around every corner of the continent bestowing gifts on good children.

“I do not understand it.”
Cetus — who back then had a free hand, with neither shackle nor chain, to scratch the back of his head — had gathered his subordinates to find something he might talk about with the children.
“But it is not as though all children actually receive gifts together on that night, is it?”
“Well, no, they don't.”
The subordinates looked at one another and agreed, lukewarm.
“The lucky households have their parents prepare something through the night, but that's not how it goes for everyone.”
“Then how does that hunchback faith hold together?”
“The kids who don't get anything are made to blame themselves — er, it's a crude way to put it, but the rule is rigged that way.”
one subordinate answered.
“The whole notion is that that hunch— ah, I'll catch it from the Enforcer — that He passed without leaving a gift because you weren't good this past year, because you secretly harbored a wicked heart.”
“Interesting.”
Cetus chuckled. And the present Cetus — who now, on top of the implements binding his limbs, left behind blizzards in place of warm breath, and small frozen puddles in place of steaming footprints — chuckled along with him. Recalling the self he had been then.
“The children were made unable, from the start, to think that perhaps that hunchback did not exist — that their own belief might be mistaken.”
“I am not like them.”
The latter words came out unusually low and rough. They sounded exactly like another person's voice.
“But would not every child who believes in that hunchback think the very same thing?”
The last words were better dismissed as unheard. Like a certain voice you come to believe you hear when you are facing the black beasts. Cetus covered his ears with both hands and tried. He squeezed his eyes shut and waited until the sound of his own heart, racing faster and faster, finally tired of itself and slowed.
“I must believe.”
Small mutterings kept pouring out before he knew it.
“I must believe. I must believe in the fact that I must believe….”
“I had been searching, having heard that a being half reality, half dream, walks about—”
Cetus started in alarm and rose to his feet. The chain that had lain sprawled on the ground was wrenched up roughly, sending frozen dirt and pebbles flying in all directions. Heedless of it, there stood a stranger of stately bearing, a woman in long trailing robes.
“—and it was quite literally true.”
“Who are you?”
She seemed not to be a mere beast, given that words passed between them, but that was hardly enough to lower his guard. Cetus stood with the invisible arm of the cold thrust up, ready to subdue her first if it came to it.
“They call me Polaris.”
she said. Unlike Cetus, she did not show the slightest wariness, making no effort to hide the gaze of pure curiosity in her eyes.
“The Guide of this place, the Rapids — and, beyond it, of the dream-world.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main4_Short: In the dream he worshipped all his life, he finds only fangs and chaos. And yet — who is it that waits for him at the end of the road?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main5_Content_0:
It was a question bound to be thrown out, sooner or later. If anything, from Cetus's standpoint it was what he had wanted to ask the moment they met — and all the more of someone who called herself Polaris, the Guide of the Rapids, of the dream-world itself. But why, then, did she falter on hearing such a question?
“Then do you know Primus?”
Polaris's movements stopped. Her unblinking eyes fixed on him, vacant. It resembled the curiosity from when she had first spoken to him, but it was a little different. Cetus felt that she was actively searching him. Not merely his outward appearance, but the true intent of the words he had just offered — she wished to read the background and premises of this person called Cetus that lay behind them.
“That title 'Primus'… you do not call him so out of familiarity, I see.”
Polaris said, her eyes gleaming.
“There are several kinds of titles that need no modifier… one would be the way a word naming one's own particular god takes neither 'Lord' nor 'Revered,' and your intonation, too, seems close to that sort.”
Cetus nodded, and a blank in her search was filled. Now it was time for the feeling hidden behind the conscious act to surface.
“But that name—”
In her bewilderment Polaris clenched and unclenched her fists, again and again, without realizing it.
“—how is it that you know Primus?”
“Know him? Of course. Is he not the master of this world?”
At those words Polaris's fists went white. However offhandedly the impression had been tossed out, it was hard to give a proper answer. Pressing the point, she felt, would be like pulling the plug from a riverbank with her own hand and then struggling to pour the water back in, so she decided, for now, simply to let it pass.

“…Yes, I know Primus.”
she went on, thinking that, for some reason, what was seeping faintly from Cetus's body in his unhidden excitement was not heat but cold.
“Once…… I was at his side.”
“So it is true!”
At the answer, Cetus's complexion, his tone, turned utterly different. Even Polaris, conversing right before his nose, was left bewildered. Then, abruptly, a flood of fervent questions followed. Among them were relatively harmless ones — such as where he should go to find his dwelling — but mixed in were uncomfortable ones too: exactly what relationship she had had with him, whether she still served him even now. Besides, who had ever used the word "serve"?
In any case, whether or not he truly meant to hear out the answer to each and every one, she was in fact letting her attention drift elsewhere. She was more interested in the shackles and chains, the stocks binding the body of this vast traveler — no, this prisoner — from whom a chill seemed to ooze in cloud after cloud. And then she finally realized where she had seen such things. With it, she also worked out how Cetus — though they had not yet exchanged names — could be so well versed in the hierarchy of the dream and in the place Primus occupied within it.
“You—”
“My name is Cetus, Guide.”
“—you are one persecuted by the Lucid Sect.”
'Guide,' out of nowhere? That too she decided, for now, to let pass… She was slowly losing count of how many things she would simply let pass before this day was out.
“I have seen those dragged about wearing those implements. They are the Lucid Sect's handiwork.”
“…That is so.”
Polaris's brow tilted aslant. A moment ago he had been rejoicing alone like a child, and now what was this voice gone so flat and heavy? It was a conversation hard to keep pace with.

“It seems the Sect teaches its doctrine even to prisoners these days.”
“It is because I was not merely a prisoner. I….”
Cetus hesitated. Then he let out a long sigh. Air cold enough to call an untimely winter down upon the soft new shoots, the verdant shade, the golden fields heavy with ripened grain, came out of his mouth.
“Once, I was one of them.”
To Polaris, those words served no function beyond a simple delivery of information. So she waited in silence until the grieved Cetus took it upon himself to go on.
“The Sect as it is now has lost its way. Twisting Primus's teachings, it turns its eyes from the suffering of all. It thinks only of toppling other faiths, other authorities. And yet now, like this….”
There came the sound of wind, and the view ahead opened up clear. After a moment, she could see what had happened. The vast toothed-whale beastfolk, Cetus, had thrown himself flat. He was kneeling before Polaris.
“To have been allowed to behold the mouth of Primus — I am simply overwhelmed!”
The mouth of Primus, he called her. This time it was not her fists that went white but her face. Yet it was only for a moment; soon the face, blank as a sheet of paper, flushed red.
It was, of course, not out of embarrassment.
“How has the dream-world come to be like this?”
Before there was even room to correct the misunderstanding before her, his earnest, drawn-out appeal continued.
“How can it be so chaotic, and how can the dream-spawn suffer for that chaos, and how can that suffering reach out even to the continent beyond? Where have order and harmony gone — where have Primus's teachings gone?”
Polaris gazed quietly at the Cetus laying out such words.
“I wish to return the Sect to its pure state. Further, I wish to halt the corruption of the dream in which faith has taken root, and so to root out the absurdity it forces upon both worlds — the harm at its very source. To do that, I need the teaching of the Guide, the mouth of Primus, who once attended him from closer than anyone.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main5_Content_1: The expression "the mouth of Primus" was something he had called her on his own, and somehow she had simply become it; the talk of having attended Primus was little better than baseless slander. But this, too, she felt she had to let pass for now. All the more so watching Cetus go on, pouring out an impassioned plea, his eyes drinking in the dark and his brow taking on the pattern of the dirt floor. The answer he sought could not, in any case, be tidied up into something easy to grasp. Yet instead of circling round words hard to accept to set him at ease, in that moment Polaris saw an opportunity. However wrong his direction and starting line, however blinded by a blind faith toward Primus, here he was, vowing to set right what the limits of the dream had distorted. That impulse was, in truth, a straight and proper path with not an ounce of excess to it. She began, carefully, to choose her words. “I will not treat you like a child and lay out only pleasant words.” The crown of Cetus's bowed head twitched as he listened. “You yourself must have agonized and suffered much over this. In the course of it you must have wrestled to take up willingly even some painful truth… so I will speak plainly.” All around was still. The grass-insects of the Rapids, playing their tune slow as a dream, and even the moles burrowing through the earth underfoot, seemed to hold their breath and wait for her declaration — the declaration of the Guide of dreams. “All of this is the fault of Primus.” Cetus's body shook violently. It was like a small hill writhing in an earthquake. Yet as though an unseen hand were holding him down, neither his body nor his head would lift. He was enduring it, teeth clenched. “But that cannot….” “Going to him will not solve this problem.” The second wedge of words drove in. On the two forearms of Cetus, sprawled face-down on the bare ground, sinews hard as steel nails throbbed up and sank, again and again. “Th-that cannot be.” he stammered, barely. “The dream-world is, by its very nature, His….” “The forces that make up this place are, from their very birth, thoroughly incomplete. You must have seen it too.” Had he seen it? Yes. He had seen it even before entering the Rapids. How abnormally savage the dream-beasts were, how perilous the various spells and arts originating in the power of dreams. But those he had regarded merely as the matter immediately before his eyes, a temporary obstacle — never had he thought them part of the problem he meant to face. He would meet Primus, and the moment Primus solved the problem — however he might pin down and unravel exactly what problem it was — everything would be all right. Perhaps? “Even were it Primus, he could not tame the very nature of the dream—” The words that followed struck Cetus not as sound but as light, in the make of lightning. Passing through his ears, his jaw, his throat, his breathing-hole, it drove at last into his heart. “—whereas I have found the way to resolve it.” The inside of his chest ached all over. Yet it was not pain but exaltation. Had she found the answer? The very answer he had ultimately craved? He had to wet his lips and steady his voice. “Might I ask what that way is….” “Of course. For I have nothing to hide.” Even reading the wick beneath those words of feigned indifference, no particular thought rose in him. Knowing that those words pointed obliquely at the Primus he revered as ever, at the Sect he had once belonged to, no rebellion stirred in him. “It is to scatter the boundary between the world outside and this one, and to bind the two unbalanced worlds into one stable reality.” Go out and show them you were right The note came to mind. The note his friends had left. Why did it come to him? Because of the memory of having recalled it before the villagers. Why had he recalled it before the villagers? Because he had taken the note's charge to be bound up with saving them. And from what had he needed to save the villagers? From none other than the dream-beasts, was it not? The back of Cetus's neck prickled cold. Merge the dream and the outside? Was that truly the right answer? The judgment that it was wrong, however, was hasty. On the other hand, the thought came that Polaris might be right. Such a thought began, slowly, to take shape, to congeal, to clot. Once reality became like the dream, and the dream like reality, would not the dream-beasts grow gentler in the seam between them? Then would they not also stop savaging the people of reality as if their lives depended on it? At the same time the mask of the Sect, which had monopolized the interpretation of the dream-world, would be stripped away too… On top of such views that, at a glance, made sense, Cetus was feeling a pressure. Not the worldly pressure of blood and entrails churning, but a pressure arising from abstract facts and the void at their center. What was the reason for the anguish he had wrestled with ever since entering the Rapids? It was that, though he had seen and felt the incompleteness of the dream firsthand, with his own eyes and skin, he had clung to maintaining a single narrative that contradicted it. It was that he had uncritically accepted the premise of Primus, the rightful ruler and proper master of the dream. Demote him to a mere condition and deny him, and then let Polaris and her explanation settle into the void at the center thus created, and everything sorted itself out naturally. A guide for belief that he could clearly understand and follow came into being once more. “What do you think of it?” This is different from the hunchback the children follow. That was only a figure of speech. thought Cetus, having heard Polaris's words. Still kneeling, he met her eyes, then once more bowed his head respectfully. “I will follow the Guide's will.” {IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main5_Short: A voice pulls the last ground from beneath his feet and offers him a faith to replace it. Has he only knelt, a second time, in the same old devotion?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main6_Content_0: He had never imagined he would meet a companion in the Rapids. Still less had he imagined a new object of faith would appear. In that respect, Cetus believed, he was fortunate. To believe in something, to be able to believe — it was a truly happy thing. Polaris, for her part, did not seem to mind his playing the role of her attendant, and let him follow at her side. Cetus had resolved to be a sturdy shield moving by the Guide's will, and a keen sword too if need be, but there was not much for him to do. There were scarcely any who tried to attack her, and the work of bestowing gold to aid the dream-creatures the Guide already did well enough on her own, without him. When she persuaded the travelers who now and then washed in from reality, she kept Cetus at a distance, so there was no chance to join the conversation. Treated, before he knew it, as one of Polaris's party, much of what he saw and heard was therefore not the facts she herself disclosed, but how others thought of her — of the Guide of dreams. “Our savior, the savior of the Rapids!” “She's truly a kind one.” “If not for Lady Polaris, it would have been disaster.” Each such time, he could forget, if only for a moment, the cold of the dream that wound about him. The corners of his mouth, frozen hard by the warm wind blowing through his chest, the set line of his brow, would loosen, and a contented smile would form despite himself. He grew certain that Polaris's road was right after all; that he, having chosen to follow such a person, was therefore right too; and further, that he was carrying out his friends' charge. But the decisive moment that was to be the last link in that certainty, the period that knots a happy ending, the red wax sealing a letter that bears the dispatch of an ideological victory — that moment, time and again, never came. “What sort of being was he?” Being companions, they naturally came to spend time alone together. And each such time, what was there to do but talk of this and that? Of Primus, of the role and responsibility he carried out in this world, Cetus threw out so many questions that even he tired of himself. But if the aim of the two of them was to right the absurdity of the dream and save everyone, then surely a great many discussions — enough to tire of — ought to pass about that world, about the master of that world. Mostly, though, answers like these came back: “Let us discuss it later.” “It is a complicated subject. I cannot sort it out at once.” “There is something more important.” “You will not like the answer.” Not every attempt was brushed off in that way. There were, of course, times the conversation came together. “Is he indeed the master of the dream?” “I should say he is the being closest to that.” In his Sect days there had been many metaphors for the almighty dream-god Primus. If, for instance, all creation of the dream were molten pig-iron and the mold that encased it, and the casting formed as a result, then Primus was the furnace endlessly producing the molten metal, and the very fire that breathed life into that furnace… To call that "closest to the master" might be one way to put it. “If the dream is to be set right, is not his will the most important thing?” Cetus pressed on. “It seems to me he is the one to seek out first and to spend oneself persuading to the very last… I cannot quite understand the fact that you left him like this.” There seemed to be something more to say, some point passed over untouched, but he made an effort to ignore it. Sometimes not every passing notion need be 'brought to mind' in the form of words and writing. “Is not his cooperation essential?” “Not necessarily so.” Polaris answered. “For I, too, have my own means and the facts I have grasped.” “Did you not try to persuade him repeatedly, as you did me and the other travelers?” “I tried, but from the start he was looking elsewhere.” For someone to look elsewhere than oneself… it was an expression too laden to describe a difference of clashing discourse and viewpoint over one concrete problem. Cetus chewed over when he had first met Polaris. The nature of the dream, she had said, could not be tamed even by Primus. “If these phenomena are now the limit of the dream itself… then at the least, should we not say it is not the fault of Primus?” “If one stubbornly turns away from that, one is choosing to do wrong oneself.” “By turning away you mean…?” “It is a common enough thing — let us call it sharing one bed and dreaming different dreams.” Likewise, the talk threatened in the end to lose its way, dribbling off into a maze of laden expressions. He did not want to pry into every little concrete detail, but he still could not understand it. Had she given up on persuading the master of the dream — or at least the one closest to that — with nothing more than the words "he looks elsewhere"? Or was there a part of the matter she did not wish to reveal? That Primus had flatly rebuffed her, perhaps… And that very notion was precisely the kind of thought that need not become words or writing. But once such things break their channel, they cannot be stopped. Like dragging up a tuber, the linked impressions, the petty suspicions, must be pulled out in a long string until they lie nakedly exposed — only then is one satisfied. Could it be that the Guide is avoiding Primus on purpose? Cetus bowed his head before such a thought. Perhaps the conversation with Primus is not yet finished. The possibility that Primus is right and she is wrong, that it could be so…. The silence had stretched too long. He looked up with a start. Polaris was smiling, soundless, with a quiet grin.
