ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main6_Content_1: “It seemed you had more to say.” “Ah, no. My apologies.” Cetus bowed his head. “I will see that there is no more of this.” “Is that so?” Polaris's manner had changed, Cetus felt. It had grown lighter. Was she amused? More precisely, she was trying to spur something on. “You must ask more of such questions.” she said. “Pick and probe at every point, relentlessly dig into the weak spots of the logic, until in the end you throw out every uncomfortable question I cannot brush off with a smiling face like this.” Cetus was so astonished that he could not even go on speaking, aghast. His bowed neck felt as if it would freeze stiff just so. “How could I ever do such….” “When I meet alone with the travelers from reality, I do not keep you close. Why do you suppose that is?” It was a riddle out of nowhere, but this, at least, was the easier one. “Is it not because, if I stood there planted before them, I might overawe them?” “Hm, there is that too.” Polaris laughed, as if it were a curious reason she had never considered. Suddenly Cetus knew that some force — unknowable, resembling his cold but more subtle, and above all far mightier — was working near the two of them. “Mostly it is so that you might clear your head alone.” When he glanced up, the Guide had already withdrawn her gesturing hand, and the trace of the force had faded as well. Only her words went on. “So that you might brood deeply, alone, on whether this road is truly the one you have chosen.” “I brooded my fill outside as well.” “You yourself will not see it so, but you are still a long way short.” Polaris declared. “In a strange place like this, having met a stranger like me, you need a moment to clear your head by force before you are wholly swayed by that strange thinking. After you have seen, heard, and above all thought as much as you possibly can, you must be ready either to hold to your decision yourself, or to overturn it whole.” I had wanted to ready more things…. With that muttering, Polaris fished out and laid down something or other. It turned out to be a bundle of odds and ends she had gathered here and there about the dream-world. “What are all these?” “Take them.” For an instant Cetus realized that, even before her words had fallen, he had taken it for granted that these things were his. The inside of his black, sleek skin tinted faintly, fair, with a flush. “These are signs and clues and stories. Stories of the Rapids, stories of Primus, and beyond that the many stories of the many who wander this world — the very things you need now.” Cetus looked from the several objects placed in his grip to Polaris and back. He could not make sense of any of it. “In the Rapids there are several who can recognize those objects. I tend to keep my distance, not wanting to stir up a fuss for nothing….” Polaris gestured toward the wide world. “But for you, who wish — who must — hear the ins and outs of this world, they are made to order.” “Guide, surely you don't mean—” Cetus rose, wobbling somewhat ungainly. So great was his haste. “—surely you are not casting me out?” “I am saying we should move apart for a while.” Polaris said, gentle and soft. As if soothing a child clinging to her. “So that you may make your own decision, one not forced upon you… Believe me. It is hardly to my liking to go out of my way to give such a chance to you, who would become my faithful ally if I simply left you be.” She smiled, bitter. The crooked corner of her mouth hung the blade-point of a mockery aimed not at anyone else but at herself. “But later, whether the plan succeeds or fails, whether you affirm your past choice or come to regret it… should that choice itself not be wholly your own decision, your own responsibility?” Cetus gazed at her in silence. He looked at that face, lonelier than ever before — a face he had not seen even once since the day he met her and, in his haphazard way, declared himself her attendant and fell in beside her. He had thought he had at last found an object of faith — but in truth, had he not merely found an object he wished to believe in, a pretext for not having to think for himself? Notions that need take no form of word or writing welled up once more. There was the sudden thought that, in fact, he was repeating exactly the thinking and the deeds of his Enforcer days. It was only because she had led him about so loosely that all had been well; if one day she were to point at someone and say, “Cetus, kill that one,” would he have tried to learn the whole story of the matter? Would he have agonized over whether there was some other way? Or would he have moved without hesitation, just as ordered? As in the days he worked as a tool of the Sect? At that thought, he came to himself with a jolt. “…Understood, Guide.” Cetus said. Faintly, he heard Polaris's laughter. “I will set my thoughts in order and return to attend you again. It will not be long.” “Are you certain of both sentences?” the Guide chuckled. There was a hint of playfulness at a glance, yet it carried, intact, the troubled feeling of a fool who 'goes out of her way to give the chance not to' a person who would otherwise become her ally. Even so, he had no intention of letting the conversation they had just shared slip away in vain. I am not simply going out to become the Enforcer of somewhere other than Lucid, to punish those who do not fit the ideology of that place. Cetus thought. And he chewed once more, over and over, on the note he had pored over so often he no longer needed to look at it. Go out and show them you were right Yes. He had to go out. He had to be wary not only of the Sect but of having his thought bound anywhere at all. Rather than absorbing another's words as they were, he had to translate them into his own language, his own justice, and be able to make sense of right and wrong. Only then, even should he fail through some lack of ability, could he be at least a failure who stood with his chest held high. “Keep yourself well for the time being, Guide.” At his words, Polaris bowed her head alongside his. “You too, Cetus.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main6_Short: Just as he is ready to follow again, she sends him away to think alone. What remains of a man who answers to no one's hand?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main7_Content_0:
“That choice is, after all, the wrong one.”
While wandering alone after leaving Polaris, he came upon an empty clearing. He was looking over the bloodied packs and tents, the weapons, or what was left of them, that remained there. Something caught at the tip of his foot, and he saw it was the hem of someone's garment. Not laid out neatly or folded, but with its wearer still inside it — whatever had been done to it, layer upon layer of clinging flesh gave off a horrid stench.
“…I cannot agree to the premise of merging a place like this with reality.”
The dream is dangerous because it is a corrupted world. Because it is dangerous, it harms what lies outside. If so, one should first work out how to mend the corruption, then discuss exchange between them — but the notion that "merge it with reality first, and the corruption will heal and the danger vanish with it"… he could not bring himself to nod along easily. If only for the sake of the faces of the villagers he had greeted and left behind — it was a conclusion that came almost too late. Not a single fact had changed from the start. Only that, having left Polaris's side, having cleared his head and thought, as she would put it, had it become plain.

“There is still much I do not know about Primus.”
He did not believe everything taught in the Lucid Sect was thorough deception. It was not that he wished to believe so, but that the realistic likelihood seemed to point that way. How could there be a faith founded from the very start on nothing but bald-faced lies? Cetus recalled the Primus of Polaris's stories. When spoken to, he listened; when something appeared that did not fit the theory, he thought on it; and having seen what differed from his own thinking, he fell to brooding. He was certainly not like the almighty dream-god of myth, but neither, conversely, did he seem the sort of blind tyrant to wield reckless misrule.
“I need only meet him and lay it out, step by step. That is where I must begin.”
It did not matter if he failed to persuade him at once. For now the goal was to learn what he had not known, and to make known to Primus what he himself knew. It would be quite enough to fill in, step by step and by his own strength, the parts he did not know, and only then to think on what came next.

“Well met—”
Somewhere or other he met another harmless-looking stranger, a woman who greeted him just so.
“—I was drawn by the power of the Relics you carry… you go about with all of that?”
Seeing the woman blanch, Cetus too looked over what he was lugging about. The bundle was now crammed not only with the things he had received from Polaris but with all manner of — literally all manner of — odds and ends from the Rapids. Come to think of it, she had said there were those who could recognize those objects, the stories held within them. Cetus handed over the various objects in the bundle and waited. He waited still, with the cold billowing off him. He waited patiently until lotus-shaped frost-spikes bloomed wide all around where he sat on the bare ground. Of the many stories he heard that way, there was one that left the deepest impression.
“This… is the token the master of this world bestowed on every rebel.”
the woman said, choosing her words with interest.
“A symbol of those who defied the heavens.”
“Were there many such cases?”
“You could say so — but they were never enough.”
{IMAGE}
Wandering the dream-world, he had several times seen a bottomless sea of mist. Here and there amid it, peaks sharp as needles thrust up their heads, swathed in eternal ice and snow. If what Cetus made was hard ice, then what those peaks held was a blade that had ripened without ever knowing spring's light, and an armor polished to a sheen. At their very heart he glimpsed some monster swinging a sword thick as a river. To think that one had once raised a banner against Primus and been defeated. More astonishing still was the fact that that one was merely the beginning. A god of somewhere, an emperor, a conqueror, a gatekeeper, the mother of a clan… many who had once governed the dream by setting up their own particular order had in the end knelt before Primus's power, the Dream Teller told him.
“He took their oaths of subjugation, giving such tokens in return.”
“So he broke them all, every one.”
His mouth fell open and would not close. To the worry of whether the dream's corruption could be halted without Primus's help, what had Polaris said again? Not necessarily so… But could Polaris truly free herself entirely from the influence of a Primus like this?
For his part, Cetus was skeptical.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main7_Content_1:
Even after parting from the storyteller woman — “You really do carry the whole lot off as it is.” — Cetus thought of Polaris. But at the same time he thought of Primus too. More than the Polaris he had met and spoken with in person, the Primus he still knew only through the verses of scripture kept rising in his mind. If he must serve someone, he felt it ought to be not the Guide of dreams but the master of the dream, who had defeated so many beginning with the Lord of the Snow Peak… and Cetus shook his head to throw off the notion.
“Still thinking such thoughts.”
He spoke of it as if it were someone else's affair, but it was a tendency by no means easy to shake — he was, again, trying to serve someone. He had unconsciously believed that to be the right conduct. And only just now, parting from Polaris, he had vowed that 'he must not be bound to any thought.'
“I will meet him and talk. Explain the whole story and find things out. Not serve him outright.”
What had the meeting between Polaris and Primus been like? An amiable discussion, a fierce argument, a heated debate… Perhaps she had failed to persuade the master of the dream because both held something neither could give up. With something neither could ever set down, with a place from which neither could retreat at their backs, no amount of endless wrangling would change a thing. But if that were so, this was not a matter of right and wrong. It was a matter of wholly different approaches to solving one and the same phenomenon.

“In what way does Primus see this problem?”
He could not know.
“It may be that, in a way Polaris simply cannot accept, Primus has a solution of his own.”
He could not know — and now he could admit that fact a little more at ease. Each time he met the myriad things he could not know, had not seen, could not be sure of, how comfortable it would be if he could scurry off to believe in something, and with that entrusted certainty drive every last shadow from his mind.
In the beginning, the object of that faith had been Primus — more precisely, the false Primus reinterpreted within the Lucid Sect's lies. That had shifted, upon entering the Rapids, to the true Primus, and most recently to the Guide who criticized that very Primus. Cetus chuckled. At this rate, was not everything he had done until now — escaping the Sect, helping people, even entering the dream-world and rushing about — all so much wasted effort? For from the start he had merely been wandering in search of some emblem of authority he could follow without question. He had left the bit jammed in his mouth, the reins cinched so he could not toss his head, and only roamed in search of another hand to take hold of them.
“I too was trapped in the very thinking of those children who blamed themselves over the hunchback.”
Cetus went on bursting into laughter. Clear tears turned at once into pearl-pale ice and rolled about the ground.

In some Rapids of some later time, the two met again.
“I can tell just from your eyes.”
The first to speak was Polaris, mischievously rolling her shoulders.
“Did I not say it? That I would ask whether you were certain of both sentences.”
“The objects you gave me, Guide, and the stories in them, were enormously useful.”
Cetus said, calm.
“And so I wish to share such stories with Primus as well. To learn what I do not know, and at the same time to tell him the things that perhaps only I yet know.”
He would tell a great many stories. How Primus's name had been distorted out in the world, how that, meshing with the corruption of the dream, had fed what harm… And if the master of the dream — or at least the one closest to him — having heard it, stirred to action, that would be a thing beyond compare.
“If he shows the will, I believe it is possible.”
“Do you suppose I never made such an attempt?”
Polaris's tone was easy and warm, ill-suited to the content. Cetus, for his part, was startled to find himself hearing those words with unexpected composure. More startling still was the fact that he had heard such words countless times, going back to his days as a Sect Enforcer. As it happened, those who chiefly spoke such words were, there too, called the Ushers of dreams. Just as the Guide of dreams before him now was.
“You, Guide, have those you must protect, and I have a record of sin I must wash clean.”
Cetus said.
“Until I wash that sin clean in the right way, it seems I cannot readily lend my strength anywhere.”
“Will the one who sinned decide for himself the manner of his making things right?”
This stung a little… struck to the heart, Cetus fell silent. Yet he knew, too, that Polaris was not truly doing it to break his will or to wound him. The point was something he had failed to do himself. He had, in the end, failed to put such an uncomfortable, brazen question to Polaris, and above all to himself. So she was, in effect, taking that role upon herself.

“The greatest sin I committed was, rather than any concrete deed, my meek following of others' words and the conclusions within them.”
Cetus said.
“And so I mean to break free of such conduct. I will confirm the whole of the matter with my own eyes and make what amends I can within it. Only then can I answer, this time, that I tried to the very end — that I pursued a justice that did not betray my own conscience.”
Polaris laughed. She laughed simply, purely — with no how, no what attached to it, leaving no aftertaste behind.
“I cannot say I look forward to it, but… very well.”
Hearing that, Cetus, who had reflexively begun to lower his neck, stopped himself. Polaris was holding out one hand.
“Let us meet again.”
“Yes.”
He straightened his neck and put out a hand large as a cauldron lid. The two hands clasped together so.
“We will meet again.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main7_Short: For the first time he chooses neither obedience nor flight, but a road that is wholly his own. Yet can a hand he reaches out himself ever wash a sin clean?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main8_Content_0: “Are you all right?” asked Cetus, the most faithful Enforcer of the Lucid Sect. Before him stood a Usher of dreams, just come out from interrogating an unbeliever. “Did nothing happen inside?” “If it had, you'd have been the first to know — why ask?” Cetus bowed his head, feeling he had played the fool for nothing. It was, after all, only natural. The unbeliever had come out first, and as had been arranged beforehand, other believers had come and taken her off somewhere. “At any rate — truly, ah, I envy them.” the Usher said, smacking his lips. “It's a posture to learn from, not doubting oneself to that degree.” “What?” Cetus asked, dumbfounded at hearing the unbeliever's attitude praised. All the more so since what had carried through the door was the very opposite — the Usher's tongue ceaselessly working over that stubborn unbeliever. “You don't agree, it seems?” “As one who follows the faith, I think we cannot leave the doubt in our heads unchecked.” “Enforcer….” Trailing off, the Usher looked up at the towering Cetus and clucked his tongue. “This is exactly why you, brother, stay forever an Enforcer.” His tone said he hardly knew where to begin. “Do you suppose I, too, did not sink into some suspicion the whole way up from a lay believer? But it has all been done before.” Done before? What? By whom? As if reading that very question, the Usher's hand swept over Cetus, over himself, and then over the walls of the facility and all the Lucid Sect believers who would be within them. “Everyone other than me, and everyone who came before them too — they all doubted, threw themselves into it with passion, tried to find something out and change it. It's what remains after all of that has been passed through, what is now 'kindly serving' as the object of my own clumsy doubt.” Merely following the stride of that imagining was enough to make his head spin. A single mouse standing before a soaring mountain, sunk down before its overwhelming majesty — and to it the voice went on speaking. “So at a certain point, you see, my own thought, my own viewpoint on the matter, becomes not worth a whit. Everything one knows turns, at some moment, into something one believes, and after that into something one must believe.” Their eyes met. One side seized the other's and would not let go, one-sided. “So you too must believe, brother—” the Usher said. “—you must believe.” “B-believe what?” At Cetus's stammering question the Usher broke into a grin. Bringing his two hands together playfully, he answered: “The fact that you must believe.”
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Main8_Short: A smile, a gentle voice, and every doubt dissolves back into devotion. Who first taught him to believe that he must believe?
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Short0_Content: Branded a heretic, Cetus volunteered to become the test subject through which the dream's power would be forced into his own body, deep within the order's dungeons. And the order spun this spectacle into a story of its own—a tale of a wayward heretic who begged for his own punishment to atone, the kind that tugs neatly at the faithful's heartstrings. Yet upon the operating table, Cetus said nothing at all. Whether he trembled because of the repentance the order spoke of, or simply from the agony of being crushed and cast aside, not even he could tell. Only one thing was certain—no one else would have to stand in this place in his stead.
ui.TravelerStory_Cetus_Short1_Content: On the day he ended the beast's final breath, the villagers clung to his arms and cheered. That night, alone, Cetus once again drew out the worn paper he had folded and unfolded countless times. Even as he secretly pictured a future of settling down in this place, he stopped short each time his fingertips brushed against the sentence. Go out, and show them that you are right. As long as the faces of those he couldn't escape alongside lingered in his mind, the word 'settling down' still felt like a luxury to him.

ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main1_Content_0: What must always be present in a doll-maker's workshop? The dolls. What can the workshop do without? The doll-maker himself. And what must never, ever set foot in a doll-maker's workshop? An assassin who has crept in to take the doll-maker's life. You watch the doll-maker absorbed in his work. Only a single oil lamp, small enough to nestle in one hand, glows faintly—yet for some reason the room is bright enough to read the fine print of a book with ease. That is thanks to the enormous ritual circle ringing the floor beneath your feet and the doll-maker's. Against the radiance pouring from it, crammed as it is with all manner of strange and wondrous characters and designs, the amber cast of the oil lamp looks closer to a shadow supping at the same table as the dark. It is precisely at such a moment—when all around lies silent and everything seems to be running as it should—that the thread of an incident appears. Before your eyes and the doll-maker's, an assassin steps into view. A doll-maker with the uncanny gift of bringing even the dead back to life. Had that very renown invited his untimely death upon him? There was no telling. An assassin does not ask his client this or that. He merely counts, once the mark is dead, the weight of silver ingots he stands to collect. In a single bound he closed the distance as if flying. He drew the dagger he had kept hidden and swung. The blade, gleaming in the light of the ritual circle, clove the room like soundless lightning. Between the doll-maker's throat—frozen, unable even to scream—and the assassin's hand there was nothing to stand in the way. So it had been. But the man-sized dolls planted all around, those glossy wooden scarecrows with no expression, with nothing at all, stretched out their arms and barred the assassin's path. You watch the assassin falter, unlike himself. For a moment cold sweat beads on his brow, his pupils shrink to pinpricks, and the mouth behind his hood gapes wide. Even if he does not know it himself, it is a moment to be savored to the full, however late. After all, a skilled assassin who until now had done nothing but startle others to the bone has, for nearly the first time, found the tables turned. But the effect of the ambush does not last. You think the assassin murmured something in that instant. What is certain, at least, is that he resolved—rather than slitting the doll-maker's throat—to first do some damage to the grain of the wood. The dagger, hurling itself at a changed target, traced narrow, deep arcs in and out of the dolls' bodies. Made of soft wood for ease of handling, they may have been better than yielding flesh, yet they were helpless before a blade honed sharp as a night bird's cry. The assassin sneers, and you laugh too. "Wait—wait!" says the doll-maker. His shock has settled, and only now does his breath seem to return. He flings aside the thing he had been tending so carefully within the ritual circle and backs away. "I can fill your void… I am telling you, I can help you!" The assassin sneers again. Whatever vows and oaths those with death before their eyes may make, they are not to be believed. Into the knees and thighs of the last doll—arms thrust out like a reanimated corpse, hopping as it walked—the dagger drives, again and again. As the round ball-joints slip out of true, the doll, unable to bear its own weight, topples; the sight, fittingly enough, is like a puppet collapsing with its strings cut. No need to drag it out any longer. The assassin kills the doll-maker, who is absorbed in some scheme, working the ritual circle. Quickly, and without loose ends. But something is wrong. This is the story of an assassin and a doll-maker. If, once the ending has been tied off, the assassin who killed the doll-maker remains alone in the workshop, then who is "you" within it? Who am I, watching all of this? When it opened its eyes, the doll-maker's final work, the one that had stood at the center of the ritual circle—that was itself. In a body resembling the other dolls yet sturdier and more solid, and at the same time more supple and more free, it looked down at the floor. One of the dead—dribbling scarlet in fitful gouts from throat and mouth—was the doll-maker's corpse. The other—without a single wound, eyes rolled back—was the assassin. His face looked somehow off. A face reflected in a mirror is, after all, flipped left to right. It was the rare experience of beholding itself from outside itself for the first time in its life. What am I doing over there? the doll thought. It imagined gasping, drawing in a breath, but its throat would not budge. Its chest did not swell. Its nostrils did not flare, nor did its belly heave. What am I to do from here on? it thought. That "from here on," it already knew. This was the story of a dead doll-maker and an assassin who had, for some reason, become a doll. A memory of a past one wished to undo. The time had come to stop remembering. Coming to itself, the doll turned its head toward a sound from outside. Beyond the window, clear slanting threads gathered stitch by stitch, then poured down as if a hole had been punched in the sky. The rain, soon coming down in sheets, hammered at the window and the walls of the room. But could it get inside the house? Looking at the wall, the doll noticed that the two streams of water were different in color. What flowed outside was clear. What flowed within, fouling the floor, was murky and unclean. The room was drenched in blood. Those who seemed to be the original owners of that substance—or parts of them—lay strewn about, sparing neither furnishings nor walls nor floor. The doll resolved, for now, to leave this house. When it reached the doorway and stretched out a hand, the back of the hand, the wrist, the grip—all of it was smeared with blood. Within it the doll could see the difference between blood that had been scattered and blood that had been splashed, blood that had run down and dripped, blood gone stiff and blood gone dry, blood that had beaded and blood that had congealed. It came to it anew that it had killed everyone in the room, every last one. A fact is simply a fact. Not a trace of needless sentiment or lingering feeling remains. It pulled the door open and stepped into the corridor, but the house only revealed yet another wall and window and shutter, and beyond them a wall and an inner courtyard and a floor and a corridor stretching on. It twisted its head left and right, but could not tell which way was out. The doll crossed back over the path it had trodden and approached the window, where rainwater still streamed in profusion. It took a firm grip on a long piece of junk rolling about nearby. Perhaps because it had applied force in the wrong way, its fingers bent into a strange shape. An ominous sound came from the thumb. The doll fixed its gaze on them, set the arrangement of the five fingers that made up its fist back in order, and gripped the object again. It meant to swing it and clear a path through the window. And then it stood there, blankly looking at its own hand. Wood and steel, brass, and unknown materials drawn from all manner of living things and things that had never lived… If the workshop's other dolls were trifling handicraft, the one at the center of the ritual circle was the single masterwork, the great piece. It was the most intricate, the most powerful, the most beautiful doll, into which the doll-maker had poured his skill without reserve. And yet—whence this void? For a moment the doll admired the way that, each time it curled and spread its fingers, each time it tensed and released, the various taut-drawn strings and the assorted pieces hung upon them meshed and moved. The doll threw away the object it held. Then, with its bare hand, it struck the glass window directly.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main1_Content_1: A cool wind laden with raindrops rushed into the room, each gust vying to be first. Like jets of water that strike the bowl of a ladle, collide at its center, and leap back up, the fierce winds tangled among themselves and fell upon the various light objects and furnishings near the sill. Something flew off, something toppled, and a commotion broke out; the thick rain that came clamoring in through the broken hole soaked this and that in an instant. The door at the back, shuddering at the bone-freezing chill, slammed shut with a bang! For an ordinary person it would have been a stimulus vivid and brilliant enough to startle them and, for a moment, steep them in an inexplicable sense of release. It was a situation in which one ought to relish that surge of the five senses, as when a cunningly crafted dish is laid upon the tongue. And yet the doll only approached the window in silence. When it gripped the sill and bore down, shards of glass crunched beneath its palm. Pressing its weight onto its braced hand, it cleared the ledge, but, not knowing in what shape or where its two legs were set, it pitched into the bare ground in a heap. It tried to right its posture, but the more it tried, the more the oddly misfired efforts only repeated themselves. The doll rolled over and over, striking the ground again and again with various parts of its body. Mud caked all over it. Fist-sized clods of earth, twigs, fallen leaves, and sedge clung to and dropped from the skin of wood and steel and brass, over and over. And yet it was not cold. It did not hurt. The doll simply could not know anything at all. It could hear the sound of the falling rain, but when the drops ran down its eyes and wet the bridge of its nose, its features did not so much as wince. There was no sensation of water shattering against bare skin. When a thick drop falling from the eaves struck it square in the eyes, it felt no urge to blink. Everything was dull and flavorless. It was merely loud. The sound of rain. That fretful tune, ceaselessly chewed over without the slightest change in pitch, grated on its temper. The doll took shelter beneath the eaves, out of the rain. And it looked at the little puddle pooled at its feet. On the surface an unreadable stain had built up thickly, forming a shimmering pattern. Standing as it was, bending neither knee nor waist, the doll tried to stir the puddle and fell again. It crushed the puddle flat with its body and once more pawned half of itself to the world of the rain's sound. Letting both arms hang, it raised one leg and hooked it against the wall, drew the other up to its shoulder and braced it beneath its trunk. Using its arms to lift its upper body, it had to go through a stretch of trial and error. Rising to its feet without knowing what shape its limbs were in, which of them lay beneath which, was quite a grueling task. It was unlike fighting. In a fight there was a clear enemy, and a weapon to reach that enemy, and the arrangement and sequence of one's own limbs connected to it—so one had only to think it through and carry it out. But righting one's own posture alone, refining one's own movement, was hard enough to cramp the whole of one's mind. But what kind of experience was it, to have a cramp? When it returned to its place, the puddle—its level a little lower now—was waiting for the doll. It had gone still again, belying the stirring it had taken, yet the risen pattern had not vanished. If anything, once the muddy water settled, it grew clearer. The doll quietly leaned its head toward the pattern. The pattern grew larger. When it tilted its head, the pattern moved to one side. When it tilted the other way, it shifted accordingly. When it drew its head back, the pattern grew steadily smaller. That pattern was not, in fact, a pattern. It was the thing pulling its own body up out of the puddle. When it sank back down, it heard the clatter of light things from somewhere. It looked and found, at its side, a string of masks carved from wood. A hole had been bored through one corner of each and a cord run through it, the whole hung at the waist. The one hung at the very front—the mask of a brightly smiling person—the doll picked up flatly. Then, as though it could not make up its mind, it threaded it back onto the cord. "Is this me?" The doll looked at its idle hand. The back of it, sunk in the cold mud, was bent flush against the forearm. It worked the fingers it could not see, but all that came was a slick, somehow unfamiliar sound, like rubbing a fruit left to soak in a stream. It was all like that. Seen and heard, but nothing felt. Neither cold nor sodden. Nothing pinched or pressed or throbbed anywhere. No hot breath felt through the sound of the rain, no pounding beat of a heart. More dangerous was the doll's own manner of recalling such things. It seemed almost like an attempt to rummage through a text written in an untongued language and fish out words. But can the sensation of one's heart dropping be reconstructed without sensation? Can the feeling of something in the mind being stung and gouged be reproduced without feeling? How long would it take to forget it all? {IMAGE} "Is this me now?" said the doll. The repeated sound was not that of a human throat but of something in nature. Rain pouring down, a pebble rolling down a slope, a pestle pounding grain… And yet there is something within that voice. It is still there. It was there. It was there once? The doll hurriedly put on a mask. It was the broadly smiling wooden mask it had drawn out earlier. Wearing it, it mirrored its appearance in the puddle again. A person who looked happy appeared. "Is this truly me?" With its hand it unfastened another mask and donned it. This expression was a little harder to read. The corners of the eyes drooped low and the line of the mouth turned crookedly down. The carver's skill had depicted even something on the verge of trickling from the scrunched eyes and nose. This, then, was a person who looked unhappy. "No. It is not me." said the doll. That hand, almost spiteful, yanked the mask off and let it fall. Once again there appeared a roundish something with no expression and nothing at all, slick as the surface of an egg. "It is not me." the doll repeated. "It is a husk. An empty thing. A hollow thing…." said the doll, looking at what was reflected in the puddle. "It is Shell."
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main1_Short: One by one, it lays mask after mask over the face in the puddle. If neither the smile nor the tears belong to it, what remains inside the empty shell?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main2_Content_0: "A monster spawned by the doll-maker's senile greed!" An ominous rumor drifted about the place. As a rule it is the monster's cry, not its true nature, the villain's renown rather than the villain, that frightens most—and rumor alone was enough to ruin a once-bustling village. Since it was a village made up of the peddlers and drifters who habitually trail after an artisan, it grew all the more fragile once its center of gravity was gone. It was nearer, in truth, to a cluster of mud huts and storehouses raised around his mansion by people who bought and sold such things as fine timber, copper hammers and chisels, coarse sand, and blocks of marble cut square and smoothed white as bean curd. Every last one of them vanished in a hurry once the doll-maker's comings and goings ceased. Fearing to be caught in the eye of the living doll—the mad doll that wandered about with its victims' garments wound around its body—they would not set foot in the area. But there are always those whose ears, for one reason or another, are dull to rumor. "Do you not know what kind of place this has become?" "Of course I do!" the old man answered cheerfully. And so saying, he moved his feet toward the side from which the voice had come. Shell drew its body back, gathering close the layers of garments wound about it, but seeing the old man's face it held its ground. The two eyelids, shriveled inward and collapsed, were stained black like dried fruit peel. The staff in one hand had worn white—both the tip that scraped the ground and the grip held in the hand—rubbed bare by the grime of much handling. "And yet today it is awfully quiet." The old man came closer, sweeping his staff to feel out the path ahead. "Where has everyone gone? Around this time of year the ones hauling wares to show the doll-maker would be in full swing…." "This place has been abandoned." Shell did not bother to disguise its flat, pitchless voice. As things stood, threatening with a voice like that seemed likely to help drive off the unwelcome guest. And as it did so, it gazed intently at the old man before it—that was a lie. At some point that had become impossible for Shell: to gaze was impossible. To listen attentively, to pay heed, to give one's heart—impossible. What remained was merely a bisected perception, or ignorance. Seeing or not seeing, hearing or not hearing… With a body that had no eyelids it had to imagine closing its eyes, with a body that had no ear-holes it had to imagine stopping its ears, and so force its senses back to life. Otherwise, at some point it could not even tell what it was looking at, what stood before or behind what, what was moving or still. It was to prevent this, if nothing else, that it had settled into the mansion. It had to comb through the texts kept there and find out whether what had been done to it could be undone. It had to return to its original body as soon as possible. And it had not the slightest intention of recounting any of this in detail to the unwelcome guest before it. "After a plague swept through, the people all fled." Folding and unfolding the arm that gripped its weapon, Shell reckoned the old man was lucky. Had he been a man with two sound eyes—the sort who, even from that distance, would have looked at Shell's body, sensed something amiss, and spread the rumor—it would have made a corpse of him the moment he came into sight. "If you'd rather not go hungry yourself, be off elsewhere." "A plague, you say!… Are you all right, sir?" "The poison has all drained out." It struck Shell, suddenly, that it was not uncomfortable just now. Not uncomfortably—and, above all, skillfully and naturally—it was telling lies. Even with a body whose voice issued from a mouth without a single hole bored in it, whose ball-joints—not covered by a single layer of skin—creaked all day long. Was it really so undisturbing that the one before it could not see it? But did the phrase "not uncomfortable" even fit this case? A word meaning "not uncomfortable" seemed to have once been in its head, but it could not remember it. "Someone's standing guard to keep folk out, so don't come anywhere near." "You're a rare kind soul these days… oof." Shell watched the old man wipe his brow and bend his legs. A hand groped backward, feeling out a spot. He set his backside fully down upon a low rock and let the strength out of his legs. Whew. A sigh of relief escaped the old man's mouth. Shell understood that he had just sat down, and interpreted sitting down before someone as meaning he had no intention of leaving anytime soon. But why? Shell drew the well-whetted knife. With a sidelong glance it scouted for a place to bury the corpse. Sprinkle quicklime over it in the burial and it would even keep wild animals from digging it up.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main2_Content_1: "You'd best hurry off before the sun goes down—" The old man, smiling broadly, turned his head toward the side where Shell's voice had come from. "—you thought just that, didn't you, without meaning to!" Empty eyelids, curled inward. So whether the sun set or not, the old man—still steeped in his own private darkness—grinned playfully, but Shell could grasp neither that smile nor the true intent behind his deliberately turning his face squarely toward it. So it stepped forward. It raised the hand gripping the knife before its chest. "I came thinking I might tell folk what I'd newly learned, and earn a coin or two for it in return…." The old man let out a low sigh. "A wasted trip. Do you happen to know where Master doll-maker is staying?" There was no reason to answer. Had Shell still been human it would have prattled some reassurance that it would soon bring them together, but for the one it was now—with a brain of wood and a belly of brass—that was beyond it. Now it had only to bring the knife straight down… Shell quietly withdrew its arm. He'd meant to tell what he'd newly learned and be paid for it? Then did that mean the old man before it had been about to disclose something that might be of use to the doll-maker? More specifically, knowledge that contributed to perfecting his craft or some technique—or to grasping its nature? Shell fully withdrew the knife and pressed it to its side. "You had something to tell the doll-maker?" "It's a tale many would find interesting, and not him alone… Have you heard of Murung, the Peach-Blossom Haven?" Shell looked at the old man. And it felt that it ought, perhaps, to do something while answering. In the past, while answering or listening to another's words, it seemed it had naturally done, or not done, something… But it merely spoke flatly. "I have heard of it—" For an instant it thought its words could be twisted, by their intonation, into two entirely different meanings, but it felt no need to correct them. "—that strange world made of things that exist nowhere under heaven." "Ah, but what if, within it, you could have a single wish—any wish at all—granted?" The old man chuckled and rubbed his two hands together. At the sight of him hunching his body, Shell looked him over to see if he was ailing somewhere. It would be a disaster if he dropped dead before getting to the heart of it. "A wish?" "I mean to say there is a way to grant any wish whatsoever, using the power of Murung." At that point, Shell watched its own arm stretch out to seize the old man's wrist. Gripping and twisting the spot where the various smallish bones interlocked seemed appropriate. It was the most efficient way to coax knowledge out of others, and all the more so since it had taken this body. But in this case there was no need for such a procedure. Shell's absent eyes surveyed the old man's appearance once more. His shabby figure, the bundle slung over his shoulder paltry, and blind besides. Above all, when he was telling all of it freely now, was it not enough simply to listen well? Shell never once realized for itself by what a strange process it had arrived at so sensible a conclusion. "Do you know the specific method for granting a wish?" "Whether you'd call it specific I can't say, but every last rumor going around, I've packed in here." The old man tapped his temple with a finger whose knuckles stood out in roughly even ridges. "By one account, Murung is not merely some wonderland but the estate of a certain master, and at his will that boundless power leaps and plays." Shell listened without nodding, without offering any prompt, without chiming in agreement. "And so, to grant a wish, they say one can tame that power by seeking out the master and bringing him down. But…." The old man drew it out. Shell waited. Doing nothing. "You too seem to have some wish of your own, do you?" "Who hasn't one?" There had been a someone who would have parried so glibly, but the Shell here and now was not it. So Shell simply went on being just as it was. Neither cold nor warm, not knowing where its limbs were hooked or touching or not touching, simply looking at the old man. So nothing more happened—until the old man abruptly read Shell's presence and, with sightless eyes, reached out his hand for that hand, and drew Shell's hand before him. "What are you doing." "Let me have a look…." Their words crossed, but the old man's actions did not change. Shell watched its own hand, set without any sensation into the old man's grip, be examined inch by inch. "It's just to see what sort of person you are. No ill meant." In that instant Shell knew it had made a mistake. Just because its own body could not truly handle anything and savor the feel of it, it had underestimated others as well. An old man trying to read the palm-lines of a doll made of wood, steel, and brass—could he possibly fail to notice the wrongness of it? Unaware of the shape of conspiracy stealthily forming right under his nose, the old man was diligently rubbing the hard, flat hand he had drawn before his eyes. Clasping it with both hands, drawing his thumbs together to stroke the center, his lips quirking once; sweeping again, long, down to where the roots of the fingers were, the bridge of his nose crinkling once; pressing hard with his stiffened fingertips, only to meet firm skin—no, a husk—that did not yield in the slightest, his brow furrowing in fits. Shell drew its knife again. After all, it had to kill him before he spread false rumors all over the village. But before that, the old man opened his mouth. "It'd be a downright lie to say I wasn't startled—" Imperturbably, he went on to unfold whatever came next. Hearing it, Shell felt nothing. As with very nearly every moment up to now, it thought, all the same, that it ought to feel something. But it felt nothing.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main2_Content_2:
"That means…"
Here and there across the old man's calloused grip, the skin grazed white for a glimpse. That was because Shell had snatched its hand back.
"……it was 'a negative meaning,' then."
To its own absent ears, too, that voice was creaking. It was awkward and absurd, but it was the most precise expression it could summon in that moment. The old man had meant those words in a negative sense. It could not have been otherwise!
"Surely not!"
"You deny it?"
The old man stuck out his tongue and then tucked it back into his mouth, as if this were some kind of game.
"It was the honest truth, not one mote of falsehood—I never said a word worth denying!"
Shell moved its feet to set its stance. The ground beneath its heels had more of a slope than it expected, and its body tottered. Nor was that all. The stray notions came pelting down all the same—that one arm should waver, that it ought to blink its eyes often, that it should purse its lips and flare its nose a little more frequently, or narrow it. Why did those notions obstruct its decision at this very moment?
It merely chewed over the prior grounds on which it had decided not to kill the old man.
First, it had gained a breakthrough in another direction. The way to seize the power of Murung. That might well be a faster, easier road than wrestling alone with the doll-maker's texts in solitude. By whatever means, so long as it could recover its body. But once the body returned, it would need a base where it could put down roots and live. To that end it had to guard, above all, against too ghastly a rumor spreading. Then again, it might yet have business at the doll-maker's mansion, and if word got out that a blind, harmless traveler had been murdered nearby, the cleanup would grow troublesome. That left, then, one thing to do and one thing not to do, each.
It must not kill the old man before it, and it must leave this place at once and prepare to set out for Murung.

"You've fallen suddenly silent… is something the matter?"
the old man asked, concerned. The cheekbones drawn taut along his sunken eye-sockets quivered.
"Are you unwell, perhaps? The plague after all, is it still…?"
Since it had resolved to leave this place anyway, there was no reason to humor the old man further. Shell made a shooing gesture meaning simply go, then realized, with a start, that a blind man could have no way of seeing it. To fail to understand something, to fail to do something one ought to do, to fail even to perceive that absence… since taking on the figure of a doll it had not rubbed shoulders with many, but these were things it had keenly known every time it exchanged words. To think that, here in this moment, it was the other way around—unbelievably, its heart seemed to grow a little less uncomfortable.
"Go now, old man."
Shell rose, making a deliberately loud noise. It hinted that, having said all it had to say, it would now end the conversation and take its leave. Too convoluted though it was, it presumed offhand that the old man had understood well enough. And so, as it turned its back and drew away, it meant to ignore outright whatever else the old man might prattle—when, all at once, it stopped in its tracks.
"May your journey be an uncomfortable-free one."
A greeting without a single flaw to fault—save that it was delivered with the neck, not the body, cranked a full hundred and eighty degrees backward.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main2_Short: A blind old man's hands read the shell like a stranger's script. Before the rumor of a faraway land that grants every wish — must it really set out?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main3_Content_0: This place, Murung, is full of astonishing things. One day Shell's fingers wrote just that. The string of characters carved into the dirt looked unfamiliar. Shell waited a moment, then rummaged through the masks at its side. Ignoring the creak of its joints, what it drew out was an expression with the brows knit and the lips working in a fretful curl—the brooding mask, then. Shell erased what it had written before. This place, Murung, is full of marvelous and curious and novel things. To that it added one more line. Quite truly, exceedingly astonishing. Shell did not cock its head, or make a sound with its mouth, or scratch the back of its head. It merely looked. There did not seem to be a problem with each individual form, starting with the handwriting. If anything was awkward, it was a matter of the overall structure, or of the very form that is writing. "In its past, the conception would have been different." A voice without emotion, like a boulder rolling. Enduring the wrongness of it, Shell went on speaking. "The present it remembers. Looking at the sky, it remembers that it was not a color like that; hearing the birdsong, it remembers that it was not a sound like that." It remembers how different something out there is from something here. And what remains? Shell looked at Murung's sky and remembered the fact that its color and form differed from the sky outside, yet it could not engrave that impression into memory. The feel of soil burrowing between the toes, the warmth borne on the wind, the unfamiliar scent rising within it—for an impression of something to remain, in the end, such things had to be there. But how important a matter was it, to leave that impression behind? Shell took up a fistful of Murung's soil. Some of it slipped out between the fingers, and some packed firm in the grip. Seeing the rim of it rise into ridges and furrows along the fingers, some food came to mind. It had been a thin wheat-flour dough stuffed with this and that and sealed, then warmed with hot steam, and the past one had enjoyed it well enough. Had there been something good in its taste, or shape, or smell? The shape of the clod molded by hand had something about it that struck one as crude and unpleasant rather than appetizing. It had no wish to put such a thing in its mouth. "Everything in the present need not be marvelous, or curious, or novel." Shell unfastened the brooding expression and put on another mask. One with the mouth pursed small and the eyes lit bright—the expression of insight. "To know the past and remember how different it is from the present—that alone is enough." said Shell. "It is enough to know for certain what life it will return to once it recovers its body." And so, in place of Murung's soil or trees or aggressive beasts, Shell settled on something to observe. The adventurers and expedition parties—or simple wanderers—who had flowed into Murung from elsewhere in reality. It helps to hide far off and observe the passersby. The Shell of one day wrote that in the dirt. Writing down what helps was itself a help. It occurred to it that ordinary folk tend to organize their thoughts in that way. And with its free hand it was busily choosing a mask from those slung at its side. It picked the plainest of all—the blank one, mouth and eyes and cheeks and the bridge of the nose all fixed flat in their proper places. That one seemed least likely to cause trouble. Shell imagined that if someone were, say, a passerby exploring an unknown world, and resting in their lodging, were to discover some expressionless wooden puppet glaring at them from a thicket, and the reaction they might then show. Since nothing came to mind, that was enough. "That's exactly what I'm saying…!" "I said it then too, but…." "Who's arguing? What I want to do is…." "Everything we've gained in here…!" The expression of a passerby in conversation was a truly astonishing material. Actual matter, by its nature, must have its fitting form and use determined for it. You cannot make a kite from a lump of iron, nor weaponry from mulberry paper. But a passerby's expression, merely by being pushed and pulled here and there about the face from within, could turn as severe as the blade of a fodder-chopper, or, conversely, as soft as long-worn cloth. Several times Shell, eavesdropping on the passersby's talk, laid out several masks in a neat row. Each time their countenances changed, it readied itself to whip the right masks on and off and on again. Having a knack for switching its weapon from sheath to hand and into an opponent's throat in the blink of an eye, it thought this would make good practice for loosening its creaking limbs—but it was a miscalculation. It was a rout.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main3_Content_1: "I was too… earlier…." "I did nothing right either, friend. I'm sorry…." "Quit your sour faces, drink this and let it go!…" Shell watched the various passersby. Those who laughed and chattered for all sorts of reasons, then lost their temper and quarreled at last as if they'd never see one another again, only to somehow smooth over the grudge and press on into the depths of Murung—it watched them. And afterward, what lay sprawled before Shell was always several masks reduced to ruin, their rims gone ragged from being gripped and hung and unfastened over and over. "With its handiwork, that skill cannot be imitated." Even if it were impossible, Shell thought, it must always study and adopt the face fitting to the situation. That, as its past self had done, must become a 'habit.' But why? Shell thought, without standing and gazing blankly into the distance or propping its chin on its hand. Why is it important to inquire into why a certain passerby wears a certain expression in a certain situation? Shell's fingers scratched at the dirt. "It must remember the state it is to return to." A voice chopped into pieces, without high or low. Presently the doll's hand, clenched into a fist, was seen to approach its own face. Watching to see what it meant to do, the inside of the grip—where thumb and forefinger curled—lingered a while at the mouth, then came down as if nothing had happened. Faintly it occurred to it that this was some ritual connected to a certain alien voice, but it was far from the subject it was thinking on now. "If it can naturally imitate their situations and their reactions to those situations, that is good preparation before recovering its body." Merely knowing how its past self had behaved was not enough, Shell thought. Those things were always somewhat… off. Clumsy. There had been, for instance, a moment that came to mind upon seeing people eating. It was the memory of something it had enjoyed eating. You scooped a water-dwelling fish from the water, let it drain, and killed it. Then, when you set it over a fire, presently there came the smell and sound of some substance burning and scorching. When the fish's insides hardened white and firm, you chewed it hard in your mouth until it was small and slick enough, then swallowed it down your throat. The name attached to that procedure Shell still remembered: grilled fish—in the old days the mere word would make the inside of one's mouth less dry. Why? Was there, objectively, anything to prefer in that whole series of steps? The passersby's talk had grown noticeably scarcer. There was little to gain from observing only the monotonous sound of food being chewed. Leaving the spot where it had hidden, Shell sought out a quiet waterside. In Murung's streams too lived various fish. Shell looked at them quietly. Perhaps if it broke the procedure of grilled fish into smaller steps, it might likewise find the appeal its past self had known. First the urgent task was hauling out what was in the water. The fish's narrow, pointed snout and the hook pierced through it sprang up over the water's surface along the line, tracing a parabola. The fish dropped to the ground, thrashing, shaking the thin flesh of its flanks. Splashing wet water dampened the soil and rocks. "The hand, then, toward the side where the tail is." Shell mimed the motion from memory. It seized the fish's tail—more precisely the slightly fleshy root inside it—and swung the fish. Once you'd stunned it by slamming its head down hard, it was time to prepare to eat. Carry it within the walls, and the household folk waiting for their meal would welcome you. Finding it hard to chew over the several passersby's expressions all at once, it decided to skip that part. In fact, eating it coated in seasoning they'd marinated in advance was good too, but better still was eating it grilled raw and clumsily by the stream out of hunger. It was nonsense, but in the old days it seemed to have made sense. There were other various moments to do with grilled fish, but all of them were crude. So much so that it could not tell why they remained in its head even now. For instance, if you didn't pick the bones out well, you had to keep mumbling a tangle of white flesh and spines in your mouth, twisting your lips and curling your tongue. And then you couldn't escape a scolding from your elders. But it could not tell why you got scolded. The entrails taste bad, but a fresh-caught, quickly-cleaned one tastes good—a sentence like that came to mind. But what was the difference between the former taste and the latter? It tried to recall the two different tastes, but the thought went nowhere. Yet what is thought? Does thought have some shape or direction? How can thought 'go' anywhere? Bitter, astringent, warm, mushy… at some point these became words that could not modify taste. Just as thought goes nowhere, so too does taste. Where is taste? What color is taste?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main3_Content_2: If taste were the fish, then the body—the real body, not the present doll—was the fishing line. Once that connection was severed, it could not be reeled in. Thinking this, Shell saw that the stream had gone clean and empty. The fish had vanished without a trace. With nothing left to look at, it straightened its waist. Just as one hand had come up to its mouth clenched in a fist, this time one hand lay open across its lower belly. It occurred to it that it should part its absent lips and press them together again. It had to rub its absent tongue hard against its absent palate and release it to make a sound. "Something seems like it should be there." Shell went back to the hideout from which it watched the passersby. They were, however, still eating. They even seemed to be putting off the end of it, as though loath to let something go. Surely by now they had been giving off a smell in every direction, and the bustling clatter must have spread as far as it would spread. Shell watched as the group—having gone to the trouble of moving as a single body—all alike let down their guard and grew slack. "Be ambushed at a time like that and it's a disaster." Shell guessed that they had been hungry. Come to think of it, the present body did not have only drawbacks compared to its past self. Hunger, for one, was an example. To think that merely eating a single meal threw them into such disorder—even granting that the sensation brought a fleeting pleasure, how could one not count it among a passerby's greatest weaknesses? By contrast, was not the doll's body, which could fight without eating or drinking, already past the point of having overcome the hardest foe to surmount—the foe that is oneself? Perhaps Shell started to set its thoughts in order by writing, then stopped. It was too clear to capture in writing. "Perhaps there is no need to return everything to how it was." Watching Murung's explorers, it came to know their weaknesses—above all, weaknesses of its own that its past self had never known. If one tamed the boundless power and used it to grant a wish, then rather than merely restoring its former life by rote, might it not be possible to excise the harmful elements within—weaknesses such as hunger—and only then be reborn as a better self? And on top of that, it would be possible to add the knowledge it had gained from contemplating a passerby's weaknesses and make it a strength of its own. "It thought the same in its past as an assassin." said Shell. By now its thoughts came obediently into order without its having to write them in the dirt. "It is, after all, a body that lives by killing others; perhaps it does not need rich feelings and moods in every petty particular." The goal of recovering its original body and life was, fundamentally, a compromise with reality. It was a bare-minimum stubbornness, trying to make all that had happened simply not have happened. But if, through what it had newly realized after becoming Shell, it could envision and seize an even more complete life, was that not a thing beyond reproach? Through such a chain of thoughts Shell at last grew not-uncomfortable. Without a sound it rummaged at its side and donned the mask fitting to the situation. The happily smiling expression, however, soon slipped out of place. One side of the mask, near the ear, gradually came apart and at last cracked and fell off. Hung by only one corner, the mask, turned upside down, slid askew down Shell's cheek and the line of its mouth. The corners of the mouth, which by rights ought to have been smiling broadly, hung there swaying, bent instead toward the floor. {IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main3_Short: From a distance it copies down the laughter of others, their quarrels, the warmth of a shared meal. That taste it can recall but never savor — will it ever win it back?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main4_Content_0: Watching the wanderers of Murung and observing their talk, one could pick up various names. As is usual with things overheard, most were no more than phonetic strings—so blurred and out of context that you couldn't even tell how they were written. The dear things they had left behind outside, the reasons they had to go back… But there were also names that held currency only within Murung, not outside, and that recurred frequently at that. The Guide—'Polaris,' that unfamiliar ring—was one of them. "The Guide will save this place…." "For our sake she gladly gave up the power of gold." Among those who spoke that name were strange and wondrous creatures of which one could scarcely tell where they ate or where they looked upon the world. And now and then, wanderers who had plainly come from outside would keep up their hasty, premature praise of the great feat that he—no, perhaps she—was yet to accomplish. "Long live the Guide, long live Polaris!" "Long live Polaris our savior!" On the other hand, there were those who, quite the opposite, clicked their tongues in disbelief. "It's far too reckless a thing—there's no way it'll go right." "If only it were that simple." "She's a gentle, kind soul, but… does even she truly know all that she's doing, I wonder." And so it heard and remembered a rich array of opinions from a diversity of people with a diversity of viewpoints. Gradually Polaris came to seem not just a string of unfamiliar phonetic letters but someone's name. It grew accustomed, too, to the fact that most wanderers, for some reason, called Murung the dream world, and that the Guide's plan was to mingle and merge that place with reality. Now there remained only Shell's own appraisal of all it had grasped, and the decision that would follow from that appraisal. "If Murung and reality are mingled, what will happen?" said Shell. The answer had been set from the start. "This has nothing to do with it." In the past something might have come to mind, but now the very attempt to form such a thought was uncomfortable. It has no interest, the expression came suddenly to its absent tongue-tip. A declaration that it was not merely a matter of no relation but that no such perception even formed—a declaration that, to its past self, might have sounded a touch aggressive. Yet now it was a genuinely upright declaration. The thought came that as reality merged with Murung, its various properties and aspects would be corrupted and at last vanish, but it still sounded like incomprehensible fuss. Someone might have a person left behind in reality, or some precious thing they had to protect. But would a solitary assassin turned into a doll have such a thing? Did it matter if reality was twisted and deformed? To the Shell of now, that was like a passerby who, sitting by a river plinking little stones into the water, abruptly turned to a passing stranger and asked— "May I keep throwing this stone?" And why not? "If reality changes, that may even be the better thing." Shell rummaged at its waist. The masks grazing its hand rustled lightly, like grains beaded along a stalk. One in particular—a single mask, set apart from the others so it could be told front from back—was a nuisance. It was a relief that this was not the thing it had to draw out now. Shell's hand seized what it sought. A mask with both eyes closed, the expression sunk in deep thought.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main4_Content_1:
"If reality changes to be like this place, then for one who has more or less adapted here, it is an improvement."
A body in which only thought and memory remained, after impression and feeling had vanished, found it hard at any rate to weigh the right and wrong of a thing. As with the metaphor of the one throwing stones by the river, here too it needed something to liken it to… a knife, for instance? Shell looked at the folding knife affixed along its forearm like a mantis's foreleg. After entering Murung and felling enemy after enemy with it, the edge had, sure enough, gone crooked. Before long it would have to find something to serve as a whetstone, re-hone it, and set it straight.
And so the corruption of reality was no different at all from the methodology of handling this knife.
A long-used knife discoloring and warping is natural and bound to happen, yet at the same time it is the better thing for it not to happen. Likewise, in reality too there must be any number of objects that were there from the start and are natural, yet had better vanish. For instance, all the petty customs and habits that the Shell of now found hard to understand even when it tried to recall them. That when doing a certain thing you must turn your head, or conversely must not; that you must hold your arm inward, or conversely thrust it outward… One day Shell began to sort through such acts and non-acts one by one and write them in the dirt. At first it was a light sort of rehearsal. The intent was to set its thoughts in order in advance, before recovering its body. But more and more it became clear that it could not stop at merely that.
It wrote and wrote, and still the next item kept coming. The space between seated Shell's two legs was not enough. The dirt began to fill, in spans and feet and bolts and their powers, with the writhing letters trailing across it. Given only time and space, it would have stretched on for leagues more. The writing hand grew so caked in soil that little grains lodged among the wood and steel and brass, yet it wrote and wrote without end. The things to do and the things not to do, slotted into some situation, some moment, some place, some passerby or among some passersby—allowed at one time but not another… It was like trying to measure the depth of a bottomless pit by laying out the length of oneself from head to sole.

"How did the past it commit all this idle prattle to memory, leaving nothing out?"
The Shell of that time, having stopped writing, spread both arms and lay prone on the ground. Then it stretched its two legs likewise, without a bend anywhere. In that state, body shoving limbs and limbs shoving body—a bizarre but at any rate effective eraser—it scoured for a while over the string of characters it had written. The long harrowing, swept like five folding fans, raked clean to the very bottom of the dirt, and what was left was a flat surface feigning innocence, no writing or anything to be found. Shell straightened its neck, raised its shoulders and chest, then planted its elbows to the ground as well. Using the rebound it threw its lower body over its head and drove its heels down. Finally, bracing on those planted feet, it drew in its belly, then the rest of its trunk above the waist, and stood up in a straight line. The movement did not strike it as particularly strange. What drew its absent gaze more was the sight of the dirt, once cluttered with all those petty things to do and not to do, gone spotless. It looked almost—though the word was hard to recall by now—unburdened.
"Again: this has nothing to do with it."
said Shell, who, having broken free of the past, was once more contemplating the Guide's plan. It still wore the thinking mask.
"If such things are devoured by the laws of Murung and vanish, that is a positive thing."
Fundamentally it was a matter of adaptation. If Shell really became not just its restored former body but a more complete self with various unnecessary elements removed, there was no rule that reality, too, could not become a more complete reality by that much.
"In the end, the conclusion of the day it recalled 'grilled fish' holds."
Quotation marks—nothing strange about them, framing a word nothing strange about it, yet unable to shed a certain stiff aloofness—stood out from Shell's pitchless voice. At some point they had come to feel less uncomfortable. They even sounded correct.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main4_Content_2:
"No condition, no supporting grounds, has changed. It did not refuse any of those doubts."
There were things it had braced itself to find grueling on entering Murung. Someone lording over their turf, say, or cutting a path by killing vicious and bizarre creatures. Once it actually went through them, such things were rather easy. Harder were the things that could not be cut with a knife or smashed with a fist—fighting thoughts that had neither shape nor mass.
"It struck against them doggedly, dissolving and subduing them. It pressed on to seek the answer."
To seek the answer meant, in the end, to reject everything else that was not the answer. It meant honing the scope of thought and verification ever narrower. The hardened deliberation was already a far cry from the Shell that had struggled to recall the taste of 'grilled fish.'
"It will recover the body alone and discard the unnecessary senses."
The thinking mask now vanished into the string at its side. What it needed was the mask of one squinting an eye and glaring into the distance—a hunter drawing a bow, a general surveying the battlefield. Wearing it, Shell elaborated.
"To exclude sensation altogether would impair efficiency. For immediate judgment and response, a rudimentary degree of smell and touch should be preserved… but at least where emotion or mood reaches a level that affects one's words and deeds, having none is an improvement."
Was this a view that had sprung up out of nowhere? Not at all. Shell had seen it. Expedition parties roaming all over Murung making wrong choices, overcome by their own passions. There were, for instance, those who, attacking some strange creature born of Murung, let its young one go rather than killing it. Because the young one circled nearby shrieking, other predators flocked in, and after the melee they met an expedition party that had failed to clear the area quickly enough, and bared their teeth and lunged. There were also those it had seen who stubbornly insisted on keeping company with a member of their party even after he had taken an irrecoverable wound. In the end a loss that could have been settled with the death of one passerby swelled into the deaths of several—alas and alack. And the foremost of those who showed such traits was even the passerby who, taking Shell for drowning—who, more precisely, had mistakenly believed so—had come rushing up to save it.
A complete stranger it had never met, and one with a doll's body at that.

"In that respect, feeling and impression are weaknesses."
The thought it had once held in the past—the fact that it had thought such a thought—grew firmer still. Since it was a body that killed others and might die at any moment itself, a rich sensibility was an obstacle. The past Shell, for some reason, never thought to resolve that conflict, and only kept forcing an impossible goal upon itself and whipping itself on—but that too was surely nothing more than the foolery of a patient suffering the affliction that is emotion. Having now lost its body temporarily, on the contrary, it had come to perceive the problem more clearly and excise it in a single stroke.
"And so it will have the body alone."
It was a fact it had resolved upon a hundred times over, but for that very reason it struck it as that important a matter. Once again Shell's reasoning was thus tied off. Its heart grew yet more not-uncomfortable. There was no more cause to doubt anything, or to long for it achingly, or to chew over why the present without it could only be the more agonizing. As the memory of the dirt with all its writing erased was laid over the scene of this very moment, sure enough the word unburdened came to mind. The seasoned hunter's mask draped over its face now vanished too. The time had come at last for the terminus of all its deliberation, the rightful ending of Shell—to draw out and don the mask of the happily smiling passerby.
Some while ago, after its corner had cracked and fallen off, Shell had boiled the swim-bladders or grasses of Murung, or at least things that could serve as such, and made a kind of glue. It smeared that on the mask's corner and joined the fallen pieces back on. Then, threading it apart from the other masks so air could circulate, it carried it about. It was letting it dry well so it could be used again. Shell's fingers, grazing the string, came to rest on the upside-down mask. Groping, it touched one corner… but it was not yet time.
"Nothing will change."
said Shell, parting and rejoining the fingers it had brought up before its absent eyes. The half-dried glue, traveling back and forth between the two fingers, kept dividing into small, endlessly sticky strands.
"Its thinking is sound, logical, and without a single doubt."
Shell's fingers did not stop. The undried glue stuck and pulled apart ever faster, making a fretful sound. The sound of the rain it had heard on that day—the day it became newly aware of itself as a doll—came to mind. It could not quite remember why it had been so shaken to see the doll's form it had taken for a pattern reflected in the puddle.
"It made the right decision."
At its waist, the smiling mask, its corner still not fully dried, swayed in silence.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main4_Short: Cut away all that is unneeded, keep only the body — so it vows. Yet at its hip the cracked, mended smiling mask sways upside down.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main5_Content_0:
Shell was observing the passersby. There was no reason not to. Outside, when it had a body, it had been different, the thought came. First there was something it wanted to do, and then the things it had to do attached themselves in petty clusters. Sorting them out one by one in its head, it set what to do now, what to do later, what it might someday do. Now that everything had gone dull and numb, however, there was nothing. Only things that there was no need not to do, things that caused no trouble if done, came to mind. This was to be liberated. From what?
Not having to think such thoughts any further—that, indeed, is liberation.
Shell observed the passersby chatting as they ate. They must have been quite close, for even as they chewed their food and drank their water the flower of conversation would not easily wilt. Laughing; laughing behind a covered mouth; laughing while slapping a knee. Laughing with the head bowed, breath held; laughing while clutching the belly. The past Shell had found such things enjoyable. Remembered them as enjoyable. Remembered the fact that it had to remember them as enjoyable.
"This is a compulsion."
said Shell. The impulse to keep ruminating on a certain choice even while knowing that only one path is right. A compulsion hard to shake had existed even in the days it had a body. But had it survived even after becoming a wooden puppet? The string at its waist clattered. Leaving alone the one smiling-faced mask still not dried, Shell's fingertips swept over the rest. The masks twitched as if to slip free of the cord that strung them. This was a writhing. The last resistance of faint impressions that had never become thought, that had lost any foothold of sensation since it became a doll. That was the last hill the compulsion now tormenting Shell had to lean on. If only it could ignore that, it would no longer have to doubt. It would no longer have to doubt the fact that it no longer had to doubt.
"It is no longer shaken."
Shell lowered its body. An aberration had occurred mid-speech. A trembling transmitted along the ground. Beyond the passersby it watched, shadows glimpsed faintly; twigs violently snapping, toppling, scattering. For those absorbed in cooking and eating in blithe peace, the signs were noticed far too late. One—probably the one serving as the pack's pathfinder and scout—came bursting into the clearing. Behind it, two, three, four….
In an instant the area was surrounded by Murung's monsters, great and small.

Shell looked at the ones whose whole bodies were ink-black. The ones that had turned that way were always larger and fiercer than the other monsters. Shell turned its head to survey the passersby flailing under the ambush, caught in the middle of letting their guard down. One who, fumbling to don armor, dropped it and struck his own instep first, squeezing out a tear; one who saw that the black beasts blocked the space between where his weapon lay and where he stood; one who, for the urgent moment, rose trembling while gripping a tool used for working wood or soft metal… It was a sorry spectacle.
Likely not a single one would survive.
"Those things have not yet seen it."
said Shell.
"It must get away before it is forced to engage."
said Shell.
"Whether they die or not has nothing to do with it."
