said Shell. Why?
Why was it prattling these obvious things as if a hole the size of a bowl had been bored in its jaw?
Shell looked at the monsters of Murung filling every direction, gradually tightening the cordon with forelegs and snouts and tendrils and all manner of other grotesque somethings thrust forward. Within it, it also saw the passersby drawing together, hesitant, their faces gone white. Someone's face along the way looked familiar. Was it, perhaps, that very passerby? The one who had tried to help Shell when it thought it was drowning? It was not certain. Shell drew one mask from its waist and tried it on. It was the expression of a thinking person, but the matter remained as murky as ever. Since losing its face, the countenances of passersby all struck it like the underdrawing of something sketched in one and the same style.
"To the campfire!"
"Don't lose heart! Show your fear and they'll swarm in at once!"
"Hold your weapons steady! Meet their eyes! Keep your backs straight!"
The passersby had, before anyone knew it, packed themselves into a single clump, backs against one another. They looked like the last spoonful of rice left in a bowl—no, like a little ball of stray grains scraped and pressed together. Such a small, shrunken formation belonged not on a battlefield but atop a spit-wet spoon, between a pair of chopsticks gathered demurely before the mouth.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main5_Content_1:
"Is there a reason it must not leave?"
said Shell, wearing the thinking expression.
"If Murung's beasts grow used to humans, learn how to deal with them, they turn more belligerent."
The first reason came without much difficulty. But it was that flimsy.
"And so, for the sake of the future, it might be better to eliminate this pack now?"
The black beasts were belligerent and savage regardless. That, by all it had observed, was their own innate nature. To take on present danger over a circumstance that would not change anyway? It was a pitiful excuse that wouldn't fool even a toddler engrossed in playing soldier.
An excuse? Whose? For what? To deceive whom?
Erasing the thought that had branched off to the side—the doubt—Shell posited a question it had not yet resolved for itself. A question must not be avoided. It must be struck and dissolved. But why must a question be resolved while a doubt must be suppressed? And why must a compulsion be covered over and rejected? Is there any procedure by which the consciousness that doubts whether one of its own impulses is a worthless compulsion or, conversely, the sole remaining shard of truth, can itself prove which is true? Shell's mind, on the verge of nearly reaching some speculative theorem, commanded itself to rise on its two feet. It was about to turn its back and leave this place—the one and only correct action by all its grounds so far. Were it not for the second reason that occurred in that instant.
Shell looked at its own leg. The round joint serving as one knee creaked laboriously. Below the knee the shin, the sole, slowly stretched out, unable to find its place. Spread across the joint's visible and unseen parts alike was a mixture, thick as moss, of dark-red bloodstains and grime, dust, nameless grains and sticky film—and it was, literally, holding Shell back by the ankle. Come to think of it, for some time it had not been conscious of the creaking sound its body made whenever it moved. That had simply come back, that was all.
"At the doll-maker's workshop, it never managed to learn how to repair a doll."
Trimming materials themselves it had grown handy at. But properly mending wood, steel, brass, and other unknown materials already assembled into a doll's form, while preserving their proportions, function, and shape—that it could not even attempt. Scrubbing its whole body with a big whetstone would hardly make the gouges heal of their own accord and the warped joints return to true.
"It cannot maintain itself effectively."
That was where the second reason it must keep the passersby before it alive lay. Shell looked at one of those facing off against the beasts—someone gripping carving knives, a plane, an awl, a chisel, and conspicuously trembling. Earlier, in the talk they had exchanged, that one had called himself a carpenter and a blacksmith and 'the man who does all the other odd jobs that take some handiness.' Why he had been smiling while making so wretched a declaration before others it could not tell, but that was not the point.
"It is a favorable situation to propose a bargain."
Shell took a step. One foot, then another, on and on.
"If it keeps those cornered ones from dying, it can then prick their sense of indebtedness and have them repair its body."
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main5_Content_2:
Meanwhile, at the very outer edge of the cordon hemming in the passersby, there was a small beast that kept sniffing at an unsettling sense of wrongness.
It belatedly discovered Shell, which had approached without giving off the smell a living thing would give off, without making the sound a living thing would make. As it drew in a great breath to sound off like a little warning bell, the folding knife affixed along Shell's forearm ran straight through it, crown to lower jaw. Unable to make even the sound of its eyes going slack, unable to let out the dead air of its swollen lungs, it expired on the spot, and presently Shell's heel trod down its corpse. Springing in a single bound, it broke through the cordon and landed. The people watched the thing that had suddenly leapt in against the backdrop of the sky and appeared before them. It was a wooden puppet. A wooden puppet that moved, wearing a sedge hat and old garments wound all about its body.
And it began to butcher the black monsters indiscriminately.
The wooden puppet hurled itself at a large individual, conspicuous, likely the leader. Leaping up, it clasped the nape—no, wound its legs and clung. Drawing one of the single-edge knives at its waist, it drove it into the beast's temple up to the hilt. Seeming about to fall, unable to withstand the bucking of the thing now thrashing madly, it twisted its body in midair as if weightless and swapped the roles of arms and legs. Biting and gripping the beast's thick mane with teeth and hand at once, it drew its soles up close to its own waist and pulled out the other single-edge knife. Before it could find a use for that one, however, the knife that had torn into the beast's temple seemed to have done its work. With the wooden puppet still hanging from it, the beast, its pupils gone slack, crashed down with a din to rival thunder. Caught up in it, the puppet failed to extricate itself from the beast's body in time.
When the dust cleared, the wooden puppet stood impaled on its own knife, run through front to back. Before the passersby themselves could grasp exactly what that meant, the head of wood and steel and brass lifted as though nothing were amiss. It surveyed, one by one, the other beasts that came charging up bravely even after seeing their leader die a violent death. The puppet's upper body, trying to rise, lifted off the ground and then flopped back down with a wet slap. Those watching thought the puppet did not realize, for some reason, that its own leg was pinned beneath the monster's corpse. That was in fact so, but it meant nothing.
The first beast to charge became mere rust on the blade. That was after the wooden puppet had grasped the knife run through its own body—not the hilt but the keen, gleaming blade—and pulled it out. The second beast bit down on the puppet's head, but its jaw could go no further and spun uselessly. Out came the sort of sound made when a metal object strikes a shield. The puppet, its neck half wrenched out, stabbed one arm into the beast's jaw. Driving in between the narrow wedge of the jawbone, it gripped directly the muscle that supports the tongue and the teeth. With no chance even to pull free, it held fast the mouth of the beast writhing in agony, then, using that as a fulcrum, threw its weight in and hauled its own body up from beneath the corpse pinning it. It got out the pelvis and thigh, the knee, the shin—but to its astonishment everything below the ankle was still beneath the leader beast's body. Even with such a body, however, it succeeded in pulling itself free like a fish leaping up through cleaving water. In this process there was a beast left with a crash as nothing but an empty hole where its jaw had once been. Its eyes reflected the knife coming toward it. The puppet, having struck off the head, spread its huddled arm, and the beast's lower jaw, lodged on like some nasty brace, broke off and rolled away.
It went on like that.
When its arm or shoulder was bitten, it stabbed its own ankle with the knife at its side. With the knife thus driven into its leg, it slashed open the belly of the beast bearing down on its upper body. If something came at it from behind, it took the blow with its trunk and fell. Then, working its limbs like an overturned spider, it instead clutched the thing to its back and clung on. Belly, eyes, crown, brow, ankle… the wooden puppet's strikes rushed unerringly toward such places without a single wasted swing. The high-spirited beasts were gradually driven onto the defensive. One by one they dropped. Watching the spectacle, the people lost themselves in it, until at some point they thought the stillness of the clearing had been broken. From a pot set over the fire, some kind of broth dish was bubbling and boiling over. That sound had broken the silence.
In the midst of a mountain of corpses and a sea of blood, there stood a wooden puppet, quietly holding its ground.
{IMAGE}

"See to the wounded."
While no one could readily open their mouths, the puppet—which had staggered over, found its sole, and refitted it—gave that order. The one bleeding profusely seemed only then to notice his own wound, and sank down with a groan. His companions flung aside the weapons they held and rushed frantically to support him. Each carrying an armload of whatever rags they could use to bind him for the moment….
"Th-th-thank…."
A passerby making a strange sobbing sound approached Shell. It was, fittingly enough, the artisan, still gripping carving knives and the like in a hand gone white.
"Th-thank… thank you."
Shell watched the passerby rest his gaze for a moment where its own eyes might be, then hastily look away. It neither tilted its head nor shrugged its shoulders, and only when a foreign sensation grazed its head did it realize: that it was still wearing the thinking mask. Having finished thinking and moved to action, Shell decided to put on the mask of insight. But since it had entered the fight after the insight, it decided to put on the mask of anger or resolve. Since the battle was already over and things were ordinary now, it decided to put on the blank mask.
The artisan watched Shell drawing out and donning and unfastening every one of these masks in turn, his face become some strange expression that defied all description.
"Are you all right?"
Shell, for its part, could not tell why it had perceived the man before it as that figure from memory, the one who had tried to save Shell when it was swept up in the current. Looking again, he was nothing like him. He wore no robe, and his build and his voice were different. There was not a single thing in common. Was it because a passerby's face was, after all, hard to tell apart? Well, it hardly mattered. From the start it had been for the sake of a bargain.
"Repair it."
said Shell, ignoring the man who kept babbling, at a loss. It pointed to the marks of battle carved all over the doll, all the misaligned and crooked parts. Shell's finger pointed at the monsters' corpses dissolving into a whitish powder, and the party left in the clearing, and lastly at itself.
"Since it saved you, repair it."
The artisan, as if it went without saying, hurriedly led it to the worktable.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main5_Short: It tells itself again and again that this is no concern of its own — and still its feet carry it toward the dying. That last compulsion it believed it had shed: was it ever only a compulsion?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main6_Content_0:
They must have been family to one another, Shell thought. The ones who had repaired its body as payment for killing the black beasts, that is. Whether brothers or brother and sister, they were surely no mere acquaintances, it thought. They had kept trying to hold Shell back even after both sides had attained their ends, prattling all day in easy good nature, opening their mouths on any topic at all—and finding them tiresome, it had left long since. Even after becoming alone again, Shell was, however, thinking of them. It was chewing over the word family, which had risen to mind by way of them. Out there, in a world caught in the throes of war, it had had two kinds of family. A first family and a later family.
Before becoming an assassin, there had been a household that took it in—this was the later family.
Before entering that household, from the time it had opened its eyes and was haltingly learning to speak, there had been a separate family—this was the first family. This, of course, was not ordinary. But just how out of the ordinary it was, it could not tell.
With a doll's body like the one it had now, it could tell all the less.
"It had a name too."
In the work of killing people for money there was no real need to exchange names. When swapping words face to face, "friend," "you there," "hey," "say there," and the like were enough. If a label was needed in some other respect, it might be needed, but a name of one's own was unnecessary. Long before that, however—from the days when it could recall only scenes blurred of all context before and after, and a voice settling faintly upon the ear—there had been a name someone had given it. Now no one knows it. The only one who knows, however, wishes to forget it.
Is there—or is there not, or might there be, or might there not be—any ground on which one may deem that there is, or is not, or might be, or might not be, a reason it should not?

"It is a strange impulse."
Shell came to know itself anew. The doubt, the impulse, the compulsion in its head concerning impression and emotion—it informed itself, whenever the chance arose, that these were improper. And so it verified, and went back to the start to verify again, and undid the whole of that process, ceaselessly knowing itself thinking the thoughts of the self that thought the thoughts of the past. With its former body it would have had a dizzy spell, Shell reckoned. But was a dizzy spell something one had? Or was it something one saw or heard? Or felt? Seeing is done with the eyes, hearing with the ears.
But feeling—with where, and how, in the body, was it done?
"It knows that this is a yoke from which there is no escaping."
The doubt, and the doubting of that doubt, were both like that. The self thinking of the self thinking of the self thinking of the self… This is that, that is the other, the other is what… Even children's verses that latch onto the tail of a word and drag it out, on and on, must end someday. Shell's own resolve was needed.
"It will have the body alone. Excising the unnecessary senses and emotions."
said Shell.
"It will stop this thinking."
The act of ruminating on a past one could not return to was of no use and nothing but harm. The doll's palm spread flat and lay before Shell's eyes. The masterwork of a certain infamous doll-maker, made of wood and steel and brass and other unknown materials. Its purpose, however, had been only to make a sturdy, long-lasting wooden puppet, not to reproduce the whole perception and sensation of a living person. That palm was like looking at an anvil in a smithy. It would be no surprise to set upon it a casting belching pale steam and hammer it, wringing out a clangorous shriek of crying iron.
Shell recalled the passerby it had last met before entering Murung. The blind old man. Abruptly declaring he would read its palm, he had taken the doll's hand, kneaded it a good while, and then—what had he said?
"It was a negative meaning."
Shell heard an unfamiliar voice. Someone was in an uncomfortable situation. They were angry.
"He knew that plight and was mocking it. After taking hold of a doll's husk, hard and like a human nowhere, and confirming it."
The thought that there was a person nearby sent one hand toward the string of masks. It seemed a good idea to don the plainest, flattest one. Shell looked all around and fixed a mask's corner to its face, but there was no one. Not a living passerby, let alone any of Murung's beasts great or small, lingered nearby.
"An insolent fellow, a brazen old man."
Then could this voice possibly be—
"How dare a blind beggar!"
—Shell's very own?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main6_Content_1:
The doll's hand, which had been spread out in bewilderment, clasped its chest. Somewhere within the body—made of large parts and small, parts that pulled and pushed, parts that caught or slid—was uncomfortable. Somewhere inside the chest periodically took on a foreign sensation as if welling up with force and pushing it out, then returned to normal, over and over. Had something been thrown out of true while the artisan worked on it? Enduring that novel pressure for a time, Shell barely made out exactly what act it was.
"It thinks, just now, that its heart is racing."
The moment it is spoken aloud and written down, a spell that has strayed from the proper course loses its power. From the start nothing had throbbed or fluttered or busily borne clear scarlet streams of blood through the whole body, playing the rhythm of life. There was merely one doll of wood and steel and brass and all manner of other unknown materials, standing forlornly there.
"My, how long has it been since such a thing?"
Just after becoming a doll it had often happened. Even after entering Murung it had attempted it a number of times. Back then it had had a vague goal of recovering body and sensation and emotion all together. So, to revive the easiest one to rouse—the sensation of hot or cold or pain or sting—it had gone about doing all sorts of foolish things. It had thrown itself into a fierce blaze with its own feet, had surrendered its body to a raging current and rammed bare-bodied into every last boulder on the riverbed, hoping to feel something. But the illusion of "racing" it felt just now was a thousandfold more intense than anything it had felt back then, anything it had believed it felt while its body was being filthily destroyed.
The blank mask fell from Shell's face. There was no leisure to pick it up again. At a feeling so utterly unfamiliar, Shell was afraid. It failed even to notice for itself that the very act of being afraid was, likewise, alien. It was the same principle by which a freshly drawn picture may be aware of its own shape and color yet cannot recognize the brush that drew it.
"Such a thing, such a bewildering thing, is, after all, unneeded."
said Shell. It was the quickest way to settle the delusion that it seemed to have a body. But at the same time it was the most dangerous way.

Was the body it sought to recover sturdier than the present wooden puppet? More consistent? If recovering sensation and emotion was a thing that threw it into confusion, and if for that reason there was no need to recover them, then what reason was there to insist with one's own feet on crawling back into that coughing, limping, tottering, clammy, mushy body of flesh and blood, that sack of skin, in the first place?
"It is enough to know for certain what life it will return to once it recovers its body."
Shell chewed over what it had said. But knowing only what life—that is, where—it would return to was not enough. It lacked the reason for going to that somewhere, the 'why' it had set its heart on it.
"It desired a body."
Shell tried to recall its self just after becoming a doll, which felt by now impossibly remote. But had the body itself been the final and complete aim? Or no more than a part of what it truly wanted? Had that first tacit—yet surely inherent—perception merely faded, little by little, over time? While it roamed Murung in a doll's body?
"Its memories no longer felt like its own. To escape that loss, it set a goal."
said Shell, striving to recall Shell.
"It set the goal of wanting to go back, of wanting to recover its body. So what it truly wanted to recover was memory."
What is memory? It is what the present experience becomes in time. If memory derives from experience in that way, then from what does experience derive? The fusion of objective facts and stimuli given in each moment. The subjective sensation and emotion that form from that make memory. They make not some moment but 'that day on which one felt a certain feeling'—a certain moment that, quite literally, remains in memory.
"Then in the end it wants to recover sensation and emotion."
Shell went on.
"It does not want to recover the body alone. It wants to return to a whole body and a whole life that makes experience and memory through sensation and emotion, and goes on savoring them."
At that point, it was inevitable that the 'Guide's' plan, which it had once brushed off as trivial, came to mind. Shell imagined reality permanently corrupted, swallowed into Murung by her will. The feeling of its heart racing came back again. But what followed was not anticipation or yearning but the very opposite impression. Anger, rejection, refusal.
The name 'Polaris' no longer seemed as indifferent as before.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main6_Content_2:
"It desires reality exactly as it remembers it."
said Shell.
"It wants every moment it once felt to be there again."
There was no need to go all the way to the memory of 'grilled fish.' Wearing a doll's body now, forcing itself to chew over the memory of cooking a particular food with particular people in a particular way only made it seem the more vague and bewildering. What the present it could understand were far smaller, slighter—no, frankly, more trivial moments.
The stretch after waking from a sweet sleep, the cold water poured over the back of the neck in the heat, the moment of rubbing the nose after a satisfying sneeze, the moment the inner jaw twinged after putting something sour in the mouth—even the memory of a fever rising on the brow, or stubbing a toe somewhere, or shuddering as coarse sand kept filling up the inside of a shoe, came to mind. It missed all those moments.
"But those were uncomfortable moments."
Shell sank into the impression of its view blurring milky. In Murung, too, rain fell now and then.
"The past it would rather have thrown away such sensation and emotion. It deemed them cumbersome."
And the result lived and breathed here, now. No—it neither lived nor breathed. It merely existed. It was simply drifting along among 'things one might as well do' instead of things one wanted to do, among all the 'not-uncomfortable' moments instead of comfortable ones. It was vanishing little by little, like raindrops seeping into the loose soil of the earth and disappearing.
How little time had passed since it became a doll, and already the reason it had desired a body was fading. It could not remember the taste of 'grilled fish.' Being unable to recite its own name at once no longer struck it as a grave matter. If it remained a doll wandering Murung—a place like a dream, in the words of the other wanderers—it would only worsen, never mend of itself. And even if it recovered its body in the meantime, were reality, the reality it would return to, to be devoured and deformed by Murung, then would the memories from before it became Shell not be lost forever, beyond all reclaiming?

"Does it desire that?"
Shell, taking the rain, fiddled with the string at its waist. The corner of that single upside-down mask, the smiling face, was still sticky. To be sunk in this kind of thought just when it believed it had broken through every deliberation and rooted out every doubt—and with rain falling, no less, to keep the glue from drying—perhaps the day it would wear that mask had grown more distant still. Paradoxically, however, Shell realized exactly when it would mean to wear that mask, and whether, even when that moment finally came, it would not wear it but fling it away.
The glue will dry only when that day comes. Only on the day it recovers the whole reality and whole body, the life, it had aimed for. In that moment it will draw out the smiling mask and gaze at it. Not merely look, but gaze deeply, attentively, with sorrow-steeped eyes. And then it will dash it to the bare ground. Without the aid of any mask, it will move its own face and make its own expression. It will smile so brightly that no mask in all this world could ever imitate it.
"No."
Shell thought for a moment.
"It... that."
Then it hesitated again, but not as long as before. It went on.
"I do not desire that."
{IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main6_Short: The moment it believes a heart that cannot beat has beaten, a name it tried to forget stirs awake in the rain. What it truly longs for — will the day come when the mask comes off?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main7_Content_0:
"This here…."
The blind old man wet his lips and took on a thoroughly earnest expression. The person whose hand he held snickered, yet waited for the words to come.
"This is the second most peculiar palm this old man has ever felt!"
"And who's the first, that you'd say so?"
the one with the held hand asked at once. It was a touch awkward to say so of oneself, but his palm was, even by his own reckoning, an utter shambles. He had suffered much hardship from childhood, and somehow all that calamity had collected in his palm. Banged somewhere, or struck, or cut, or burned… and as a matter of course the lines too were snapped clean off here and there, or ran off to odd places. So those who had learned palmistry only by rote memorization of books would, after peering down at his palm a good while,
"You will travel to the place you came from, and in that season a beggar turned overnight-rich will envy you, and you shall be unpopular for long, long years."
spout some such preposterous nonsense, time without number. And yet a hand made like that was not the first but the second?

"Their name this old man did not ask, even so."
said the blind old man.
"And had I asked, they'd not have told me… When first I took hold of it, like this."
He gripped the other's hand with force. Using his two thumbs like dowsing rods seeking a vein of water, he swept from this end of the palm to that.
"It was uncommonly hard."
"They'd suffered much too, perhaps, and so the calluses had set in like that?"
"At first this old man thought so as well, but…."
The blind old man clicked his tongue in wonder. Then he swung one hand out in a broad arc. Spread it wide. As if sketching a shield that a battlefield general must bear upon his two arms, upon his shoulders.
"It was not flesh but plainly a plate. A plate, a shell, a husk… the very stuff of the body was such."
It had been as he ran his hand over it again to go on with his account. Along the folds of the grip, the parts that curled in, the parts that spread open, what he felt was not skin and blood-vessels but smooth wooden boards and cool metal.

"And so what did you say?"
The one whose hand was held had by now forgotten even about his own palm and was caught up in the tale.
"This old man told them just what he felt."
Sensing, perhaps, something of the other's excitement, the blind old man too answered with a gentle smile.
"It can't have been pleasant to hear—"
For what more could be said of a hand lacking its most important lines? A note of worry crept into his voice.
"—were you not done some harm?"
"That, on feeling it, I was not the least bit startled—that this old man could never say, not though it cost me my life, but…."
The old man went on, chuckling.
"Flat and hard is, in the end, but a backdrop; what, then, could a palm with no lines be, if not a boundless possibility to become anything at all?"
"You said so in earnest?"
"Aye. What had befallen them this old man knew not, but—"
The blind old man nodded.
"—since it all rests on what one makes of the days to come, they are boundlessly free, able to ponder and decide every part of themselves by their own will."
He went on, smiling brightly.
"And so I told them they bore the most powerful palm under heaven and earth, one destined to grow great in time—such a seed, that they bore, indeed I did…."

After a few more words were exchanged and they parted, it was of course self-evident that our 'shambles-palm' was quite moved by the blind old man's heartwarming tale. All that remained was to spread the fine story far and wide across the world, and so he seized upon the very first friend he met and poured out his impassioned account, only….
"That's just him gripping a wooden hand and going on with the damn thing, isn't it?"
And so, after an exchange of the sort of fervent epithets and expressions that only the closest of friends can lob at each other—though one could not exactly say it came unaccompanied by serious slander and abuse of the other's very character—the conversation at last found its footing again. Having composed himself, shambles-palm asked his friend once more for a more fitting appreciation of this moving tale, only….
"But that old man—"
he said with a smirk.
"—in the end he couldn't read your palm at all, just rattled on like that and bolted, eh?"
A heartwarming tale, if you like, of a certain blind old man and a person turned into a doll—and an empty one, if you like, at that.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main7_Short: A flat, hard palm without a single line. Whether to call it a hollow lack or a boundless possibility — who gets to decide?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main8_Content_0:
—plunged into the flames.
The wooden parts held up well. The doll-maker must have coated and treated them with something, for the fire would not catch. What became a problem, rather, was the metal. The fittings, originally assembled so precisely that not even a single needle's stitch could pass between them, swelled and grew fat. They began to push and pull mercilessly at the doll's other parts.
—felt something foreign somewhere inside its arms and legs.
Soon that progressed into the perception of something somewhere snapping apart. When it tried to turn its neck, something jutted out from the nape. When it gripped it, a glowing-red shard of metal bored into its palm. It seemed as though something might be felt.

—flung its body from a high place.
Nature abhors a vacuum. The wind rushed in to fill the gap between its belly and the ground below, but it stirred no feeling at all. It only watched the ground grow linearly larger in proportion to the distance traveled. Soon the moment of impact came.
—believed, in the instant it slammed into the dirt, that it felt something.
Merciless impact was dealt in order—head, chest, shoulder, belly. Cracks as large as full-grown grubs were engraved all over its body. Something broke off and flew somewhere. The outline of the body it had drawn in its mind was ruined. But only for a moment. Amid everything dull and blunt, it deemed there was something, some feeling, in between—but only for a moment. As dough kneaded with water fills its own gaps, the something that had glittered was swallowed up. A dough utterly numb and unfeeling, on which no color could be laid, simply boundlessly wide and deep and soft, seized it and would not let go.
—thought that there had been an improvement, all the same.

—lay with its back beneath a toppling tree.
Its face was fully buried, yet suddenly there came the perception that it could still see ahead. It thought about how that was possible, but it had never seen anything from the start. An absent face, absent eyes. The illusion of seeing was nothing but a pretense.
—hurriedly dug its way out of the ground.
Because to maintain such a state—one in which it should not see yet went on seeing—seemed likely to carry it further still from its own goal.

—leapt into the very midst of the black beasts.
It was the least stirring of all so far. Savage beasts that would not flee, and a wooden puppet that showed no mercy—between them, an invincible polynomial that nullified every sign of operation. One that, faster and more perfunctorily than any other expression, yielded nothing but zero.
—could think of nothing.
Looking at the bite-marks and claw-marks strewn all over its body, the broken forearm and the twisted ankle.

—surrendered its body to the fierce current.
Each time it reached the places where the current coiled and spewed pure-white foam—where it churned inside and out most violently and destroyed the particles within—it tried to concentrate, but could not.
—did not know how to concentrate on anything. Perhaps it had never known from the start.
"Huh?"
It was someone's gasp. A woman draped in a robe. Young, she paced the riverbank, rubbing her own forearm as if tense. And then she saw something being swept downstream on the current.
—knew its body had stopped. It was still not enough to feel anything, yet its body had wedged against a great boulder. Just like that, before the eyes of the robed someone watching, it had ceased flowing along with the current.
—mustered what remained of its four limbs and tried to move away from the rock.
"I-it's alive."
And she saw clearly the way it twitched so. Startled, she opened her mouth.
"It's not just a doll."
The young woman drew toward the riverbank, hesitant.
"Are you all right? However did you come to… Wait just a moment!"
—heard not a word. It only strained to wrench its body from the boulder. Seeking once more the path to be battered this way and that and destroyed, like a mere mote of dust within the fierce current.
"I'll bring the rest of the brothers and sisters!… We'll save you, so just hold on a little."
—was freed from the rock around then. And so it began to drift away again. And as it did, it thought. She had clearly meant to come toward —. More than that, she had tried to save it. Why? It could not tell. What if it had been the reverse? —imagined the woman it had just seen drowning to death in the water. Yet no impulse arose that it ought to do something.
But who was —, again?

"—is Shell."
said the wooden puppet, flung over and over by the current. It had just barely recalled that name again.
"It is Shell."
it repeated.
"It must not forget. It must not forget."
What it had forgotten, and how much, whether it had even forgotten the very fact that it had forgotten—not knowing, it repeated, over and over.
"It must not forget…."
In the roaring current, a vow that no one would hear rang out.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Main8_Short: Into the fire, from a great height, into the raging current it hurls its own body, waiting to feel something at last. That name the current sweeps away — can it still hold on?
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Short0_Content: Shell returned to the puppeteer's workshop where it all began, and discovered a lingering fragment of memory. Within it, an unfamiliar swordsman swung his blade toward a pitch-black void. He was not cutting down enemies. He was merely channeling the emptiness within himself into his blade. From that swordsman, Shell felt an inexplicable familiarity.
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Short0_Title: The Blade That Embraces the Void
ui.TravelerStory_Husk_Short1_Content: Somewhere in the Rapids, Shell came face to face with a crystal that reflected his form with perfect clarity. What he could not bear was not the sight of himself as a puppet, but the fact that the sight forcibly summoned memories of when he had once been human. The blade moved first. The crystal cracked and scattered, yet even each of the scattered shards held that same face. Breaking it made only the crystal disappear; he who remembered that face still remained in place.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main1_Content_0:
The aftermath that Edgar IV's untimely death brought was plain as day. The throne, suddenly left vacant with no heir named, stirred up the charming little flutters of many a "perhaps even I?" — and this, in the end, summoned a power struggle that was far from charming and that left stains everywhere, plenty of them, and hard to scrub out. When the fierce infighting finally subsided, the one who became the next king was Rogit, a distant relative of the late king.
Having ascended the throne, however, Rogit I had no intention of letting the country he had inherited coast along as it always had. The Kingdom of Draconia would be different from how it had been in Edgar IV's day. It had to be. He scrapped the advancement of gunpowder technology that had been pushed as state policy. Along with that, he resolved to redirect the enormous sums that had been poured into armaments toward more moderate ends — honing commerce and diplomacy, say. In the course of this, the dissolution of the Royal Guard — which, though it bore the name "the army that protects the king," had been deformed into a private band of soldiers thrown at the assassination of enemy dignitaries and the removal of political rivals — was, then, surely inevitable.
Yet not even Rogit I could flatly reject the whole of the Kingdom of Draconia's history up to that point. Especially when it came to the most outstanding talent of all — Lacerta, say, renowned as the Top Hand of the Royal Guard — that was all the more true.

"Is that so…."
Lacerta lowered his posture. What rang through the audience chamber was the voice of Rogit I — the one who, by the natural order of things, should have become his new sovereign.
"You are surely aware once more, are you not, that you possess every qualification?"
The king continued, not hiding his disappointment.
"The kingdom's garrison is still needed. You could become its commander. Or how about a lifetime appointment as head of the intelligence agency that is to be newly established?"
"I apologize."
Lacerta answered as humbly and concisely as he could.
"Even as your servant, this is a matter I have deliberated deeply and decided upon — please grant me your leave."
"Is your will so firm, then…."
Rogit I suddenly realized that he had been edging his body forward, as if to rise little by little from the throne. That was how much he regretted the decision.
"But to take no settlement money at all, and to go off into the deep mountains to live as a hunter — is such seclusion truly necessary?"
Without lifting his bowed head, Lacerta waited in silence for the dissuasion that was sure to follow.
"At the very least, how about a palace-cooperation post — an advisory seat? Exchanging words now and then would be enough. For one such as you, anyone would gladly agree."
"I apologize."
Lacerta answered as humbly and concisely as he could. He worked to appear so.
"Even as your servant, this is a matter I have deliberated deeply and decided upon — please accept my decision."
It goes without saying, but Lacerta was no clockwork device that moved in pursuit of efficiency and gain alone.

He could understand, with his head, Rogit I's decision to build a new country, and the logic that the dissolution of the Royal Guard was indispensable to it. If that was the choice of a new country in a new age, then it could not be helped, he thought. But reason and logic were one thing; the human resistance that welled up, all of a sudden, from his chest was another, and that he could do nothing about. To reduce the authority of the Royal Guard — into which he had poured the entirety of himself — or to rework its selection process, or to reassign its personnel… it was none of that. He no longer wished to remain beneath a new king who had resolved to fasten the first button of his reign by abolishing it outright.
"I have long since ceased to be a free man, and yet I kept behaving like a child and caused my wife far too much worry."
said Lacerta.
"For a while, I want to live an easy life with just the two of us — no other cares to trouble over — self-sufficient in some cabin in the woods."
The king gave no reply, only let out a single sigh. Curiously, it called to mind the wails Lacerta had heard some time before. It had been when he announced the same decision to his subordinates in the Royal Guard — no, his comrades, no, his friends.

"You mean to cut ties with us entirely?"
"No, that's not it…."
"If we can't see you at the palace anymore, and we can't come to visit you either, then what is it if not that, Captain!"
"It's not as though I'm vanishing forever."
Lacerta thought that his face back then must have looked unbecomingly dumbstruck — mouth open, eyes rolling this way and that, flustered…. What had he said to quiet the uproar?
"I am most certainly not trying to hide myself away somewhere because I've come to hate the world. Nor do I have any intention of staying that way forever."
Emerging from the recollection, Lacerta declared once more to the Rogit I before his eyes — the king he had not yet grown fond of, yet who was, on the other hand, the ambitious leader dreaming a new dream for the Kingdom of Draconia, his homeland and the country where everything of his lay.
Who was to say whether a day might come when he would gladly work for him?
"I only wish to catch my breath a little."
"……I understand you well."
Rogit I answered with a nod. It had become clear that no matter how he coaxed and cajoled, he could not change the end of this conversation. The king made a gesture commanding him to withdraw.
"Lacerta, may there be blessings upon the road ahead of you."
"And upon Your Majesty, I pray, may there be boundless glory and prosperity."
Once he had offered his final farewell, he felt unburdened. He left the audience chamber and set off. Now he had to retrieve the belongings he had left in storage.

*
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main1_Content_1:
"…You wish to take those things back again?"
"That's right."
Lacerta was conversing with a low-ranking royal official with whom he had left his belongings.
"What's the matter? Were they stored improperly?"
"Ah — no, sir."
"Or has some new order come down in the meantime?"
A faint unease raised its head in Lacerta's mind. The Royal Guard was gone, but most of the unit's members had been permitted, in recognition of their personal merits, to take their own equipment out with them….
"Has the permit to take such things out been revoked?"
"Th-that's not it. There's nothing at all wrong with your belongings. I merely…."
The official caught the glasses sliding toward the tip of his nose and pushed them back up to his eyes. Having corrected his appearance so, he somehow looked even more hapless than before.
"Merely?"
"Eh — since I'd heard the Top Hand was going off to live in the forest with his wife now, I thought you'd have no more need of such things… so I was carrying out the full return procedure."
The official ducked his head low and apologized.
"My apologies. I'll bring it all out, check it against the list, and return it to you intact."
"See that you do."
When his worry proved to be no more than groundless anxiety, Lacerta's heart grew lighter. And to hear his own new resolve — the life he would spend from now on with his wife — spilling out as rumor from the official's very lips, made it feel real at last. His heart pounded. Just as the Kingdom of Draconia was greeting a new age, now he too, and Iris, his companion, were taking a step into a wholly new life. Toward our home, our life, our promise.
"You're quite the desk-bound bookworm, aren't you?"
"Y-yes?"
When his mood lifted, even idle, meaningless quips came out easily. Lacerta said it with a smile in his eyes.
"To live in the forest hunting wild animals, wouldn't a man need weapons to protect himself all the more, not less? And yet you thought I'd leave 'those things' behind and go."
"Ah…. Ye-yes, yes, you're quite right, sir, yes."
The official kept cocking his head this way and that, yet ran off diligently all the same. He went to fetch once more Lacerta's "those things," which would just now be partway through the storage process.

"What've you come back for this time?"
"The Top Hand's gear — where'd you move it to?"
"Haven't moved it, not yet."
The errand-runner jerked his chin toward the heap. Off to one side was a pile of belongings… no, stacked up almost like a small hill. Rather than stow them somewhere against a wall, the things looked fit to serve as a wall themselves — good enough to build a whole new storehouse out of.
"Good. Round up some men and haul it all back out."
"What — why?"
Their eyes met. The errand-runner tilted his head.
"Weren't the two of 'em gonna wash their hands of it all and live nice and cozy, just the pair of them?"
"He says he's taking it all back just as it is. What am I supposed to say to that?"
The official ran his eyes down the list of Lacerta's belongings he'd drawn up. Firearms, custom explosives, bursting charges, all manner of chemicals and raw materials for synthesizing them, and bullets — blunt-tipped or sharp-tipped, hollow-light or solid-heavy…. It would not have looked out of place swapped for a classified shipping manifest bound for a battlefield rather than one man's stored possessions. The question that rose naturally in his mind — and, right on cue, the laborer voiced it aloud for him.
"What earthly use could all this be to him out there?"
"How should I know."
A hollow laugh escaped his mouth.
"Needs 'em to hunt beasts in the forest and protect himself, or some such… well, whew."
Arms crossed, the errand-runner watched his superior sigh.

"Me, I'm just a lowly clerk who's got nothing whatsoever to do with the Royal Guard. But I keep getting these meddlesome thoughts…."
"I'll bring it right over, sir."
"Hold on a minute — just hold on!"
The official's hand stayed the errand-runner, who was making to slip away with deliberately big, sweeping swings of his arms and legs.
"At a time like this, shouldn't you be asking me what's got me thinking so much?"
"Isn't it obvious what you're thinking, sir?"
The errand-runner crossed his arms again and gave a shrug.
"The missus can't stand this dangerous, blood-reeking stuff, so he means to wash his hands of it. But then he's got to go and pack up every last thing — the kind that fires when you press it, blows up when you touch it, punches through when you shoot it, shatters to bits when you set it off — and lug the whole lot along…. That's not exactly the right frame of mind, is what you're getting at, isn't it?"
As he listened, the official's face went pale. He had been thinking just that, it was true, but….
"It's not that he genuinely wants to be new, to change — he only wants to keep up that pretense for now. And on top of it, the unit's been disbanded anyway, so it suits him fine. Like a man slapped right when he wanted an excuse to cry, he means to use it as a pretext to just up and retire — that's the scheme, isn't it? It's not a wish to change welling up genuinely from the heart."
"You — you're being far too blunt!"
The official wet his lips and stole repeated glances over his shoulder. The glasses-frame, grown heavy with worry, began to dangle at the tip of his nose once more.
"It's hardly our place to be saying this and that about the Top Hand's affairs…."
"I may be penniless and ignorant, sir — none of the Top Hand's deep cultivation in music or art or whatever it is — but I know well enough what becomes of a man who forces himself against his own heart."
The errand-runner took the document from the official's hand and clicked his tongue. They were, of course, a fearsome feast of munitions in their own right, but the spectacle only grew once you looked into the details. None of it was the kind of existing matériel that — its reliability verified — had been folded into the supply system; it was all something or other stamped "specifics unknown." Bullets of unknown specification manufactured by Lacerta's own hand, explosives of unknown specification, machine parts of unknown specification….
"When a man fiddles with stuff like this and a stray spark singes his own hair or scales, that's a fine joke to get a laugh out of everyone. A funny little mishap. But what if that same kind of accident befalls the person most precious to him?"
said the errand-runner.
"Whether it could end then, too, as something to simply laugh off and shake away… that, I truly cannot say."
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main1_Short: A man turns his back on everything and walks into the forest—yet the scent of gunpowder still clings to his hands. Can he really leave it all behind?
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main2_Content_0:
"You call that an excuse!"
At the bellow from the one seated in the chair, the man standing there wobbled and flinched. Head bowed deep, shoulders hunched in, both hands clasped at his navel in a servility that bordered on the abject — he looked less like a subordinate operative who had botched a mission than a schoolboy being scolded before his teacher.
"No, truly, Captain…."
"Truly or not, if you didn't ruin the job, then what was it?"
A clenched fist hammered the desk, and the documents piled atop it jumped soundlessly. They were the records of those who, over the past weeks and months, had doggedly tracked a single lizardman. Not when he was mingled among his comrades and subordinates, nor when he walked through villages thronged with ordinary folk, but when he spent time alone, away from others' eyes — especially when he threw himself into grueling training by himself in the forest where no one was around — that was the moment marked as the perfect one. The perfect moment for what?
For assassinating Lacerta, the commander of the Kingdom of Draconia's Royal Guard, the very paragon all men looked up to for his overwhelming martial power.
"Do you have any idea how much effort we went to, just to find out where a man who's the Top Hand himself trains alone, out of everyone's sight!"
The bellow gave way to the fist, and now to a jabbing finger. Thinking that if he watched a moment longer that finger might not stop at carving through empty air but go on to gouge cleanly into the inside of his eye socket, the subordinate flailed both hands and hastily widened the distance between them.
"No, Captain, truly, I really am being wronged."
"Cut the nonsense!"
"I really didn't do a single thing wrong, I'm telling you!"
A cheeky note of self-defense, tossed out in his utter disarray. That creaking, half-rattled sanity paradoxically lent credence to his sincerity, and the captain — who had been huffing like a bellows about to burst — gradually leaned back against the chair once more.

"Go on, then—"
His coldly settled voice granted a second chance. One hand waved listlessly.
"—out with it, then."
"I planted all the traps real careful, real secret — buried 'em, tied 'em, hid 'em, set 'em, the whole lot!"
That much he'd said before too. If that was the end of his defense, it was time to scratch behind his eyes again….
"I tied branches to my ankles so I'd wipe out my own footprints every time I passed, and worried about any smell coming off my body, so I scrubbed myself raw in the stream, and then smeared and scattered forest leaves and dirt all over myself, made a whole fuss of it the whole way there."
"Mm-hmm."
So far so good. So then — whatever it was — he'd made some mistake after that?
"Didn't you just cover your own tracks well and botch the trap-laying? Otherwise how could he have dodged every last one of them?"
"Well — honestly, I gave it my best, but maybe it wasn't enough…!"
Amid the rambling, unpersuasive babble, the subordinate forced himself to rally. Now was no time to be professing wholesome self-doubt and reflection.
"Maybe it wasn't, but?"
"But the way he moved, it wasn't like he noticed the traps and dodged 'em."
the subordinate appealed earnestly.
"From way off, see — meaning he didn't come anywhere near the traps in the first place, just roamed off along some path, some direction, totally different from the intel we had."
The captain sank into thought. Lizardmen are famed for their keen senses to begin with. Even granting that our flawless Top Hand was renowned for his particular intellectual cast, that wouldn't have dulled his innate nature. But even so, it wasn't something that could be explained. The structure and contents of the prepared traps were a far cry from the level of skewering a single hunk of smoked ham on a spear-tip to catch some boar half-starved for days. They had been made strong enough, and above all fast and small enough, to suit a lizardman's constitution and senses from the start. Other lizardmen who'd been marked for assassination in the past had been left utterly helpless — but never had there been a case of one acting as though he'd spotted the traps from a distance like this.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main2_Content_1: "Spotting from a distance there's no way to know a trap is there — and yet veering off down other paths all over the place…." "Maybe — um. May I say one thing?" The captain gave no answer at all, but the personable subordinate went ahead and mumbled out the rest of his thought on his own. "It's a place where he trains alone, after all…. Couldn't he just have, on a whim that particular day, wandered around all over the place?" A new view. Impudent, but interesting enough that it was hard to dismiss in a breath. The captain cupped his own jaw, then worried for a moment whether some fever had broken out — but, realizing it was the very fist that had just pounded the desk a while ago, was reassured. "He'd prepped the training grounds real thorough all over the place, too. He's a tough one." The subordinate, taking the captain's silence as a lifeline of salvation, fluttered his lips all the more. "Cliffs to hang and strain on, spots to shoot targets from far off, places to climb ropes up and down barehanded…." "Hold on." When the captain cut him off with a sweep of his arm, a strange sound came from the subordinate's throat. It was exactly the sort of sound you'd expect when an outgoing breath, ambushed by a frightened gulp of saliva, makes the windpipe and gullet wring at each other. "Y-yes?" "The cliffs and the ropes… couldn't you have just made those things weaker? Instead of laying out traps and all that." "Oh, come now, Captain." As if he'd been swinging between nightmare and sweet dream in that short span, color returned to the subordinate's face. Had he loosened his grip on sanity a touch more, he looked ready to spread a hand and slap the captain's shoulder — slap, slap. "It's not like you can drag something out into the middle of primeval forest like that, and am I a lizardman myself? How am I supposed to follow him up a place like that and put a knife in him?" He had a point. "Keep talking. He just wandered around, you said?" "Yes — even if it's called a training ground, it's not like someone's standing guard there ordering him do this, do that, is it?" Whether there even existed, in the Kingdom of Draconia — no, anywhere else on the continent — anyone who could openly command such things of Lacerta, other than King Edgar IV, was doubtful. "So he doesn't strictly stick to some order or path — he goes whatever order he feels like, down whatever path he wants, gets there somehow and trains alone, and that's that." "And not knowing that, we laid traps along the one 'path' we'd figured out, and so he dodged them all?" The captain lowered his head. He watched his own two hands fidget at each other in thought. Then he raised his eyes again and glared at the subordinate. "You — you know my temper." Crrr-ack! That kind of inaudible sound seemed to come from the tendons of his wrist and the back of his hand. "If you're just spouting whatever comes to mind…." "But really, truly, he went off down some completely different path way over yonder, I swear!" The subordinate beat at his chest and pleaded, all but sobbing. "They say Lacerta himself is strict to outsiders but jokes around and mingles freely in front of his men, don't they? With no eyes on him anyway, what's so strange about him strolling along — taking paths he hasn't tried, skipping the one that just doesn't sit right with him that day?" It was true enough that the man, hidebound as he was, was not a wholly emotionless battle-maniac. To begin with, there was a rumor that the reason a man who was the Top Hand bothered to throw himself into training alone was precisely that he feared his own such conduct would become silent pressure on the unit members he ordinarily treated with warmth. However much it was training he himself wished to do, with the captain at it right beside them, it was plain his men too would one day end up following along, swallowing the bitter pill. "Well, all right…." The captain drew a breath. A failure was a failure; what remained was cleaning up the aftermath. "Were the traps recovered?" "Not all of 'em — how am I supposed to do it right there beside him while he's coming and going from the grounds and starting his training?" the subordinate added in breathless haste. "The moment I confirmed it'd failed, I came back as fast as I could, hiding my presence. To report to you!" "So you're saying some are still left out there?" The captain sank into thought. Whether Lacerta's next training would come tomorrow or a week from now he didn't know, but perhaps there might be a second chance, he thought. You never know. Maybe his dodging the traps from a distance this time was because some alien scent — one they, being still human, couldn't detect — had wafted off them, and if left alone, that scent would naturally fade, and that would be the moment he'd let down his guard. "Will it be a problem?" "No, you did all you could." said the captain. From here on there was no reason to ride the man too hard. He'd done his level best within his means and improvised. "It's not over yet, so don't let your guard down." For some reason the back of his neck felt tight. The windows were shut tight, yet a chill night wind seemed to blow in through the thin glass. The captain casually drew his coat collar closed. "We'll watch next time, and if it fails again, we can recover them then."
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main2_Content_2:
"There is no next time."
said Lacerta, watching.

He was not, however, inside the same room as them. Nor was he eavesdropping on the two of them with his face mashed flat against the windowpane, nose squashed pug. He was far, far farther away. So far that only his gaze, leveled parallel along the barrel, remained, and it was impossible to actually "hear" the two of them speak.
Could Lacerta overcome that distance with supernaturally keen hearing? He could not.
Could Lacerta read minds, or at least read lips? He could not.
Their purpose was simply obvious. The context of the conversation the two would now be having, its contents, lay plainly visible to him — just as the traces those fellows had erased to the best of their own ability lay plainly visible to the Lacerta of the training ground that day.
His own footprints, his own scent — was that the whole limit of their imagination?
Lacerta, heading along a familiar path toward one of his own training grounds, had spotted a branch about shoulder-height snapped at the mouth of some slope. A four-legged beast that, even on its belly, stands tall enough to naturally snap a branch at a person's shoulder-height would of course have to be enormous, moving and leaving a far larger swath of wreckage in its wake. There was no such trace.
The forest had been a place where a great fire broke out a few years back and was barely brought under control. It had been the blunder of some greenhorn poachers who'd made light of a Barasus's instincts; in any case, as time passed the vegetation had more or less recovered, but fundamentally the soil quality had changed from that point on. So if you dug into the ground, buried something inside, and tried to fill the pit back in, you had to take greater care — lest the scar-like mottling of mismatched soil colors, or the slick stench peculiar to ground baked nearly to pottery and then made to hold moisture again, come stealing up.
Lacerta, having chosen a different path than usual, slowed his step at the sight of a great girthy tree off in the distance. One thick branch of the tree was bearing force in a strange direction. An attached vine had vanished up among the higher trunk and leaves — and no doubt something hefty, like a weight, hung there, eyeing only the moment to crush whoever passed thoughtlessly beneath. So he had simply dodged it all.
Not on a whim, not on a stroll — but because he had, truly and early on, seen straight through every last bit of it.

"I'd thought there might be some instigation from those Volcania dogs… but a third-rate assassination — no, a thug outfit like this."
It was an irony indeed. Had it been even that much of an affair — that is, had there been so much as a whiff of another nation or people involved — he'd have kept them alive longer to ferret out who was behind it.
"There is no next time."
Lacerta pulled the trigger. With that, the one who had been sitting in the chair died.
"Huh?"
"There is no next time."
The other man, who'd spent that precious crossroads between life and death on a few seconds of bleary staring, soon met the same fate. Lacerta drilled through the light fixture hung from the ceiling and the head of the man who'd set the traps in a single shot. It was deliberate. He'd made that room a single, brightly lit target, so that in dousing the light he could strike it from the list at the same time.
Lowering his firing stance, he stood straight up and gazed at the building far off. Only the captain's room on the top floor was gripped in pitch-black silence; all the other rooms and corridors were still abuzz with crowds of people. He sank into thought for a moment. Those men, close to common rabble, had — though it ended in failure — dared to attempt the assassination of the head of the Kingdom of Draconia's Royal Guard. And in the course of it, they had obtained real intelligence as well.
"…There is no next time."
His mind made up, Lacerta whipped out what he'd brought along. Several guns, each designed for its own purpose in subtly different ways. And bullets.
A great, great many bullets.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main2_Short: They believe they're hunting him. But the snares were read long before they were laid—and one truth waits in the dark: there is no next time.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main3_Content_0:
The thick fog of the forest at daybreak called to mind a sheet of hazy, cream-colored paper. Whatever story someone carves onto that paper, it can become anything at all. From a fleeting moment of happiness to a shudder-inducing tragedy…. Having finished setting up camp, Lacerta shook his head to drive out the stray thoughts, but it was futile. Always, these moments — when the surroundings fell quiet and there was nothing more to be done — were the hardest. He chewed over the moment, three years ago, when she had vanished.
Iris — the pillar of his life and the greatest reason he had resolved to change, his companion — had vanished. Vanished, quite literally, like smoke.
"It wasn't an accident."
Lacerta muttered.
"It was deliberate. Someone is behind it, without fail."
At first he'd thought her body had caught fire. She hadn't touched anything dangerous, and it was a little odd that the flame was a dazzling blue, but that wasn't the important thing. Surely the thing to do was to save her first. He'd scrambled to his feet in a panic and just then… the flames vanished. Not caught, not put out — they simply vanished, like the blink of an eyelid.
Along with Iris, wrapped up in them.
Lacerta forced his hands against his face and dragged them down. The brows of his eyes, gone hard as stone, kept catching at his fingers. What was the use in retracing a moment already gone, like this? It was nothing but tormenting himself.
And yet it was not as though he could sever the thought with a single stroke.

"What sort of sign there was… if there was one, I couldn't see it at all."
He didn't know — and that was all. For three whole years he had thrown the same question at himself, and every time arrived at the same, unchanging, unmistakable answer. Iris had suddenly, simply been engulfed in flames, and suddenly, simply vanished. What remained was some unidentifiable powder that at a glance looked like a heap of ash, yet held a pale, bluish glow. Beyond that, there was not a single clue. The strange blue flame had not spread to anything else. It had left not a speck of soot in the house. With an ordinary fire that would have been utterly impossible.
The Lacerta of that time could not accept such an ending. There was simply no way he could. Believing he had to find something, he'd rushed frantically about, inside the house and out, as though the secret of her disappearance were hidden away somewhere. He'd overturned and flung open every piece of furniture. He'd combed, fine-tooth, through the objects that bore his wife's touch and the places her footsteps had passed. After repeating it for a long while — until the shadows had swung the opposite way — he'd returned, spent and exhausted, to the house, to the room where she'd been until the last. Then he'd slumped down and, like a madman, scraped together that powder, those pale-blue grains, and put them in a glass bottle.
Was that Iris? — rather than believe so, he'd sooner follow after her. Not for an instant did he think it.
Was it a clue by which he could trace Iris's whereabouts? — yes. That was it. That was the way it had to be!

A blue fire that appears in an instant and swallows a person whole, a flame neither hot nor spreading, and some powder left behind once it goes out. With only those for a guide, he set out on his journey. He had to dig out some reason Iris had met such a fate, the one behind it. And before he knew it, three full summers and winters had passed.
There had been no gain whatsoever.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main3_Content_1:
Along the way he'd even met sorcerers who used blue sparks. They, however, could tell him nothing. Even after, partway through, he was left with no choice but to "speak" directly — not to their ears but to their fingers and wrists, shoulders, knees, and such.
It struck him, suddenly, that he was treating the matter quite drily, as though it were no more than digging vegetables from a field. When in truth it was nothing but the cruel torture of a band of sorcerers who'd protested their innocence to the very end.
"…If Iris had seen it."
He didn't want to put such painful words into his mouth, but he couldn't help it. The thought kept coming.
"She'd never have done such a thing."
There was no need even to picture her clinging to his side like a cicada. Simply — if Iris were still home waiting for him, if he thought he had to return to her side once the work was done, he would at least have given it deep thought before doing something so cruel.
What kind of person was he becoming?
"Stop, stop it!"
Lacerta struck the bare ground with a fisted hand. He must have hit a stone, for a sharp pain shot up, but if anything that was for the best.
"It's meaningless, all of it. Drop it."
After breathing deeply for a while, his head began to settle calmly. Soon, easing the strength from his tongue and closing his mouth quietly, upper and lower teeth aligned, only the sound of his own breath answered the forest's stillness. The silence of the dead of night drew near to him. Good. This is good.
"I have to conserve my strength, so I can keep up the search tomorrow."
Beyond his half-closed eyelids, he saw something. No — felt it. Not a shape or a situation but a color. A dazzling blue light that rose for only an instant and vanished. Just like that day he could never forget.
It was enough to make him cast aside everything else he'd been meaning, or not meaning, to do, and run in that direction.

In the middle of the fog-laden forest at daybreak — yet what else, who else, was there besides him? Lacerta recalled the group that had been loitering about the area in broad daylight. They'd been in the garb of the Lucid Sect. At that thought, his neck somehow went stiff with tension. His back teeth ground hard.
"Those damned bastards!"
he said. His chest felt tight, constricted. Not from fear, not from shrinking back, but the opposite. Lacerta noticed his breath turn ragged, every muscle in his body swelling taut to ready itself for a fight, as though watching someone else's affair.
"It's all because of them, if not for them, I'd never—"
A feeling that something was off came over him. Had he only the leisure, he'd have wanted to stop still and dissect the thoughts in his own head first. Where had this anger toward the Lucid Sect suddenly sprung from? It wasn't as though he stood at odds with them — as one who worshiped Elpiros the sun god, say — so why was he raging so wildly? Just then, right on cue, he saw a fire flickering up ahead — lit, most likely, by the Lucid Sect. Realizing he'd reached their campsite, Lacerta slowed his pace and so won a chance to put his own thoughts in order.
Come to think of it, mightn't the Lucid Sect be victims of the blue flame too?
That a thing called the Rapids had opened and become a stepping-stone between dream and reality — even Lacerta knew of it. Since when, he couldn't say, but he had the sense that, faintly, such a thing had become common knowledge. For the Lucid Sect, who had worshiped a dream-god to begin with, things had eased a little — but for all that, branded heretics in the open as they were, the most they could do was drift from place to place like this, hiding. And in the midst of that, wouldn't it fit better to say that someone wielding a more powerful force was, without compunction, testing their power on the sect's members?
Just like that day when Iris — gentle Iris, who in all her life had never once wronged another — became, out of nowhere, the sacrifice to some cruel deed!
Was the one who'd attacked the Lucid Sect still nearby? He couldn't tell. Since he didn't know how an attack using the blue flame was carried out, he had to be as cautious as possible. Crouching low, Lacerta drew toward the clearing. He could hear the bustling stir of presences moving about, as though some were still left. From the forms of address and the contents passing between them, it was indeed the Lucid Sect that had made the camp. Only — the way they spoke to one another felt more composed than he'd expected. Had they succeeded in subduing the attacker before he arrived? Or else….
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main3_Content_2:
"For the glory of the Lucid Sect!"
The instant those words ended, a blue halo of light flared up again and vanished. The heart of the watching Lacerta sank.
"Just now…?"
he repeated despite himself. Forgetting he was in the middle of hiding, he thrust his face out openly between the twigs and leaves. As if worried he might not have seen well, the other sect members went and repeated the same thing.
"For the glory of the Lucid Sect!"
"For the glory of the Lucid Sect!…"
He watched the gathered ones, the Lucid Sect members, intone the words one after another. And each time, a dazzling blue flame embraced their bodies and then vanished.
Everything was a dead copy of that day three years ago.
Lacerta struggled mightily to hold back the urge to charge in at once and subdue them — no, to speak truly, to kill them on sight, every one. Gnawing at his tongue until the taste of blood swirled in his mouth, he held himself in check. It wasn't certain yet. There might be another reading. His blazing, inexplicable hostility toward the Lucid Sect was on account of frayed nerves. It was the air of the forest at daybreak. There couldn't possibly be some further unknown reason. So he had to confirm every last clue, leaving none.
Was there someone of another affiliation among the sect members in the clearing? Had that someone threatened the members in some way? Were they being forced to use the incantation? Or was some procedure being carried out, one unwelcome even within the sect? Were they, too, in other words, no more than victims of the blue fire?
None of it.
That blue flame was plainly the power of the Lucid Sect, and they were willingly, of their own accord, becoming the objects of the rite.
Lacerta waited until the clearing fell silent.

"They were the kind you can't deal with after all…."
After the last sect member had vanished, he approached the empty campsite and examined the ground. It wasn't hot at all. Once he'd confirmed even that, holding his emotions down became impossible. His vision went pitch-black, and his tongue swelled so plump and bloated it was hard to keep it lying quiet in his mouth. With that, every other thought and feeling in his head was driven clean out. It felt as though thorns sprouting from inside his body were tearing through bone and flesh, jutting out to drive him on.
"These bastards — this is what they did to my Iris."
When he slammed the rifle butt into the bare ground, dew-soaked earth flew up and fouled him to the shins. The cold, damp feel of it ran down his ankle, licking down over the top of his foot and toecap, then down the lining between ankle and boot to the very sole — so vivid it was a curse. Lacerta trembled, shaking, unable to master his rage. Every scale along his body stood on end like blades. The tendons of his neck, his forearms, his brow swelled as if to burst… and then all of it, at some point, abruptly ceased.
Lacerta drew a breath and stood in the middle of the clearing.
He barely steadied that absurd desire to seize and smash something without reason, to drive anyone who chanced near at that moment into a corner and see their blood. Then he quietly regarded his own breath, not yet cooled. White as the fog, yet the color of iron heated to a glowing red… something disturbed that pure hue. A bluish halo of light still lingered. It spilled from something in one corner of the clearing — quietly flickering, not burning at all and not hot, yet lighting the spot more brightly than a campfire.
{IMAGE}
"Is that the place?"
he said. For some reason this thing he was seeing for the first time felt neither threatening nor strange. If anything, he recognized its function rather quickly — that it was not a single object but the entrance to somewhere.
"Is that where it went in?"

The rift in the air looked like clumsily blown glasswork. Like some nameless beast, it ceaselessly curled and uncurled its edges, swelled and pursed, stretched out and shrank back. Above all, the color of what lay inside it — and beyond it, the place the rift connected to — captured his gaze. The very same blue as that flame.
The strength drained from the hand that had been gripping the barrel as if to crush it. The rifle butt was driven so deep into the ground that the gun, standing slanted like a stake, didn't even topple. He pulled it back out of the earth. He brushed off the unsightly clinging dirt and gripped it just right. With eyes sharply on edge, with a voice frozen cold, he asked, then.
"Inside there — is that where you bastards flee and hide?"
No answer came.
"Are all the answers inside there?"
No answer came.
"Is she — is Iris — inside there?"
No answer came, and from the start he hadn't hoped for one. Lacerta took a step forward.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main3_Short: A flame that doesn't burn took her, and left only a pale blue dust behind. Three years on, a rift opens—and on the other side, the color of that fire.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main4_Content_0:
"You, by any chance — were you born not long ago?"
It was the question of some storyteller he'd met while roaming the Rapids.
"What exactly is that supposed to mean?"
To Lacerta's counter-question, however, it answered only with silence. No matter how he pressed, it would just go on reeling off whatever it wished to say, while at his actual questions it merely cocked its head. He couldn't afford to be caught up by such a thing and squander precious time. So he ignored it and moved on. Still, the memory of that day remained, distinctly, as a strange moment.
And yet by that measure — were the oddly strange things he'd encountered since entering the Rapids one or two in number?
At first he could manage to ignore them. Since this was the border of dream and reality, not everything would make sense, he reasoned; there'd be parts whose meaning escaped him. But that subtle unpleasantness, that wrongness, only piled higher and higher.
"How do I know this?"
It was the question Lacerta had stubbornly repeated ever since setting foot in the Rapids. What gave him still more pause was the doubt of just what, exactly, he knew. The things he knew, the things he believed he knew, were mostly nothing more than fragments that couldn't be shaped into words. Premonitions, signs, impressions, threads he couldn't clearly express… such things crammed his head, prickling like white, hard teeth pushing up through the gums.
To know something out in the world was made possible by observing one's surroundings keenly enough. For Lacerta, hardened in the bone by grueling training and experience from his Top Hand days — no, from long before that — it was nothing strange at all. He had always striven to read his opponent's movements and prepare. But here it was the very opposite. Before he could grasp the unfolding situation and rack his brain for a countermeasure, the result already hovered before his eyes. In the Rapids, this strange and uncanny place, he felt he dimly knew what awaited him, and how he ought to break through it.

"It's that I haven't rusted yet."
At times he tried to soothe himself, saying so. Fiddling with the glass bottle in his pocket.
"Because I spent long years on the battlefield as the Top Hand."
Every time, it felt just like making an excuse. The cynical thought rose that he was forcing a logical, rational explanation, trying thereby to avert his eyes from the true wrongness. If that was how it was with the enemies of the Rapids, then what of Polaris, who'd styled herself the Guide of this place?
Lacerta did not understand how he could have behaved so unruffled. In a perilous place, the border of dream and reality where anything might happen in any manner, something he'd never seen in his life had led him to where it was, in the form of an ownerless voice. And how had Lacerta reacted to that? He hadn't attacked. He hadn't trained a muzzle on it in wariness. Nor had he so much as glared at it with suspicious eyes and waged a probing skirmish to fathom its intent. He had docilely approached it and meekly accepted its goodwill.
As if he'd dimly sensed it was all right to!
There was no shortage of other strange points besides… but it was about time to put aside such brooding.

"Caught up to me again."
The screeching cry the Hunters made — come to think of it, this name too was one the Guide had taught him — drew near. They resembled the monsters of the Rapids but raged more savagely, and above all that dark, murky color, like thoroughly rotted river-mud, was their greatest mark. The deeper he went into the Rapids, the more — as if they had some hierarchy of their own — a hazy miasma, like a shadow, came welling and seeping out, worse and worse. Whether it was actually a substance that mixed into blood and flesh and took effect, he couldn't tell; nor did he much care to find out.
"Damned things, can't take my eyes off them for a second."
The Hunter pack was charging from off in the distance. Even at that fearsome speed, though, a fair gap still remained. Lacerta braced the gun against his shoulder and fired the first round at the head of the formation. A dazzling spark was inscribed along the bullet's trajectory.
