The blow that plunged down like a meteor splitting the sky struck home handsomely. Surely its windpipe had been cleanly severed. The Hunters, however, hadn't the wit even to be cowed at the sight of their fallen comrade and pull back. Like kneading clay, they slid their bodies forward to fill the hole opened in their ranks, then, feigning innocence as if nothing had happened, came lunging in. The narrow, keen wedge of an attack formation had its tip aimed precisely at Lacerta.
Just what he wanted. It was about time to test the many skills he'd gained roaming the Rapids.
At an unbelievable speed, drawing and chambering bullets, Lacerta reckoned the structure of a curtain of fire to halt the Hunters and the force it would carry. Then, scarcely conscious of his own movements, he delivered a second shot. Soon, giving the other side no room even to recover their formation, came three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine in a row…. The booming reports followed without a breath between them, until his ears throbbed.
When the battle was over, Lacerta frowned, gazing at the mood of the Rapids ruined by the thick haze of gunsmoke.
"From here on I'd better pick up the pace."

*
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main4_Content_1: His resolve to keep the Hunters at a good distance as he moved did not, however, always succeed. And at some point, ominously, a voice that whispered in a sly, insidious murmur began to follow along with them. "Lacerta…." "Who's there?" The first time he heard that voice, he was startled enough to lose his composure and waver. Was that the very aim? In place of any reply from the voice, a Hunter that had crept up close thrust out a great forepaw. Lacerta twisted aside to dodge, then drove his muzzle deep into the brute's armpit — a spot where, with no bone or other hard tissue, only flesh gouges away — and pulled the trigger. As the joint rooted into the torso was sheared off whole, as if filleted, the Hunter toppled with a skin-crawling scream. From the remaining part of its shoulder, instead of blood gushing like a fountain, a whitish, glowing dust came pouring out. Seeing it, Lacerta's face contorted. The feeling was strange. "I told you never to set foot in this place again, didn't I." That voice again. Lacerta flinched, trembling. He felt his heart pound violently, the blood rushing to his head. As if it weren't enough to feel that wrongness at every single thing he did and saw, now he had to take similar reproach from a voice of unknown origin too? "Not now — not now." Letting a single Hunter come up that close had already been a blunder. Spurring his halted feet, he widened the distance and resumed firing. His hand, which had been chambering rounds with a smoothness like a living thing, suddenly stopped. Looking down to check, he found a bullet caught crosswise at the mouth of the chamber. His breath grew ragged. "Steady — I have to steady my mind… yes." he said. And, pressing the bullet down with force, came a precise and crisp "click" — the sound that returned the focus of his breath, his heartbeat, and the thoughts in his head to their starting point. "This is the border of dream and reality. This voice too is, in the end, an auditory hallucination mimicking my dreams, my heart!" A Hunter with flame flung over its face staggered and pitched forward. Thanks to it, the other Hunters' feet were snagged, and Lacerta could keep forcing the enemy to bleed from an advantageous position. "I won't listen any longer to some hallucination that spits back the words that unsettle me, like a mirror." Was it that those words were logical enough, and above all satisfyingly rational? Was that how he'd succeeded in driving out the hallucination? In any case, the Hunters were all dead, and the voice was heard no more. At least for that while. * "Still wandering, are you." "You again?" Lacerta, grown used to it by now, smirked and shot back. "What a persistent hallucination. Won't vanish even when I keep quiet and ignore it." Perhaps he ought to answer? Perhaps even hold a conversation? If his own hallucination was the problem, perhaps he could browbeat it logically and make it stop being heard? At the thought, a dry laugh escaped him on its own. "So now I'm to sit here alone in self-questioning, asking and answering myself? The Guide would think me a fine sight." "Lacerta…." "You've got the wrong man!" He planted himself in place, the old leather coat flapping. From that stance he cleanly blew off the head of the Hunter that had drawn nearest. "I'm neither so weak as to be bewitched by a phantom like you, nor of any mind to let it happen!" The nearest, he'd said? Either he'd erred, or these dark, murky brutes were growing more cunning by the day. One Hunter lunged from his blind spot. Not what he'd wanted, but he had to use the barrel laid crosswise between it and himself as a castle bar to shield his body. "The phantom is…." The voice — no, the auditory hallucination. It was babbling something again. "The phantom is you and your purpose, Lacerta!" Biting the gun — no, gripping it? The forms of the Hunters clinging on were warped so grotesquely there was no telling which part was mouth and which forepaw. In any case, the part it had pressed against the gun clenched, and sparks began to scatter, faint and steady. They could pass the time a while in this romantic tug-of-war between the two of them, but unlike the Hunters, Lacerta — who had no pack to call his own — had to end a one-on-one standoff as fast as he could. A pity for the thing that had finally worked up the courage to choose a partner, but from the start Lacerta had meant only to play along a moment and then stand it up. He drove his knee up into its… lower belly, or whatever, the part left blankly exposed. Seizing the gap as the force on the gun loosened, he reclaimed his weapon, widened the distance, and fired off rapid rounds. At so close a range, aiming was meaningless. That isn't to say his shots were wasted on parts of the brute that weren't its vitals, though. From the Hunter's body, now a riddled shadow-honeycomb, a whitish dust came showering down. "And from your second tragedy too, you mean to turn your eyes away." "Second tragedy?" He sank into thought. At those words, sprung so out of nowhere, his mind wouldn't readily turn. For someone in the midst of so frantic a melee, he mulled the new phrase, "second tragedy," for quite a while. "How fitting of a half-baked hallucination, to step right into a hole." Then he scoffed. A little stiffly. "Losing the new dynasty's trust, or whatever… compared to the day I lost Iris, that's no tragedy, nor anything else." Combat with a gun is monotonous. And for that very reason it is all the more dependable. Having shaken off the Hunter that had asked him for a private tryst, Lacerta took early stock of the battlefield's state. What remained was half of them reduced to half-corpses staggering about, and half latecomers charging in from afar, mouths reeking of exhaustion. For a gunman, an ideal sort of opponent. Bringing the full measure of the skill he'd built up roaming the Rapids to bear, he thus formed his signature curtain of fire — no, an outright no-man's-land of fearsome explosions and roar that severed every scrap of scenery, inside and out, of attacker and attacked alike. When the smoke lifted, the Hunters caught in the fan-shaped curtain of fire centered on him lay sprawled together, literally torn to shreds. And when he'd confirmed it, his heart sank — for exactly what reason, though? "Still…." Was it because he'd thought he heard that hallucination murmur, faintly? Or because of the dust — that whitish, glowing, accursed dust — that he saw spilling out, surging like waves, from the Hunters who'd lost their lives all at once, their bodies heaped layer on layer into a little hill? "…It's the border of dream and reality." He didn't know how many times he'd repeated those words, he thought. Lacerta turned his eyes away from the sight around him. "Nothing to worry about, absolutely… I can just forget again." What was there to forget, why "again" — why that cursed "again" should have stuck itself onto the sentence without his noticing, he could not say. Whether the wrongness in his head was slowly eating away at his sanity, or whether some part of himself, a part he didn't know, had taken hold of his tongue and spoken in his place, he could not tell. One of Lacerta's hands, unawares, rummaged through the coat pocket and then stopped. The glass bottle in his breast — the very bottle into which he'd scraped together his wife Iris's last memory. That powder, like ash yet pale and bluish. If he took it out now and touched it, if he sat quietly gazing at it, he felt he would commit the one doubt he must not.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main4_Short: Among the hunters, a voice keeps calling his name. He swears it's only an echo of his own mind—so why does it know what he's trying so hard to forget?
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main5_Content_0:
"Do you remember me?"
At the familiar voice that drifted in, Lacerta raised his head. A woman in long, trailing robes — Polaris, who had called herself the Guide of the Rapids.
"Yes, I remember."
he answered.
"At the threshold of this place you taught me this and that. I was grateful."
"Has your cold gotten any better?"
"It was just an unfamiliar environment — I only needed a little time to adjust."
At her question Lacerta gave the tip of his nose a brisk rub.
"I'm fine now."
"How has your journey here been?"
A sudden appearance, then a question, then another question… and yet Lacerta was resting, mind empty. The warmth of the fire was pleasant, and his two legs, stretched out where he sat on his spread mat, were at ease. He felt no inclination to break from that mood. On the other hand, though, that itself was plainly odd — the self that simply assumed this moment was not dangerous.
"If you ask how it's been — what do you mean, specifically?"
"Is there anything you've newly learned, any fact you've come to realize?"
Lacerta bowed his head and sank into thought. For a while only the sound of the campfire he'd lit to warm himself could be heard.

"…You."
Without lifting his head, he rolled only his eyes to follow her, Polaris's, trace.
"What I've learned. No — what I already knew… I knew you would appear."
"Now, you mean?"
"Now I'm not sure. What's certain is that time. When I saw you for the 'first' time."
The emphasis stamped crookedly onto "first" felt ominous. Lacerta drew a breath. Then he hesitated a moment.
"Why is it familiar?"
he muttered, as if talking to himself.
"Why is it familiar, I'm asking? Why does everything rise up naturally as a feeling, before I see, hear, or know it?… You definitely know something I don't."
Polaris's eyes trembled slightly, yet in the end she did not avoid Lacerta's doubt-filled gaze. Not until his next words came.
"Has what lies ahead been decided?"
"It has not been decided."
she stressed with force.
"You are free."
"Then why doesn't it feel that way?"
The Dream Teller's words came to mind. The one who'd called him an untold story. At the time he'd dismissed it as nonsense, but now, having come to his present plight, that single remark became, on the contrary, a strange comfort. An untold story, an undecided story — that meant, in other words, that he was free.
Or was it merely that the Dream Teller's own ability fell short?

"You know a great deal."
To Polaris, those words sounded almost like a jeer, a mockery of her.
"Do you know the end of my story too?"
"Do you mean to repeat even the second tragedy?"
For all her insistence that he was undecided, that he was free, she promptly slid off, evasive, into another question instead… and beyond that, this "second tragedy" refrain again? The very one the hallucination among the Hunters had babbled? It was enough to make sour bile rise in his throat.
"Fine — let me set everything else aside and ask about that first."
Lacerta tilted his jaw as if sick to death of it.
"If, instead of a proper answer to this, another question comes back, that's the end of the conversation. What exactly does 'the second tragedy' mean?"
"You do not wish to know it."
"Beyond the Guide of this place, do you now aim to be the guide of my heart as well?"
For all his open sneering, no sign of agitation could be felt from Polaris. Or should he say she paid it no mind at all? Because her attention was given over to something more important?
"Am I not asking precisely because I want to know?"
"The you of now does, yes."
Polaris answered.
"But the you of some time ago — the past you — would not have wanted the you of now to want that."
"Enough — enough!"
What more words could pass between them from there? Lacerta waved a hand as if shooing off a bothersome insect and turned to sit away from her. Forcing the exchange would, at best, be a waste of time; at worst, his already churning mind would only be locked deeper into a maze of doubt and denial, left to flounder.
From that mouth, shut tight — lips with disappointment, jaw with resignation — soon a flippant little jest began to leak out.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main5_Content_1: "Go and tell the Hunters you sent, then — that they failed." With his gaze fixed on the campfire, Lacerta went on idly. "A scheme to stall for time with nonsense talk and corner me…." His back prickling, Lacerta glanced sidelong — and then, startled, looked back at Polaris. The stone-like eyes peculiar to lizardmen, famed among other races for seeming devoid of feeling and often called a "cold, ruthless stare," went wide. Lacerta's mouth fell open of its own accord. Polaris's expression was contorted into a wreck the likes of which he'd never seen. "How — how dare you, say such a thing!" The formless aura wrapped about her began, little by little, to take on color, to take on sound. Like drawing too near a boiling crucible, his skin stung and tightened, and the grains of bare earth and the pebbles began to be shoved this way and that in a frenzy, like fine powder sifted through a sieve. And at the heart of that aura stood only the two of them — Polaris, and Lacerta, who had drawn her wrath. "What is this, all of a sudden?" Quick as lightning, Lacerta snatched up his gun and drew away from her. The finger laid across the trigger was already half pulled. "What's the matter?" "I have nothing whatsoever to do with the Hunters or the will that made them!" The distance between them closed. "I am not trying to torment the beings of reality who come into this place! I only want to give the products of dreams a safer, surer life—" Her words slowed, little by little. "—to give them the power to grasp and decide their own fate — that, is, all…." Polaris's inexplicable anger vanished as fast as it had come. The aura that had radiated from her gradually withdrew its trace. What had flared cooled, what had surged subsided, what had raged grew calm. All of it vanished, and what remained was once more only Polaris, the Guide of the Rapids. "I apologize." Even as she looked at the muzzle aimed openly at her heart, she bent at the waist in a bow. "I am truly sorry. I showed you something I should not have." She's embarrassed? That was the first explanation that came to Lacerta's mind on seeing it. That she'd lost her temper and… no, that was too personal a reading. He had clearly seen the expression Polaris let slip for that instant, the glint that flashed in her eyes. It was, without doubt, closer to the regret of someone who carries a great cause — yet who, from some day on, has come to doubt that very cause, who could not help but doubt it. After long service in an organization like the Royal Guard, which bore far more authority — and the duties that came with it — than an ordinary army, one saw plenty of comrades and subordinates wearing that very expression. And the reason such a problem was never simply tied off was that the cause itself was either too abstract to begin with, or bound to clash, one way or another, with any number of other "righteous ideals." So then — what of her? Was Polaris, too, in the grip of such a conflict? "…Shall we, please, return to our talk." Lacerta thought there was hardly a talk worth returning to, but she seemed to think otherwise. "The you of now wishes to know, but the you of some time ago wished that the you of now—" "There's no need to repeat your childish riddles." he cut in, with a shudder. "I said the conversation was over there… or do you, from your side, have something more to say?" "Yes, I do." Polaris, having fully recovered her usual composed manner, paused a moment as if choosing her words. So all the talk until now — the you of some time ago, the things newly realized in the Rapids — had been nothing but bait, and this was the real matter, was that it?
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main5_Content_2:
"Wandering this place, you must have seen how fierce and powerful the creatures of dreams are."
"I have."
"But at the same time you must have seen, too, how fleeting they are."
Lacerta had seen some greenhorn explorers. Most likely fellows who'd barged in without careful preparation. With no clear plan or aim, they'd merely shuffled about the shallows of the Rapids, and so had built up no skill to speak of. What fate such men would meet should they truly run up against real danger was self-evident. From their dying bodies a flood of glittering pure gold spilled out, and the dream creatures that until then had been attacking them with terrible ferocity came scrambling in to devour it — Lacerta had seen the sight.
There was something stranger still.
A dream creature feeding on the explorers. Among them he saw one, the smallest and feeblest, all but cast out of the pack. Shoved aside by the brawnier others, it fretted, unable to so much as catch a single crumb of pure gold that rolled to the bare ground. After whimpering a while in that state… it simply died, on its feet. He could not have misseen it, for its body even broke down into a whitish, glowing dust.

"Some beast died because it couldn't eat the gold of reality."
"And if it were not such a beast, but a person born wholly of dreams — what then?"
said Polaris.
"Those who awaken to a self, who learn the words to reach one another and live together, those precious to me, those who hold me precious — beings who live amid such bonds, yet who, all the while, fret over when they might lose something within them — wouldn't this fleeting nature of dreams come at them all the more cruelly?"
Lacerta watched her clench a fist.
"If there is hope for such suffering ones, it is the power of reality — the power of gold, which fixes form and disposition. If we could share that power with the products of dreams to their fill, what a great help it would be."
"It sounds well enough."
Polaris seemed startled, as if she hadn't expected an immediate reply.
"Every wicked scheme sounds that way at first… you haven't said anything of the concrete method."
But Lacerta, for his part, hadn't finished speaking either.
"Exactly how do you plan to loose the power of reality, the disposition of gold, into this place?"
"It's simple. We break down the boundary between dream and reality."
she said, as though it were quite a simple matter.
"I think it would be no bad proposal for you, eith—"
"You spout something that irresponsible, and then call it a proposal?"
Lacerta frowned. Without even reaching for the Hunters that chased him at every chance, all manner of bizarre — and therefore all the more dangerous — dream creatures flitted across his mind.
"And so these dreadful monsters, once they eat a little gold, will trouble no one in reality and sit quietly holed up in their nests?"
"I understand your wariness."
said Polaris… and, oddly, with eyes that somehow seemed to pity Lacerta.
"It will be hard to understand for now. 'The second tragedy'… you will come to know that those words, in the end, hold a story of returning somewhere, of coming back from somewhere. The method I pursue can resolve even such a looping ending."
Lacerta watched her two hands interlace and clasp together. What had been two becomes one. And yet it sounded like nonsense — an overly romantic reading of the claim that she'd break down the boundary of reality and dream.
"When dream and reality blend, within it every question and answer can likewise be found. Your last doubt, too—"
"Enough."
He deliberately gripped the brim of his hat and blocked his view. With that he severed the line of sight between himself and Polaris. And deliberately held his silence a while.

"You may not, but I am tired. This is no easy place to be."
"Yes, of course I understand."
She read between the lines obediently and withdrew. The light sound of her footsteps grew faint, little by little.
"It is only right to give you time to think. I would not force my opinion while you yourself do not yet know your final answer."
"Yes—"
As he spoke, Lacerta felt Polaris's presence grow faint. And, at some moment, sever completely.
"—thank you."
All around fell quiet once more. What remained was only Lacerta's own breath and the sound of the campfire crackling, throwing sparks. He pulled his hat down low, covering his whole face. With the lights and shadows flickering before his eyes thus shut tight away, he sank into his own thoughts alone.
The glass bottle in his pocket dragged heavily, that day of all days, at his coat.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main5_Short: A guide offers to fold dream into reality, two made one, every question finally answered. The proposal sounds gentle. So why does it feel like a trap?
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main6_Content_0: Lacerta cursed his hand. That trusty, nimble hand of his, the one that had always been his most faithful comrade, with which he'd brought down countless enemies. At the same time he cursed his eyes, too, and the inside of his head. The eyes that had thoughtlessly turned that way; the head that, having once seen, could no longer forget. "Why of all places?" His outstretched arm trembled. "Why here of all places? Why now of all times did I drop it?" Why had he had to take it out at all to begin with? The glass bottle holding his wife's trace — and there, of all places, amid the heaps of dream dust scattered from the dream creatures he'd dispatched? Lacerta hurriedly drew his arm back. The movement was as if a red-hot poker had touched his fingertips, but he could not unsee what he'd already seen. The scene that left no room to deny or evade lay spread before him. {IMAGE} At a glance, above the low-piled hill of dream dust, the mouth of the glass bottle and the stopper that sealed it had suddenly floated up into the air. An illusion of the Rapids? The working of some incantation? Neither. It was simply the glass bottle Lacerta had dropped, half-buried there. And the glass surface he ordinarily stroked and cherished was so transparent that the naked eye could pass right over it, missing it in a blink. Thus the bottle holding the dream dust of the Rapids and his wife's last trace melted, before Lacerta's eyes, into a single substance — the two, touching inside and out across the bottle's thin membrane, were without doubt the same substance. "No, it isn't." said Lacerta. He shrank back, recoiling as if he'd seen a monster. "I saw it wrong. It's a trick of the light. This is different." Because one is a "whitish, hazy dust" and the other a "pale, bluish-white dust"? Just as shallow water is clear, but deep water turns a deep blue? A fictional tongue, gleaming like a dagger, stabbed painfully into his head. He wanted to flee from that question. He wanted to stop doubting. But however fast a horse may gallop, bit in its mouth and reins fastened, it cannot flee the rider on its back, the sharp, jutting spurs digging into its haunches and thighs. "I knew it from the start." he repeated. The moment he first entered the Rapids — or at least the day he resolved to believe so. He had seen the Lucid Sect members handle the blue flame. He had even drawn close to examine the traces left behind. A robe folded on the bare ground, a branch set in an odd spot, a clod of earth bearing the mark of a toe that had struck and passed it… he'd combed the campsite, scrutinizing all those things to the point of obsession. And there was one fact he'd ignored to the very end. Unlike Iris, those sect members had not vanished leaving dust behind. Once you reach this point, it is no longer the domain of inference or logic. This is already arithmetic. The unbreakable rule of addition of one fact and two terms. The dust that appeared when his wife vanished did not appear in the case of the sect members. And that dust resembled the dream dust composing the fictional beings within the Rapids. Was similar. Was alike… no, was the same. How much longer was he to keep feigning ignorance here? "W-when did it begin?" he said. He'd thought the ground was rushing up at him, but it was his knees that ached. The cold earth pressed into his shins. Before he knew it, Lacerta had sunk to his knees and crumpled down. "When did it come to this?" Surely not from the very start? he thought. From the time he was the Top Hand of the Royal Guard, while Edgar IV still reigned, when he spotted Iris — strumming an instrument and singing in the market, a woman whose name he didn't even know then — had he, all along, been chasing a being of dreams? "No." He clenched his teeth. Less a renewed denial after coming this far than a honing of memory grounded in evidence he could be sure of. "Then, it truly wasn't… too early; the timing doesn't fit." Time. That, too, was a subject worth pondering.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main6_Content_1: It bears restating, but in the Rapids — with no one to talk to and no trifling chores to mind — there were many moments when one fell to thinking alone. And each time, with a hand stroking the glass bottle, if not chewing over his past, what else would Lacerta have done? No matter how he thought it through, there was a part that didn't fit. The dates in his memory lay still for weeks, months — no, for several seasons — and then suddenly leapt all at once to some "next" point in time. He simply could not explain that gap. Take, for instance, the death of Edgar IV — a moment so eminently suited to serve as an objective reference point, being a part of history. That was where it started. "I took my leave, came down, and together built a cabin—" Yes. Not long after, he'd left the palace and entered the Hissing Forest. They'd built a cabin. He'd thought to step away from the world a while and live a carefree, self-sufficient life — time for just the two of them. And then a string of happy days with Iris followed at once — a life conveniently sealed away in the forest, with no chance to compare the mismatched points of memory against anyone? Right up until she was engulfed in blue flame and vanished? Where had all these intermediate stages gone? How does one build a house? Roughly fell some trees, dry them, lay them lengthwise, stand them on end along the border, lay a slanted pitched roof over that, and done? Where, and what sort of house, and how had he decided to build? What opinions had Iris added in the process? What of partway through building it? Among the boards and posts and beams, half-built, what words had they exchanged? Where had they eaten? What had they made and eaten? Hadn't they, wolfing down food so hungry they could eat a horse, dropped crumbs or broth onto the floor? Hadn't some mark of it remained somewhere in the house, so that later, whenever Iris saw the spot, she'd pull a sulky face and scrub at it with a lye-soaked brush or some such? When Iris came in while he was hard at work, where and how did she sit or stand to lend a hand or trade idle chatter? Where was the chair she used then? Had he padded the windowsill — its sanding not yet finished — with a cushion or the like, so she could perch on it easily? Sitting there with the sunlight at her back, gazing over at him — how had her laughter sounded? When he mashed up paste to use for plastering this and that as he built, and lumped it all into a pail too heavy for her to carry alone, so that he had no choice but to ladle some into a smaller dish for her… while building, with his own wife, the house they'd live in together, had there truly not been a single one of such trivial little things? And if there had been, why did he not remember them? Is it possible to forget such things of their own accord? "It's empty — the whole… the whole stretch of it." What had Lacerta done during that time he couldn't remember? Alone, leaving Iris behind? Or — or could it be that there was already no Iris to leave behind by then? Had he, to find her, set out on a journey much like the one he was on now, arrived at much the same place, and made much the same discovery? There's a place called the Rapids where the border of dream and reality lies; go in there, and even a wish that out in the world isn't worth a half-penny can readily be granted… such stories had drifted endlessly through the world — so however much he forgot, in the end could he do nothing but come walking back here on his own two feet? "Did I find this place, find my own Iris, and take her away?" The second tragedy, no second time. And what else had it said? The voice the Hunters murmured. "Lacerta, I told you never to set foot in this place again, didn't I." Inside his ears rang and rang like a great bell. Lacerta clutched his head. He couldn't breathe. He wanted to forget every thought rising in him now. And so he grew all the more certain. His past self — "the you of some time ago," as Polaris put it — had, for that reason, truly forgotten. Not of its own accord but by begging some source of power met in the Rapids and forcibly erasing his memory. Forgetting even the fact that he'd forgotten, and now wishing to forget like this once again. A foul reek rose from his chest. Unable to hold back the heaving, he abruptly vomited up his insides. The retching went on a long while. Hot tears welled up, blurring his sight, and he had to simply hold his mouth open and endure until his jaw throbbed. When the spent Lacerta lifted his head, the thing came into view again. His wife's last trace… no, the glass bottle holding the dream dust. Without even knowing what he was doing, he picked it up and tucked it into his breast. The coat's inner lining stretched into a snug, mold-like shape and received it. "Polaris." he said, dazed. "Your words… is this it, now? Is this my 'when you yourself know the answer'?" He drew out the hand he'd put in his pocket, but the sensation didn't fade. Lacerta found himself rubbing his fingertips against the rough part of his clothing to wipe it clean. Not the glass bottle but the thing he'd touched in drawing it out and gripping it — he wanted to erase the feel of raw, naked dream dust. As if he, who'd until now succeeded in erasing, averting his eyes from, and forgetting plenty of things, were at last content with his lot. "Do you think I can answer your proposal now?" For a while no sound came at all.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main6_Content_2: "…That I awoke so painfully is, in the end, because I'd pinned my hopes on dreams to begin with." Lacerta opened his mouth. "I craved the power of dreams so badly I forced my way through my own head… and ended up like this." Merge dream and reality into one, was it? It was a plan with its own pull. If painful truth was to be realized in the end anyway, why not just cram all of reality into the heart of dreams, and all of dreams into the cracks of reality, mashing them into one lump from the outset, leaving no room for misunderstanding? Then dreams would be shown to be not a world where anything could be achieved, but merely another kind of incomplete world bearing its own kind of suffering. It stings? That's reality. It's unfair? That's the truth. "Better to bar a thing from ever starting than to realize it this painfully… you might think so." Lacerta rose unsteadily to his feet. "But I, for one, don't want to negate every single decision my former self made." He loaded the gun. Lose himself staring at the heap of dream dust and he'd run into the Hunters again. "However hollow it may be, even if I've forgotten it, it's my choice. It was the best the me of that time could do." Would there be worth in it, even if it repeated itself wholesale? It was a question not easily answered, yet at the same time a wrong question. In the end, every decision is the only choice he himself could make, having experienced, felt, and agonized over it directly. So, dreadful as it might sound, he could only admit it. That even if this were the second tragedy, even if someone in the Rapids looked on a Lacerta like that and laughed coldly, the self of now had not the slightest mind to turn back until he himself reached the end of the dream and dug everything up. "It may look foolish and witless, but this is my way." Lacerta put in a bullet. "Whatever waits for me at the end, whatever choice I make—" Lacerta put in a bullet. "—before that, I have no intention of swallowing someone's proposal whole, clapping along, and stopping my walk." Lacerta put in a bullet. How many? Which round was it? He bowed his head and stared blankly at his own hand. He repeated clenching and unclasping it. With no gun gripped in its hold, just toying at empty air, the sight even felt awkward. To the wrist a palm, to the palm fingers, curl them and clench a fist and inside it the gun's grip…. A song came to mind, the sort little children might sing, pointing to parts of their own bodies. Since entering the Rapids, had that hand ever held anything other than a gun — the small copper awl used to service it, say, or even the chip-rimmed wooden bowl and blunted fork used to eat? When was the last time he'd felt he ought to? "…Ah." Lacerta sighed. "Is this it — yes, this is it. Polaris." Was she hearing these words? He hoped not. This one doubt he chewed over now, he did not want to find a clear answer to. "This is my last doubt, and my last answer." The sentence that rose next he could not bring himself to carry to the tip of his tongue — if that was so of Iris, then what of the me of now, who's roamed the Rapids this long? "If I dreamed Iris, then might I be able to dream myself, too?" Lacerta asked. "Have I, too, at some point, fallen from a being of the outside to a product of this place? Is that why she said it? 'A proposal that would be no bad thing for you too'?" Do you think so? — she, forever turning a question back with a question, would probably offer up some such cryptic line again, he thought. For some reason the imagining was so brazenly funny that he laughed a while, crinkling the corners of his eyes. The sound of the Hunters began to drift in, faint and far. This was no time to be lounging in idle thought. "…The problem snagging my ankle right now is a separate matter." Lacerta raised the barrel and set his feet, one before the other. So he took his firing stance. The wind was still and the target was growing larger. Shoot at any spot on the horizon and you'd be called a crack shot. "I don't know if you're listening, but it's fine if you appear again. My answer is set—" When he pulled the trigger, a dazzlingly bright meteor plunged into the heart of the Hunter pack. "—whatever choice I made or come to make, having reached the end of the Rapids, I have no intention of going along with your plan right now." The glass bottle in the coat's inner lining swayed and softly tugged at Lacerta's collar.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main6_Short: Some truths are no longer a matter of reasoning, but of arithmetic. When the dust in the vial matches the dust at his feet, what answer is left to give?
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main7_Content_0:
Lacerta finished his warm-up and left the house. Gun in hand, he made his way to the training ground. The forest, not yet over the night, was rather chilly. Dew-beaded blades of grass bent and trembled as they struck his toecaps. Open his mouth wide and breathe out, and he could see his breath rise faintly white and vanish. He thought of putting on a thicker coat, but decided against it. A touch of cold was better for training. He suddenly chewed over since when he'd kept up this habit.
The training he did in the morning, hauling his huddled body along, was the most important part of the day. He had never once skipped it. Even the day after that incident, the moment he opened his eyes, reflexively
….
The Hissing Forest, which he'd made his nest after retiring, lay far from any great river. Yet for some reason a thick water-mist came stealing up almost every morning. The ground wasn't especially damp, nor was there a marsh nearby — it was a strange thing. Reaching the training ground, Lacerta figured the soles of his boots were surely caked with sticky mud.
"Still, better than the ground freezing solid, or snow coming down in sheets and stranding you."
He wondered since when he'd taken to talking to himself so often. In truth he knew. Ever since the one who'd kept him company at his side was gone
….
He looked at the target set off in the distance, raised the gun, and pressed it tight to his shoulder. Squinting one eye, he laid his line of sight parallel to the barrel. There was no reason to drag it out long. Since it was something he did without fail every day, he quickly pulled the trigger, bore down against the recoil, and lifted only his head a touch to check the result. A perfect score. A black hole was bored through the dead center of the target. For his sake he'd deliberately painted the boulder behind the target black. Using the brush carelessly, he'd gotten black smudges caked all over the handle, too. Later, seeing it, she'd grumbled at him to be more careful
….

"That'll do."
The morning training was done. So he made to head back. But Lacerta didn't lift his foot. Instead he bowed his head and stared. He looked down at the gun, still wheezing with leftover heat. Come to think of it, what a secretive weapon a gun is. To handle its visible part properly, one must understand its invisible part precisely. At times one must even have faith.
A blade has no such suspect point. It shows its rust where it rusts, its nicks where it's nicked. But a gun — there's no telling how the inside of the muzzle may be, whether the hammer will move at the exact speed and bearing intended each time the trigger is pulled. Even if the heart of the muzzle were packed full of jelly-like soot and powder residue, not even the most seasoned marksman in the world could grasp the fact until he actually fired. So what was the point?
"I'd better fire again."
No reason not to. Training was the most important part of the day. If he could begin his day more safely, more surely, that was no bad thing. She'd think so too—Lacerta held his breath to drive out the stray thought. He forcibly reined in his chest, swelled until his ribs creaked. In that state he slung the gun to his shoulder and fired one more round. A perfect score.
Was it, though? In fact it might have missed. All that could be seen from here was the black hole in the target. Had the bullet slipped right inside it and left no trace? Or maybe it had struck somewhere far from the target and only kicked up a puff of dust. The temptation rose to go up and check. But if it had truly missed, was he to find out where that bullet had lodged, or whether it lay rolling about, and confirm it?
Lacerta was no child who shut his eyes each night yet behaved as if he had no logical way of knowing the sun would rise tomorrow too. In his Royal Guard days he'd made bets, day in and day out, that he could drill a coin dropped from shoulder height before it even hit the ground — before it had even passed a man's shin. There was no way he'd fumbled so badly at a target standing still, far as it was. So it's a perfect score. So training's done. He could head home now. And yet, and yet….
If he fired just one more round, wouldn't that be the moment he could be sure?

Lacerta felt he was fixating on this. Rather than training in the morning for some purpose, before he knew it he was throwing himself anew into morning training merely to keep up the form of morning training. This was unhealthy. It was the figure of a man held captive by habit. He thought it over carefully. He pondered why, today of all days — no, lately, more and more — he couldn't finish his training and head back with a fresh, clear mind. But in fact it was no matter of just today or tomorrow, nor confined to lately. He had always felt, deep down, that it wasn't enough. Fire one round, ten rounds, a hundred in a row, and the hundred-and-first after might still miss. That's what a gun is.
{IMAGE}
What had let him put a stop to it was that, right about this point, the voice of someone calling for him would, as a rule, come drifting in.
Lacerta quietly closed his eyes and waited. For what? For the light footsteps, for the voice crying out his name, for the smoke of cooking rising from the cabin chimney and the gentle breeze that carried it all the way here, for the moment the owner of voice and footsteps drew near the training ground — when, lest the stench of gunpowder cling to her, he'd hurriedly beat at his shoulders, his forearms, his coat collar, fretting and fidgeting. Like a little brat caught at some mischief just as the person he liked was about to find out.

"Iris?"
His own voice felt awkward. He tried not to mutter. He had to smooth out his roughened voice first.
"Iris? Are you there?"
The fact of speaking to someone felt strange somehow. Unsettling. He was confused as to how he'd ever held a conversation with Iris. The softened voice rang unfamiliar in his ears.
"Where did you go, Iris? Are you looking for me?"
She said nothing.
"You haven't forgotten the way to the training ground, have you? I'm right here."
Everything had gone wrong.
"Iris?"
A sudden whirlwind gusted up. Lacerta started and opened his eyes. Strength flowed into his arms and shoulders of its own accord. His aim must have been thrown off. He had to steady his breathing. But the finger that had tensed in the moment, before he knew it, blinked and pulled the trigger. The gun fired. Reflexively he checked the target off in the distance. The round hole at the target's center — only now a little more ragged.
A perfect score.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main7_Short: Every morning he fires one more round at a target he cannot miss—waiting for a voice that never comes. How many times must the song begin again?
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main8_Content_0: "Hey, you know what I just went and saw?" "The top of your foot." The two lizardmen traded words like characters out of a joke. "Huh?" "Lose some of that belly fat, man…." The lizardman who'd shot back teasingly chided his colleague. "Desk job or not, we're still the Royal Guard." "Look at this guy — I'm telling you, the moment I put my mind to it, I'll be solid as a rock in no time and you'll be calling me big brother." There was something hard to take at face value about the rotund lizardman's grand proclamation. All the more so given that paunchy build of his, which somehow made even his kind's hard, characteristic scales look soft and fluffy as wool. "Anyway, quit talking nonsense — you know what I saw? Our Top Hand, I swear to you, was off gazing at something, lost in it!" "Weren't we just saying no nonsense." he sneered at his fussing colleague. "Him, lost in gazing at anything — and how would you even see that? Did you clock him on the back of the head or something?" "Are you out of your mind?" the wide-eyed lizardman shot back. "And even if I had swung at him, you think it'd land? He'd have snatched what was in my hand and beaten me half to death with it on the spot." That did seem likely. It was hard to picture anyone — and not just anyone, but the Top Hand, whose renown rang inside the Royal Guard and out — being subdued, even by a surprise attack aimed at the back of his head. And yet a man like that, lost in gazing at something? "Lost in gazing at what? Something the matter with him?" "There was this woman in the market, some musician from outside, singing a song. Name's Iris." The easygoing lizardman mimed strumming an instrument as he spoke. "And he was just completely taken with it." "Yeah?… Well, even the Top Hand's allowed a hobby or two, I guess." "But it didn't look like just a hobby 'or two,' I'm telling you." As if even recalling the moment astonished him, the easygoing lizardman wiped the sweat from his brow and went on. "He didn't notice me at all until I got right up close to say something. Just kept staring at that woman musician, riveted." "Oh?" That was decidedly no ordinary thing. Running into the Top Hand outside the unit usually meant not other Royal Guards approaching him but rather the reverse — that is, while carousing in the street, failing to keep up Royal Guard dignity, raising a ruckus drinking and shouting, you'd suddenly feel a gaze sink into the back of your skull, and turning around, you'd meet the Top Hand's stern eyes skewering you like a spit. Not someone you happened to spot or someone people went looking for, but someone who'd already found everyone — a man who never, ever let his gaze wander. That was the general image of the Top Hand, Lacerta. "So did you clear your throat or something? Ah — he was mid-performance, so even that wouldn't carry, I suppose." "That's just it… and what's more, I stood behind him a good while and he still didn't notice, so it was only after I tapped his shoulder to call him that he turned around!" "What?" his colleague cried. The Top Hand not merely letting his attention wander, but noticing nothing until another's hand touched his very body? Now the distinction between the lizardman telling the story and the one listening dissolved, and there remained only the lumped-together categories — the lizardmen astonished together, the easygoing lizardman, the fussing lizardman. "Really? That far gone?" "That's what I'm saying! So taken with a street musician, his whole mind carried clean away…." "What's got you all having such a grand old time gabbing?" Other colleagues drifted in one by one, and of course it was hardly a tale meant for just the two of them. "He was smiling? I can't picture it." "This is earth-shaking stuff!" "Seriously? Our Top Hand? The one who puts a knife in you with his eyes every single training session?" They all roared with laughter together. Not so much that the unexpected side of their captain was funny, but that the proof a superior who'd seemed almost inhumanly flawless and airtight also had a warm heart was, in a way, even gladdening. "So even the Top Hand, with icicles hanging all down his heart, knows what spring is, eh…." "But how come you came back empty-handed?" The colleague who, at the story's start, had ribbed the easygoing lizardman, singled him out again to ask. "Hm?" "Weren't you — didn't you go to the Top Hand because you had some business with him?" he asked. "You said you even tapped his shoulder to call him. So why'd you come back with nothing?" "That's right, I left that part out. That's when I learned the musician's name, too. What he said to me then was—" The lizardman snapped his fingers. Having, unintentionally, drawn every colleague's gaze to himself in one stroke, he lowered his voice like an actor about to perform the climax of a play, drew out the pause to the fullest, and then…. "—'What is it? I've arranged to meet Iris after her performance is over, so let's talk later.' — and sent me right back!" A boisterous cheer rang out. {IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main8_Short: Spring seeps even into a heart carved from ice. The man who never once looked away stops, for the first time, before a song in the street.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Main8_Title: A Flower That Met a Butterfly
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Short0_Content: With the throne left empty by a king who died suddenly and without an heir, the court seethed with a thousand competing voices. Some invoked bloodline, some their backing factions, some old debts owed. Lacerta watched all their scheming and felt an unfamiliar disillusionment. All his life he had upheld a single loyalty above any cause, and those he led had followed him believing in that one thing alone. Yet here, in this place, loyalty was nothing more than rhetoric to mask self-interest. Was this truly what he had spent his life protecting? For the first time, Lacerta found himself asking.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Short1_Content: Concerts, paintings—none of these existed in Lacerta's world before he met Iris. Dressed in plain clothes and settled into an unfamiliar place, he still felt out of place, yet even as the orchestra began to play, his gaze fell not on the stage but on the seat beside him. Those eyes, so used to scanning his surroundings with sharp vigilance, now followed only one person's expression. Quietly, Lacerta was coming to understand that there existed something more beautiful than anything else in the world.
ui.TravelerStory_Lacerta_Short1_Title: On the Way to the Recital
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main1_Content_0: A film of pale dust, settled near the doorway, was all that greeted Eleanor. She stared at it so intently that she forgot everything else. Forgot to shut the door, forgot to go in and do what she had meant to do in her room, forgot to set down somewhere the sack she clutched in both arms. Without thinking, she called the name of the maid who used to work at this hour. "There's dust on the floor; sweep it again—" But whom was she calling? In this house, now. In a desolate ruin where no one would come and no one would listen. Would she squander the last breath of a dying house? Eleanor closed her mouth. And as she did, she understood why the dust had gathered in that one spot alone. There had once stood a large writing chest there. The space left beneath its feet was where the servants, ordinarily, had never troubled to clean with much care. The dark-brown chest, giving off the faint scent of linseed oil, had been purely ornamental; most of its drawers did not even open. Above its four curved legs spread a carving of grapevines, broad and coiling about the lower body, and the upper portion was trimmed in thinly gilt bronze—little eaves, a railing, surging-wave filigree and other such fussy ornaments. The handles of every drawer had been carved like the braided hair at the back of a woman's head, so that the fingers would not slip. And to sell off furnishings like these, for only— Eleanor thought, and tightened her arms. The sack she held against her chest rustled. At that sound—which no flattery could have called heavy, or full—her eyes burned hot and her lips threatened to crumple. "N-no crying." Eleanor said. She sniffed and shook her head. She let the cold wind wash over her and steeled the rims of her eyes. "Just keeping our lives is a miracle. Sheer fortune…" What had happened? She knew it all—and yet was there some part she still did not know? Or was there some part she only wished to believe she did not? There had been the Princes' Revolt, and it had come to nothing. A witness surfaced claiming that the lord of House Verdesilver—her father, Sir Loren Verdesilver—had known of the plot of rebellion beforehand and yet had not reported it to the Crown. Living power is at its most venomous after it has wandered to the brink of life and death and come back: that is, just after it has put down something like a prince's treason. Loren Verdesilver, who had sheltered traitors, was executed at once. The house, too, had to pay for the crime. The vast family fortune was, for the most part, confiscated. Every individual and faction that had once kept close ties with them—out of need or out of friendship—turned their backs all at once. Even the retainers, the knights foremost among them, slipped quietly away and abandoned their posts. "We should count ourselves lucky we escaped the extermination of the line." Eleanor's grip went white. How fine it would be if she could simply declare that this was righteous anger. It was closer to humiliation. Worse—though she would rather die than admit it—it was even fear. How could she have failed to feel the uneasy current that surrounded her the whole time she carried that sack out of the manor and through the village? The villagers had once bowed and scraped at the mere passing shadow of a Verdesilver retainer—whether they were tenants of the demesne or free farmers with no connection to it. And today? Eleanor heard them spit, loudly enough for every bit of it to reach her, behind her back. A stone came flying and tumbled at her feet; people who had been chatting amiably until she drew near hardened their faces as though they had spotted a plague-carrier and slipped away. And after suffering such indignities, what was it she held in her hands? She looked at the contents that left the sack hanging slack. Bread so black and coarse her teeth would not sink into it unless it were soaked in soup, and a lump of cheese gone hard as candle-tallow, yet giving off a sour reek it could not hide. And to get even that, what sort of conversation had she had to have?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main1_Content_1: "Th-this is all?" Eleanor could not even remember the last time she had stammered. Under her mother's strict instruction she had held silver tableware by day, a perfumed feather fan by evening, and a wooden practice sword by night. And all the while—at the dining table, in the salons of society, on the training yard—she had been lectured without end on her bearing and her composure. She had heard, until it was beaten into her ears, how always to speak calmly and with decorum. "That's me payin' meself back for all the bother." The proprietor answered carelessly, working something between his teeth. "Don't like it, take it elsewhere." Thwack! The cleaver he swung split some lump of meat in two on the block. He flung the severed meat into the pot beside him, and the foam splashed up. "Even so." Eleanor cleared her voice. Why her throat kept closing up, she truly could not say. It was not as though she were committing a crime, nor as though she had anything to hide. She was only asking a fair price for what she sold. "Even so, this is far too low." The proprietor pushed back his grease-soaked forelock and shot her a glance, never stopping his chewing. "Even if you melted the ornament down and sold it again, you'd hardly be the one to lose—" "Said take it elsewhere if you don't like it." Thwack! The sound of meat being cut again. For a moment Eleanor did not understand what had happened. The proprietor had turned his head slightly, and something thin trailed down the side of his workbench and hung upon her face. A moment later she realized it was spittle he had spat through his teeth. Her face flared scarlet. With eyes gone milky and pale as a dead fish's, the man then looked at her—straight on. At Eleanor Verdesilver, eldest daughter of a noble house, whom in another time he would not have dared to meet in the eye, let alone hold his head up before. "Makes no odds to me." Elsewhere… but where would she have gone? To whom could she hand over goods and receive a fair "price"? What renowned trading house, what family, what guild of craftsmen would wish to be entangled with House Verdesilver? There, in that spot, Eleanor had had to stuff whatever the man handed her into the sack and carry it back to the manor. It was wretched beyond words. "Eleanor?" Her mother, hearing someone, was calling to her from the sickbed. Roused from her reverie, Eleanor tucked the sack away and stepped toward the head of the bed. And as she went, she looked for the other member of the family who ought to have been keeping watch there. "Is that you, Eleanor?" "Yes, Mother… where has Astrid gone?" "She said she'd be in the garden out back." Her mother whispered, barely, in a voice all but fading away. "She'd forgotten to water the flowering trees, you see… such a good girl." Eleanor smoothed her skirts and sat on the chair beside the bed. The backless chair had been knocked together carelessly from the gardener's leftover timber; its legs were uneven and its seat tilted crooked. When you sit in a chair, you must always keep firmness in your chin and your lower belly! Her mother's voice came back to her out of nowhere, from memory. Knees together—yes. Keep your back straight. A grown lady must never let herself slump, nor carelessly drape her arms across the table…! But this chair was different. It creaked. It went on creaking. No matter how she kept her knees together and her back straight and folded her hands demurely upon her thighs, it creaked. It creaked on and on. It creaked without stopping. It creaked ceaselessly. The short leg, against the floor, creak, creak, creak, creak, creak, it beat. "Gone… to water them, you say." A hollow laugh escaped her. Astrid, her younger sister. She had always been a good, gentle child, but now that was a curse. Quietly she looked about the room. Like the writing chest that had vanished and left only pale dust behind, the room—no, the whole house—was slowly withering. The well-tended flowering trees of the garden would go the same way. Soon footsteps, and then all gazes, would cease entirely. In the end they would feed on nothing but the falling rain or the slop the women threw out. The branches would grow jagged and ugly, the roots wreathed in the smell of wet earth would heave up hideously over the beds, and in place of swelling buds and the petals that would shyly show their faces within, only overgrown stalks and insect-gnawed leaves would spill down in profusion. Her mother's coughing filled the room. A gloomier sound had cut off the gloomy imagining.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main1_Content_2: "Eat a little, Mother." Eleanor set the bread and cheese on an earthenware dish and held it out. The potter must have fired it any old way; a small chip of stone clung to the bottom of the dish and pricked her palm. Her mother gazed at it a moment, then turned her head away. "You must eat." "I've no appetite." Suppressing a cough, her mother went on. "A little rest, and I'll be well." "You've eaten nothing for—" But words could do nothing. Eleanor drew the dish toward herself and considered it. Then she tipped the water jug beside her and soaked the dish through. Taking up the wooden spoon, she began to press and mash together the bread and cheese bobbing within. The spoon, now that she thought of it, had also been salvaged from the belongings some servant had left behind. Its shape was uneven and far too deep; in ordinary times her mother would have been the first to forbid its use—it made a "slurp" with every mouthful of broth. The result was not so lovely as to compel admiration. A marsh of cheese, pale and runny as snot, an archipelago of finely torn islands of bread, and the filthy, foam-covered sea that joined them—such was the state of the dish that Eleanor, helpless, pushed once more toward her mother. She no longer knew what she had been thinking at the start, why she had imagined this would help, but there was no other way. "This way it'll be easier to chew… get even a little of it down." Please. She remembered the first day she had set foot on the training yard alone with her mother. Sword-strokes that ran out straight as a great old tree. Beside them, her own childish straining had felt like a thread of water dribbling crookedly from a teapot. The demonstration her mother gave that day had seemed a goal to chase for a lifetime. Above all, so that the burden of the house should not fall even upon frail Astrid, she had to try all the harder. And now that same mother received the shabby earthenware dish as though it were a precious treasure, and began to eat what was in it, gulp after gulp. If only she would snap at me, even in irritation. Eleanor thought, gnawing at her lip. If only she would shout and fling it away. If only she would spring up from her place and rage, stamping and seething… "Sister, sister." From the doorway came the voice of her younger sister, Astrid. Eleanor hurriedly wiped away the tears that had begun to well and turned her head. "Sister Eleanor…!" "What—what is it?" Her heart dropped. Leaving behind her mother, who wrestled alone with what was little better than muddy water, she rushed headlong to her sister. She searched her from head to foot for anything amiss. "Did something happen?" "No—no, nothing." "Tell me straight!" Eleanor took Astrid's hands and met her eyes. Her two hands began to stroke her sister's palm, her wrist, her forearm, slowly. She stroked and stroked again, in time with the pit-a-pat throb of her pulse. It was a signal that had passed between them since the two were far younger—their way of soothing each other. Little by little Astrid's breathing settled. "Did something happen?" "Nothing happened. It's just—just that all of this…" Astrid's gaze seemed to steady for a moment, then clouded over again. Then she looked about the room. Eleanor did the same, following her sister. There was not much to see. For there was not much left. "Nothing happened, but—sister, sister." There was no one left in the manor now. No one to come, no one to look up to them. Nothing at all. The jewels, the gold coins, the power, the name of House Verdesilver and the footsteps that had once flocked to that name, vying with one another—all of it had been cut clean away. The family demesne, the rights to everything it yielded, the promises made with the guilds and the houses—every bit of it had vanished. "What do we do now? Sister…" Eleanor folded Astrid's slight body into her arms. She rubbed her back hard as though soothing an infant, even making a hush, hush sound, but it was useless. The moan she had heard behind her ear turned to sniffling, then to sobs torn loose from the throat. "What do we do now? What do we do now?…" Beyond the door left ajar, the armor stowed alone in one wall-niche suddenly caught Eleanor's eye. The past glory that had proudly borne aloft the teal cloak and banner of House Verdesilver—the glory she had barely managed to keep, burying it in the earth and hiding it when the King's executioners came battering in. She realized, of necessity, that it had become the one skill left to her. The etiquette of noble society was good for nothing now. She could not borrow the family name. What remained was the swordsmanship she had honed on the training yard. No—the brawling. I can't simply put it on as it is… I have to find a way to hide who I am and earn money. she thought. A hired blade, a fixer, a brawler? Through her mind passed the vague roles of a vague world that she—a proud knight and the daughter of a noble house—had until now neither known of exactly nor needed to know. Eleanor was no mere naïve girl. She knew that fighting in someone's stead at their command—and, beyond that, taking the life of whoever stood against that someone—could be turned into money. Now she had to know it. {IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main1_Short: A name that once opened every door now only closes them. When all that's left to sell is the bread you cannot eat, what does a daughter take up instead?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main2_Content_0:
A sack heavy with money was flung down with a clink and a clatter. Not a single coin spilled from it, yet that alone made for a fairly forceful message. All the more so when the place it was flung was the broad desk that some gang boss kept for himself alone.
"You knew all that yourself, so why the fuss, Fog?"
Hearing those oily words, "Mist" quietly bit her tongue behind her armor. She could not, of course, use her real name while swinging a blade for pay in some dim back alley—but even if it was a name she had made up, it galled her every time some lout tossed it about as he pleased.
"Look here, friend…"
The speech that did not fit her mouth came out coarse and grating. This, too, was the same. In an outfit that took on jobs to break something or kill someone for money—or scouted out and brokered such work—if you addressed your counterpart with refined words like "sir" or "your honor," you stood out far too much. She made an effort to pitch her voice with a hasty, low sort of anger, the kind her former self would never have shown.
"What's that supposed to mean?"
"Means you were turning a blind eye yourself, that's what."
The boss spread one hand to take the weight of the heavy money-sack. He bobbed it up and down as if to gauge its heft, then quirked one eyebrow playfully. As if to sneer—after raking in this much, what have you got to whine about?
"And what is it about this job that doesn't sit right with our Fog's temper this time?"
"…I heard it was about stopping kidnappers."
Mist said.
"Sending a little girl back to her hometown—guarding her, along with her escort, against the gangs that'd chase us till we crossed the border."
"You think I don't know that?"
The boss, chin propped in his hand and glaring listlessly at Mist, rapped the stack of papers in one corner of the desk. A few slid free and slipped to the floor, but he did not even spare them a glance. That was just how much people sought to foist off on others some task they could not see to with their own hands.
"Get to the point. Don't go beating around the bush for nothing."
"…The child."
Her throat threatened to close. Feeling that a voice belonging to some other name, and not Mist's, was about to come out, she cleared it.

"The brat, what about her?"
"When the gang came at us, I cut them down. Before any of them reached the carriage. But the girl who was supposed to be asleep inside threw the door open and came running out. Before she could be dragged off, she looked at the gang's leader—the man who came at me to the very last—and his face, and she…"
Mist shut her eyes tight.
"She called him 'brother.'"
"She saw wrong, no doubt."
The boss had already lost interest in the tale and was reading the papers before him out of the corner of his eye. That perfunctory jerk of his chin, pointing past her toward the back door, brought her blood within a breath of running backward in her veins.
"Once you've said your piece, take your pay and clear out."
"Their faces were alike."
"Coincidence, no doubt."
Her voice sank lower still. Mist was seized by the sensation of her own face, inside the armor, growing hotter and hotter, then all at once turning cold.
"The girl's fingertips were black as soot. So were the dead lead— that man's nape and behind his ears."
Mist chewed over, anew, how she had come to see it. The attacker who flings himself in without regard for fire or water is the easiest to face. Step aside from the line the weapon cuts, then go for the flank or the back left wide open—it is as easy as eating cold porridge. So it was that the helmet of that man—who for the leader of somewhere was clumsy indeed—came off, and through the streams of blood pouring down, what caught her eye for an instant was…
"Soot-smell and grime clung black to him. And his hands were a charcoal-burner's hands."
"What a remarkably keen eye you've got!"
The boss, sneering, glowered at Mist where she stood across the desk.

"You know another thing you're good at—that you'd best be good at? Moving your arms and legs for pay, not your lips!"
He pressed both hands to his forehead and rubbed, as if his head ached.
"Let things roll on the way they were rolling, eh? We pull a tidy broker's fee, and you—didn't you say you'd got some family to provide for?"
Mist held back the foul, bitter taste rising at the back of her throat. However suspect an outfit—one that kept clear of the eyes of the watch and the private soldiers of nobles—she had feared that papering over and hiding everything with false names and pretense would look too suspicious. So she had let slip a word or two about a plausibly desperate reason: that she did this work to support her family. That had been a poor choice. Had she invented an outright, brazen lie instead, she would not have had to think of Astrid every time a moment like this came.
"Seems you've got some kind of conviction of your own—fine, noble's all well and good. You think the world'd be beautiful if everybody belched and farted to high heaven at the table after a meal, and dug out what was stuck in their teeth and smacked their lips over it? I take your point."
The boss spread both hands and spoke jeeringly.
"Somebody's got to protect the weak, and stand his ground without kneeling before the strong. But… you set your mind to it here, of all places?"
His gaze raked Mist up and down. She came within a hair of flushing and shielding her body before him like any noble's daughter. To hide who she was, she had clad herself head to toe, leaving no gap, in shoddy cheap armor and a sword with its edge gone ruined—but it sat dreadfully ill on her. It was a disgrace. She felt as though she stood naked before everyone.
If only she could one day again shoulder the teal cloak of House Verdesilver, its banner, and march onto the field of battle—if only, wreathed in sword-light that gleamed like emerald, she could practice a justice not a hair's-breadth astray…
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main2_Content_1: "If you wanted to keep justice, you should've taken that polished swordwork of yours, bared your face, and gone into service under some house! You think the ones who've really got cause, the truly wronged, come to us? They'd go to a lord or to the royal castle and plead their case…" The boss's caustic words shattered her musings without mercy. "Or—do you actually want to help that sort? The real 'weak' that are too piddling for us to take on? A man driven out for the crime of insulting some lord's son, scratching dirt to live in the forest; a widow whose husband was whipped for failing to hold back a cough when the castellan passed by, and who took sick and died of it, leaving her to feed the little ones alone—people like that? They'll thank you from the bottom of their hearts and say this is all they have to give—a strip of tree bark you can choke down only after chewing it all day, a few wild mushrooms not even bugs will touch—and you'll live off that?" He smirked. "For the sake of that little sister waiting with her neck stretched out for you, you might want to hold your tongue, hm?" Mist found herself taking a step back without meaning to. Her mind—and likely her hidden face along with it—went just as white. "You—how could you possibly know that—I beg your pardon, how did you—" So thoroughly rattled was she that she did not even notice her manner of speech, the shallow disguise peeling away, the self of that other name laid bare. The corner of the boss's mouth tore oily along his cheek. "You said so yourself, didn't you? You went so far as to say you had family to provide for. Didn't you let it slip in passing, a word or two, with the other lads around? Or… did you?" She watched the boss's fingertip tapping the papers. What was inside them? Writings. Above all, information. Who, where, had hidden what weakness; who, where, stood to gain some profit or to swallow some loss… and perhaps even a record of a background-check run on some able blade desperate to hide her identity. Go further, and their names, their surnames, might come to light. That I be put in danger, that I stain my hands with unjust blood—that I can bear. But if Astrid is dragged into it, then we are past the stage for thinking. "Mmh." The boss jerked his chin up sharply, ill at ease. The very tip of the sword Mist had whipped out—the part where the edge narrows to its keenest—was pressing up into the soft underside of his jaw, denting it. Every motion, from the instant the blade left its sheath to the moment it leveled at the boss, had flowed like water, without a trace of waste to be found. Now, with a mere twitch of Mist's finger, the livid blade was a breath away from skewering more than a hand's-span through the boss's tongue and the roof of his mouth at once. She had to strive without ceasing to keep her limbs from trembling. "How dare that mouth of yours—" "And once you've done it—what then?" The boss licked his lips and smiled uneasily. Anyone is apt to, faced with death. Paying it no mind, Mist made to bear down on the hand gripping the sword—"What then"? She imagined what would happen after she killed the boss. To get out, she would have to deal with the underlings barring the way. Or, before they learned he was dead… no, that was not the point. Even if every gang in the place rushed at once to punish her, she could still slip away. The outfit teemed with men trained in weapons other than the sword, in all manner of styles, but not one of them came close to Mist's swordsmanship—was not even fit to be compared. In a narrow passage she had nothing to fear, even facing dozens at once. So then—what next? After running every last one of them through single-handed, boss and lackeys alike, and slipping away? Was she simply to become a fugitive for life? It would be the wholesale annihilation of a criminal outfit. It could not fail to draw the eyes of those who held power. After that, how long until the two daughters of House Verdesilver—vanished since their mother's death by illness—were uncovered? And what of the rumors in those secret places, where a wink and a cipher and edge-shaved counterfeit coins wield more power than any decree of the mighty? She had already been taking jobs under the name Mist. And every brawler and hired blade, every fixer and go-between under heaven knew it. Who, from now on, would entrust a commission to one who, the moment things displeased her, turned an outfit she was on speaking terms with into so much stain upon her sword? "Good thing your head hasn't gone completely stiff." The boss smiled, carefully easing the slackened blade aside.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main2_Content_2:
"As it happens, there's a certain personage curious about who you really are."
It was like a bolt from the blue. Her legs went weak and she nearly toppled.
"…About me?"
"Someone highborn… a noble, they say. And yet well versed in this world of ours, supposedly? Could be just idle talk, I don't know."
The boss carried on as though he truly saw it as nothing more than idle talk. And in truth, why not? Even from Mist's standpoint, whether the rumor was true or false was not what mattered.
What mattered was that, right now, there was nothing she could do.
Her head was a blank. Mist re-gripped the sword and turned its tip straight down toward the floor. Then she drove it in with force. Winding the blade against the thigh-plate and greave she had cobbled on and strapped over—padding made up only because she'd had no occasion to ride—she fixed it fast, gripped the hilt with all her strength, and wrenched. The nameless, worn-out sword she had picked up roughly and worn only to hide her identity snapped clean with the supple, ringing twang peculiar to metal.
"You're not taking this?"
From behind her, as she walked off plodding and dazed, came the clink and clatter of the money-sack. The boss was calling out from inside the room.
"That's a part where your head ought to go a bit stiff… it's money you earned with your work! Tsk, tsk."
Mist walked. She kept walking. Through corridors joining room to room, through rooms joining corridor to corridor, past the gatekeeper standing watch, she came out from inside somewhere. And so she began to walk, aimlessly, through a remote alley where no one stirred in the dead of night. Inside the armor her own heartbeat echoed. To her ears, her tongue, her head, her throat, her shoulders, her flank, the soles of her feet—to every part of her body the heart, swollen fat and bursting, raged. She was out of breath. Her face was burning. Mist clawed at her own throat like a mad woman. She could not breathe. Wrestling with herself, she leaned against a nearby stone wall. Suddenly she looked up at the sky.
It was a moonless night.

{IMAGE}
No one would be about at this hour. Every window and door within sight had its light put out, and even if someone had stayed up late, unsleeping, they could not have seen her, buried in the dark. What did that mean? She was alone. There was nothing remarkable in it. There was no one here. No one could see her.
Astrid could not see the self she was now.
"…Astrid, our good Astrid."
She said under her breath. This morning, before heading out to work, the girl had chattered up to her as though something delightful had happened. While she was at the market she had helped some blacksmith with an errand, and it had suited her hands better than expected; perhaps, she had said, she could go there and lend a hand at odd tasks little by little, and be of some help to the household. And to that admirable sister of hers, what had she said?
"What kind of useless nonsense is that, I said."
The present Mist, sorry now for having flown into a temper—telling her to speak up if she lacked for anything, to put such dangerous ideas out of her head—fumbled at her waist. The money-sack was gone. She was bewildered as to why she had reached for it, but the memory came soon enough. Today she had passed a house that baked and sold bread. The proprietor white to his very eyebrows with flour, and at the same time the smell of fresh-baked bread drifting over his shoulder—it had made her mouth water. She had thought to go home early, get hold of some dried fruit, and leave it with the baker along with the dough—to lift the girl's spirits, even a little, with food that mimicked the sweet tart they'd eaten as children. That money was, by now, settled snug and safe in the boss's strongbox.
In that very place she could never, ever return to again.
"…What do I do, Astrid, what do I do."
She buried her face in her hands. With her back against the stone wall, she crumpled. The old armor rattled and shifted with an ungainly clatter.
"What do I do now, Astrid?"
Eleanor sobbed.
"Astrid… what do I do? What do I do now?"
The sound of her stifled weeping trickled softly, softly along the alley where no one heard.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main2_Short: A face behind a borrowed name, a blade for hire in the dark. But when the wrong word slips out, who has been watching all along?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main3_Content_0: Mist held her throbbing head and stared at the dust on the windowsill. She swept it away absently with a finger, then, realizing there was nowhere to put it, simply flicked it onto the floor. The room was narrow and dark. Even without being shut up in the state of a prisoner—head pounding, throat cracked dry, no strength in her limbs—it would have been uncomfortable enough. "I'm sorry to end up like this without a word, Camilla." She said. "I'll be back soon… with Astrid." Camilla Highgate, head of a venerable countly house, had had little connection with House Verdesilver. Still less with the woman who, after the fall, was no longer Eleanor Verdesilver but "Fog," the back-alley brawler. So it should have been. Driving someone out, taking something away, helping another to a death they did not want—Mist had scraped by drifting from one such job to the next, forever on edge as to when her secret would be exposed. And then, one day, an offer came. Would she care to become the household duelist of a count? There was no need to recount one by one the petty suspicions, the background-checks, the feeling-out. A duelist's may not be a comfortable post that wins the respect of all, but it was better than a life of fretting, hour to hour, over when her identity would come to light, trailing the scent of her secret in every direction. Only—the conversation she had once had alone with Camilla—no, with the woman whom Mist, the lone disguised brawler, would have to call Lady Camilla the Countess—had always lingered in one corner of her heart.
