"If you are more at ease that way, you need not remove your visor even before me. Not now, and not ever hereafter." Camilla Highgate said. Without thinking, Mist let the two hands that had drifted toward her helm fall, careful that it not show. And as she did, she breathed a long, long sigh of relief. That a mere duelist should stubbornly keep her face hidden before a count—and her own master at that—was, needless to say, a breach of etiquette. In the worst case she had been hardening her resolve to prepare for the moment her Verdesilver blood was found out. "Thank you, my lady." "There was a blacksmith who once served our house." What was this, all of a sudden? Mist, then, sharpened her every nerve. "He had no heir all his life, yet for some reason a rumor always went round that he had a child. I'd been wondering whether that rumor might be of use someday… and I think it would do nicely for the two of you." Camilla said. "I'm not sure I follow." "It means you may, for the world's eyes, give it out that the two of you were in truth the sisters in that blacksmith's care." And then she glanced at Mist—as if measuring how she meant to take the command. No—the request. "Will that do?" "Yes." The Mist of that day bowed her head. It was not mere courtesy but sincerity. To think that the very problem over which she had lost sleep and agonized for days on end, Camilla should have been the one to tie off in a single stroke! "I thank you for your deep kindness, my lady." But why? Why bestow such kindness on a mere duelist? She knows something. So Mist had thought, then and now. But it was no time to be choosy about the kindness she accepted. Securing armor and weapons had grown harder and harder, and the days Astrid spent gripping hammer and tongs at the anvil herself were on the rise. In the end the girl would not bend, and—having picked things up here and there—she had set out to forge her sister's sword and armor with her own hands. Amid all that, what did it matter how, or what, the woman who had become her new master knew? That she did not press the matter and let it lie buried was already a mercy to be grateful for. And just when it seemed a moment to catch her breath, however briefly, had come at last…
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main3_Content_1: "Astrid." The present Mist clenched her fist. Her flank ached. Not merely a strained muscle—she suspected something was broken. Someone had surely brought more than a kick's worth of force to bear there while pinning her down. "I'll get you out of here without fail, Astrid." Behind Mist—as she gauged, looking out past the windowsill, the placement of the other walls and fences, the height of the room, the points she would have to break through or skirt to get out—came the sense of someone there. Soon the hinges creaked and a thick wooden door dragged across the floor. "You're awake." Said the one who entered. He wore the robe peculiar to the Lucid Sect, but a natural dignity and gravity steeped his every gesture. A man of some rank, then. Mist kept her guard up, clutching her aching flank. She did not lift her wary eye until he had seated himself in one of the backless chairs arranged around the gaunt sunlight that came climbing through the window. "Do you mean to go on like that and kill me outright?" "And if I said I did?" "Then the Enforcer standing guard outside would come storming in with the force under his command." The high sect official spoke in a lukewarm tone. "That fellow—he's Anguillian. Ever seen one? One swing of his fist and—" He hushed himself, as if at some idle remark. Then he made a gesture of turning something round and round. As though to say that, since wrangling would change nothing, he would return to what he had meant to say. "Thanks to your splendid rampage, our losses are staggering." "I merely made you pay the price." Mist declared coldly. "Because you would not give up the truth." "Your sister—she who has now become a member of the Sect—left a letter herself, as I understand it. Did you not receive it?" "I received it." Her teeth ground. To swindle her with so flimsy an excuse—one transparent from the very start! "How am I to know it was not written under the duress of those who follow you—no, by your own command, gracious sir?" "A fair point. Then shall I ask the reverse?" The reverse? Ask? Mist knit her brow behind the visor. Something about it smelled foul. "Had there been some proof in that place, would you have believed it?" He pressed on quickly. "A signature from your sister? You could simply dismiss that as written under threat. A lock of hair, or a fingernail… how would you know she cut it herself, and it was not thrust there for show? By the same logic, a hair-tie or a sash or a ribbon among her belongings—all unbelievable as proof. In fact, is there any proof at all that you would—" "Spare me the excuses." Mist drew near to the high Lucid Sect official. She shoved aside the chair set out for her. It caught on the uneven floor and toppled with a crash, raising a clamor, and beyond the door came the sense of someone hesitating a moment. Anguillian or no, only one or two could come at her at a time. Take away their weapons, and after that… "I only want to speak with my sister. That is all." It was still too soon to imagine the worst. "Speak with her, you say?" "I'll meet her myself and judge. As for some letter, or some object you claim was entrusted to you—" —because you'd obviously forge it, she had been about to say, then forced the rest down her throat. Said aloud, would it be any different from the nitpicking the high official had just rattled off in his sneering way? "Bring her here yourself." "And then, may I remain in this place?—Ah, no, that would be awkward, wouldn't it." The official spoke, rotating his palm. "If I'm in the same room, your sister will be too tense to talk. So leave just the two of you in this room and—ah, but then you'll say your sister is still under our influence, in our building. So you take her out by main force and live with her some weeks, perhaps some months, until she's had quite enough time to forget the Sect, and then you say let's talk again—and to that, why, we'd hardly know how to answer." Mist's bare face flared scarlet. It was righteous anger. There was not the faintest trace of any other feeling in it. There could not be. "You are not thinking of your sister—you are thinking of yourself thinking of your sister—" A loud clearing of the throat. "…I've strayed from the point. The excuses of those colleagues of mine that set you trembling with rage—the reasons you cannot come face to face with your sister—are, in truth, no excuses at all." The high official went on. "Your sister has, truly, gone missing in the Rapids right now." "That is the lie!" Mist, unable to contain herself, burst into a roar.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main3_Content_2: "An expedition gone missing, red-eyed monsters… that world of dreams—is it not, in the end, as good as your own Sect's backyard? And in such a place you don't even know her whereabouts." "Do people usually die doing something utterly inexplicable in a place they know nothing of?" The high official answered. "Most people die doing things they know very well, in a place they know very well—or at least believing they do. It's a pity we aren't more erudite about our own place of faith, I'll grant—but isn't that the very nature of a life devoted to faith?" Her head spun. Mist was not a person of deep piety, but moments like this she found hard to bear no matter what. This whispering devil's tongue, this banquet of word-games that slipped away slick as an eel. "Your sister becoming one of us is a loss from our side too… You remember that room? Where you were caught." "The place where you sprayed a gas to induce hallucination and delusion, you mean." "Is that what you fix on? Well, that's your affair… but that room is, in fact, where your sister truly lived." Mist chewed over the things she had seen before losing consciousness. There had been what looked like Astrid's travel bag, and the various belongings that had come out of it. The instant she set foot inside, the mind-clouding gas had come pouring out, so naturally she had taken it for a trap built to lure her in— "When you abduct someone, you don't usually pack up all their belongings and haul them along too, I'd think, probably?" Mist pressed her brow behind the helm. She was dizzy. Unlike the foes in the duel-pit who came charging blindly, this sort was far more troublesome. She must not lend an ear. She must not be beguiled. Astrid had been threatened. Or, at the very least, she had been deceived somehow and dragged here. A place called the Rapids, and within it the granting of wishes, the turning back of everything to the past—whether that was true or not, surely Astrid could never want such a thing? Because— "…You are stubborn indeed, I must say." The high official's sigh cut off her thoughts. He shrugged as though he had thrown up both hands in surrender. "If it galls you so, you could see for yourself, you know." "See what?" "The Rapids." He said. "If you're so inclined, I'll guide you to a passage through which you can enter." This is a trap. It was the first thought to rise in Mist's mind, and there was little reason to doubt it. "You'll let me into the Rapids?" "Yes." The high official nodded. "Why not go look for yourself? The expedition records lay out the route as far as the last confirmed point, after all." "It reeks of something rotten." Mist said. "You've no reason to give me such a chance. There's some other scheme behind it." "I mean to recoup as much as we've lost. Information about the Rapids is a great help, you see." Thinking, perhaps, that the conversation was at last meshing on both sides, the official laced his fingers and smiled, well pleased. "Once you return alive from within, you report everything you've been through, seen, and learned—and that makes up for it. If you find your sister in the process, so much the better for you, and this very conversation gains its proper momentum. Well?—" The high official gazed out the window and went on. "—give it some thought." "I accept." A little startled to find her suddenly right before his nose, the official flinched. The thought rose in Mist's mind that she had, for the first time, done something he had not foreseen. "…Very well." It was a sentiment that did not suit the situation, but it was secretly satisfying. "Rest a while and wait. As soon as preparations are ready—" "If it's all the same, I'll go at once." Mist stretched herself out and steadied her breathing. Seeing that they had not stripped her armor after pinning her down, had he meant to make this offer from the very beginning? The thought sent a sudden chill of fear through her. What if even this, in some larger frame, was swindle and lie and trickery? What if, however she combed that Rapids place fine as a flea-comb, she would find no Astrid but only do the Sect a good turn? Yet the doubts that came welling up like a burst dam no longer had any effect at all on Mist—no, on Eleanor Verdesilver. If Astrid was in the Rapids—at least, if there was no other reason to think she was not—then she too must go there. She brushed past the official with whom she had just struck the bargain, stepped up, and knocked on the door. It seemed the matter had been settled outside as well; she heard the bar lifted, and the door rolled inward. Would entering the Rapids by way of a "passage" be just like this? And after crossing the door, what then? Would it be hard and grueling? Painful and bitter? Yet she was not in the least afraid. Not in the least troubled. "Astrid, I'm coming." She said.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main3_Short: Every kindness she's offered seems to ask for something in return. And when the only door left leads into a dream, would you knock?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main4_Content_0:
"Tenacious—the brutes!"
No matter how often she fought them, battle with the dream creatures never grew familiar. Gritting her teeth, Mist climbed up over the great beast's body. Ignoring its struggling, gone visibly weaker, she ground her heel into its shoulder-blade and, putting her weight into it, pulled free the blade buried in the back of its neck. As she drew the deeply lodged sword straight out, blood gushed in spurts, the way water is spat through a narrow reed. That something—surely not even real blood—turned at once into the strange substance peculiar to the creatures of this place: a thick, pale-glowing dust. Strangely, the sight of it brought home to her, anew, just how hard she had been pressed.
"Hahh, haa…"
Mist caught her breath and looked around. Among the alien creatures sprawled dead were ones taller than Mist, ones with thicker thighs or calves, ones bearing longer and sharper claws, ones that ran faster. And yet—once they trusted only to their own strength and came at her with eyes gone red, once they took the foe before them for prey rather than a match and let their attention slip, they themselves turned, in reverse, into prey whose weak points lay flung wide open.
That is what battle is. Even with superior force—even after winning once—it does not simply end there. You must chew over the memory and reenact it without end, until the experience becomes wholly your own.

"Are they truly just beasts?"
Mist said. At the presence she felt behind her, she gripped the hilt hard. On the blade, weeping its blue tears in streams, something glinted for an instant. A dream beast, baring white teeth and charging at her—not yet finished off.
"Or do they have some purpose of their own?"
She curled in tight as a clamped shell and took the first impact. There is no need to parry or dodge a foe's attack outright. As long as you do not lose your balance and fall, even the fiercest collision divides its damage in the end—between you and your foe alike. Merely twisting its direction a little is enough to make the attacker, unable to master its own momentum, tumble. As if sliding down a slope, the beast's body, "parried" along Mist's slender, supple armor, floated up into the air for an instant. She was not one to let that pass. Twisting clear so as not to be pinned, she came naturally to be positioned at its back. She drove down the wrenched blade, but instead of severing the bulging spine, it only cut shallowly to one side. At the beast's thrashing her vision swung hard, and the grip of the hand holding the sword went slack.
"No—!"
When the balance held taut between the pierced beast and her, the piercer, broke, the blade tilted alarmingly far. Try to force it back into her grip now, and the stance she held braced at the beast's back might collapse—or, worse, the edge might set in place for a moment in that warped shape. Luckily the sword run through the beast's neck had stuck into the bare ground, restraining its movement. With every thrash of its four legs—or, at any rate, of the decidedly-more-than-four it had—as it lay gazing aslant at the sky, the beast's living flesh and bits of bone were shaved away, grinding, along the line of the blade's force. A dumb little thing it might be, but she had no wish to leave it like that for no reason. Mist drew the weapon at her flank. The dagger that slid from its leather-lined wooden sheath gleamed with a chill. She re-gripped it so the edge faced not toward the thumb of her fist but the opposite way, the better to take the force of a downstroke.
"I'll finish it quick."
Astride the beast's spine, she settled in as if to throw her arm round its throat. Pressing her body flat to the ground alongside it, she bore down with her weight. Cinching one arm to crush its neck and the thick vessels coursing within, she worked the blade with her free hand. A long cut across the throat, then a stab to the crown, one to the temple, one behind the jawbone… each time the thrust-in edge snagged, she twisted and pulled it free, scattering arcs of blood-water in every direction. Soon the body, its will to live cut off, went limp. When even its death-throes had faded, all around fell silent but for the rough heave of her own breath.
At last, truly, it was over.
Mist rolled off the beast's back. Drawing the sword and finding it undamaged, she sheathed it, then did the same with the dagger. And on the flank of the thing, which had begun to crumble away into dust, she found a long scar. It seemed to have been made—and to have healed—long before it met her.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main4_Content_1: "…Made by a blade." Kneeling, Mist traced the beast's scar with her fingertips. The flesh had risen rough and knotted; it had been a fairly deep wound. That such a thing had healed meant this beast had either kept its life from one who held a weapon, or had somehow turned the situation to its own advantage. Which is to say, the one who held the weapon—likely someone come from reality—had died in its stead. When her thoughts reached that far, her heart lurched. "In a place like this, could Astrid still be alive?" She bit her lip till it bled, but that could not turn her from the words that had come out. Even unspoken, she could not ignore the thought that had held her captive all along. Mist walked, stamping hard at the ground with deliberately large movements, putting more force into it than when she had trodden the great beast, taking it out for no reason on the dirt and pebbles. Her heart would not settle. Now, having let slip from her lips a thought she should never have voiced, was more agonizing than the moment before, when one slip might have meant her death. The information the Lucid Sect had given was of little use. Advice that might serve in an ordinary forest or mountain—that when lost you should follow a watercourse, or that with no watercourse you ought not to descend blindly lest you end up wandering along a ridgeline, but should find the nearest high ground and check the lay of the land—none of it fit the Rapids. Reading the terrain of this place was not geography but the caprice of small children. It felt like joining a game two friends had made up as they pleased, partway through, and guessing at its rules. "What would I have done?" Mist looked about her. She imagined where she would go and what she would do, were she trying to survive in Astrid's place. Either the expedition had been scattered to the winds and she was alone, or, by good fortune, she was with some other experienced sect member… First she would have to find a hiding place. For the moment she would dig the ground shallow at least and cover it over with something for camouflage. Where to get drinking water? The memory of training on House Verdesilver's training yard came to her. After sparring with her mother from the small hours and coming out, spent, for breakfast, the fruit trees in the back garden would be heavy with a water-mist mingled with dew. Though no tree or wild grass is visible to the eye, she had learned then that they exhale tiny droplets through their leaves. That could be put to use. If thirst grew urgent, one could also hold a small pebble in the mouth and work it about to keep the saliva flowing. It was something she had learned in her knight days from a squire, while directing operations in the wilds. But would Astrid know such things? "That girl, probably—" Nothing came. She had to admit it. She—as Mist or as Eleanor—had no way of knowing whether the girl would have done a thing or not. More than that, she had not the faintest idea of exactly what the girl knew or did not know. Scraps of memory, things they had done together in childhood—of those there were plenty; but could one really take it as a clue that someone stranded in the midst of the Rapids most loved to eat fruit tart, or that when they had to step out before grown-ups they would pull funny faces at each other and giggle to ease the nerves? And after that? What of Astrid a little further on in time? Mist sank into thought, stroking her own forearm. Since the fall of the house, she had been—an odd way to put it, perhaps—too busy to so much as draw breath. She had gone from Eleanor to Mist, from proud noble knight to back-alley brawler, and after that to the household duelist of a count. And Astrid? While her sister rushed about ready to take any commission to protect her, what had Astrid done, left standing alone and idle at home? What had she newly learned and understood? Or wished to? Mist recalled a certain day. That morning Astrid had said she wanted to help with odd jobs under some blacksmith at the market and add to the household. "That's useless talk." Mist said to herself without meaning to. "If you need something, just say… that sort of skill's no use in a place like—" The words broke off abruptly. In the end this was the Rapids. It might not be the place where all thought begins, but it was the proving ground—and the final reckoning—that every thought made here must someday meet. That painful little remark, which she had nearly managed to forget by burying it in idle thoughts, rose again. Isn't Astrid, after all, already dead? Mist halted. Her limbs went stiff and unbending as wax. Her neck, her gaze, her very breath all locked rigid, and in that frozen posture she could do nothing more. This cursed thought, however, did not stop. It raced on and on, raking through her head and leaving it all in tatters.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main4_Content_2: If she is dead—and then, behind that purely innocent-seeming hypothesis, came truly hideous words—then it is my fault. Mist stood face to face with the thought. "Me? My fault, you say?" Mist said. "And if it isn't my fault, then whose?" Eleanor said. "I—I should have sheltered her more closely." "This weapon, this armor… when Astrid made them and held them out, I should never have taken them so readily. I ought to have refused to the last, and chided her—told her never to speak so." "It was wrong of her to take a liking to the smith's work. She kept going back and forth, her head filled with empty fancies, and so she was lured in by all this talk of the Rapids and wishes." "It is my fault, for standing by and letting it come to that!" "I should have kept her shut within the house… it's my fault for letting her know I worked as a duelist. It was impossible to hide it from her anyway, wasn't it?" "Even so, I should have hidden it—held out to the very end. That girl need not have known a thing; I alone could have borne the unfairness, I alone the hardship!" "If only I had tried more desperately—!" Just then, passing along the verge of the path, a small and harmless dream creature—one resembling a cat—caught Mist's eye. {IMAGE} It sat perched on a broad rock that took the full moonlight of the Rapids, absorbed in grooming itself. As if there were nothing in all the world but itself and the moonlight upon it—even though there was no surface anywhere to admire the body it tended so prettily—it gave itself wholly over to licking its fur smooth, to laying it flat, to drying it soft and downy. Mist's quickened breath, as she watched, gradually subsided. "…A cat is a cat, even here." Small of body and short of muzzle. Not an animal you could call strong or mighty. Yet nimble of movement and full of cunning, kept for catching rats, and so to be found wherever people live, high or low. An animal that can pass through the narrowest gap, and that—even against a creature larger than itself—turns that very strength against it, burrowing underneath to fasten at once upon the nape. Indeed, had not she herself, from her Eleanor days, watched the movements of cats and applied them to her swordsmanship? How then could anyone swear that Astrid, too, could not have shown such valor—the steadfast will and clever wisdom peculiar to House Verdesilver? "I'm sorry, Astrid." When some uninvited guest watched it groom so openly and then began making some unfathomable crying sound besides, the Rapids cat, its mood spoiled, cocked its head and looked her way. "She's not a child anymore. Is she?" Mist asked. "She'll have survived splendidly even in here. Maybe she's even leading what's left of the expedition! Don't you think?" The Rapids cat, indifferent, having confirmed that the two-legged thing before it was no threat, sank back into tending its fur. That unconcerned air was, strangely, more trustworthy to Mist than any promise in the world. "Maybe she's made a friend within the Sect… haha." For a moment her tongue felt uneasy at its tip. She sensed some faint sign of something, but alone she could not tell what it was. What was certain was that this something hung upon the words she was about to speak. It was a crucial moment, yet of it she herself was utterly ignorant. "I'll have to take them both away together, won't I?" Ah—with that, Mist made her decision. Though she might never know it, that one remark was enough. "A friend she made sharing every trial and joy, that girl." Her muttering trailed on, dim as a dream. "Surely a child as good, as gentle, as well-mannered as Astrid herself…"
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main4_Short: In a world made of dreams, the sharpest blade can't cut the thought that follows her. If the worst has already happened—whose fault is it?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main5_Content_0: "Do you believe me?" "There's no reason I can't." Mist answered curtly—to the woman who had appeared from nowhere and introduced herself as the Guide of this place. "I've wandered this place a good while. I've seen creatures stranger than you, and people trying to bring about stranger things, beyond counting." Mist quietly loosened the grip half-draped over the drawn hilt. For all that she said, she did not let down her guard. "I'm familiar enough with the Rapids now that wanting to merge this place with reality doesn't strike me as so very strange." Splendid!—as if to say just that, the Guide watched Mist with shining eyes. Her name—Polaris, was it? Yet her manner said it was not enough. She acted as if more words ought to come from the other side. Bewildered, Mist looked at her, then thought that someone of all things the Guide of the Rapids would not be merely too bored or too flush with time on her hands—and so would not simply prattle out her plan to a total stranger and then go their separate ways again. Then did she wish for Mist to step forward as a fellow-conspirator in that plan? Mist looked at the shadow cast behind herself, standing with her back to the fire, and behind Polaris, who faced her. She needed time to order her thoughts. Hearing talk of sharing out gold to the dream creatures and the like gave her no real sense of it. To put it somewhat roughly, she did not care. The "dream creatures" she had met since entering the Rapids had, for the most part, treated her as nothing but prey or foe, and she had no cause to grow fond of them either. The only thing that troubled her was this: when dream and reality were merged into one, exactly what effect would befall the people within—and could one escape it? More precisely, not herself but—again, even now—Astrid, who must be drifting aimlessly somewhere in the Rapids, was the problem. "If that plan is achieved, what becomes of Astrid?" "Astri—? Ah, the sister you mentioned." Polaris sank into thought, her head tilted. For a while only the crackle of the campfire broke the silence. "As I said before, when dream and reality become one, what specifically happens to each single person within is something I cannot know." So it was. They had already touched on this. Had she not said herself, from the start, that it was something without precedent? Only, the aim of it was to help the dream creatures escape their fleeting lives. By sharing out the power of reality's gold. And Astrid, then? My good, gentle sister, who must be trembling among those fleeting dream creatures? "You truly have never seen my sister? Think once more, please." The voice that leaked out a little was Eleanor's, not Mist's. "You're the Guide of this place, are you not. Recall it again and perhaps it'll come to you. She looks like me—" "As I said a moment ago—" Polaris gently spread a hand to check Mist. "—I have never seen anyone resembling her. You needn't worry too much." Sensing, even through the armor, that Mist looked disheartened, Polaris quickly added more. "Even apart from the Lucid Sect, it happens often that an expedition come from reality meets misfortune and scatters to the winds. And such people do not all… come to a grim end." It was a comfort that did not sound the least bit welcome. Each time, Mist chewed over the Rapids cat she had met by chance and the thoughts she'd had watching it. "An expedition scattered like that might meet again, might join forces and survive. Don't you think?" Trying to speak hopefully of Astrid put her at ease after all. Her words stretched longer, and her tone began to soften. "As much as I'm looking for Astrid, Astrid is looking for me. I'm certain of it! Once we're out of here, she'll cast off the Sect or whatever it is and come home." "Yes." Polaris smiled and nodded. "I believe she will, too." "As the Guide, you must be well versed in the lay of the Rapids everywhere. And you must meet many along the way." Mist went on. "Will you help me? I mean to take all the help I can get in finding my sister." "Of course I intend to look for your sister as well. Only…" Only what? Mist's gaze followed the eyes of the woman who let the rest trail off ominously. She had thought, for a moment, that Polaris was guessing her sister had met some ill fate—but no. That gaze was sweeping over Mist. Over Mist's armor; over the full plate that had begun to flake thin here and there; over the breastplate where cracks too small to see were spreading, little by little, into fine white threads; over the mail at the armpits, beginning to crack and rasp with dried, caked blood. Above all, it was looking at Mist herself. At the woman who, with a frame and a hardiness that were nothing great, had made up the difference with nimble movement and supple swordsmanship and quick wits, and had somehow come this far into the depths of the Rapids. But in the end, at some point, the limit would come.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main5_Content_1: "…Before you find your sister, why not first go back and tend to yourself?" Polaris opened cautiously. "Spend too long in this place, and in the end, even should you wish to return, you'll no longer be able to take your place in reality." "There's no battlefield that isn't dangerous." "That's not what I mean—" Mist saw Polaris gaze off somewhere, then give a faint chuckle. It was the attitude of one for whom something did not sit well. "These are the words of someone I'd rather not bring to mind, but—stay long in the Rapids, and your self vanishes. What remains is not you, but only the memories of the one you've come to believe yourself to be." And what was that supposed to mean? If it was so dangerous, then it only gave her more reason to find Astrid quickly and get out… "You mean beings of reality become assimilated into the dream?" "In the end it comes to much the same, but not exactly—" "Then could Astrid become so too?" Mist asked, drawing close up to Polaris. "Is there a way to prevent it? Could Astrid have learned it on her own? Is there some material, some technique, needed? If I learn it, then meet Astrid and teach her, that would do, wouldn't it? And if the assimilation has already set in, is there a way to reverse it and undo it?" She fired off her hurried words without pause, as fast as the breech-loading rapid-fire cannon being experimentally studied in a few kingdoms of the continent. Polaris tried several times to part her lips midway, then gave it up and chose to keep silent throughout. Hisss… The sound of water droplets drying away fast came strange to her ear. Polaris looked at the campfire behind Mist. Something had been propped against a green branch stood at a slant by the fire. Looking closely, it was a scabbard set upside down. Whatever had pooled inside it was running down the channel and vanishing the instant it touched the flames. From the black, dried stain at its mouth and the smell of iron it gave off, it was clear enough that this was no clear, clean spring water. Hiss, hiss… Setting the scabbard close to the fire to dry it, leaving it to pool full of someone's blood-water or turbid filth—both, of course, are wrong. The leather lining is apt to rot, and left longer than that, the wooden core breaks out in mottled, milky blotches, then twists past all remedy and begins to take the shape of a sick thing. What does Polaris know of the substances of reality, of the proper care of a scabbard? Nothing. And Mist? She could not be ignorant of it—so why was she being so stubbornly unreasonable? "My sister—" "Let's set thoughts of your sister aside for a moment." Polaris opened her mouth in a somewhat subdued voice. "Will you not talk about yourself?" "What matters is Astrid." Mist's answer followed without yielding an inch. To Polaris it would not do at all. "When you meet your sister, when you find her—what exactly do you mean to do, and how?" "Save her and get out, of course." "And nothing to ask her?" "Ask?" Mist asked the one who asked the question. Ask what, of all things? When even getting home together was as much as they could manage. "You said yourself, with your own mouth, that she likely entered the Lucid Sect of her own accord—or at least agreed to join an expedition—and so is here inside." Hearing it, Mist quietly curled her grip. "Why she decided to enter the Rapids, what she was promised by the Sect's people, what she's been able to find or accomplish in here and how far that matches or differs from what she'd thought, whether you can help each other from here on… above all, why she made the choices she made until now, and whether they were right or wrong—will you not agonize over it together with her?" "I don't think now is the time to agonize." "Your sister doesn't seem to think so—" Mist felt heat rush to her ears. "—seeing that she went so far as to leave you a letter and come to this place… does your sister's opinion not matter?" The eloquence of this self-styled "Guide" was fluent only in seeming, and riddled with holes and blunders. She was excluding outright the possibility that Astrid had been mistaken about something, or come deceived, or fallen for the Lucid Sect's coaxing without knowing better! And who in the world knows her own sister, knows Astrid, as well as a true elder sister? "That girl doesn't know about such things. She—" What does that girl know? She seemed to have had this same passing thought before. That time, the Rapids cat had appeared and helped her firm her resolve. Or—no, the cat had only been absorbed in its own affairs over there, and she who watched it had resolved it herself? In any case, what does Astrid know? What had she set her mind to do? Was there, among the things she knew or did, anything Eleanor herself did not understand? Having taken a liking to the work of the smithy, after her sister became the count's household duelist she had gone so far as to set up a small workshop, growing busy in this way and that. To picture Astrid groaning and dripping sweat in a place where sparks that bore holes through cloth and iron-filing-stained fire-tongs and the limpid copper liquid bubbling up in the moulds all passed about—it did not please her, but if the girl said she liked it, there was nothing to be done. Getting hold of materials for her now and then, and wearing the armor and weapons made from them herself—that much she could accept. For it was a fun thing the girl wished to do. Surely she did not mean to make a trade of it outright. For she was forever the good, gentle little sister who must be cared for. "…There's no way she truly understands Lucid, or the Sect, or the Rapids." Mist said in a strangled voice. Her breath grew shorter and shallower. She felt as though her sight were spinning round and round. "She came in without knowing better, and lost her way—" "Your sister has not lost her way here." Polaris said. As the Guide, she dared to pronounce it. "The one who has lost her way, it seems, is you."
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main5_Short: A stranger by the fire offers to remake two worlds into one. But she has only one question—and what if she's the one who's lost her way?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main6_Content_0:
At the dying gasp that came suddenly from the brush, Mist tensed. It was a beast's, not a person's, but that was no reason to let down her guard. Yet after it, no further sound, no further sign, could be felt.
Her curiosity roused, Mist parted the undergrowth and sought out the one that had made the sound—its corpse.
A creature of the Rapids, smaller than a goat, lay dead with its limbs splayed across the ground. Had it caught some plague? To the eye of Mist, who did not let down her suspicion, the harsh story of its life gradually came clear. The body, with whole tufts of brittle fur fallen away, had skin sunk hollow between the ribs. One injured hind leg had limped, it seemed, to the very last; even after the breath left it the leg stayed folded close against the haunch. The crooked teeth jutting out past its lips were worn rough and jagged, scarcely fit even to use as a paper-knife. Hard-pressed to find food, it must have gnawed and smashed up whatever it could, and so come to this.
"Poor thing."
From the corpse's nose and muzzle, a pale-bluish dust slowly seeped out. Watching it quietly, Mist felt one eyebrow twitch upward. The upper and lower teeth clamped tight, the mouth with its tongue pressed to the ground—and through what gaps remained, the body, broken down into the dust of the Rapids, had spat out something altogether out of place. A glittering lump of pure gold lay cradled in its mouth. The creatures of the Rapids need the gold of reality—she did not care to chew it over again, but her meeting with the Guide, Polaris, came back to her. When it could simply have swallowed what it held in its own mouth, why had it lain still until its breath gave out?
Mist looked toward where it had been gazing till the moment of death. The paths the beasts of the Rapids might travel, the marks they might make, the traces they might leave. Following those, she set her feet in motion. She wanted to know where that strange thing—choosing to starve to death over the gold lump in its mouth—had been hurrying off to.

{IMAGE}
Where she arrived was, predictably, what looked to be the creature's den.
A burrow dug down beneath a large rock, then filled again with fallen leaves and dry grass to lay a soft bed. From its ample size, it seemed two of them would usually climb in together, curl their bodies round, and settle to sleep… two of them?
Mist tiptoed in and probed about the burrow this way and that. The pale-bluish dust was inside it too. From the pressed-down marks and the matted bedding, it had plainly never been a size for just one to climb in and brood eggs or nurse young. Another of its kind, near the same size as the one dead outside, had been within the burrow. And at some point it, too, had died. Waiting for a companion that would not return.
Mist could not tell why she troubled herself over such a pointless thing.
One must have fallen ill and taken to its bed first. Caught some sickness, or hurt somewhere… an obvious enough thing. The other, straining beyond its strength to fetch food, had died. Nothing to pity, nothing worth making a tale of. In the wild such things must happen times beyond counting. For a moment Mist thought she was pitying these two dream beasts. It was a clear-cut explanation—but that was not it. The one that had waited in the nest for the other might have been sound of limb. Might have brimmed with more vigor than its companion. And yet might have waited, and died. Thinking it could do nothing at all by itself. Because the other had meant to care for it, that way, all its life.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main6_Content_1: "What nonsense is this." Mist muttered as she rose. "Reality is no picture-book… this is just a beast. Coincidence." A bitter taste lingered in her mouth. "Enough of these pointless thoughts." And yet it disturbed her. She could not stop thinking. She felt she had to understand something. Mist imagined the two beasts she had just seen, leaning on each other's warmth, curling their bodies and settling to sleep. And she recalled a certain day, when she had held the weeping Astrid in her arms and soothed her. She had taken the long way round, but it was time at last to admit it. She had been thinking of Astrid from the very start. "I… I'm different." Somewhere a cricket with an iron carapace was chirring. The frantic, sickening sound of two iron plates rubbed fast and hard together. Mist bowed her head, then saw her own fingers rubbing at her forearm. The habit from soothing Astrid had been about to come out. It isn't that kind of bond I have with my sister. Seizing the unguarded moment, she let slip one such thought that never quite became words. But her throat soon tightened like an axle crushed under the spokes of a wheel. Then what kind of bond is it? "Eleanor, you've certainly got time to spare, haven't you?" Flustered at the familiar, unguarded turn of phrase that had blurted out, she fanned at herself with her hand. Back when the name of House Verdesilver was on everyone's lips, the banquet halls had been so sultry and stifling. The feather fan she held had been made, in the first place, not for cooling sweat but for covering the mouth and cheeks while one laughed. Each time, she had wished she held instead some broad, flat poker in her hand… but even such trifling stray thoughts were, in the end, excuses. "My sister's in here. I have to save her quickly." Mist said, trying to gather herself again. "This is no time to be sunk in such brooding." She had said the same to Polaris. And how had Polaris brushed that excuse aside? She had said something similar, too, to the Lucid Sect official with whom she'd struck the bargain before entering the Rapids. He had needled her over her stance—asking how believable a proof must be before she would count it as proof at all. "I have to meet her and first get her out of here." And then? How to settle the matter tangled up with the Sect? While she and the Sect stepped forward to talk it over, was Astrid to stand idle behind her like a sack of borrowed barley? What would Astrid think? Will you not ask her when you meet, Polaris had said. What was there to ask? In taking her sister out of so dangerous a place… but would Astrid herself think the same? Would she meekly fall in with her wishes? She could not picture well what would come after they met. And if she said no? If she said she had truly found something in here, that she was gathering the threads to a wish that could be granted? Then was she to set aside any thought of leaving, and explore the Rapids again together with Astrid? But this thing called a wish—was it not, from the start, beyond all sense? Mist chewed over her sister's letter. A wish that could turn everything back to the past. Surely Astrid could never want such a thing? Because— No one cut in, or spoke to her, or made any sound, nor did any other thought happen to rise. From here on it was Mist's own thinking, her own will, her own decision—and so, wholly, her own responsibility. Because it is an impossible thing? Then what of all the astonishing objects and phenomena she had seen since entering the Rapids? The Lucid Sect, and every explorer and traveler and treasure-hunter who had entered the Rapids unconnected to the Sect—so they were all of them wrong, and Eleanor Verdesilver alone thought sensibly? It was not a matter of whether granting a wish was possible or impossible. It was a matter of belief, and of whether she could admit that belief to herself. Perhaps all of this was the problem of a stubborn child thrashing about, turning her eyes from the possibility that this was Astrid's own decision.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main6_Content_2: "You want to go back to the past? Why?" Mist leaned her back against the rock and bent forward. The bridge of her nose stung and the back of her throat heaved. "You don't trust me. Is that it? I'm sorry, I'm sorry. No matter how hard your sister tries, it's never enough, is it? Your sister hasn't protected you well enough, has she?" Had she actually said such a thing, what would Astrid have answered? Likely she'd have flung her eyes wide and pursed her lips and waved her hands, denying it with all her might. Saying it was absolutely not so, that she only, only… look at this. Mist could not even fill in the voice of the Astrid in her imagination. That was how bitterly ignorant she was of the girl as she was now—of what exactly she knew, and for what, and what efforts she had made. The realization pierced her head with pain. The warped guilt of the past, rooted in the self she had been until now; the present guilt that had thrown out branches at the end of nothing but excuses, far from facing that past; and, beyond even that, the guilt of what was to come—that, rather than begging forgiveness now, it might all end with her never meeting her sister again—guilt swollen hideous as a vine left untrimmed past its season had coiled and grown in the garden of Eleanor Verdesilver's heart. Who said that nothing could grow in a garden grown untrodden but sickly bluish weeds? Have you not seen, when the season ripened, the flowers of sin bloomed riotous and lurid-vivid? Have you not seen the sweeping view of lush trees—wreathed in the scent of remorse that has lost its road to repentance, in the trailing folds of confession that spread upon the wind—all at once breaking into flower, forgetful of the years? "Did you leave without a word because you feared it would be like this?" Mist burst out laughing. The sound of swallowed tears and coughed-up bitterness followed. "Because you knew I'd be like this… that I wouldn't even hear you out, that I'd only browbeat you—how could you think such a thing, never do anything so dangerous?" She had no confidence she would not have. But hounding the Mist of the past was meaningless now. What remained was what lay ahead… "I'll listen to you. I'll ask you." Eleanor said, on the edge of tears. "There's so much I know less of than you—the Rapids, the Sect. Tell me everything you were promised by those people. Tell me everything you found in here, whether there really was a road to the wish. And then let's agonize over it together." Her words went on. "Not because anyone has to do anything, but because it's something we both decided to do… because it's not my matter but ours, something we, Eleanor and Astrid, the two of us, must do together." But the thing that should have been a tale for the two of them alone had come too far. Right here there were the Rapids, and Polaris. There was her plan. When dream and reality were merged, no one knew what would befall each single person within. Then by whatever means, that plan had to be stopped. "…I'll find that girl." Mist steadied her stance, putting strength into her waist and belly. Striking the rock she leaned on with a clenched fist, she pushed herself up. "And until then, nothing unknowable is to happen. I won't allow it." You're stubborn indeed. She felt as though such an answer would come back at her. At their meeting that day, too, words not much different from that had passed between them, as she recalled. And even if they hadn't, it made no difference. The Guide, Polaris, was now her enemy. Not because Polaris was evil, nor because there was a flaw in that plan, nor even because Polaris meant to bar her road. Because there was simply no other way. "Until I find my sister, I won't set foot in any plan, any side—not for anything." Still she felt she had not advanced a single step. As if turning from Astrid's voice, this time she was turning her eyes from Polaris's, and from her own preposterous reasons for trying to stand in Polaris's way. She was being unreasonable. "This is the last, the very last time I'll be unreasonable, just this once. To find you… I'm so sorry, Astrid." She went on. "I want to see you and say it to your face—I'm sorry, I'm sorry, Astrid. I want to meet you again and say it myself. So please, never give up." She seemed to have strayed off the path and spent too long there… she heard the sound of the black beasts in pursuit. Drawing her sword, Mist took her battle stance. "Because I won't kneel either—not until I meet you."
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main6_Short: Two creatures, one waiting in a nest for the one that never came home. What if protecting someone meant finally listening to them?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main7_Content_0: "First I must reckon the cost of hiring a new duelist, and…" The voice of the woman seated in the armchair in the moonlit dead of night rang out. "I can hardly throw all her things away, so until she returns I'll have to keep them somewhere and see to their upkeep. …If she returns, that is." With those words, the voice—edged a moment ago with something like irritation—lost its edge. Then a long sigh followed. "Honestly, it stings a little. Mist." Gazing fixedly at the moon risen beyond the window, Countess Camilla Highgate spoke to herself. "And here I thought we'd grown, well—a little closer." "Close"—an awkward word to apply too literally between a Countess of high standing and the household duelist she had hired. All the more so when that duelist was no ordinary duelist but one who, on account of a past she wished to hide, could disclose neither her true name nor her face—and more still when the Countess herself dimly surmised that very circumstance. Perhaps it was for exactly that reason that Mist had left this place without a backward glance. Tossing down a brief letter—no, something nearer a scrawled note—saying she would pull her sister out of the Lucid Sect, and then vanishing utterly, alone: her heart was not beyond Camilla's understanding. Camilla had indulged her circumstances, asked neither her face nor her name. She had even gone to the convenience of fashioning a false identity for her to present in public. Even so, full and open trust would be hard to come by. Better to lie awake into the small hours wondering what scheme this absurdly generous Countess—who had appeared out of nowhere to style herself employer and protector—might be harboring… Above all, working as the household's duelist, she too would by now have come to know it. The true nature of House Highgate, so different from what was given out to the world. In genteel terms, a house of long lineage; in the more common parlance, a house that had once "thrown its weight about" a fair bit; a pitiable household whose mistress, the woman Camilla, ran herself ragged trying to prop up the prestige of a line gradually guttering out. Such was the world's estimation of House Highgate. The reality was the reverse. The house had merely chosen to drive its roots deeper and longer rather than put forth flowers and fruit and stalks that could be flaunted in broad daylight. Rather than reduce the chances of mingling with the regional powers—the lavish banquets, the horse races, the hunts—it had merely spread its influence through the world of back alleys and duel-pits. To keep one foot planted in the world of fixers and brawlers of every stripe, and above all of information-merchants, and to devote itself to the war of secrets—that was the method Camilla Highgate had chosen. She had not, of course, recited every last fact of it to Mist on the first day she took her in, nor had she ever troubled to explain it… but one has a sense of these things. Work as a house's duelist and you come to learn the parts that house would rather not reveal; keep an elder sister who works as a duelist and you come to learn this and that about the work she would rather not spell out exactly. That she earned her money, for instance, at a trade in which, if you do not take a life, your own life may be taken. Though Mist herself had asked, quite earnestly, that this fact not be let to leak. "If I'd shown such a calculating face—increasing my illicit influence even to the point of deceiving every eye—in the days when you still used your own name, it would surely have earned nothing but contempt." Camilla stroked the armrest and gave a faint chuckle. To uncover the true name and origins of the enigmatic blade "Fog" and her younger sister had required no grand stratagem. It was, rather, a matter of time; and for Camilla it was nearer to having rushed in headlong before the two sisters' fates plunged into a pit past all saving. "And if I told you it was for exactly that reason that I help you—would you believe it, Mist?… I hold your house, and your father Sir Loren, in respect." The hairs at the nape of her neck stood on end. To speak the name of a man beheaded for the crime of sensing the Princes' Revolt beforehand and failing to report it—and, what's more, to call him respected—was, needless to say, a perilous thing. Far thinner suspicions than this had been enough to bring all manner of ordeal. And yet she said it. She let it out. There were times, now and again, when one tired of being calculating. "What would it have been like, had all the nobles of Celestia been as I am… A pack of neurotics, deceiving and being deceived, deceiving even themselves, growing in the end more learned in the habits, the weaknesses, the secrets of others than in their own, and comporting themselves accordingly—and there they are, granted their titles and strutting about. Ugh." Camilla gave a playful little shiver. Gooseflesh prickled up across the body clad only in a thin gown. "…Sir Loren in his lifetime, and your house, were far from that calculating, self-serving sort. Because it is something I cannot do, I have always respected you for it." Then why? The unspoken question rose in her mind. There was no evidence he had taken hush-money or any such thing, and no other corner where he might have pursued private gain. Neither he nor his family had in fact taken part in any plot. So why had he chosen to learn of the plan of rebellion beforehand and hold his tongue? "There's something to it." Camilla said, rubbing her brow. "Your father was no traitor… he had merely come to know something others did not." She rose and crossed to the hearth. Sorting through the reports laid on the side table, she ruminated over the information she had crammed loosely into her head during the day. The places Mist might have gone; the route by which her sister and the Lucid Sect had made contact; and besides these, the matter of the Princes' Revolt that had brought about Sir Loren's death—an affair already hushed up among the powers-that-be under the name, romantic even, of "the Greensilver Treason," its inner workings on the verge of being buried. To take Mist and her sister back in again, she had above all to tie off that knot. "You vanished without so much as a word to me, the same as your sister, but…" The corners of her mouth hardened a touch coldly, yet the words ran on. "To uncover the reason your father made that choice—and so to make ready for the two of you to reclaim your lives—that would make the finest gift with which to welcome you back. Mist—no…" Camilla drew a light breath. "I'll be waiting, Lady Eleanor Verdesilver."
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main7_Short: Some debts are paid in secrets, not coin. And the kindest patron may be the one still digging for a dead man's truth—so what is she waiting to give back?

ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Main8_Short: Strikethroughs, scribbles, and a recipe written for two. In the margins of an ordinary afternoon, what were they promising each other?
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Short0_Content: When Camilla first extended her hand, Mist caught the scent of calculation on her fingertips. A bargain dressed up as goodwill, a kindness that would someday return as an invoice—that was all she saw it as. But even after learning the face behind the disguised identity, Camilla never withdrew her hand, and her genuine gestures of care slowly loosened the shoulders that Mist had kept rigid for so long. Now, between the two of them, the things that need no questioning keep growing. In this one place, seated across from each other with teacups between them, Mist could set down both armor and helm and simply smile at ease. And the same was true for Camilla.
ui.TravelerStory_Mist_Short1_Content: Four days into the Rapids, Astrid glimpsed Belpomet tearing the Lucid Sect apart and fled to safety. Even with trembling hands, she never let go of her pen. Her sister had always seen her as someone to be protected, but in this moment, even in the face of fear, Astrid was deciding what to leave behind.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main1_Content_0:
Wasn't it beautiful? The Dream Master's Host.
Taking the shoreless sea of dreams for nothing more than a sheet of drawing-paper, recklessly smearing its colors together and dragging its lines across it, until at last it stains the whole in its own singular hue — wasn't that bearing of theirs truly relentless, and truly magnificent? Making brushes of their jackboots, creative inspiration of the war-horn's command, daubs of paint of their charging hooves and the wheels of their wagons, all to complete that imperfect underdrawing called the dream-world — and most of all, your tiny little world standing against it like a lamp braving the wind, the wretched figure you cut as you thrash about trying to look away from the one certain ending — wasn't that, truly, beautiful?
Your forest, too, was one such lamp.
He saw you fall, spent past your strength in trying to keep the forest. He saw the forest's boundary pushed farther and farther back with each passing day; he saw the forest's plants turn to smoke and its animals to shadow, losing their memories and crumbling away by degrees. And he saw, too, the Dream Master's Host, advancing tirelessly, step after plodding step. When the spirits of the forest — who by nature could never be fixed in any settled state — wandered every corner of it, limping, broken and cracked and snapped in every place, his two eyes flushed as scarlet as holly berries against fresh snow: surely you, too, saw it, time and time again! Won't you permit me, at this passage, to speak the monologue in your stead — oh, thank you for your leave!
"Ah, what in the world am I to do!"
Day by day, only the sighing grew. While, at the break of dawn, every dewdrop on every leaf reflected the whole net of fate woven of all the other dewdrops — dare I declare that the image gathered within was not the splendor of daybreak, but the grief-stricken faces of you two, sister and brother? The Dream Master had no reason to leave your forest in peace — a forest that had already raised up the Cycle of Birth and Death and, with it, a history that does not wither. For all order in the dream-world must converge upon his name, and his alone.
And so the time simply slipped away, helplessly. Though no clever remedy was anywhere to be found.
His Host is not one to fall back so easily before the struggling of a mere two Forest-Keepers. Even if you dug in your heels to the very end, what you would meet is not the sweet fruit of victory but only the bitter wall of reality. For the dreadful Dream Master himself would, in the end, descend in person for the sake of your forest, that festers in your hearts like an aching tooth. Could you, who were helpless even before his Host, stand against the very wellspring of that Host? You know well enough, don't you, what miserable end befell the Lord of the Snow Peak — who commanded countless giants and wolves — after he came to grips with him?
And so he — the one of the two Forest-Keepers who was, of course, the wiser, the finer, the more admirable — resolved at last, so they say. To reach out his hand to another source of power, one as mighty as the Dream Master, perhaps even more profound. To drink that power in to the full and so gain, for a time, the strength to defend the forest. No doubt he meant to strike some sort of bargain — but understand this clearly. A bargain is struck, from the first, only between two parties who each have something to offer.
Not when the one side, hopelessly in want, lays all his cards on the table alone and then grubbily begs.

What a pity that you never saw with your own eyes the moment he received that power and was reborn as a new being. How mouth-wateringly lovely it was! Some will fasten clumsy little moral sermons onto it — that he was swallowed by an evil force, that he lost himself and turned ugly, deteriorated — but pay them no mind! By their nature, the instant one perspective is negated, it is bound to put on a show of hating, however reluctantly, all that has slipped beyond itself and newly deteriorated into — a slip, "reborn" — into all things newly reborn. Ah, but the talk that, in that instant, a long rift was carved that split the forest's spine in two; that a scream that tore the very eardrums of the Rapids rang out; that the death-cries of the ignorant beasts of field and air caught up in it — even of the spirits, who ought to be eternal and undying — scattered like the ashes that trail a great blaze — that talk, at least, happens to be true. I don't know what all the fuss is about. On the contrary, I cannot bear how pitiful you are.
For you will never, ever know how sweet that moment was.
Now you must face the other half of the reborn Forest-Keeper. Those two eyes scarlet as burning coals — and what of the gaunt limbs that call to mind a sheer cliff's edge, the claws of hand and foot so sharp they could shear even radiance, casting no shadow? But what is most admirable of all is his bearing in defense of the forest. He is no longer the irresolute, half-a-Forest-Keeper of old. Armed now with searing grudge and obsession, he has become a warrior who will do anything to keep the forest! He'll tear to shreds every living thing that loiters nearby, dig out the curious eye and bestow upon it an eternal darkness, hunt down the humming melody and carve away whole the tongue that murmured it, the ear that opened to it — and have strength to spare. Oh, how admirable! Thanks to him, you too must have felt one weight lifted.
And yet — no — you began, on the contrary, to behave like the most brazen of fools.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main1_Content_1:
"………?"
That is the name you call out, so earnestly. Would you believe it if I told you that only at this passage does the story's latecomer character — you — at last come crawling out, limp and dazed, with eyes that know nothing? This is the punishment given to such a latecomer.
Then again, the you of back then is gone now anyway, so what does the name of the remaining half matter?
"What is all this?"
Why did the two of you not come together, hand in hand, to borrow that power? If you had poured out even half the effort you spent then, calling his name in desperation, searching for the thing already reborn — if you could only have gathered all of you into your arms that way — the forest would have become wholly mine!
"Why is the forest like this? Where are you? …………?"
Everything you met and suffered with that thing was nothing but a misunderstanding! So come back to the forest that was once yours. Right now! What you heard then was not the cry of a beast starved for slaughter; the blow it struck did not topple, root and all, the great tree the two of you cherished together; it did not butcher, without a trace, the many beasts that waited, innocent and trusting in their master's embrace, for only the moment of being loved! Well — in some tellings, they say that in that moment you sensed something. That, sensing this forest, and above all the bond between the two of you, could never return to what it once was, you wept for the first time, overcome with grief — and that the teardrops which fell that way turned at once into small, hard pebbles, where no seed, no rainwater, not even a spore could ever come to rest. Or some such thing.
Don't you find it a touch shameless, even to your own ears?
"I can't just leave you like this."
After whimpering for a while like a runny-nosed child, you barely gathered your wits and said as much — so they tell me. You set your most loyal Leaf-Pup spirits to baring their fangs and snarling. At none other than your own other half!
"I — we — have to protect the forest…."
And so you, sniveling so wretchedly, and the Leaf-Pups, and the rest of the half-taught spirits who had still not severed their grubby ties to you, joined forces to stand against the thing, and so on and so forth… now look here, isn't there a limit to ingratitude? Shouldn't you praise that admirable thing, who offered up himself to gain the power to defend the forest? Shouldn't you, I mean to say, be grateful to me, who granted that power!
One day, surely, the day will come when I too receive my thanks.

The outcome of the fight? Yes — you won. For the thing did not yet know its newly reborn self well. After all the uproar, there came to you a moment when victory and defeat were plainly divided — the moment you so wished to believe in. The spears and blades of vine and moonlight, the assorted spells of your loyal spirits, bound and lashed and bit at the thing and worked every kind of low interference upon it, until it could not so much as twitch a finger. There, you had only to wring out your last strength, turn your eyes from its exhausted face, and make one final decision, just one more….
You hesitated, didn't you?
Did you try to set it free again? To speak to it? To shut it away somewhere and nurse it back to health, bringing it dew-soaked raspberries and the like? Watching that farce would have been delightful enough to make me clutch my belly with laughter — what a shame I couldn't see it for myself. Ah, I'm glad I can at least pass on this one thing for certain. That moment of your hesitation was, for the thing, the perfect chance to turn the tide of battle. Wringing out the last strength it had, counterattacking, the thing rejoiced so hard its mouth all but split open.
What were you thinking, as you fled, mortally wounded by the thing that had been your other half? In the moment you crossed the forest's boundary in a frantic scramble, with only the half-a-Forest-Keeper's staff you had once shared with him, and the spirits under your protection, tucked under your arm? How did it feel to hear, at your back, the roar of that thing — the red-eyed monster, drunk on the elation of victory, become at last the forest's true master? Tell me, please! I think that, having heard it, my dreams will be most foul for days.
But you are gone now. Even if you wished to tell me, you could not.
For the last thing you remember is yourself, sprawled on the bare ground. As the strength drained little by little from your whole body and your eyelids came down, everything — everything seen and heard and felt — grew smaller and dimmer and slower, on and on, until at last it shriveled to a tiny dot, barely there at all.

"Ah, but, but…!"
The you of back then might cling to me like this, perhaps, stamping your feet. Unable, in the end, to let go of your regret.
"How could you just forget all of that?"
That's right. You may have forgotten, but I remember. Because you — the you of back then, to be precise — are no longer here. Who on earth are you, you ask?
Hm. There, you see. You don't know yourself — so it's only natural you can't remember what you went through. It does seem I'm right after all, doesn't it?
Ah — then who am I, you ask?
Who else could I be, but the beginning and the end of this story, the source of power your other half reached out his hand to, the forest's new master — and the true master of this dream-world, not that clown? None of it will reach you, the you of now, but the truth happens to be just so, and what can be done about that? So let us take our leave of one another now — farewell, nameless wanderer!
Sweet dreams — no, very bad dreams. May yours be days of nightmare so foul that you break out in cold sweat, your mouth twisting like a storm-cloud, until at last you wake screaming a terrible scream. Don't go sinking into resentment, fancying that only you must endure such a thing. There's nothing to feel wronged about. You and your forest are neither the first of this, nor the last. You were merely marked down as someone's next, and somewhere's before. Surely by now you can guess who I am?
I am the Nightmare.
And one day, all of the Rapids will be mine.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main1_Short: A voice recounts a ruin as if it were a triumph, and calls the horror beautiful. But who whispers, once every witness has long fallen silent?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main2_Content_0: When she opened her eyes, the world was still there. This was a clockwork spring rewound to its place, taking its first step once more; it was a wandering whose beginning and end were not yet fixed; and it gave birth, then and there, to the first question within a system of thought belonging to oneself alone — the sole subject able to doubt and to prove a world of one's own — Who am I? It learned that it had a body it could move, and so it became someone. That someone, after looking down at its own body, became her. Gazing at the torso that ran on below the neck, the limbs attached to it, the cloth she wore, the ornaments and the rest, she marveled. She was full of color. She was wonderful. The sight of her was like a rainbow of every hue, or a waterfall cradling the ever-shifting rapids. A moment like this — reclaiming a self once forgotten — was the equal of discovering a whole unknown world in one stroke. She was rewarding. To recognize her rewarding self was more rewarding still! When she began to move her body, still more interesting things appeared. The marks, for instance, where the horns on either side of her head had gouged the ground. When she thought something was fluttering at the edge of her swaying vision, it turned out to be her own long braided hair; and besides that, the cords and bands that flowed down around her body, and the little carvings of stone or wood hung from them…. She thought she must be very skilled with her hands. It also occurred to her that she had lived a most leisurely and contented life. "And just who am I, then?" she said. Her voice was soft, but firm. It was the speech of one who was capable, steady, and strong of will. This, too, she liked. But the thought carried in that very voice grated on her. It troubled her that nothing came to mind. That the first thing she had said was 'Who am I?' Then, all at once, something flashed up. "I am…." A word of an instant flickered across her mind like a spark struck from flint. "I am… 'Nachia.'" She remembered someone calling her that. It had been a man's voice. Not an old man's, nor a grown man's, nor a young man's, but a boy's, still tender with youth. Nachia looked around, wondering whether the owner of that voice might be watching her from somewhere. "Where is he?" Suddenly there was a throbbing ache in her chest. There was no one in the forest clearing. As her focus shifted from herself out toward the rest of the world, her curiosity only grew. "Where is this place? Is it somewhere I know?" The forest was just a forest. An ordinary, plain, unremarkable forest. Just somewhere, holding no fateful encounter or secret, neither the mouth nor the threshold of a journey leading to some great event. Again and again Nachia took that impression of it — and yet she could not stop looking around. She wanted desperately to believe that this was not just somewhere. She wanted to find out what she had done within it, what she had been meant to do. Not a single trace remained of the cry of insects, the beating of birds' wings, the footfall of beasts. The trees were weeping. The leaves were sighing. The flower-petals, wearing the faces of the guilty, stubbornly refused the bright sunlight. Everything left in this place was like that. There was nothing but those bound fast by root and mycelium, unable to flee of their own accord. Prisoners of a fate that could only suck their fingers and watch some irreversible change approaching from somewhere. "Do I know what that thing is?" For some reason, it made her sad. When she changed the ending of the words and said it again, her heart felt a little easier. "I know what that thing is." But what could she do to find out? There was no one here to speak to. Thinking alone in total ignorance would only deepen the questions. Yet to summon someone else… summon? Why, of all expressions, did that one come to her?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main2_Content_1:
"If I… do something…."
Nachia gestured. Fast and large, then slow and small — there was an order and a rhythm to it. There was a swelling and softening of dynamics, too. It was something like playing a piece of music.
"Like this, like this… something should happen."
The thought struck her suddenly that she ought to keep her mouth shut. Such memories are always the hands' work rather than the head's. And so, not knowing what she was doing, Nachia performed a swift sequence of gestures. From beginning to end — though she hadn't even known there was such a thing — she carried it off without a single falter. She had not clapped, yet the sound of clapping rang out. Just as she was thinking she would come to hear such sounds often from now on, something appeared before her.
"Come forth!"
It was a thing she'd said on a whim, unable to tell whether it was working properly. The things that appeared looked to be some kind of four-legged beast. In place of natural fur, though, they wore tough, hardy leaves, set as densely as armor. Their claws were blunt but straight and hard, and beneath two yellow-glowing eyes a tongue lolled, dangling, as if for some reason it had no mind to go back in. Could it be they had no lips…?
"Smaller than I'd thought?"
There had been many such moments since she woke. Moments where she'd say something offhand, then trace back her own past through what she'd said. As Nachia reached out to stroke the head of the beast that had come closest, she saw her own arm flailing far above the crown of its head. She had the feeling that 'originally' that was how it should be. Did that mean the beast had once been that big, or could grow that big? Meanwhile the beast, seeing the hand dangling at such a dizzying height, seemed to have misunderstood something: it hunched its body tight, twitching like a chestnut burr, then kicked off hard with all four legs and leapt. And so it succeeded in touching the palm Nachia held flatly out, blankly, at the very top of its head.
{IMAGE}

"Oh…."
Nachia drew her hand back. Then, looking troubled, she glanced back and forth between that beast and the others around it, their eyes shining with bright curiosity.
"Good job… puppies?"
If she sounded unsure, the truth was that the beasts — no, the balls of fur that had just been given the pretty new name of "puppies" — were no different. Apparently deciding that this single phrase was enough to newly define the relationship between the two sides, the "puppies" watching Nachia all began at once to wag their tails. Then, in no time, they pressed up against her, friendly.
"Did the old me call you puppies too?"
No answer came back. Well — they were puppies.
Instead, that tongue — a tongue somehow moist, though it had surely been taking the cold wind this whole time, with no telling when it had gone back into the mouth and out again — began to lick her. Nachia crouched down to their eye level and gathered the puppies up, stroking them, scratching behind their ears, their brows, their chins. It came so naturally that this, too, seemed a memory carved into her hands rather than her head. That peaceful, almost happy, innocent scene — the first she had met on opening her eyes. Nachia laughed out loud despite herself. As if the feeling were catching, the puppies, too, rolled onto their backs and wriggled, brimming with delight. That was why her gaze fell anew on all the little jingling ornaments hung about their bodies.
"Did I put these on you?"
The puppies neither denied it nor confirmed it. Either they couldn't make out her meaning, or — seeing that they'd been summoned in answer to her will — they had lost their memories along with her…. Nachia rattled the thing she held in her hand, then compared it to the other carvings fastened about her own body. Their features and style matched, exactly.
"I didn't just give them to you — I made them and gave them to you!"
It must have been her imagination, but the puppies seemed to be agreeing fervently.
"This is fun. Shall I try a little more? Are you my… children?"
The response — or what passed for one, the puppies' spirit — was lukewarm. Did that mean it wasn't the answer?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main2_Content_2: "Then are you my underlings?" This one she sensed was wrong the instant the word left her tongue. Wasn't it too… formal an expression for such lovable beings? Like calling the old tree the two of them had planted and cherished together a 'jointly-owned specimen of timber'! Why had such a comparison come to her? "Are you my friends?" The most convincing response yet came back. Seeing it, Nachia stroked the puppies all the more fervently, and her hands in turn spurred on, again and again, the dance of the puppies as they responded with delight. "Could it be that you're my—" Before she could even open her mouth, her chest throbbed. "—family?" "I had a family." Her voice, gone heavy, sounded like another's. Nachia abruptly set down the puppy she'd been holding and rose to her feet. The puppies, who had been so thoroughly steeped in her touch, in her gaze, splashing about in their joy, circled her at a loss. Come to think of it, the very name Nachia was something borrowed from him. Had there been no memory of him calling her that, Nachia would still not be Nachia. "The one who called me that… why isn't he anywhere near here?" She scanned her surroundings for any likely place he might be, but the meaningless heart of the forest, this nowhere-in-particular, had not changed in the least. No matter which way she went, no matter what she followed, going would be no better than not going; and yet standing still and waiting would change nothing either. At such a dilemma's crossroads Nachia stood. She turned her head. She had marked several places where the grass and jutting stones were sparse — the closest thing to a path leading on from the clearing. Then she lowered her eyes and studied the puppies' faces. "Still, I have to go somewhere, don't I?" Even if she only wandered aimlessly, if she could go anywhere other than here, she had to move. She had to set out, somewhere. She had to go to the place where he might be waiting — the one who had given her back her name, while not yet having a name of his own. She was skeptical whether she could convey all of that without trading words, but luckily, judging by the impression they gave, the puppies seemed to have more or less understood. "Let's go somewhere." The puppies leapt and bounded in agreement. "But where should we go?" The puppies, more demurely than ever before, planted their rumps and sat. Somehow they even slyly avoided her gaze, as if some urgent business had suddenly come up, as if some grave matter had occurred to them. "What's the matter? I only want to ask… is there somewhere you'd like to go?" When she singled one out and asked, it only tilted its head aslant. Nachia idly pointed to one of the paths she'd noted earlier. "How about this way?" The puppy stayed quiet. "Then this way?" The puppy wagged its tail happily. Seeing it, Nachia snorted a laugh. "What — you could've just said so from the start."
