But perhaps that had been impossible. Not the elementary objection that a puppy cannot speak, but rather that perhaps a puppy has no opinion of its own about wanting or not wanting to go anywhere. It had merely watched Nachia's reaction and fallen in with it. Yet how could it 'fall in' with her pointing down a path that might lead anywhere, when she herself had no idea where to go? It was possible. If Nachia were the old Nachia, the Nachia of the days when she knew everything. Maybe the me of now doesn't know, but my body might remember where to go. she thought. It made sense enough if, while in that state, the response shifted ever so slightly as she pointed somewhere, and the puppies, seeing it, fell in with her. Nachia moved off in the direction she'd pointed. She left the clearing. She vanished into the gaps between the dense undergrowth and the trees. "I almost forgot!" And then she came hurrying back at a trot. "This must have been mine, too?" She looked at the long staff that had lain beside her unconscious body. Not just a stick, but a staff, marked off into a plainly made base meant to touch the ground and an ornamented top meant to be raised aloft. "The handprints… mm, yes, this is what I used to carry." When she wrapped her grip around the smooth, worn part and stood, the height was just right. It was hard even to imagine how she could have thought to leave it behind. Just as she made to set off at last… Nachia hesitated again. On one side of the staff was a flaw, as if it had been cut and broken off unnaturally. "This is…?" She looked around, but there was nothing that resembled a fallen piece. The flaw was no small thing — it would catch the eye at once. It felt almost like the staff's missing other half. Nachia put her hands to her knees and bent down. And so she asked the puppies. "Do you know where the rest of the staff is?" No answer came back. As she turned her gaze to the staff, her attention began, little by little, to be drawn to other things. Her arms ached. Her throat was parched. Her legs trembled. Her eyes stung. She had risen and walked only a little, yet at once she was short of breath. Perhaps from panting so hard, her chest throbbed too, beyond all comparison with before. She felt, for no reason, as though tears might come. She must really have lain unconscious, like one long dead, for a very long time — so she thought.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main2_Short: She wakes in a forest said to be hers, answering to a name that isn't quite her own. And in her hand, a staff missing its other half — who once carried it?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main3_Content_0:
Between forest and forest, mountain and mountain, there was no clear boundary line. So if she walked wherever her feet led, she soon reached a limit. With no sense of any specific where — at the very least, no sense of heading toward some somewhere — she could spend time on the road until her feet swelled fat, and still feel no closer to anywhere.
But that well-fed sort of worry ended, too, once the uninvited guests began to appear, one by one.
Looking back, there had been things here and there that ought to be called the omens of those uninvited guests. The increasingly grotesque shapes of the trees, for one. The hideously bent branches thrust out strangely thin, sharp thorns. With them they were whittling and shearing away their own selves and the trunks they'd grown from. Inside the bulging burls lurked things that looked like the dark pupils of animals, staring fixedly at her. The fruits hanging from the branch-tips had swelled until their skins thinned like oilpaper, but instead of a sweet fragrance they gave off the stench of slop-water. Even the moss in the rock-clefts and the shade wore some wrong shape there. Watching that landscape — bristling black cilia rippling in periodic waves, as if breathing — was enough to leave her with the impression that she was slowly sliding down some monster's gullet. This deterioration was simply something the beasts of that place — the aforesaid 'uninvited guests' — had been unable to escape either.
The twisted form of something exhaling a black aura; or else the shape of many fused into one, hurling their resentment and hatred of one another at the intruder before their eyes. Nachia was startled to see several necks — unable to look in one direction at the same time — squawking and lunging at her. What touched the ground was two legs and one stump, one tail. Such a thing came bounding and lunging, dragging its whole body. And there was more than one or two of such things. Things filled with nothing but the urge to bite, claw, suck in, smother, coil around, cage, and crush every living thing that was not themselves. A string of abominations rampaging, having forsaken the will to grow and live, the reason of nature. And yet, at the same time, victims swallowed up by some unknown deterioration.
{IMAGE}

Nachia ground her teeth and made a particular gesture. It was a command directed at the puppies.
The small, shaggy balls of fur that had barely reached her knee vanished without a trace. What filled the empty space were beasts with broad-set shoulders, four legs like the pillars of a house, and jaws clamped so tight that no spring or lever or cudgel in all the world could ever have pried them open by force. Keeping every nerve fixed on Nachia's movements, they lowered their stances and put strength into their legs the moment she tilted her head ever so slightly. Their long, slit pupils were like beholding balls of bright-yellow fire. The deteriorated forms did not falter in the least at that menacing sight. They had no presence of mind left to weigh such things. And so Nachia, too, had no choice.
"…Put them to rest."
Her lips barely managed to stir, but that alone was more than enough. The puppies kicked off the ground and shot out like arrows, tangling with the wave of deteriorated forms. The foam that crashed white as it struck the ground, the fiercely surging current and the curling crests of its waves — but this time they were all tough flesh and hard bone and shrieking throats. On that battlefield there was no distinction of inside and out, no proof of will, no clash of strength. There was only unrecognizable outer shapes, a vicious stench, ear-splitting screams, and hot bodily fluids that pattered down against bare skin. Nachia, her face gone pale, clenched both fists. From the crown of her head to the tips of her toes she trembled so that she could not even hold her gaze still in one place. And yet she held on. She must not turn her head away, not to the very end.
There rose faintly the impression that the self she'd been before losing her memory had borne some kind of responsibility.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main3_Content_1: "What did this to you?" The deteriorated forms did not speak. If something could reach as far as near her, it was a fragment, a remnant of something. Things that had been flung, or sent sprawling, or had come rolling over and over. "What happened here? Does it have to do with my past?" Nachia wrapped both forearms in her hands. Gooseflesh had risen on them. It was unsettling. All of this was unbearably unsettling. It suddenly struck her as strange that when she breathed out, no white vapor formed. She lifted her head and looked at the sun. The strong thought rose in her that its position and the present hour, the feel of her surroundings, did not match. The season was wrong, the month was wrong. This forest was wrong. And its former shape — that, Nachia's body remembered. At a thought that came to her, Nachia signaled the puppies and had them ease their fury a little. The distance between the forms and herself thus narrowed, bit by bit. "You — do you know me?" And so Nachia spoke to one form that lay half-dead, wheezing. "I was here, wasn't I? Wasn't I?" She went on, pounding at her chest. "You remember me, don't you? Hm?" What had she been hoping for? The form had been trodden and bitten by the puppies until it was reduced to a rag. There was no strength left in that thing — shaped like chewed-up, spat-out food — to work even an outward show of spite. Nachia watched the form's pupils drift away from her, up toward the high sky, then roll back behind the eyelids altogether, heading for the land of death… and then, all at once, it all stopped. It came back. The dark pupils spun back around to face front once more. For an instant, but completely, the clarity returned to those eyes. "You — you do know me, don't you?" Nachia threw herself forward. She fell to her knees. Seen up close, the deteriorated product — that ugly, pitiful thing, the pupils of its many eyes clustered thick as frog-spawn — she all but gathered into her arms. "What happened here? What was I supposed to do? Can this be undone?" The questions that poured out as if a dam had burst were every one of them weighty, but they all feigned ignorance. There was still one left. There was a question that had hung in her throat to the last. The one she had refused to speak aloud until now, but could no longer look away from. "The man who called me 'Nachia' — where did he go?" The shards of perception and thought within the form's head, the pupils where clarity had returned, shuddered. Then the thing scraped together all its strength and shut its eyelids again. Grinding its broken bones, it drove its head down into the bare earth. It chose instead to swallow the sticky pool made of its own dream-dust, hastening its own death. Had it not understood Nachia's words? No — it had understood. It had understood precisely, too, what answer it would have to give to them. And so how could it dare speak the thing that must not be spoken? "You know me, don't you? Don't you?" "Did you know that child too?" "Is that child among you?" And so it went, over and over. "Please, just answer me…!" But forms that recovered their senses even at the brink of death were rare, and stranger still was the fact that even those which did come to their senses did not welcome the situation in the slightest. Forms whose bodies were relatively intact rather strove all the harder to lunge at her. And such cases of desperate, last-ditch resistance appeared more and more the deeper she went into the deteriorated forest. They're stopping me from going farther. Nachia thought. For what? For my sake? To that, no answer came. She wanted to ask even the puppies that followed her, but it was wasted effort. If she had forgotten something, it would have been erased from their heads as well. In her frustration, Nachia's grip clenched the staff tight. A staff made of wood. A staff whose split half lay somewhere or other. A staff that must have been carved from the wood of this forest. But the trees of this forest had now become hideous somethings that blinked, lashed tentacles and whips about, and shrieked. "Here, I…." The ranks of puppies guarding Nachia had loosened greatly. For the deteriorated forms crowding doggedly in, it was a chance not to be missed. One form burst through the ranks as if flying and lunged abruptly at Nachia. She raised her staff at a slant to take the blow, but could not keep from losing her balance and toppling. For a brief moment she writhed at the pain of something hard and angular jabbing the center of her back, as if a stone had jutted up from the bare ground. Nachia saw the form's maw and snout and tubes coil round and round her staff, chewing. The staff trembled, taut, as if about to snap. Her head went hot in a rush. "Get away!" The staff loosed a dazzling flash. She hadn't even known such a thing was possible. To that thing, now seared golden-brown without leaving so much as a scream, the puppies came running, having hastily torn apart the forms grappling with them. They were half a beat too late, but it was a melee — there was no helping it. "It's all right," Nachia said, rising to her feet. The puppies studied her with eyes full of worry. "It's all right, I'm all right…." Pulling herself together, checking whether the staff had been damaged, reassuring the puppies… as Nachia staggered about in a daze, her foot brushed against something. It was the stone that had gouged the center of her back until it bled when she fell. Only — was a stone ever that light? Did a stone ever tip and topple over to the side like that? Nachia lowered her head to confirm the thing's true nature.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main3_Content_2: It was a block of wood worked by someone's hand. It seemed to depict some animal, though that wasn't certain. The pigment painted on, made of withered petals and dead insects mashed together, had faded all over. Its smoothly worked lines had gone rough and risen, while its corners, conversely, had worn dull and away. Half-swallowed by the bristling moss, there was no telling which was the front of the body and which the back. But it was somehow familiar to the eye. "…This." Nachia chewed over the moment she had first opened her eyes in that unknown place. The ornaments that had hung jangling about her body. And the little carvings hung likewise about the puppies' necks, in their braided fur, after she had summoned them. She hurriedly looked around. In that place filled with pale, bluish pools, she tried to read the forest's original shape. Small carved figures of similar size, material, and form lay here and there. In that nightmare of a forest — where the trees had gone mad, the grasses wailed, and the beasts could no longer die — certain pieces of evidence, not yet wholly crumbled away, remained like this. "……I made this." I mustn't go in any farther. The moment she felt this, her chest throbbed. This was a place where the very figures she had made with her own hands lay. So surely this was the deepest part of the forest, the place where she had usually stayed? She had barely reached its threshold — why must she not? What had she forgotten, and what did she so dread to the very end? A red flame rose up in her head. Two flames burning separately, set apart at a distance — a campfire? The candle-lights humans use? The heart of a forest scorched through by lightning? All at once she remembered what she had thought, looking into the eyes of her stalwart puppies. That they were like burning balls of fire. And so, in the innermost part of the forest, something with two eyes likewise burning like balls of fire was waiting for her, too. "Not now." Nachia said. The commotion around her had more or less died down. It was thanks to the puppies fighting their hearts out. The tide of forms had noticeably weakened. There would be no better chance than this. If only she set her mind to it, she could storm straight through to the forest's center. Her faithful puppies would, without a word, follow her command and kill the enemy and kill again, carving out a path. Even if, in doing so, they were spent past their strength and their breath was cut off. "Not now." Nachia's will was conveyed to the puppies. The things that had been stamping their forepaws and gouging the soil in triumph turned, by and by, to look back. They drew in those snouts and claws that had been turned outward, the manes and back-fur that had bristled up in a fluffy mass, and came back to her. Their great striding steps became a 'plodding,' and then again a 'toddling.' The puppies, returned to small balls of fur, began to follow Nachia back along the path they had walked thus far. "I can come back later. Later, again." She was short of breath. As she made her way out of the forest, she muttered without cease. Though she knew well enough that a glance and a sigh were enough to command the puppies, still she muttered. "I'll come back, for certain. Not now." She was reciting it to herself. "I'll come back later, for certain, for certain…." * Meanwhile, on the battlefield Nachia had left, one form not yet wholly dead opened its eyes. This was the heart of the deteriorated forest, true, but the shock Nachia and her puppies had dealt it had — if only for a moment — awakened in the form the memory of a time when it had not been a form. The form recalled the days when it had worn no body, when it had not had to keep spitting something out or doggedly swallowing it down while bloating fat or shriveling small. And it recalled a certain scene — the last thing the self of that time had ever seen. "…I have to tell her." The little spirit that had opened its eyes within the form's body cried out. It looked around. She was not there. Then it had to find her. It had to follow after her. It had to find her before the aura of the deteriorated forest made it once again the puppet of the ignorant Nightmare. The spirit, gasping for breath, made its way out of the forest. It absolutely had to find her. "I have to tell her, I have to tell her." Before this memory, only just surfaced, could grow dim again.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main3_Short: The deeper she goes, the more desperately the dying try to turn her back. What waits at the heart of the forest that even the broken would shield her from?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main4_Content_0:
Even after she made it out of the deteriorated forest, Nachia could not, in fact, make it out of the forest. A curiosity that had become like a sticky pit of tar kept clutching at her ankles. The instant she thought she was standing still, lost in thought, she would find she'd turned her head. Looking at her own footprints, not yet erased, she would suddenly think she could still go back, that it wasn't too late — even though she knew she mustn't.
That, too, was no insight she'd reached on her own. Watching the puppies pace about, Nachia realized she was circling the same spot. Lingering at a vague distance — not even far from the forest, but where its aura could not surge out and reach her — she was doggedly tormenting only the soil beneath her feet. Nachia's steps came to an abrupt halt. From afar she gazed silently at those black trees, listened to the faint cries of the deteriorated forms, and sank into thought.
"I mustn't go back recklessly."
She told herself, sternly.
"It only drains my strength. Nothing gets solved."
So she had to find out. At any rate, she had to learn what had become of what, and how, and how it could be undone. She had to learn what she would have met had she gone inside, and exactly what those familiar traces left there meant. She had to learn, too, where the man in her memory — the one who had given her back the name Nachia — might have gone. They were all questions that the Nachia of now — no better than a bare, leafless tree that had shed the foliage of memory — could never resolve alone. And so she needed someone to tell her the story of the deteriorated forest. And who could be more fit for that than the explorers of the dream-world? Especially the outsiders, come from beyond, who roamed about so actively, carrying an unquenchable curiosity about this world.

Of course, there were trials and tribulations before she found explorers to travel with.
At first, the way Nachia saw it, to travel alongside them she had to show how useful she was. And in the dangerous dream-world, surely the forces one could command were everything. Thinking this, Nachia instructed the puppies to keep their burly forms at all times. But the explorers who saw that took fright and steered clear early, or even leveled their iron at her first, making to attack. The next thing she thought of was to appear as a savior. By bursting in to the rescue the moment the explorers were, say, set upon by some belligerent beast. For a while Nachia tailed people in just that way, looking like a gray rat that hid in the shade, crept on all fours, crouched low, and scrambled out of sight. She would wait, doggedly, until they fell into some crisis.
And, to her surprise, she arrived at the conclusion that the dream-world might be more peaceful than she'd thought.
Most of the explorers were rational agents, not fools. The greenhorns took fright from the start and scurried out, while the fairly seasoned ones, to match their skill, made full preparations in supplies and support, pioneered as much of a path as they could as quickly as possible, and then withdrew. In a situation where most of those entering the Rapids knew their own measure all too well, decisive peril was rare to begin with. Trailing various explorers and their bands, Nachia, her thinking somehow gone numb, found a small satisfaction in growing better and better at erasing her presence and hiding her body. One day, having spent her time crouched behind a thick bush, she sat for a while with her arms wrapped around her knees, gazing blankly at the ground. Then it occurred to her that it might be fun to doodle on it a little. And she just barely came to her senses.
This was no good, any way she looked at it.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main4_Content_1:
"If I lead dangerous beasts over and make them run into these people, and then…."
It was a wicked scheme not worth a moment's consideration. If the puppies had been beside her to hear her words just then, Nachia thought, they'd have drooped their ears and shown an all-too-human disappointment.
"Now what do I do?"
Her head was a tangle. She wished she could have the help of the puppies, whom she'd told to stay out of sight while she hid.
"I'm sick of following them around. But I can't just throw caution to the wind and walk up out of nowhere and talk to them, either."
At some point, unable to bear it any longer, Nachia did exactly that. She threw caution to the wind and walked right up. And in that moment she abruptly spoke to the explorers in front of her.
"What do I even say, popping up out of nowhere like this?"
Contrary to that bit of muttering, from Nachia's mouth in that moment there flowed, smoothly, lie after lie — bright red, but harmless all the same.
"I don't know a thing about the world all these people come from. I can't convincingly fool them about the things they take for granted, or about who I am and what I'm trying to do."
And yet she could!
A made-up name and borrowed pretexts; and though she knew little of the outside, she had at least a rough sense of the flow of things, learned from all her observing. And so, in a nothing-to-lose frame of mind, Nachia threw herself in, revealing that she too was an explorer and introducing herself, then patiently building common ground before at last showing them the puppies. In this way she staged a scene that — while not the whole truth — at least accorded with the facts: that she had a knack for taming the creatures of dreams.
And when she'd come back to her senses, she found she had companions traveling with her.

"It was a hard first day, wasn't it?"
One of the expedition members struck up a kindly conversation. The sun was sinking low, and everyone was bustling about lighting a campfire for a late meal.
"I'm fine. It's only my first day joining you—"
An unscratchable spot in Nachia's head began to itch. In the past she'd fabricated a little while ago, when she'd given a fake name, she couldn't remember how she had 'set' the length of time she'd supposedly explored the dream-world alone.
"—so I've already gotten used to it."
"Have you, now? In that case, maybe—"
"Dinner's ready!"
The shout of those on cooking duty rescued Nachia from the awkward moment. She let out a sigh of relief and followed the others' lead. She took a bowl and stood in line. After receiving some boiled concoction of water and who-knew-what, she found a spot and sat down. One on a broad, flat boulder, one on a dry stump, one on the bare ground swept clean of dust… and so, naturally, a circle formed around the campfire, an arrangement where each could see the others' faces across it — a truly ideal setting for conversation. Only, for a while there was nothing but the sound of people busily chewing and swallowing, so Nachia had to wait first for the others' hunger to ease.
While she waited she stared blankly at the bowl steaming up at her. Then she made a reluctant show of taking a few spoonfuls, but felt nothing more than that. There was an impression that in the past, something small gathered or sprouted somewhere had been enough. To put it bluntly, the very act of harvesting a great heap of something, cooking it by artificial means, and putting it in her mouth felt unsettling to her.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main4_Content_2: "Ahh, you mean the Forest of Turbulence?" That was how the expedition members understood Nachia's question about 'the place with the deteriorated forms and trees,' and they nodded. So that's what it's called. She drew in a breath. Did it have that name back when the old me was there, too? "That place has a lot of tangled stories, they say." "So many they're useless, I hear." "…Tell me anyway." Nachia said. In a low voice that sounded almost solemn. "Even the trivial things — tell me all of it." "From what I hear, it wasn't that kind of place originally." One member spoke up. "There were two Forest-Keepers seated there — sane ones, of course." Was that the two of us? Nachia thought. Nachia, and some… man. She wanted to bite off and swallow her own tongue, still unable to call up even his name. "But one of them, they say, turned into a monster." "The way I heard it, that one was an off-kilter, out-of-its-mind Forest-Keeper from the start." Someone cut in, bringing up something none too welcome. "Is that so?" "Yeah. If the other one was order, that crazed one was chaos that never knew its bounds from the beginning." The fingers of the hand holding Nachia's bowl curled, crooked. For a while she scraped at the rim where no food was held… then they returned to where they'd been. "Why keep a child like that on as a Forest-Keeper?" "How should I know? The sound one barely held it in check, apparently. Whenever the broken one destroyed something, the sound one would keep cleaning up after it — that was the way of it, they say." "Could've just cast it out, you'd think." "That's how all myths go." Her lips curled higher and higher. Her heart pounded. Nachia, feeling dizzy, pressed a hand to her brow. Even so, she wanted to hear more. She had to hear it. "Anyway, that, ah, the out-of-its-mind one finally caused a disaster and turned into a full monster, they say." "The 'red-eyed monster,' you mean?" Nachia did not miss the quotation marks wrapped around that phrase. So it meant the thing itself was a proper name. To be called the monster with red eyes… Nachia, realizing her bowl was trembling violently, set it down beside her. "And what happened to the other, sound one?" "Got killed when it went on its monstrous rampage, what else. Couldn't even recognize the one who'd looked after it." The explorers' conversation went on as though it were a thoroughly trifling matter. "Its name was, maybe, Belpo—" "No!" At the cry shouted out at full voice, the explorers looked, startled, at its owner. Baring her white teeth, Nachia had sprung up from her seat. "He's not — he's not a monster like that — watch your mouth!" Her hair, the downy fuzz all over her body, stood straight on end. Her clenched fist was white as blank paper. From her tight-shut lips leaked a low groan like a beast's. The tendons of her throat rose taut as a bowstring, and her whole body, unable to master its fury, began to creak as though about to collapse. And then… at some moment, all of it stopped. Nachia plopped down hard, landing on her backside. But the damage was already done. Why am I like this? Nachia thought. When she heard the others murmuring in bewilderment, her face went hot enough to burst. She ducked her head awkwardly and avoided their eyes. She put off answering. The very one who had poured cold water on their cozy chatter had thus lost all her strength and shriveled up, and now the suffocating silence of that place seemed as if it would, in due course, stretch on forever. "Something must be eating at her, I'd guess?" At the sound of someone cautiously approaching, Nachia raised her head, blotched red and blue with indignation and shame. The strapping great explorer picked up the bowl Nachia had set aside and held it out to her, just so. "It's still warm — finish it." At a loss, she looked back and forth between the offered hand and the bowl resting on it, and the face of the one offering it. Now that she looked, the cuff of his sleeve had gone red, soaked in the broth that must have slopped over a little as he picked it up. "A full belly fixes everything. Just eat, for now." Nachia blinked. He held the bowl out again with a broad smile. "Fill your belly up good and proper first, then sleep till you're stretched out flat. Then you'll have the strength to think, too." What could she do, when he put it that way? Nachia took the bowl, hesitant and shy. Then, seeing the other explorers strike up their talk among themselves again, she felt reassured and took a spoonful. She put it in her mouth, chewed. And swallowed. And she repeated that, several times over. My belly's not filling up. she thought. Something was strange, more than could be put down to mere distress. Somewhere inside her own body was utterly empty. The more she sent food down past her throat, the more, on the contrary, an appetite rose — a very strange appetite that could never be filled by eating food — creeping up by degrees. Her mouth filled, for no reason, with saliva. She had the feeling her teeth were going sharp, sharper. The food she actually ate tasted not the least bit good. This was strange. She wanted to eat nothing, yet she was hungry. So very hungry.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main4_Short: Strangers trade the legend of a red-eyed monster, and one name in it belongs to her. So why does her mouth fill with hunger the longer she listens?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main5_Content_0: "Nachia?" Nachia woke. It was a familiar voice. "What is it?" "Come look at this." A voice somehow downcast. She tidied her bedding and went outside. She could feel that her eyes were bloodshot. Her two feet, treading the ground in turn, and the insides of her thighs, were all thick and heavy. It was because she'd slept poorly the night before. Her dreams had been thoroughly fitful. She couldn't remember well, but she seemed to have had a bad dream. When she stepped out of the hollow old tree, bright sunlight poured over her face. As she shaded her eyes with a hand and frowned, she saw the one standing a little way off. Belpomet. "Just look at this…." "What's the matter? What is it?" Her little brother was making a whimpering sound and pointing at something. A hill she'd never seen had cropped up out of nowhere in the ground — but on a closer look, it was an old tree that had toppled, clods of earth hanging in clumps from its roots. So the thing Nachia had taken for a hill was a portion of the ground heaved up high, tangled in the roots. "Why is it like this… mmm." Having more or less guessed the whole story, Nachia curled the corner of her mouth, looking troubled. "Belpo—" When she folded her arms and gave Belpomet a teasing sidelong glare, the boy — already cowed — shrank even more pitifully. "—what did you do this time?" "…I didn't do anything." Nachia couldn't help but break into a smile. Even this clumsy excuse, with no gift for words, was just like always. So had the tree really keeled right over of its own accord when he'd done nothing at all? "Really?" "……No." A long, long sigh. And then it was time for the confession to begin. The gist was always the same. Trying to do something a little better. Trying to paint more, raise more, dye deeper, heighten and stir things up, Belpomet would produce fruit so overripe it gave off a sour reek, or a mountain of vines run rampant without end until it looked like a graveyard of serpents, or a marching procession of swirling wind and rain. And every time, it was the hapless grasses and trees, the beasts of field and air, the spirits that stood for nature's own true form, who suffered for his pushing. "I did it again…." "I know, I know, little brother." "The outsiders are right after all." What do you mean? A strange thought began to rise in Nachia. "What did the outsiders say?" "That I'm a monster…." On this bright morning — rising late, walking with her little brother through the Forest of Reverie where everything was just as it had always been — a strange thought began to rise that this single day was not real. "That I'm a monster who smashes and kills everything… that the real Forest-Keeper is just you, big sister." "Tell them to stop talking nonsense." Nachia said sternly. "How many times have I told you? You don't just recklessly run wild — you're chaos as a part of the cycle!" Belpomet turned his head to follow his sister's gesture. He looked at the tree-roots, caught up in the upheaval he'd caused and now, willy-nilly, taking in the cool breeze, and at the tree lying flat and neat along the line of those roots. "This was a dying tree to begin with — old, dying." Nachia went on. "Its bark grew so thick the burls put out no branches; the inside rotted and never recovered, leaving it full of sunken hollows. Remember?" "Mm-hm…." "And it doesn't end with this falling over — look here." The wormholes bored into the trunk; the grubs that borrowed the roots' sap with no apparent intention of ever paying it back; the rodents that had dug their burrows in turn; the ants that, without a word of complaint about their sudden eviction, were silently carrying their eggs and larvae away… one by one, Nachia pointed them out to her brother. "These little ones will go find new homes and build new nests, hunt new prey, meet new mates, and so they'll add to the story of the whole forest. The tree falling is the same!" Near the old tree, in a spot that had usually been wrapped in thick shade where nothing grew but bryophytes with neither stalk nor flower, the blazing sun now beat down. Even in soil that all looked alike, that same dark and dingy color, surely there slept — with a faintly bitter feeling — the countless seeds of other trees or herbaceous plants, borne in on the wind only to be thwarted, unable in the end to put down roots. "And from here, just that quickly, sprouts and saplings will go poking up their heads… to fill the forest's empty space. And right on time…." Nachia gestured. She didn't much care to force the flow of the five seasons, the twenty-four months, into acceleration. But a thing that had already lost its life, that could no longer return to its place — to 'caress' it ever so slightly along the natural course of things was nothing to trouble over. The wood of the fallen old tree loosened into a slightly softer, more pliant shape. It moldered and crumbled and was bored through. It became a form better suited for other creatures to take as nourishment. "With me here to turn your chaos into birth and flourishing like this, what's there to worry about?" "But what if you're not here?" Belpomet looked up at her. She couldn't see his face. "Then we just stay together. We just don't go anywhere." As she answered, Nachia narrowed her eyes without lowering the hand shading them. It was too bright. But why? Why should she be dazzled, looking down at her smaller brother, and with the sun at her back overhead at that? Because there was no sun there. Because in the midst of darkness on every side, the only light was her brother's eyes. Those two eyes scarlet as burning balls of fire. "Even if I become like this?" Nachia woke.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main5_Content_1:
For a while she had to figure out where she was and what she'd been doing. Staring blankly at the tent-cloth that walled her in, the strange material cut by human hands, she remembered: deciding to learn the story of the deteriorated forest; tailing the human explorers for that purpose; being accepted as a companion at last and dozing off in their camp. Outside it was bright. A daylight so dizzyingly brilliant.
"Why didn't anyone…."
Her hoarse voice sounded strange to her. Nachia cleared her throat, hacking. Oddly, she had no strength.
"…wake me?"
Nachia parted the tent and went out. The worst case, she'd been sure, was that the explorers had simply abandoned her and gone. After she'd shattered the mood the night before by suddenly bellowing, wasn't there a profit in cutting their losses — ditching one woman of unsound mind for the price of a single tent? But that wasn't it. All their packs and the tools they'd brought, though a little in disarray, mostly held their places.
Only the people were not there.
A dusty hot wind churned through the clearing. Heat-shimmer rose toward the blazing sun. At that rippling, writhing landscape before her eyes, Nachia shielded her eyes. A tongue that crackled like a dead leaf licked her cracked lips. Her grip rose, by degrees, to the bridge of her nose, to her brow, then to the crown of her head. Her head ached. Her throat stung. Her chest throbbed. Nachia clutched at the spot that surged with the sharpest pain. It hurt as if teeth, sharp fangs, were lined up in rows and ranks inside her belly, carving away her own flesh. She was hungry. So very hungry. And then, the moment she spotted something, her mouth flooded all at once with saliva.
{IMAGE}

"This is it, this is it."
Nachia moved her feet, swaying. Then she knelt before the something she'd found. Her grip, tightening with a sound like beads cracking, her bare face plunging in heedlessly, began frantically scraping that something together.
"This is what I have to eat. Not food."
She raked at the dirt and piled a fistful onto her hand. With the other hand she made a pincer-shape and carefully picked out strand by strand — then, oh, to blazes with it, she shoved the whole clump, twigs and pebbles and all, into her mouth and worked it about. With no time even to chew, she gulped it down. A single spoonful of priming-water poured onto the dried-out bed of a spring. Still not enough. Nachia brought over what looked like the rinds of some large fruit, stacked together. She clutched the ones strewn here and there about the clearing. A mouth-watering substance clung in tantalizing little bits to their insides and out. Nachia turned the large rinds this way and that, inspecting inside and out. She began to dig out everything stuck to them and eat it clean.
Her belly grew easier and easier. A primal happiness, like a strain of song, welled up in her head. It was rapturous, as if a whip of rainbow were drumming all over her body. By degrees her eyes opened. And at last she recognized what that 'rind' she had so longingly clutched really was. It was a garment. Part of the clothing worn by those who had taken her in the day before. These delectable things — the golden, hardened lumps and the seared-on films and the finely scattered grains now crusted thick beneath Nachia's nails, on her palms and wrists, at the corners of her mouth, on her chin, on the tip of her nose — why were they tangled together with that tattered clothing? Scattered every which way across the bare ground?
The look of it called to mind not solid particles but something that had once flowed, thick and viscous. Something that gushed out violently, spread out in a haze, streamed down and down to stain everything all around in a spreading mess. Those delicious things, for some reason, clung only to the inner side of the clothes, the part that touched bare skin. To the place where her companions' bodies should have been, and remained until the last moment. Nachia turned over the garment she held. And she recognized the reddish stain, soaked with broth, that remained on its cuff.
Her pupils narrowed to the width of a needle's eye.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main5_Content_2:
"Then I."
She must not think of what came next, she believed. But how could she not?
"No, no, it can't be. I…."
Nausea surged up. She covered her mouth, but couldn't hold out long. She bent at the waist and opened her mouth. The dry heaves came pouring out, but only clear, sour bile dripped, drop by drop. Nachia's body refused with all its might. That precious sustenance — not a grain, not a drop yielded up — it was devouring it inside her, morsel by morsel, savoring every crumb. So unbearably revolting was this that Nachia clawed at her own body. Pinching, striking, scratching, gouging, she scored stinging wounds across herself. She wanted to ram her arm in to the elbow down her throat and wrench her whole gut out and split it open. Because she couldn't, she wept, and wept hard.
It had not been so before. That much was certain. Using that moment in the dream as a lever, she had at last summoned up her whole, intact memory of her days as a Forest-Keeper. She and her little brother Belpomet — the two Forest-Keepers, sister and brother — had not craved any food to eat. A single drop of dew, a pinch of flower-nectar, and then, some day, one cluster of raspberries, was enough to keep them full for days on end.
"I'm changing into something wrong."
Nachia pursed her lips, turned inside out from the retching. The tears she'd shed had built a little cairn of stones.
"I think I'm becoming a monster too…."
Sobbing, Nachia buried her face. She wrapped both arms around her knees. Hunched small and frail, like a caterpillar that has no other way to guard itself from predators, she trembled and shook. Now everything was ruined. Belpomet would become a mad god, and his sister — the only one who remembered his story — would likewise become a wandering man-eating monster, sunk to nothing more than a ghost story to send a chill through travelers….
"Arise—"
Out of nowhere, such a voice came.
"—Forest-Keeper of the fallen forest."
Nachia lifted her head, smeared all over with tears and bodily fluids.

"Wh-who are you?"
"I am Polaris, the Guide of dreams."
She was beautiful. Not her features, but her bearing. That radiance and spirit, that serene, unruffled poise that only one who has wholly brought the power of dreams under her command — the power and its workings that Nachia had felt vaguely in her Forest-Keeper days — can give off, this woman before her, Polaris, possessed it all. And once you have seen such a sight, you cannot help but ask. You cannot help but cling, frantic.
"Why have I become like this? Hm?"
Polaris looked down with a pitying gaze at the woman who had crawled, wriggling, up to her.
"Tell me, please."
"It is because the focal point of your power — your forest — has lost its original purpose."
The explanation that followed was, to Nachia, needlessly long-winded. But it was enough to grasp this much: that, barring a place with a fixed purpose, like a Forest-Keeper or her forest, every product of dreams requires the power of the Gold; that this power of the Gold flows in by way of the outsiders from beyond; and that Nachia, having lost her focal point, would come to depend on the power of the Gold more and more. She mentioned some plan she was dreaming of, but Nachia could not keep her wits about her enough to hear that far.
"I don't want to become a monster…."
Nachia said, sprawled at her feet. Sobbing. Beseeching.
"Help me, help me, please."
"Yes. I will help you."
Nachia could no longer hear anything. Could no longer see anything. Everything was shriveling, by degrees, into one small period. She had the thought that she'd felt something like this once before.
"I don't want to become a monster."
"Help me, help me."
Her voice, rough and ragged, grew smaller and smaller. Nachia's pupils trembled, fluttering, then were sucked away behind her eyelids.
"Help me, help me, help me…."
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main5_Short: She meant only to save her brother — but the hunger inside her shows no mercy. When the keeper herself becomes the monster, who is left to guard the forest?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main6_Content_0: "This time, I know." she said. She rose from where she lay. Inside the hollow, withered tree she usually used for a bed; outside, the weather was bright and clear. A warm spring breeze was blowing in soft, rolling waves. The smell of fresh green shade and leaves not yet come to fullness drifted in. She could hear the cicadas, clinging fast to the trees, singing their song. And on top of it all, a downcast voice calling for her…. "This is a dream. An illusion." Before any more stray thoughts could rise, she went briskly outside. The sky had darkened. This time there was a clearing. She could see the camp she'd set up with the human explorers. Every scattered pack and tent and implement glittered greedily. It was because, one and all, they'd been draped in a film of gold. And surrounding her as she glared at it, unsettled, were great hulking beasts, growling. The four legs that trod the ground were like the rock-clefts that send a stream curling. Their bared teeth were like beholding long, yellow fruits. The trouble, if there was one, was that they were her puppies. "What's wrong?" The puppies' low growls swelled louder still. In those bright-yellow pupils she saw her own throat, her own head reflected. Their burly, muscled bodies had finished readying to spring at any instant. "You don't like me?" That trifling little phrase seemed to be the final wedge: the puppies all lunged at once. Before them, howling as if mad, she stood limp and still. Those keen-edged fangs, the claws and forelegs taut with strength, the eyes burning bright as they hurled themselves at her, looked so… so utterly trivial. She raised one arm and struck aside the puppy at the vanguard. Belying its great bulk, it was unexpectedly easy. Light as a feather. The thing, flung off like a slender stalk of sedge, took a great old tree square against the middle of its spine. With a sound of breath knocked clean out of it, it curled all four legs like an insect, then closed its eyes and slammed into the ground. "Stop." she said. She wanted to go somewhere else. She no longer wanted to call up the bright, familiar forest, or the clearing she was supposed to know, or any name at all. She just wanted to go anywhere her feet led and revel, to her heart's content, in whatever could be had there. If she had eyes, she wanted to shut them; if ears, to close them. To never open them again. By and by the other puppies came charging like a plow turning soft soil. "I said stop." She swung her hand. One was laid open across the belly and fell. Another's neck was broken. By some reflex, perhaps, its gulping lower jaw was chewing, over and over, on its own lolling tongue. Seeing the marks left by its sharp front teeth filling the tongue at regular intervals, like the traces of some handicraft, she laughed. The next puppy lunged. "I told you to stop, didn't I?" This time she seized it by the throat and drove it straight down. The ground caved in a hollow, and all around her shuddered, trembling. Something in the puppy's body made a snapping sound. A groan so pitiful it was almost comical leaked out of it. Yelp. She waited for the puppy to close its eyes. And in the end she saw it. Her own face, reflected in those pupils. The face of a mad monster with eyes burning scarlet as live coals. "I don't know this face." she said. "It has nothing to do with me — stop." she said. "It isn't me, it isn't my doing. I don't know anything about it." Nachia said. The instant she let go her grip on the throat, everything vanished. The puppy that had been suffering, and the face of Belpomet reflected in its pupils. On the dream's stage, halted halfway and frozen, Nachia stood weeping alone.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main6_Content_1: "Belpo…!" The bridge of her nose stung. Everything before her broke apart in beads. Even in a dream — even in a dream within a dream — she wanted to be someone else. She wanted to forget that name. She wanted to fling away Nachia and everything else. But she couldn't. "Belpomet, my little brother…." That had now become, just so, the legend of a monster. Didn't like the phrase 'the red-eyed monster'? No matter. Then teach the travelers of the Rapids the proper name. So that they might all remember it clearly and spread it far and wide. "This is where Belpomet is. Don't go near." "These are the corpses of the people Belpomet killed." "Belpomet waits — in the forest become a snare, in the starving thicket of thorns." "Belpomet is coming, Belpomet is coming!" Nachia knew that she had once truly stood there, with the puppies. To strike him down — to bar the way of Belpomet, become the puppet of a wicked source. She had braced herself. She'd believed she had braced herself. And yet, when the moment truly came, she hesitated. The question every frog holds before the serpent's maw, the question every rabbit cries out before the kite's talons come down on its back — now, then, it was Nachia's turn. "Isn't there another way?" This pressed at Nachia's thoughts with talk of the natural course and order. Soon it stirred a chain of association with the words of Polaris — who must be looking down, even now, at Nachia's swooned body from outside the dream-within-a-dream, which was to say still within a dream. The products of dreams need the power of the Gold, Polaris had said, speaking it as though it were a proper law one ought rightly to obey. But was it truly so? No. Nachia thought. "What that woman's trying to do is the strange thing, if anything." When Nachia — when Nachia and Belpomet had been Forest-Keepers, there had been no such thing. The Forest of Reverie had already been one small, perfectly everlasting world. It could not be said that its products all enjoyed eternal life, but at least there had been no abnormal fixation upon the Gold. To pin the present of this world in place forever with power dragged in from another world in the first place — such a stopgap trick could surely never be the right way. What had to be restored was the order, the purpose, the cycle that had existed all along. Not a makeshift measure. And what else had Polaris said? She'd been in no state to take it in at the time, but, ironically, only after she'd fainted did the rest of it slowly surface. The claim that the power of the Gold was needed had — by Polaris's own lights — completed its proof; so now it was time to lay out exactly by what means that power of the Gold would be granted to this place. That means was merging. The outside world… recalling that far, Nachia's two eyes flew wide, bulging in a sudden start. "Merging them?" Nachia was aghast. The Dream Master still stood firm, and so did the unknown source that had defiled Belpomet — so where, in the plan the Guide of dreams was sketching, was there any place for them at all? How did she mean to block their interference, their meddling? And succeeding would not, in fact, solve the problem. If anything, it was far from any solution. "Belpomet…." If the worlds were made one in this state, if that vast Gold came pouring in, if the power that fixes the present form and nature in place pervaded everywhere — then what of Belpomet? Was she saying he should be left to remain in that state? You will come to depend on the power of the Gold more and more, Polaris had said. The rest of it had moved on to explaining her plan, but the implication she'd left unspoken between the lines was plain. Now Nachia had to follow her. If she wished to keep her life, there was no other way. "To save myself alone… I'm to look the other way from my brother, turned into a monster?" The memory of dreams grows dim. It is forgotten. With the Forest of Reverie gone, it would be no exaggeration to say that Nachia alone now remembered Belpomet's true form. If the two worlds were merged as Polaris intended and came rushing in like a flood, what would come would be only the travelers and explorers who knew nothing of that place. Only those who knew Belpomet's name as a monster's from the very start, brimming with the urge to spread the infamy of a mad, red-eyed god. In a dream-world ruled not by matter but by perspective, not by structure but by the force of sentiment, this was fatal. So Belpomet, crushed beneath the Gold, would not merely remain a monster. He would utterly lose, beyond all stirring, even the road back. "To leave him like that forever?" That it could not be an easy choice, even she knew. For the resolve to bring something to an end and the declaration to return everything to what it was before, in truth, sketch out entirely different prospects. The ending she would meet if she refused to bend her stubbornness now might be not an easy salvation but a final moment, endlessly repeated. The memory of that one instant when, in the end, she had hesitated. Her past misjudgment, which had, in the end, consigned Belpomet and the forest to a longer, more agonizing ordeal. Nachia gripped her staff with all her strength. Its other half, she thought, must by now have vanished forever, or be rotting away buried somewhere in the forest. For there was no way that Belpomet, who had forgotten even who he was, would be cherishing a half-a-wooden-staff like a treasure. Once she'd settled it so, her heart, if anything, grew calm. It became clear and bright what the right thing was, the necessary thing. At least for this one moment. "I have to. I have to see it through." Rubbing the one remaining staff in her hands, Nachia said. Her palms burned as if set alight. Her face must be drained white, she thought, and on that ashen brow, thick beads of sweat must be standing out, dripping. But she could feel nothing more. As she ducked her head and gazed at her own knees and the tops of her feet, the bare ground, the view before her grew dimmer and dimmer. Because this was a dream within a dream, the last refuge Nachia had found to flee to. Because it was her final attempt to look away from reality. And because that had now failed. And because from a daydream that had lost its reason to linger, one must, at last, awaken. When she opened her eyes, Polaris was still there.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main6_Short: A safe road lies before her — she need only look away from what her brother has become. But what if duty and love do not answer to the same name?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main7_Content_0:
"No."
It was the most out-of-nowhere word — perhaps the most betraying word — one could hear after keeping vigil beside someone who had fainted.
"I can't follow your plan."
Polaris, met with the first words of the just-woken Nachia, showed plain bewilderment. Naturally so. Nachia herself would have felt the same. But, astonishingly, that look soon passed.
"I see…."
Polaris gave a bitter smile. And that, in the end, was the last thing the two of them had in common.
"It's a familiar thing to me — though hardly a welcome one."
"In the end, I'm his sister. Belpomet's sister."
Nachia had to strain to put that name to her lips. She had to keep struggling, ceaselessly, to hold the original meaning carried in the name 'Belpomet' — not the red-eyed monster, but some warm, familiar feeling she knew well. That struggle was, on the one hand, meaningful; but on the other, it filled her with self-reproach.
"…Ah, this makes no sense to you, does it? To you?"
"It does."
Polaris was still smiling. Out of delight, out of satisfaction, out of amusement… it was none of these. If the earlier one had been a bitter smile, this one was a smile of pity. Nachia thought that she felt sorry for her.
"As the Guide of dreams, I know the story of the Forest of Reverie, and the story of the two Forest-Keepers, sister and brother, all of it… and that is why I can only pity you all the more — as a fellow product of dreams, a friend."
Nachia wondered whether she'd been avoiding Polaris's gaze. She could have said she'd merely looked elsewhere just then, that something had suddenly come to mind, that her attention had simply been caught by something else. She could have. She had to.

"And what of the others who suffer because dreams have deteriorated — the weak ones your forest cannot look after? What of them?"
Polaris said.
"If only you can reclaim your forest, are they something you can ignore?"
"I'm a Forest-Keeper."
It was a meager answer, but the right one. The closest thing to it, Nachia herself believed.
"If I can save the forest, I'm content with that."
But hadn't Polaris just said it herself, a moment ago? That she knew it all — the Forest of Reverie, and the story of the two Forest-Keepers.
"Are you saying that what you're doing now arises purely from a wish to save the forest?"
she went on.
"Can you be certain your actions aren't, rather, an act of forsaking the forest?"
"What?"
Nachia shot to her feet. Stiff strength rushed into her neck. But exactly what the Guide's words — the Forest-Keeper's story — pointed to was no unfamiliar truth to Nachia herself. Because, well, it was her own self. Even if her memory was not whole, at the very least various impressions and moments and feelings remained, however much they took a form she could not put into words.
The forest a Forest-Keeper guards is the cycle of order, which is to say the reason of nature. It is not a matter of blindly soothing and protecting and cradling everything — sometimes there is letting something suffer and die, however often it comes to that; that, precisely, was the Forest-Keeper's story. Then, with that cycle of order now thrown out of joint, what was the right choice, the one that truly served the forest — and the doubt that rose in Nachia's mind, that very doubt, Polaris pierced straight to the core.
"Don't you think the only road left to save the forest is to remove Belpomet, the very core of the deterioration, as quickly as possible?"
Nachia's mind went white.

"That — that remains to be seen."
she opened her mouth with effort.
"There may be another way… there will be."
Going out of her way to backtrack and revise her words, it was becoming all the more a declaration she couldn't answer for, a promise she couldn't keep — drawing nearer to the bluster of a windbag who wasn't even half a Forest-Keeper.
"Without removing the greatest wedge blocking the cycle of order, what other way could you possibly find?"
"I'll put it back the way it was."
"How?"
Her breathing grew shallower and shallower. The view before her threatened to stain yellow. It was hard to refute. No — she couldn't. Because it was nothing but the plain truth, point by point. Nachia was a Forest-Keeper, and a Forest-Keeper had to protect the forest, and to protect the forest she had to kill the monster that had swallowed it. Not some cloud-grabbing talk of a final moment that must someday be faced, a resolve readied for that time — she had to move right now. Right now she had to set out toward the monster — no, toward my little brother Belpomet. And if it came to it, here was even a powerful ally, the Guide of dreams; wasn't it simply a matter of joining hands and going to dispatch — no, to murder — him together?
But Nachia was Nachia.
If she had to choose, if she had no choice, then in the end Nachia had to be Nachia. She had to admit that it was not the identity of a Forest-Keeper, nor the cycle of order, but the story of Nachia and Belpomet — herself as Belpomet's sister — that she did not want to give up.
"Then how about this?—"
Nachia smiled. She'd realized just what kind of stubbornness she'd been clinging to all this time. She could finally lay it down, but it brought no relief at all. There was only the throbbing ache in her chest. It hurt enough to bring tears.
"—I throw out the forest and everything else… and say I'm just Nachia, Belpomet's sister, and so I'll set everything else aside and save him."
The corners of her mouth tore open hatefully and she let slip a faint, mocking laugh. Sneering like that, she must look pitiful enough that one could hardly bear to keep one's eyes open, Nachia thought.
"So — what are you going to do about it?"
"The Forest-Keeper's story, that cold and pitiless order — I know it, and the dreams I came from know it, all of it."
Polaris, however, was not the least bit shaken.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main7_Content_1: "Do you mean to make such an appeal, now, at this late hour?" "I don't want to hear it. I have nothing to say." Nachia said, shaking her head hard. "If you mean to break me by force, then go ahead. I won't listen anymore." She couldn't believe what she was saying. Her stomach turned queasy. She trembled. Her voice, in turn, began to tremble with her. She must surely look naive and clumsy and pitiful. "And besides — wasn't it the Dream Master who broke the balance in the first place? If there's a fault, it's that wretch — yes, that's right!" Tears welled up, blurring everything white. Nachia began to pace where she stood. And all the while she kept jabbing a sharp, accusing finger at the Guide. "That craft of yours, the way you handle the power of dreams — I've seen it before… in the Dream Master's Host." She let it hang a moment. So that the Guide could guess at the meaning beneath her words. "What's the connection?" "…It's true that I originated from him." Polaris answered, as though it were none too agreeable to her. "After we confirmed that we held different aims, I left him." "Anyway — hmph, fine. You, born of that power, mean to remake this world however your own heart pleases too, don't you? So that makes you—" And the rest of it finally forced its way out of her mouth. "—in cahoots. With the Dream Master." All around froze over like thin ice. Polaris, unable to do anything at all, only gaped, mouth fallen open. She wanted to believe she'd misheard. "That… that's offensive—" And because she couldn't, she fumbled open lips paralyzed with fury. Now and then she gritted her teeth, chewing her words to pieces. "—profoundly so." "That's exactly what I meant it to be." Nachia forced out a snort. The corners of her stiffened eyes crumpled as if rubbed raw against something. "Clear enough now? I'm going to put my brother back the way he was. Whatever you say, that won't change." She threw out her chest and declared it boldly. Wiping again at her reddened eyes, sniffling. "All the way, to the very, very end I'll try everything, and if all of it turns out to be impossible — then by my own hand I'll…." The words wouldn't come. Because she'd hesitated. Because she'd hesitated again. Because no matter how she vowed it and vowed it again here and now, it would be utterly worthless the moment it actually came to pass in reality. "That is the better road." The Guide seized the gap and cut in. "With so little certain, so little brought to light, wouldn't it be better not to thrash about first, but to save yourself, to save the dream-world, and then look for another way? All the more so if you'll arrive at the same conclusion in the end." "Don't you dare." Nachia said. Leveling the half-a-Forest-Keeper's staff at Polaris. With her remaining empty hand she summoned the puppies, filling the clearing with them. The burly beasts — appearing this time from the first with every intent to fight, to threaten the enemy — drove the Guide back with low growls. "Don't. You. Dare." But the rays of light at the staff's tip dimmed by degrees. The puppies, too, reading the irresolute, unripened core in their master's mind, grew confused, little by little. It was hard, after all, even once she'd made up her mind. It was hard even though she'd already thought it through, already steeled herself. If anything, that made it harder. Polaris was, without doubt, offering the safer road. Wouldn't it be all right to follow her even now — to first take in enough of the power of the Gold so as not to die, and then think it over slowly? Because her brother had become a monster anyway. "You're a monster now anyway — just wait a little longer the way you are, hm?" The voice of a Nachia in her head shook Nachia. "It's not as if you can get any worse now. Right, Belpomet?" "Get out." Biting her lip, Nachia put strength into the staff. The puppies, having gathered themselves into form once more, drove Polaris to the very edge of the clearing, their eyes blazing fierce. "Is this truly your choice?" Polaris said, softening her wrath. Hemmed in by the whites of eyes bared toward her, by fangs whiter still, by bristling leaf-stalks, she backed away, step by faltering step — yet her gaze, far smaller than the puppies' but far more steadfast, stayed nailed to Nachia's face to the very last. "It is." "You'll come to think, later, that this was your last chance." she said. Plainly, and with pity. "You will regret it." "I'm regretting it. Even now." A wall built up, a dam so thick and impregnable as that — for it to fall, all that's needed is one last step, one last drop, one single trigger added on. For Nachia, this one phrase became that trigger. The tears wetting the rims of her eyes began to fall, streaming down her cheeks and chin. Through her uncontrollable sobbing, a faintly intelligible voice leaked out. "If you've nothing more to say, then go." The tears pouring down did not turn to stone. They remained to the last as the tears of Nachia, who had not the products of a Forest-Keeper but a will and a heart — even a selfishness — of her own. The streams that struck the bare earth flowed on to wet the stones and seep into the soil, doing all the things real tears ought rightly to do. "If you mean to stay, then stop talking. Fight. Fight to the end and kill me." Nachia's hand, drained white, gripped the staff's cut end so hard it hurt. So that its shape might be carved clearly into her bare palm, pressed down like dough. So that this unfamiliar pain might let her forget, if only for now, the throbbing ache slicing through her chest, the hot tracks of tears clawing at her face. "And if you don't think you can do that, then just go, anywhere at all… please." It was the last farewell she offered to Polaris — and to her own self, who had once been an unshakable Forest-Keeper. {IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main7_Short: Made to choose between her calling and her blood, she lets go of everything but one. Will she come to regret choosing the sister over the keeper?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main7_Title: The Forest-Keeper Who Left the Forest
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main8_Content_0:
"I have to tell her."
the little sprout said. Like an arrow, like a gale, like a rumor of some mighty being that had torn through the edge of the Forest of Turbulence and vanished, it ran on without stopping. Pushing through thickets, riding down slopes, scrambling over mountainsides and rivers in a frenzy… and then it stopped, blankly, somewhere.
"I have to tell her, I have to tell her…."
Its two eyes shrank small. It had happened often before, but the intervals were growing shorter. It couldn't remember.
"I have to tell… but…."
It couldn't tell where it had come from, where it was supposed to go, to whom and what it was meant to tell. The little sprout began to pace. It couldn't stay still. If it did, it would be caught. By the black grasp creeping out, by inches, toward the bond-servant that had defied it. The little sprout shuddered all over. It had an impression of a place it had come from, a place it must never go back to — a place that had not, originally, been so. A forest swallowed by an eternal night. That night was hunting it. Licking the bare earth with its yellowish underbelly to read the stirrings of its prey, a night drawing near with a crescent moon hung in its eyes and, at the tips of its venom-fangs, coldly gleaming meteors, even in the pitch-black dark. It was biding its time to make the thing, once again, not itself. Just then a realization reared its head in a flash within its mind.
"I remember now!"
The little sprout scrambled away in flight.

"I have to tell her, I have to tell her."
Ever since the day the Elder Keeper vanished without a trace, it had thought everything was over. Forgetting its own name, its purpose, its original role, it had become nothing more than one of the starving Nightmare. It had romped and rampaged about, drinking the blood of all things that were not the Nightmare. One day a being appeared that looked to be one such prey. The bond-servants of the Nightmare, delighted, threw themselves at the new plaything.
"…Put them to rest."
The thing, struck down by some great beast the woman commanded, soon returned to the source of the Nightmare. And then it should have had to rise again in a body new but still horribly twisted… yet this time it was not so. Only the memory of being overpowered and losing its body rose up as it was. And it just barely realized. What it had originally been.
"Elder Keeper!"
The little sprout looked all around. Its fingertips, clasped anxiously together, made a small squeaking sound.
"Where did you go… I remember it, I do."
And from that moment the little sprout broke into a run.
"But I have to tell her."
It had to search the whole forest, the whole of the Rapids, and, if need be, the whole of the dream itself to find the Elder Keeper. Because it had been there, that time.
"He told me to say he's sorry — to Nachia, to the Elder Keeper."
Because it had heard the one last word the Younger Keeper left behind before he lost himself.
"I have to pass that word on. The Younger Keeper is still in there—"
the little sprout said, gasping for breath.
"—so there's still hope, and I have to tell her."
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main8_Short: A tiny sprout races against its own forgetting, carrying one last message. Will there be time to speak it before the night swallows it again?
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Main8_Title: The Whole Forest, to This Sprout
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Short0_Content: In the Forest of Reverie, Nachia carved fallen ancient trees into masks shaped like spirits and beasts, and scattered them throughout the woods. Spirits, the Leaf Pups among them, gathered at her side, and travelers came to call her the Goddess of the Forest. It was Nachia's way of expressing the love she held for the world. She moved her hands not to protect anyone, but simply out of a cherishing heart.
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Short0_Title: A Moment of the Forest Keeper
ui.TravelerStory_Nachia_Short1_Content: Mortally wounded while defending the forest from Primus's armies, Belpomet stood alone before an unknown source of power, driven by the desperate resolve to give up anything if only the forest could be saved. It approached gently, offering a deal in the sweetest of tones. The moment black claws sprouted from her fingertips, Belpomet sensed something watching her from beyond her sight, smiling. Before she could even give it a name, her hand had already reached out.

ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main1_Content_0:
It was the day he would see the sun for the first time.
Young Vesper and the children his age had awaited that day until their necks ached from the craning. And how could it have been otherwise — among children their age, indeed among every orphan the hand of the Order had ever touched, there could not possibly have been one who did not count down the days to it. For the Order of the Sacred Flame, which had gathered up these orphans with nowhere else to go, it too made every possible preparation for that day.
That did not mean, however, that all the Order's ten-year-old children were reared like mere worms beneath the earth. A life that at its root never touched the sun at all would wither and end like a faded flower — not at ten, but before an infant could so much as hold up its own head. The point, in the end, was this: to preach how great the sun god El'pyros is, those under instruction had to be placed, for a limited time, in surroundings where the sun could not be known.
And so the orphans the Order had gathered remained, from the moment they learned speech and began to recite their own names — that is, from the moment they knew themselves as themselves — only in places where the sun could be neither perceived nor praised. Outdoor activity took place in an inner courtyard whose high, translucent roof permitted only the faintest gradations of light and shade, and when the day's labor was done they had to seek sleep in the crevices of thick, swollen stone walls without a single window. In that place the thing nearest to the sun — that is, the thread-thin candle flame — when it was snuffed out, the darkness that then settled bore a color much like the underside of a grime-caked fingernail. On the rare occasions they had to move elsewhere in broad daylight, the venerable priests and the stern teachers always came along. As though handling beasts, they fitted the children with uncomfortable garments and blindfolds, with manacles and leather straps bound across their chests, and led them here and there.
Young Vesper, on every such unexpected excursion — a true outing, not into the courtyard but into the real outside — would screw his whole face up into a comical expression, everything drawn toward the tip of his nose. Because he never knew what thunderous reprimand might come down if he so much as cracked his eyes open beneath the blindfold, he tried instead to gather all his senses into the remaining parts of his face that could touch the outside — the nose, the cheeks, the lips, the tongue, the chin.
When he walked outside, there was a certain steady pressure in the air of that place. That force, pouring down at a slant from the sky, would tug at bare skin or press upon it, carrying a ticklish sensation. Added to that force were the smells of some inexhaustible world — utterly unlike the stone walls that gave off only the scent of damp moss — smells that tangled and welled and burst forth, that slipped in through the seams of his heavy clothes and made the down on his skin prickle and rise, a warm wind that gently stroked the throat and the nape where beads of sweat ran down… these things he devoured greedily, the way a starving man gulps down the water of life.
After living like that for whole years on end, when at last he turned ten and would see the sun for the first time — how could he not be beside himself?

"Slowly, slowly!"
The words of the venerable priests reached him. His turn to remove his own blindfold was drawing near. Vesper wished, if only he could, to stop his heart then and there. For the fist-sized thing lodged behind his ribs pounded so insolently, thump upon thump, that it threatened to devour every sound around him!
"Uh, waaahh…."
The sound of someone bursting into tears reached him. Strangely, though they had all lived together this whole time, when the weeping was set apart on its own he could not tell whose it was. The children who turned ten and saw the sun for the first time made all sorts of other sounds besides. The sound of crumpling to the ground, the sound of frothing at the mouth, the sound of gasping for breath and then stopping dead and toppling over headlong where they stood… hearing it, Vesper was suddenly seized with fear. Why? That he too might faint? That he might bawl and disgrace himself? More frightening than that were the adults.
The most frightening thing of all was the fact that the watching adults had not yet laid any expectation upon his name, upon the ring of the word Vesper.
Vesper believed himself the most valiant, the sturdiest, the most loyal and the most devout among the children his age reared by the Order. He had no reason to doubt it. Even so, that did not make the day of first seeing the sun any less harrowing. Vesper thought he might weep, or faint. What frightened him more was the indifference that would follow — that the teachers, or the venerable priests, might simply let it pass with a "well, that's a child for you." He had to be braver than anyone. He had to be more upright than anyone. And so the watching teachers, and the priests too, ought to be disappointed in him and set him straight. They ought to bear down on him — was he going to whine like the other children? — and demand that he rise at once on his own two feet and receive with his whole body the grace of the sun god El'pyros. That, at least, would be better.
He had heard it in doctrine lessons until it was branded into his ears. His parents had cast away children like himself, and the Order — though it had no need to — had taken Vesper, taken all the other children, into its broad embrace. So Vesper had to repay it. He had to draw all the adults' expectations upon himself. He must never disappoint them; without fail, he would see today's rite through with dignity….

"Vesper… Vesper!"
Hearing his own name called out ringingly, Vesper started violently. How long had it been?
"Y-yes! Priest!"
"Slowly, carefully now — remove the blindfold!"
His two arms, which had stood rigid as though bitten by a spring, jerked into sudden motion. In his fluster he struck his own cheekbone and the rim of his eye with his own hand, but did not even feel the pain. Groping, he moved his hands to the back of his head. He found the knot of the blindfold tied across his eyes. Following the words the teachers had taught him, he could quickly tell which cord to catch and which to loosen. Turn this so, and pull, and….
"Slowly, slowly!"
Listening to the words of the venerable priests, Vesper had to strain ceaselessly. It felt as though some strange monster hung from his forearm in place of his own hand. That monster was tremendously fast. Swift as an insect hurling itself at a candle flame, as a stream of water running down a parched, burning throat. And yet here it was, held forcibly back, sentenced to the punishment of loosening the cords slowly and slipping the loosened blindfold down over the bridge of his nose by mere degrees. He recalled the tale of a certain apostate who had mocked the sun god El'pyros and was made to roll a boulder that would never, ever cease.
"I am no apostate. I will not become one."
Vesper's lips stirred.
"I am His child. I am… I will be the one He is proud of."
So Vesper resolved. Breathing deep, he slowly released the force he had clenched into his eyelids. Patterns like shining muddy water, come from he knew not where, gradually faded, and at last the world was there.
It was a world of daylight, met for the very first time in his life.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main1_Content_1:
All around him was …….

All around him was what? He could not tell. He did not know what he was looking at, nor by what words he ought to point to and describe which things. With knit brow and lips, mastering his whole trembling body, he could barely manage one thing. He turned his neck so that the scene right before his eyes shifted. That was how Vesper looked around at the first midday he met beneath the sun.
Bright — that was the first word that came to him. But it was a word he had learned when a candle was lit in the schoolroom where the children stayed. Was there, then, a candle here too? Was a single, very strong candle lit somewhere? No. The outside world reflected in Vesper's eyes was such that everything in heaven and earth, every place, was bright all at once, without remainder, without a gap. The original colors of the world he had known could here be seen only by borrowing the form of thin, small shadows. So much vast matter, and the connections between things, came into view all at once that he grew nearly dizzy with it.
It was a world apart from counting, one and two, the lines scored into a stone wall in the dark to make out a number. Everything was too open, too far, too high. Vesper, not knowing why he did so, lifted his head. His spine bent back with a crack, as though it would break. He held a perilous posture, the back of his head pointing toward the ground, yet had no awareness of it. And up above, where he happened to gaze, there was
a cliff with no end.
Vesper thought he was looking down from an upside-down ceiling into a bottomless pit. Above that pit of sky made of a very strange light, a few white, billowing masses drifted. Once he saw such a thing he could not tear his eyes away.
