He thought that in an instant he would plunge headlong into the void, that those pale-white masses would come scrambling at him like the yellow, long, legless things that lived in the crevices of the stone walls, and begin to gnaw at him. Vesper's two eyes tried to curl back into his skull like a hermit crab shutting its shell. Shallow, faint breaths bubbled up. To anyone's eye it was the very picture of someone about to throw a fit. At this the teachers and priests who had watched from a distance flinched and moved toward him, but….

"I have not fallen."
Young Vesper was speaking. As though it were no longer possible even to whisper, he was crying out, ringing and loud.
"I have not fallen yet."
But what, exactly, could be known from those words? The conduct of those fallen into madness and that of practitioners sunk in religious ecstasy were at times exceedingly hard to tell apart… most unpleasantly so. And so what set the watching adults at ease was the speech and conduct that followed.
Vesper knelt down with both knees pressed tight together and began to pray.
"Because my body, and the bodies of the teachers and the venerable priests, and all manner of other things have weight, I have not fallen."
Phrases learned from scripture, the words of the venerable priests, and sentences the child had understood and memorized in his own way were all jumbled together, ill-formed and rambling, yet their content alone everyone could hear.
"Thank You for protecting all things that have weight, all things that have substance."
The expression "things that have substance" was, of course, a concept a little too difficult for a ten-year-old child to utter on his own. It was borrowed from a word learned in doctrine lessons. What, then, is that which has no substance, that which has no weight, the opposite of that which has substance? Light and fire, warmth — fittingly, are they not all the infinite powers of the sun god El'pyros!
"El'pyros's light and fire do not bear the sin of weight laid upon all the things of the earth. And yet I believe that, in order to keep company with all things that have weight and to save them, even the weightless light and fire willingly come down from there to here."
Vesper went on in a hoarse, cracked voice.
"I believe in El'pyros's merciful grace. I believe in the grace that keeps all from falling from here into that blue pit, and that pours down eternal fire and light alike upon all sinners born with the sin of substance…."
One is meant to close one's eyes while praying, but that day Vesper did not blink even once. He did not bow his head and bury it in his chest until that long, rambling prayer was finished. All the while Vesper kept his two eyes wide open and watched the scene around him — the scene in which every place, every thing, had ripened into its own most rightful and resplendent color. He knew and praised that the very harmony of all those colors and qualities is the foremost blessing the infinitely merciful El'pyros pours down upon this world.
"Look down upon us, look down upon us…."
Those who watched would say there were three suns in that place that day. One was in the sky, the original sun in the place where it was meant to be. As for where the other two were — when they came to the part where, in the eyes of a mere child, two other suns each took up dwelling, one in either pupil — even the most barefaced storyteller had to fold in a snicker or two. There were almost none who believed they had truly seen, that day, the fire of the sun welling and pouring out of a mere ten-year-old's pupils, that wellspring of undying faith.
Save only the master of that faith himself — Vesper.
{IMAGE}
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main1_Short: A child raised in windowless dark, counting the days until the light. But what kind of faith is born in a boy who has never once seen the sun?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main2_Content_0:
Only a few weeks had passed since becoming part of the Order of the Sacred Flame — in fact, strictly speaking, only a few days since being stuck with the ambiguous label of "probationary member," not yet an official post — and the man, who was diligently cleaning his own small room on the first assignment to come down to him from the Order with his head full of grand dreams, stared open-mouthed at the colossal figure that had appeared from nowhere. There was no name tag or anything of the sort, but who it was was beyond doubt. What knightly order was it again? That personage of such resounding renown, said to be the future head of a newly founded regional Order-level organization — who else could it be but Vesper?
The other rampant rumors about him went like this. That a blade brought down to strike bare flesh stopped of its own accord before it could reach the bone; that during every rest period he crushed stones to bits with his bare hands, so that the lines of his palms had worn away entirely flat… He and the other probationary members would only put on a show of taking such things seriously when they were in a room with the venerable priests. They figured someone had singled out one of the august personages to load with cringeworthy overpraise, just to haze the newcomers.
Who could have known that this was, in fact, the very opposite — an underestimation?
A height and frame so imposing that it was not as though he had several extra heads on other men, but rather several extra calves' worth of bulk. That broad-set upper body in particular looked as though he could go about with the bar that braces a castle gate strapped on as a breastplate, and a blacksmith's anvil set atop his stiff neck as a stand-in for a helm, with no trouble at all. The golden two-handed hammer he was said to use as his main weapon? One could only heave a sigh of relief that he had not brought it along. For one thing was certain: if a weapon broken in to that man's hand were brought indoors, it would call for major construction, tearing several handspans out of both the corridor and the doorframe. Such was the overwhelming majesty Vesper possessed — a majesty that made one heap upon him, without realizing it, the most preposterous praise, like a meek lamb standing before a beast of prey.
And yet — what business did so proud and high-ranking a member have in the quarters of a mere probationer?

"Brother."
He spoke in a voice that was heavy, yet that left one unable even to scheme an escape from it — a voice that felt for all the world like the blazing sun of a sweltering day.
"I hear you have only just begun your life in the Order. Is there anything troubling you?"
"There is not."
The probationary member answered with a deep bow of the head. It was a reply that had sprung out reflexively, but it seemed to him the right one.
"I am in a position where there is still much to learn, so I mean to think of such things rather than my own comfort. Thank you for your concern."
"I see."
Vesper's head, which had been roaming this way and that about the cramped room, then halted abruptly upon one spot. And the armor sculpted in the shape of golden flames flinched, for just an instant. As when a low gasp at a mountain's peak swells into a thunderous echo by way of the slopes and foothills, the body of the probationary member, who had been minutely observing his every move, trembled with a violent start. The Vesper himself, reacting sensitively — perhaps with displeasure — to something somewhere in his quarters? Wondering whether there was some part he had left untidied, he hurriedly turned his gaze to follow that head. There stood a wall.
The wall was just a wall. A black, thick stone wall like any that made up the Order's buildings, nothing special about it, forever beading with dew and giving off the scent of moss that trailed limply down with it. Only — the thought that, had it been a different building, somewhere in that wall a window would have been set to let cool wind and downy sunlight loose into the room, and further the thought that such a thing would be desirable, never once occurred to the room's owner, who had every nerve on edge so as not to ruffle Vesper's temper; and to Vesper, who had unwittingly shown an unusual reaction, it was forcibly ignored.
The tale of a certain small child, shivering in the cold of the dark and forcing himself to seek sleep, back in the days when the name Vesper was not naturally called the Order's greatest pride, the favored child of El'pyros — that tale was no longer there.
It had to be so.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main2_Content_1: "It must be stifling. You have it hard." Vesper, who had stepped up to the firmly sealed stone wall, stretched out his arm and stroked it. The watching probationer had no sooner shut his gaping mouth than his jaw dropped again. Vesper's armor — the thin plates of metal protecting the back of his hand and the base of his fingers — passed over the surface of the brick, softly shaving it away like a chalkboard ground down by chalk. What in the world was it made of? "Ah, n-no." He answered with another bow of the head. There was nothing to be gained from letting his astonished expression show. "A place untouched by the sun's flame is the very place best suited to recalling El'pyros's grace… I, too, wish for nothing more than to one day become El'pyros's pride!" Too hasty. Would he be scolded for nothing, taken for empty flattery? Fortunately Vesper paid it little mind and drew away from the wall, moving toward the doorway. From his bearing, it seemed he had said most of what he had to say and meant now to go elsewhere and devote himself to whatever it was he ought to be doing — slaking his dry throat, perhaps, with sand wrung from a crushed boulder. For the member, the situation was cause to breathe easier at last. Had he just chided himself that his words had been too hasty? Regrettably, that judgment of his was hasty too. Vesper, who had carried on as though about to leave the room, stopped in his tracks once more. Then he gazed fixedly above the desk lit by the dim candle. Where his eyes had turned, several sheets of old paper were bound with a thin straw cord. The bundle was rather thick. "Ah, ah. It is nothing." The expression on Vesper's face as he gazed at the bundle of paper on the desk could not be seen. Naturally so, for even indoors he never carelessly removed the face-guard that hung down from his helm. But who could know whether, behind it, some look of displeasure was seeping out — whether a stern rebuke was about to come, asking how a probationer dared to keep some private possession to read and idle away the hours with? Guilty in his own mind, the member had no choice but to start explaining, even at the risk of jumping the gun. "It was brought in with permission. It is… a collection of letters from my mother." "Is that so?" Vesper said. For some reason the thought that there ought, after all, to be a window in the wall surfaced again, but he did not let himself dwell on it. "Yes, well…." Taking courage from the fact that, even as he watched warily, no anger colored Vesper's voice, the probationary member went on. "Even before I became a probationer I often had to stay in distant parts, and each time I gathered up what my mother and I exchanged. When things are hard, there is nothing like reading them to steady the heart." So that is how it is. Vesper thought this and, saying nothing, folded his arms. Then he soon unfolded them. He swore that he had not moved so out of any thought of his own. And the way one arm then began, unthinkingly, to reach out was likewise far from his intent. "Does your mother cherish you greatly?" Vesper's movement stopped all at once. The hand that had been advancing toward the bundle of letters hung half-extended, cutting through the air. Being the youngest and yet the eldest son, she frets over me wherever I go, I suppose, ha ha…. Such a reply reached him in passing, but that was not the reason. The reason Vesper could reach no further was not that he had learned something more, but that he could not know. It was that he could not gauge precisely what value such a thing as a letter sent from mother to son possessed, nor what one ought to do, or refrain from doing, in order to honor it. Was it acceptable to pick such a thing up and read it as a matter of course? Or was it better to confirm the owner's wishes before touching it? Was a letter a mother had written to her son an intimate object that an outsider — even one high-ranked in the Order he had sworn to serve — must not lay hands on carelessly? Asking permission first might make it all right. But was the very act of asking such a thing of someone beneath him already a discourtesy? If discourteous, how discourteous? Even taking into account that he was this man's far superior, was it an act with a moral flaw, one that must not be forced upon a subordinate?… To Vesper, a true orphan who had been gathered up by the Order and raised "memorizing" his own name and role and responsibilities, these were all unfamiliar matters. And yet to some — no, frankly, to most people — there is surely a certain sense that comes wholly naturally.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main2_Content_2: "What sort of person is your mother?" "My mother, I suppose…." Some reply or other rattled on again, but this too he let in one ear and out the other. Even had the member, his tension eased, prattled on with the giddy gestures one makes with a friend, Vesper would not have so much as noticed. In place of the probationary member's reply, which did not enter his ears, what he recalled was the words he and the other orphans gathered up by the Order in childhood had whispered to one another. No matter how thoroughly they recited the doctrine, no matter how lustily they sang El'pyros's hymns at the top of their lungs, in the end children were children. Those children could only speak of a certain name they had not all experienced together — a name that ordinary children all know — and the feelings that arise around it. Whispering more faintly than the smoke that climbs the wick of a freshly snuffed candle. "What was my mom like, I wonder?" "How did I even come to be here?" "My mom might still be alive… do you think she's looking for me?" "She's probably just forgotten us. Back then we wouldn't even have had names." "She might have given some other child a new name in place of ours by now." In the crevices of the moist stone walls, the children grew wise as fast as a flat, dark stain spreads. Long before they ever saw the First Light, they had aged enough not to blindly yearn for what they did not know. Having been reared in the Order of the Sacred Flame, which held sway over more than a few kingdoms and guilds, they could not entertain the thought that some wealthier true parent would appear out of nowhere to "rescue" them and carry them off at last into the embrace of a real family. The children simply wondered. They could only wonder, as naturally as anything, about the thing that was a given for other children but was absent for them. What it would have been like, if we too had had a mother and a father. "Brother?" Without realizing it, Vesper raised a hand to his broad breastplate. "Um, Brother?" His heart was pounding. It felt as though the pounding could be heard right through the armor. "Brother Vesper?" His own name seized Vesper by the ankle and set him back down upon the earth. And so, in an instant, it forged him anew into the Order's mission and duty and responsibility, into one of the proudest children of El'pyros. "You seemed lost in thought… my apologies. I have gone and rattled on with too much idle talk, have I not?" "No." Brother, Brother, he says… By rights it was not a word a probationary member should yet be using so freely, but just now the ring of it was very pleasant to hear. Surrounded by countless brothers, he passed each of his days. Raise his head and there were the merciful Round Table of the Sun and their Eminences the Cardinals of Radiance; lower it and there were these countless younger brothers, fervently looking up to him and burning with devotion toward El'pyros — were they not all bound to one another in love truly without limit, in a bond more complete and full than any familial affection? In a lot so overflowing with blessing, what was there to be at such a loss over — to wonder about, or even to long for? "You had best rest well, Brother." The probationary member, in a thoroughly tensed manner, pressed his limbs tight against his torso. As though to belie the somewhat easy mood in which they had been exchanging words a moment before, a voice heavily laden with menace flowed out from behind the face-guard. The man himself, Vesper, did not know that whenever he addressed a subordinate without much thought — that is, at ease — he came to open his mouth in just such a tone. "Yes!" "From tomorrow there will follow arduous days of forging anew a faith all too prone to slackening, of hammering it into shape with merciless blows." "Yes, sir!" The probationary member stood stiff as a poorly planted scarecrow and answered. "I shall keep it well in mind, Brother!" Leaving the member's spirited reply behind him, Vesper opened the door. By the faint lamplight kindled in the room, his own long shadow was cast. That sturdy, loyal body, filling almost without the slightest gap the space between ceiling and floor, between wall and wall, bent long and stretched out along the narrow, dark corridor. Looking down at this other figure of himself, Vesper pretended not to see the faint stain shimmering shallow upon the surface of his armor that shone resplendent and golden — the stain that his own sigh had grazed in passing — and hurried his steps along. The sound of his heart gradually subsided. It is only when speaking of such things that my heart is ever at ease. So he thought.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main2_Short: A bundle of a mother's letters, and a giant who does not know how to touch it. What is the name of the thing the Order never gave him?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main3_Content_0:
Vesper and the Solar Flame Knights under his command, who had pursued their quarry for so long, had now come to the very brink of writing the final period to that mission. That the head of the Lucid Sect — who had each time slipped his keen, ruthless pursuit by the narrowest of margins — should have chosen for his last refuge some remote underground hideout was most fitting indeed. Was it not the very picture of a wily mole, frantic to bury itself out of reach of the farmer's hoe?
"You have come, Captain."
"Mm."
Vesper arrived at the site where they had seized control of the entrance to the underground. The knights under his command had pitched their lines without a gap and held a stern watch. Few in number though they were, each one of them was more than a match for several dozen untrained rabble.
"An immediate breach being difficult, we are first clearing the surroundings. We assess the fortress interior to be not very large."
The report followed at once, without his having to ask one way or the other.
"As the terrain is isolated from the other ridgelines, the escape routes are likewise limited. Since we are watching every side without the slightest gap, the moment any suspicious movement is detected anywhere, we can coordinate and respond. We believe there is also scarcely any food within the fortress."
At this Vesper's brow twitched. So then — what was it, what in the end was the point, the thing they really wished to say? Was it not these two lines?
Wait it out, and the cur will come crawling out of his own accord. So there is no need to force our way in.
"I see."
Vesper cut off the report there was no need to hear out further. A knight under his command looked up at him with a puzzled expression. Every one of the knights had to. Indeed, some of the knights, even mounted, had to lower their heads — not raise them — to meet Vesper's eyes.
"Captain?"
"There is no need to 'force' our way in."

Vesper set his steps forward, tread upon tread. So he approached the entrance to the underground. The gazes of all the members under his command soon turned that way. With countless eyes converging upon a single small point — taking the very shape that signifies the great El'pyros's sun — Vesper raised high both hands and the enormous hammer they held. Unsuited to its ponderous form, finely shaped ridges and grooves ran along one face, but this was no artistic flourish — it was simply so that the face could be swung against an enemy and pound them into a pulp of blood. Meanwhile, at the sight of that enormous hammerhead floating as lightly as a seed borne on the wind, it was not Vesper who held it but the onlookers who felt dizzy and shifted their footing again and again.
"Hrrgh!"
The hammer, raised in a flash, was driven straight down. The other knights nearby braced, clenching their backs and hips with all their might. It was a tremor that made one's knees go weak of themselves and shook one's very joints. The result, too, was beyond reproach. Not only the door that had firmly barred the entrance but the whole area around it caved in wholesale, baring the bare flesh of the underground. Setting the hammer down, Vesper put a knee to the ground and folded what looked like a thin blanket over his arm. In truth it was no blanket but the door itself, crumpling like a sheet of paper and spewing out heat in waves. When he flung it aside — its tattered crossbar still hanging — the last barrier blocking approach was removed as well.
"We search."
Watching his subordinates enter the quarry's hideout, Vesper fell to thinking. To bring the head of the Lucid Sect himself before a heresy tribunal and execute him there was needed, and so they were to track and capture him alive — this was the mission handed down by His Holiness the Archbishop of the Sun, or more precisely by the "Voices of the Sun" who acted in his stead. Regrettably, until now they had had to content themselves with weighing various incidental gains against each other, somewhere between large failures and small ones. For instance, discovering and hauling in a wandering merchant in league with the Lucid lot, or learning that some figure of a certain kingdom had ties with the Lucid faith and sharing the information with the Judicators of Purification.
The chief target himself, the head of the Lucid Sect, they had let slip again and again.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main3_Content_1: To the Solar Flame Knights, failure is not permitted. For a time they had been able to realize that aim quite literally. Those caught in their net of surveillance, however secret, could not in the end escape pursuit. Organizations that set themselves in opposition to them vanished overnight without a trace. And yet that same vaunted force found, of late, its pursuit dragging on listlessly over the mere matter of capturing a single king of heretics. Had they grown soused on success too swift and too easy? It struck him that the resignation and doubt spreading among the troops were reaching a dangerous pitch. There had even been knights plotting desertion openly among themselves; Vesper, who had handpicked them himself, had wished with all his heart to stop them, but to set discipline right he had had no choice but to execute them. To be made to treat precious comrades who had given themselves to El'pyros in such a fashion! Rage at that rat of a Lucid head boiled up within Vesper. "Search thoroughly." He spoke in a voice colored with anger. "Yes, sir!" Watching the backs of his subordinates as they rushed busily into the underground, Vesper glanced about and picked up a stone of suitable size. Crunch, crunch…. A truly pitiable stone — guilty of nothing but having happened to lie there in that place at that time — began to crumble with a blood-chilling shriek. Cruuunch…. * The search drew to its end, but the harvest was meager. As the report had said — that it was not a very large facility to begin with, and the food situation poor — it seemed the place had not been built to receive a figure as great as the head himself. Even so, it did not explain where the man had vanished to without a trace. The prisoners dragged out were for the most part riffraff, rank-and-file members at the level of vagrants who had only just finished an initiation rite in hopes of getting a meal. They had merely been hauled out to be taken prisoner, yet that alone had been enough to terrify them into fainting and frothing at the mouth — there were no end of them. "What is your judgment, Captain?" A member under his command asked Vesper thus. "Shall I wake them at once and interrogate them?" "There seems no need for that." Vesper looked upon the prisoners without hiding his contemptuous expression. Before any harsh torture — indeed, before anyone had so much as laid a hand on them, busy as they were just hauling them out — they slumped of their own accord, shoved this way and that, a truly pathetic sight. Having roughly looked over their appearance, he was the more certain they were worthless. Vesper knew well that the Lucid head could not possibly be hidden among their number. "These are not men holding any useful information." And so, in the end, only the first question remained, with no way to be resolved. Where in the world had this cur bolted to from an underground facility sealed on every side? Unable to master his fury, Vesper drove the tip of his foot into the bare ground. Failed again? Have I failed again? he thought. As his clenched fist trembled, the grains of sand still left inside bid farewell to one another's brief lives. Crumbled into fine dust, they at last escaped Vesper's grip and went sailing off on the wind. "What report am I to send up this time." It felt hopeless. The Solar Flame Knights were, beyond doubt, a tremendously successful unit. But as cases of missions accomplished piled up one upon another, ever greater expectation was always laid upon them. Officially their Captain was accorded honors equal to those of the Cardinals of Radiance, yet Vesper himself was, in the end, the head of a mere force of arms. Compared to a regional parish overseeing several houses of worship, to a regional Order overseeing those parishes, to a Cardinal who is the supreme authority over that Order, his standing within the Order was weak. He had no intention of taking up political struggle, but such was the fact. Even so, for a time he could be content. With each victory dispatch of the Solar Flame Knights he had felt, if anything, all the prouder. Since the Cardinals could not take up arms and go out onto the battlefield themselves, he believed he was doing the work only he could do — that with his own disciplined body he was directly condemning heretics and putting into practice the great cause of El'pyros. But what if, at some moment, he failed to distinguish himself any longer in such a domain? What if the Order no longer needed him? If, drinking in the sun's daylight every day, he could yet sing no hymn of praise for it; if, while all creation cried aloud to bear witness to the great El'pyros's order, he could not take his place as the trumpeter of salvation in the very heart of such faith — then what meaning was there in all the rest of life's grubby, trifling little tasks? "Captain, we have found something." Perhaps it was because he had been sunk so deep in such thoughts. The moment he heard those words, Vesper went running as though he would take flight.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main3_Content_2: "It appears to be a door." "A door?" "Too much to call it a door made by human hands — it is an entrance. One leading somewhere." Exchanging such words testily, Vesper and several knights arrived at the room in question. Though he had charged at full sprint for some while in his armor, he came to a stop bolt upright without pausing once for breath, and Vesper gazed upon the "too-much-to-call-it-a-door entrance, leading somewhere," that his subordinate had reported. A bluish light poured out and filled the room. The edges of that entrance fluttered this way and that, deforming feebly. It was an entrance not drawn or hung anywhere, but simply floating, suspended. So then — this was a Rift. A Rift split open in the air — no, in reality. "Thinking it might be of help, we brought a fellow caught near here." Vesper nodded with satisfaction and then glared at the captive bound tight in ropes. A scrawny build, a shabby robe. When the hood was thrown back to reveal the face, the terror written upon it came through all the more clearly. "Heretic. What is this?" "It is a Rift." Just as Vesper was loosening up, deciding he had better demonstrate a more impassioned technique of conversation, the captive seemed to catch his own blunder and hurriedly added the rest. "Th-this is a Rift leading to The Rapids. It is connected to that place." The Rapids. He had heard well enough of it, yet it remained a horrifically irreverent place. The boundary between dream and reality, object of longing for countless unbelievers and heretics, the very Rapids about which absurd rumors circulated — that reaching its end let one have one's wish granted, and the like. It struck him of a sudden that this might become another thread for the pursuit. "Did your head flee in here?" "That, I do not—" "Could he have fled, or could he not?" "H-he could have!" When Vesper kindly took hold of one of his own fingers, the captive seemed to grasp that warm sentiment too, and began to pour out a string of more earnest replies. "He most certainly could have! Please, my lord… I have only been in the faith a few days—" Take him back. Having said so with a gesture, Vesper poured his whole mind once more into the matter before his eyes — the Rift leading to The Rapids. True enough, with every side sealed off, it was the one lifeline the fugitive could grasp. The trouble was that there was no knowing what sort of environment lay within — the Rapids he had only ever heard tell of. Perhaps the head of the Lucid Sect, joined within by allies, lay in wait, sharpening himself for the moment this side came in. Might it not turn into driving his subordinates to their deaths? Vesper looked upon the loyal knights who had run without rest at his heels for seven days and seven nights. His judgment as a military commander told him that here and now was, for the moment, the time to withdraw. He ought to relieve the fatigue of all this time and request resupply. Only by devoting himself thus to reinforcing his strength and dressing his ranks before setting out would the mission's rate of success be higher. Was it, then, the rightful thing to extend a hand to the Order yet again midway through a mission? "I am the pride of El'pyros." Vesper said. "I am the brightest-burning flame. I am the sunlight that never ceases." Was the sole reason not to advance nothing but the unwatchable excuse of "because we are tired"? This man, the head of the Lucid Sect, is now driven into a corner. Give him more time and he will only hatch yet another scheme in here. So it is fitting to bear down on him as swiftly as possible and beat him to a pulp. Such was his judgment as a man of faith who follows the great El'pyros. "Though there be shade the sun for a time does not touch, there is no place where it never rises at all." "What did you say, Captain?" Vesper turned about, his back to the Rift. He looked upon the elite members of the knightly order who followed him. "Do you remember the oath you swore upon joining?" No one answered, but everyone knew it. That for the sake of conviction they would gladly lay down their lives, and that upon finding a heretic they would burn him without hesitation. Vesper looked upon the members; the members looked in turn upon the other members. They exchanged glances and nodded. Vesper turned around. "We breach."
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main3_Short: Seven days, seven nights, and a quarry forever slipping the net. When the only door left opens onto somewhere no sun has ever reached, who would dare step through?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main3_Title: There Is No Place Where the Sun Does Not Rise
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main4_Content_0:
"So you are Polaris, the Guide."
It was one of the precious rests he took now and then since entering The Rapids. He had unpacked his load by the fire and was in the midst of a meal — though it was no more than the last field ration dug out from a corner of his pack. And in the midst of it he had spotted someone. A woman, fair of skin, long robes trailing down… Vesper soon withdrew his suspicious gaze and fixed her identity. She was without doubt the very being whom the various unbelievers and heretics he had met roaming The Rapids had praised with one voice.
{IMAGE}
"I have no memory of guiding you."
"Yet you do not deny that you are the very 'Guide.'"
One was merely eating a meal, and the other merely happened to be nearby, yet a tension needlessly taut flowed between the two. It was Polaris who broke the silence.
"Your subordinates failed to appear here."
"They are only scattered for a time."
Vesper retorted with an indifferent shrug of the shoulders. Owing to the deep shadows of the campfire cast over him, at a glance he looked for all the world like a small copper hill heaving and swelling.
"I await their rejoining. Some… by forces beyond control, fell in the line of duty, slain in battle. A common thing."
Beyond the face-guard, opened only to the minimum for the meal, a mouth rough as a boulder parted to bare white molars. They bit off a mouthful of the Order of the Sacred Flame's field ration thrust long into them — a ball of grain kneaded with honey. One might well savor or relish a little longer that sweet and nutty taste, yet from Vesper's blunt face, with no change of expression above or below the lip, and his limbs that never loosened slack at ease, it seemed that even some delicacy of land and sea many times more delicious would be no different to him than chewing weeds mixed into muddy water.

"Just as I begin to grow accustomed to this irreverent place called The Rapids, only now do you come to guide me?"
"Not in the least."
At his question, Polaris answered with her head tilted aslant. For a while she eyed askance the golden radiance pouring ceaselessly from Vesper's armor.
"You already follow your own 'light of guidance,' do you not?"
There was something of a sneer to it somehow, but Vesper could bear with it. For now, that is. The other was not an unbeliever cut from the usual cloth, but a being more complex than that. If she was one with whom words could be exchanged, then even one in the bosom of the Order might have no cause to oppose her unconditionally.
"Many unbelievers born and raised in this place hold you in high esteem. That you kept them from losing themselves and decomposing into a heap of dream."
He said.
"Is it true that, by such deeds, you have to all appearances cared for the unbelievers?"
"Unbelievers — even come this far, you still gather up the words of your scripture?"
Polaris said, pressing a hand to her brow.
"To have lived through all manner of phenomena and powers, things and creatures, and the somethings in between, none of which appear in your scripture, and yet still to believe in strings of letters frozen upon paper — how very hollow."
"Experience cannot come before faith, nor phenomenon before the Word."
Vesper answered, crunching his field ration.
"By that reasoning, your name too appears nowhere in El'pyros's scripture. That is no reason for me to disregard your existence."
Hearing this, Polaris gazed fixedly at Vesper. It seemed an unexpected answer, and she looked not a little surprised.
"You are… more temperate than I thought."
"Then your thinking was mistaken."
"I have seen you fight."
Fight? Who with whom? To Vesper, those few words alone were as good as granting him the right to launch into a whole sermon. The members of the Order of the Sacred Flame do not "fight" with other outsiders. They only "render Judgment" upon wrongs already done, or "Purify" the ravages of sin. Moreover, had not all the creatures of The Rapids grown up just as they were, in just that state, without even the chance to know El'pyros's order? It was always right to attempt instruction and conversion first and foremost. Even so, if the other was not moved to grace, then what came next was merely what was necessary to defend oneself.
However cruel it may be, must not what has to be done be done?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main4_Content_1:
"Honestly, the moment I came upon you, I thought it would be that hammerhead leveled at me, not words."
Vesper followed her gaze to the two-handed hammer set down at his side. However gently it was set down, it was a cumbersome thing that gouged a hollow into the bare ground — yet a convenient one too, for the bone and flesh of unbelievers and heretics who refused El'pyros's Word to the last ended up in a much like state before it.
"That I conduct myself as I do now is because you, Guide, have plainly done deeds near to good works, at least on the surface."
As Vesper spoke, he chewed over the record of Polaris that he had reconstructed through the residents of The Rapids he had seen and through their voices. The various frail dream-beings seemed to Vesper like soft tufts of cotton. The strongest among them, at best, differed from the rest only as a water-soaked tuft of cotton differs from a dry one. Such beings, far from rising up resolutely at the decisive moment to seize their own will, would find even defending themselves day to day a hardship. And yet if a being such as Polaris had embraced and protected such ones with no clear demand in return… then surely, certain unbeliever though she was, she could not be called wicked out of hand?
If there were a chance to win such a one over and draw her into the Order, it ought by all rights to be seized.
"As one who spreads the Word of truth, I have bought such misunderstanding until I am sick to death of it."
Vesper said in a voice tinged with regret.
"Narrow-minded heretics prattle that our Order, for the sake of faith, disregards even the standards of good and evil and applies its own arbitrary measures. Do you think so too?"
Polaris did not answer. Whether she had resolved upon it from the first, or whether she had pondered something and let too much time pass, there was no telling — but to Vesper, both alike were already answer enough.

"A pity, that you would cast away so precious a chance."
He lamented.
"Though your aim is unknowable, your deeds are upright, and from the way you speak you can discern reason well enough. That is why I — none other than I, Vesper, Captain of the Solar Flame Knights — offered you in person the chance to have your sins absolved, and yet…."
The two gazes met.
"Have you no thought of turning to true faith and walking at last the right road?"
"You already know the answer."
Polaris drew herself up still more erect where she stood.
"I am this place's Guide and interpreter. Learned in the world your cherished scripture has never told of, can never tell of, I want for nothing in unfolding my own will — so under whose faith would I place myself and become the mouthpiece of that name?"
"Then you know well what is to come hereafter."
No sooner had the words left him than Vesper sprang that tremendous, colossal frame up nimbly. He had set down the field ration in his hand at some point and stood now on both feet — already, what is more, having taken up the two-handed hammer and assumed his stance. Marveling for a moment in pure admiration, Polaris saw him go one further and sling the hammer's haft across his own shoulder. Had an ordinary man borne such a thing atop his shoulder in addition to the weight of his thick iron plate, he would have crumpled where he stood into a reddish pickle.
"However much you make a habit of seemingly good works, you cannot wash away the original sin of beguiling unbelievers and tearing them from the name of El'pyros."
Vesper said in a terrible voice. Standing to face the campfire he had kindled, deep shadows lined up dancing along the contours of his armor. It was a truly grim sight, ill-befitting the name of the Order's foremost warrior.
"And since you have refused even the chance for atonement granted you, only one road remains."
"I have no mind to fight you—"
"You yourself just now relinquished the right to that choice."
A dazzling golden flame began to blaze across the whole of Vesper's body. He set one leg back and drove his weight into it. Now he would kick off the ground and lunge, swinging the hammer so swift and deep that she could not dodge it in a single stroke, taking her whole body at once…. Of a sudden his gaze reached the ground behind Polaris. Though a flame so dazzling that the campfire he had kindled was scarcely visible now blazed and crackled, upon the ground behind her not a single pattern, not a single shape, had formed.
However closely he looked, he could find no shadow of Polaris.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main4_Content_2:
"—Not yet, that is."
Letting slip a curious afterword, and a curious look as well, she began slowly to withdraw. Her speed was not fast. Were it merely a matter of opening distance, he could overtake her any time he liked. He could even outrun Polaris well ahead and pound the path before her to a fine mash with his hammer in advance. But she was not merely withdrawing, or drawing away. That shadowless body was, little by little, growing faint. It was vanishing from sight. It struck him that to give chase would be to chase a mirage. Perhaps she had not truly shown herself at all from the start, but was some kind of spell conveying only voice and form? Vesper ceased tensing his body and rested one face of the hammerhead against the ground. From beneath it came the sound of a single jutting stone, which had held out rattling to the last, splitting with a crack.
"It is not a situation where chasing you would stop you, nor where attacking you could do you harm?"
"No."
It was a simple, almost perfunctory answer. For Polaris's part, this was because her mind was occupied elsewhere. She was studying Vesper closely. She studied his attire and his bearing, the story glimpsed in the belongings he had gathered, and the journey he himself believed he had taken thus far. That golden, blazing armor; that hammer gleaming as though new; the not-very-large pack holding field ration and canteen; the load bearing no trace of the other members who had failed to rejoin or of fallen comrades; and yet the countless marks of battle profusely covering every part of the armor; and above all the memory of those other knights, of whom not a single one remained at his side — these were plainly laying out, each to the other, stories that did not add up.

"Countless souls lose themselves in this place."
Polaris said, looking once more straight into Vesper's eyes.
"They lose their names, and even their essence. And afterward they forget all of it."
With a suspicious look Vesper glared at Polaris. He seemed unable to fathom why she should suddenly say such a thing.
"And after that, it usually grows a little easier to talk. You…."
"You mean to say you will come to me again, after I have become so?"
Vesper cut off her words with a snort. With the possibility of Judgment gone now, there was no reason to hold the hammer any longer; he set it down and crossed both arms before his chest. Tilting his chin up to the full, he met her — met her preposterous delusion — squarely, head-on.
"That impudent imagination of yours has grown almost pitiful now. There will be no such thing."
He went on.
"I am not like those feeble souls. With faith that shall never wane, I shall, by the Sacred Flame…."
"We will meet again."
This time it was Polaris who cut off his words. But she did not smile in the least. Even that gaze — meeting Vesper's face within the helm head-on, yet with the corners of her eyes drooping low, that sorrowful gaze — was utterly out of keeping with the situation, yet felt almost as though she pitied him. When was the last time he had been the object of such a look — no, when was the last time anyone had even dared to look upon Vesper, the Order's foremost warrior, with such eyes? He was dumbfounded.
"I never thought I would say this of speaking with you, but — yes."
Still bewildered, he waited for the words that followed.
"…I find myself looking forward, a little, to that moment."
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main4_Short: A stranger who casts no shadow offers him neither battle nor surrender, only a sorrowful promise: we will meet again. Why does she look upon him as one already lost?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main5_Content_0: Pleasure may be the result of atonement, but it can never be a part of it — was that how it went? Vesper remembered the words a certain bishop of the Order had spoken. It was a phrase not to be forgotten in rendering Judgment upon hostile dream creatures, especially the innate unbelievers who had hardened just as they were, just so, without even the chance to be awakened. Pain and suffering are but for a moment; once Purified, they would surely accept El'pyros's merciful hand and find pleasure within it. "The black ones again." He took his stance and stood. Though he had performed the rite of absolving their sins any number of times by now, they were tenacious unbelievers indeed. Those things, charging on while gushing out an aura turbid and filthy as slop-water in roiling clots, were met by Vesper standing firm without a hair's wavering, and by the two-handed hammer he swung. "You do not seem to be mere beasts — yet you have no mind to repent…!" When the hammer, swung in the shape of a dull bow, was driven down into the ground, a crater opened up. Hairline cracks ran out around it like a spider's web, and before long the whole broad stretch of earth caved in. The black horde did not halt at a mere thing like that, but at the least, whether to leap the crater or to skirt around it, they needed time to respond. They had to soften the charge that had run so fast their feet could not be seen, and the black things at the very front had, one after another, to form a new line and lunge for the golden prey before them. That instant of hesitation was the very thing he had most desired. Without any run-up, Vesper sprang from where he stood and leapt clear across the crater. Then he shattered outright the front ranks of the ones milling about stalled before it and drove deep into their innermost depths. Once one can infiltrate any formation, throwing it into disorder is child's play. With the targets swarming on every side, Vesper swung his hammer without stopping to weigh this or that. As he bore down and crushed in every direction, all three hundred and sixty degrees, without a gap, over and over, a strange dust and a mist of death-cries welled up thickly, along with a sound like great leather sacks bursting with wet thuds. Anything struck square by the hammer was, as a matter of course, left without so much as a bone to recover; even those merely grazed lay floundering, heads driven into the ground. Small hills made of the bodies of dying black things soon formed. "The host of the faithless — thus unable to bear even the faintest, frailest ray of the sun's light." A bone-shard of something or other, burst as though exploded, then tapped against the lower part of Vesper's breastplate as it flew past. When he dropped his gaze on a sudden, he saw a faded mark scored there. It was no great matter. An old scratch happened to be there, and a bone-shard happened, unthinkingly, to strike it again. But there had been a member who had taken the same wound in the very place that scratch was…. In the very midst of rendering Judgment upon the unbelievers, Vesper sank thus into recollection. There had been a member. The name did not matter. He had, in any case, entered The Rapids together with him, a comrade-in-arms to whom he had entrusted his back. He too had been wounded in that part, the lower breastplate, and so he died. The wound itself was not deep, but his body was ruined. Every time he coughed, livid blood gushed out; every time he opened his mouth to speak, his gums, his palate, his tongue were all smeared with sticky streams of blood. There was simply no means to stanch the bleeding. There were no bandages to bind it in haste, and the juice of the leaf that clots blood was all used up. Vesper remembered that moment clearly. The pack that held the medicines was empty. He had thrust his forearm in and frantically rummaged, and when something the size of a pinch caught at his fingertips he hurriedly pulled it out. Out came some dark, blackish lump of powdered medicine — probably several medicines that had trickled out little by little and clumped together inside, something with no medicinal use whatsoever. That moment of futility was vivid even now, and around then that member closed his eyes. So he gathered up the body and buried it. When, and where? Vesper could summon up various peripheral scenes, fragments of scenes, but he could not bind them into a single picture. What tree had cast its shade, what color the earth he buried him in had been, what the smell on the wind had been like… Could I find my way back there? he thought. Meanwhile, even while his mind was occupied elsewhere, his body dealt with the enemies of its own accord. One black thing pressed an absurdly large tusk against Vesper's armor and strained hard at it. A strange sound began to come, little by little, from the tooth's root and the gum, and before long it broke. Not the armor — its tooth.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main5_Content_1:
Vesper's fist seized the throat of the thing as it tried, dumbfounded, to pull away. Then he drew it back toward himself. Lowering his head, he dealt it a headbutt with the sharply jutting rim of his helm. Aiming exactly between nose and brow and ramming it, he split the thing's face wide open. The golden flame Vesper then poured out swallowed up the thing as it toppled, spewing blood. It died having cast off its once dim and bashful guise, turned now into a shape brighter and more radiant beyond recognition.
"When, and where, and how, did all my other brothers die?"
he muttered. What he had just recalled was the story of a mere single member. But the members who had followed him in — how many were they all told? The first to enter were, by rough reckoning, a dozen and more; before setting out on the proper expedition, several more joined. If a good many of those members had already become the bodies of martyrs, then when and where had they become so? Each single moment might be no more than a small, vivid point, yet stringing all those points together made a long ribbon of memory. And memory implied the passage of time. He had the impression that weeks, even months, had passed since he entered The Rapids — but that made no sense.
A black thing came rushing in low, body hunched. It seemed to be leading with hard bone to lessen the impact, but Vesper struck up the hammer he had rested against the ground and countered the thing's flimsy trick. The nape of its neck caved in with a hollow, and its whole head was thrown back nearly behind its shoulders. Vesper drove the hammer down upon the back of the thing as it writhed in pain. Using the hammer, now become one with the ground, as a counterweight, he twisted his body and turned toward the far side of the corpse. The instant both feet touched the ground he wrenched the hammer free and swung it sideways.

"It was not like this."
That was Vesper's reflection upon seeing the black things sent tumbling all at once in a heap. He was speaking of his own members. In memory, the moments of pressing his troops to form up and assigning their roles came back to him. And he had several times, for slightly different reasons each time, had similar thoughts. He had judged that a certain formation could no longer be formed now, that a certain role would now have to be divided up little by little among the surviving members, and issued his orders accordingly. So the members' deaths had not come at any one particular moment. As they explored The Rapids, injuries slowly accumulated, and there came to be those who closed their eyes. The memories he chewed over — mourning someone together with someone, and then that someone falling in turn — linked together densely and let him reckon the passage of time between them. So he had been wandering within this place at least weeks, months?
That could not be.
What of the shortage of supplies, then, here and now? If bandages and medicine were lacking, what of food? Vesper, grown strange in mood, groped at his waist in the midst of the fierce battle. He swept his hands over the bound pack this way and that, trying to find something snagging within it. There was nothing. Come to think of it, had he not eaten the last field ration a little while ago, upon meeting Polaris the Guide? That had been the last. He was certain. And yet had he not thought it the last before then, too? And had he not, perhaps several more times after that, chewed away with the same thought at the same field ration, that ball of grain kneaded with honey?
There was a black thing that, seeing one of Vesper's arms plainly idle, came rushing in at once. It managed, against the odds, to avoid the hard armor and bite down on the thin chainmail that wrapped the joint, but was soon stopped by the forearm beneath it, hard as a stone painted over with pigment. Vesper smashed in the head of the thing, its panic plain, and stamped down on the spine of the thing as it staggered off-balance, finishing it. Onto the bluish mire where its long-lolling tongue still twitched he poured golden flame, putting a meticulous end to it.
And all the while, with the hand not gripping the hammer, he searched the pack again — this time opening its mouth and rummaging directly inside. It was not even very large, yet he always searched for something in just that way. And when he did, there was always something at the very bottom. But what if this truly was the last? The last medicine, the last field ration, the last canteen?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main5_Content_2: Vesper forgot even what he had been doing and put both hands entirely to wringing out the pack. He flipped it mouth-down and shook it out, every last bit. When no amount of shaking changed anything, he pointlessly set the pack upright again, waited a moment, and tried once more. A lump of field ration and a canteen fell out. They were the last that remained. Seeing a black thing coming toward them, Vesper moved swiftly. He set his back to it and drove his weight in, using his back like a great shield. In that posture he stared hard at the field ration and canteen tumbling on the bare ground between his legs. "So this is the last after all." he said. "One was wedged in a corner. How very fortunate." Just as he was puzzling over how many times one could be so mistaken, his body toppled backward. The black thing, having given up the futile contest of strength, pulled away, and Vesper alone, who had been bracing against it, fell flat on his back. To let slip an easy prey lying on its back was, for a Hunter of The Rapids, a thing too shameful to lift one's head over. But the limbs of the black thing that had lunged drooling now suddenly drooped and flopped about like sheets of water-soaked paper. Pushing the corpse away with one hand, Vesper rose. His other hand was buried deep in the black thing's chest. When he pulled his forearm out, thick clotted blood dripped from the plate armor that ran up to his shoulder. What if this is not even the first time I have had such thoughts? Vesper thought. Time had passed — passed far too much. Weeks or months, impossible as it was; yet contrariwise, there were too many moments that made no sense unless it were so. And what of his armor? Whether wrapped in resplendent flame or not, armor is a consumable. When had he last serviced it? And his weapon? When had he last heaped sand upon it and scrubbed it so it would not rust, and oiled and tended it? "What is all this?" Vesper said. It struck him of a sudden that this was a "rhetorical question." It was a phrase he had learned in childhood, watching the venerable priests use it. Not a question asked to hear any answer to something, but a question that is no question, posed in passing to underscore one's own faith all the more. That was a "rhetorical question." If it were not a rhetorical question, then it was as good as an indirect confession that his faith was not firm. He let his head drop and gazed at the ground. The radiance and flame issuing from his armor were dazzling now to the point of being more than even he himself could bear. Most black things would catch fire and fall at merely drawing near, and even his own shadow could no longer be seen. "…Light is faith; doubt is shadow." Vesper said in a low voice. He felt the face within the face-guard flush hot. In the very midst of so resplendent and pure a holy war, that the Order's warrior who bore its very responsibility should sink into vexing cares? "In the very heart of so rapturous a faith, I have committed the sin of doubt." It struck him that he had been forgetting where this place was. The Rapids — the boundary between dream and reality. The domain El'pyros's order has not reached. In so wicked and irreverent a place, was it not, then, only natural that such cunning doubt should arise beyond all checking? "This is none other than a trial from El'pyros!" He flung down the hammer and thrust up a tight-clenched fist. He had cast off the weapon, but two successive sweeps of his forearm turned one, then two of the black things nearby into "things that had been black." Sent sprawling on their backs, they expired without even time to flail. "Memory is the product of thought; thought is the product of life; life is the product of light!" A forest of golden flame burning without cease, a river of dream dust crumbling away and flowing down, and in the very midst of it, Vesper, standing firm as an immaculate spire. Meanwhile the horde of black things sprawled about suffering like so much noise lost all strength and sank down. "Without light, can there be knowledge? Without the flame of life, how can there be thought!… To seek to harm faith in Him, by the very grace of El'pyros — it is unthinkable!" Vesper roared, ringing and loud. He sought out the hammer he had flung away and took it up. Having cleanly burned away the foreign matter clinging here and there, he gripped the haft once more in both hands. It was reassuring. "Doubt is faithlessness; faithlessness is the road to apostasy!" He closed the distance to the few black victims that remained. Being himself a radiance draped in no shadow at all, he drew the shadows of everything around him. Deep, thick, ugly warped outlines were cast over everything other than Vesper himself. "I shall, without fail, see the end of this accursed Rapids!"
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main5_Short: The rations never run out, the wounds never scar, and the comrades are all gone. When a man burns so bright he can no longer find his own shadow, what is it that he refuses to see?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main6_Content_0: "I shall see the end of The Rapids!" He resolved it. That oath lasted fifty years. It lasted a hundred years. It lasted, indeed, thousands of years. But the eyelid within a dream, each time it opens and closes once, dawdles away nine hundred ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine years. And one year more passed after that. Vesper realized that all of this had been, in the end, merely a matter of time. The doubts that arose moment to moment as language, he could disregard. He could ward them off by turning his mind elsewhere before he conceived such words. But to dam up entirely the thought itself, before it took on words — the very room in which a thought might appear — was impossible. The members who did not return; the instants in which they died, and the memories of battle that nonetheless went on without cease; the weapon being sharpened ever keener, and the armor that never wore. And the wound taken from facing the dream creatures. Vesper gazed at the stream of blood pouring in torrents down his forearm. But had blood always been a thick, pale-glowing powder? {IMAGE} He glared for a long while at the foreign matter flowing out from within his own body. There was no sense of wrongness as there should have been, had such a thing been filling his body. One would think he would collapse and die before that — yet, in any case, it was the same substance he had seen no end of times while dispatching the dream creatures, and no other thought came to him at all. A pale, bluish dust was dripping out. Vesper spread his other hand and gripped the wounded forearm whole, as though to wring it. The tendons of the seized arm tightened and his fingers curled in of themselves. As blood rushed in, the fist began to pale white. And yet the blood — no, the dust — did not stop. Avoiding the gripped place, it became a fountain, a waterfall, a brook, and went on gushing out. Coursing freely like the small lines and dots that fill a map's surface in their winding way, it at last made its way out toward the sea that lies outside the body. Was the strange, peculiar scent that quivered in the air the stench of blood, or the dreamlike smell that the substance of The Rapids gives off? Vesper did not stir until the gushing of the dust ceased. And as he stood there, he waited. Strange to say — though no one had yet said anything at all — he was waiting for someone's reply. "Do you understand now?" The voice of Polaris the Guide reached him as though it had always been right there. Without opening his mouth, Vesper groped at his side. He unfastened the pack he had been carrying and gripped it. Within that pouch, gathered slim into his clenched fist, there was surely nothing left at all. It was empty. Now, holding it by the bottom, he turned it over and shook it out. Something that had been inside fell to the ground. It was the last field ration. The last — there was always something left over as the very last. Someone was deceiving someone, telling them that some provisions yet remained, that one could eat and move about comfortably for a while without any doubt. But the one who could deceive and the one who could be deceived were, from the first, until now, and ever after, Vesper and Vesper alone. "I, too, once took a fatal wound." he said. "It was not like this then. It was just blood. Like the other members." Did he just say "fatal"? His hand, pointing to the river of dream dust dried upon his forearm, trembled faintly. But there was still more. One question, whose answer he already knew, remained as his to ask. "It seems I am, after all…." Vesper drew a deep breath. He chose his words carefully. It was hard. Far harder than hoisting a boulder the size of a house to show off his strength. "I am no longer Vesper — I think I am that very memory which believes itself to be Vesper." "A fine way of putting it." With that single line Polaris dismissed his anguish. Anticlimactically. "Now that you have realized it, we can speak… To put it briefly, I am drawing up a future that holds no small benefit even for the you of now." What followed was the rather slovenly verbiage that all who lack confidence in their own plans tend toward. It was an explanation in which there was nothing new for Vesper at all. It felt like the attempt of a greenhorn to crudely string together the things she had seen roaming The Rapids and explain them as a single theory. The dream creatures that decompose into dream dust upon death; the power of gold that becomes the reason they hurl themselves at the traces of reality; and so the wish to share with them the power of gold overflowing in reality…. "All dream-beings require the gold of reality in order to fix their own memory and form." Polaris went on. "For such unstable ones — among whom, of course, you too will soon be counted — I will merge dream and reality into one…." "I have no interest." At Vesper's hasty rebuff, Polaris broke off and gazed at him fixedly. And so no one opened their mouth. "What did you say?" "I refuse, king of unbelievers." Vesper stressed each word clearly. "I do not assent to your plan." The tone was so excessively assured that it sounded almost like the tantrum of an ignorant man. Polaris cocked her head. "You do know that your becoming wholly a being of dream is now only a matter of time?" "I consider that I have already become so." Vesper looked at the forearm where the wound had been. The trace of the dried dust, and the long-gaping wound, had at some point vanished without a trace. When he clenched and unclenched his fist, full sensation and motion returned without the slightest resistance. "And besides — merge dream and reality?" However hearty it was, a scoff was a scoff. Polaris knit her brows. "You mean to fling this irreverent world, left untended without El'pyros's order, upon a reality already perfectly beautiful and harmonious? I shall stop you without fail." "Do you not wish to return to that perfectly beautiful and harmonious reality?" Polaris pressed in, pushing back. "You can no longer leave The Rapids by your own power. To return to reality, the only way is to quietly assent to my plan." "What could the mere memory of Vesper, without Vesper, do by returning to reality?" He began, out of habit, to pick up a stone and crush it.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main6_Content_1: "And what reason is there to return at all? Even without me, the Order stands firm. Faith is without end." The stone became a pebble, the pebble gravel, the gravel grit, the grit grains…. "Even with no substance called Vesper, my name and my deeds yet remain there, passing from the lips of the many members. Those tales would lead the surviving Solar Flame Knights and the other members, and at the same time stand as a warning of this perilous Rapids." The particles, become something near to soil, Vesper brushed off with an open palm. The sight of them all falling to the ground without a single unpleasant fleck left behind, returning to their place, to where they ought to be — it was truly an unburdening thing to behold. "In the end, the moment the present I forces a way back, it becomes my own obstinacy. Only if I remain in just this state, only if my name and deeds alone remain outside and take it upon themselves to serve as guide for so many, does it become the one rightful service to the Order of the Sacred Flame." "This is absurd." Polaris said. "Have you gone mad, hanging upon faith past all reason?" She shook her head. It was the tone of one who could not believe her own ears — could not believe the crude denunciation bursting from her own mouth, worked up as she was at hearing his words, that he could not leave because he thought not of himself but of the Order, and at that irrational rationalization of his. "The truth is that you are now clinging to a pointless stubbornness — you are gone. There is only The Rapids and the power of dreams." Vesper gazed fixedly at her finger held rigid, leveled at him. "So stop your stubbornness and accept the truth before you truly lose everything. My plan, for the sake of the dream-beings, is in the end the very road to your salvation." "Since entering this place I have heard no end of nonsense — that I am a hollow god, that I am a fanatic." Vesper sank for a moment into thought. He recalled the voices that had reached him from among the black things — no, the wicked doubts that had merely seemed like voices. There had been a time when they felt so truly present there that he suffered no little torment of heart. "And now, on top of that, a promise of salvation… I am no apostate so feeble as to be shaken by such words of yours." "This, however, is the truth." "Only unbelievers ever bargain over the truth as a condition of faith!" Vesper struck the haft of the hammer against the ground, forging a great resounding ring. The figure was for all the world a stern teacher dealing with a child throwing a fit. "Faith comes before truth. Faith transcends substance, transcends the vessel that held it, and endures everlasting! Are you not, even now, looking upon a living witness to that very principle?" He went on. "Even if I am not the 'real' Vesper, even if I am no more than his memory — what of it? That, after the single vessel called Vesper is gone, the pure faith it held, the devotion toward El'pyros, did not scatter but remains thus upright — this is already a thing to marvel at!" Vesper — or his memory — rose. Over a body that had bared its naked forearm, he donned his armor. No — he was wearing it. He had never once taken it off from the start. Armor in which golden flame blazed, armor unbreakable that, however scratched, pressed, or fractured, would never be harmed so long as its own will did not bend — such indomitable armor guarded Vesper and his memory. "Faith that, even without substance, presses on along the rightful road as it ought — this is surely the purest rite by which to serve El'pyros. Like the flame and sunlight and warmth that are the sun's greatest grace, I too once wore a body, but am now reborn, wholly under His name, as a substanceless power that burns itself away — reborn into an immaculate glory no one in the Order of the Sacred Flame has ever attained!" "…I see." Polaris said, narrowing her eyes. The corners of her hardened mouth opened and closed slowly, as though unwilling. "I misjudged." "Do you mean to repent before true faith?" She asked it so blithely, and yet so earnestly, that Polaris nearly burst out laughing. "It is only foolish of me to have thought I might tell you my plan and seek your cooperation — or at the least your tacit consent." "What would be more foolish still is to refuse the inevitable yet again." Polaris glanced behind her. Belying the title of Guide, her own path forward was slowly being sealed off. The golden flame pouring from Vesper's body had begun to fill the surroundings in the shape of a long ring. From the hammer raised in venom-sharp readiness spread a dazzling radiance — a radiance that, even as it erased every shadow cast over the hammer and the Vesper who held it, conversely draped everything around it in the shadow of disbelief and original sin, a shadow never to be washed away. "Come at me, false Guide." As the hammer pointed at her, Polaris's contorted expression was reflected whole upon its surface. "You who would dare offer up the reality embraced by El'pyros's order as fodder for the dream — you abominable unbeliever, who falsely laid claim to virtue while hiding such a scheme within!"
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main6_Short: If the man is gone and only the memory of him remains, can that memory still call itself faith? He is offered the way home, and chooses the flame instead.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main7_Content_0: In the dead of night, Vesper, having finished his prayers, lay upon his bed. As he gazed blankly up at the ceiling, a deep orange light like the glow of dusk shimmered all over it. He had set a deliberately short candle in a generous dish, so before long it would go out on its own, and he had no wish to rise before sleep and do anything more. From the wide-open window a cool, settled night breeze drifted softly in. The languid sound of croaking frogs put his heart at ease as well. Vesper stretched out his body, all its strength let go. His two feet and arms, slipped free of the coarse single coverlet, simply lay there, nothing more. Those boulder-like muscles, which had always devoted themselves to gripping, tilting, and hurling something, lay sprawled just so atop the bedding, with no need to bear or impart force to anything. Vesper, yawning, did not open his closed eyes again. A touch frivolously, he even smacked his lips. Reaching one hand behind his neck, he shifted the wooden pillow, fitted the nape of his neck snugly against it, and let go his strength. The feel of it against his body was cool. The fatigue of the day, the memory of the beads of sweat that, when one busied oneself absorbed in work, would trickle down a drop or two and tickle the back of the neck — it all melted softly away. Everything was perfect. Now, if he lowered his arms again and let them hang slack alongside his thighs and simply emptied his mind of all thought, he could fall straight to sleep… Without realizing it, Vesper folded his arms. The resolute shape of those two forearms coiled around each other before his chest looked as though they would serve, with no want, as the anchor-cable of a great ship. Do I desire the suffering of unbelievers? Vesper thought, knitting his closed eyes. It was a question that had tormented him for long years. Especially at a time like this, when, in a place where there was no need to mind the gaze of others, he took off his armor and sought sleep, it was a doubt that surfaced nine times out of ten. But any sound, sensible person of the Order of the Sacred Flame knows that a question can lead to doubt, doubt to disbelief, disbelief to apostasy! "And yet I cannot simply ignore it…." Vesper found it amusing, thinking his own words sounded like sleep-talk. But it was no question to take lightly. This was perhaps a measure by which one could gauge how faithful one was to El'pyros's cause. Matching his breath to the croaking of the frogs outside the window, he closed his mouth. Instead he quietly sank into thought. He posed the question once more — do I desire the suffering of unbelievers? "No, I do not." Still with his eyes closed, he asked and answered himself. "Suffering — suffering is an exceedingly useful tool." A resolute, distinct voice strove to shake off the drowsiness. "So long as one is not bound to it or fixated upon it, it is the means by which right and wrong can be taught most swiftly." Vesper chewed over the memories of his childhood. For saying his mealtime prayer half-heartedly, for taking and wearing another child's clothes, for slacking on the cleaning of his assigned area… unthinkable now, but the Vesper of those days was so. Each time, he was harshly scolded by the stern teachers, and sometimes by the venerable priests. There were times he stood out a punishment holding something heavy, and times he was struck with the switch. There were times he resented it, thinking such suffering had robbed him of his joy and pleasure, of what was rightly his. Brief though it was, there were even times he bore a misplaced hostility toward the adults who would not turn a blind eye to him, rather than repent of the self that had done wrong. But before long he gradually came to realize. That the things lost through such momentary suffering always came back as far more precious and meaningful moments. Being struck with the switch hurt. But there was a teacher who looked at the marks left by it and applied salve. There was the memory of lying face-down on a bedsheet made downy by the sun, his calves bared, dozing off as he felt the touch of the ointment settling gently upon the hurt and the hand of the teacher dabbing it on. Not being able to see the bright sun, the brilliant midday, with open eyes was stifling. But the world he met for the first time on the day he turned ten welled up all the more overwhelming for all that he had not known it. From that day on, even going off to sleep in the windowless room became a thing to look forward to. For the fact that, when he opened his eyes in the morning, he could meet the resplendent world again! The great expectation laid upon him was a burden, too. But the swelling pride he felt when, striving as though his life depended on it, he actually lived up to it — the elation and the self-esteem he first felt when he had reached an age where he could aid, and at times even lead, the venerable priests who had always seemed so far above him — he would not have traded for anything. "All the sufferings of my childhood vanished clean away as I came to believe in El'pyros." Vesper murmured. As the stray thoughts settled, a low, strength-drained voice came out. "There was a reason for all of it… it was a momentary suffering, borne in order to receive the great grace." And what of today's unbelievers, by contrast? Vesper's mood soured. Those born outside faith from the start, and the adults who grew up there learning only laws and stories other than faith — their heads had already hardened so. Such ones build families again and raise their own children by the methods they know, the methods of unbelievers. That cycle must be broken, by whatever means. Even by somewhat coercive methods! Here, in the end, the tool of suffering cannot but be brought to bear. "You can stop this suffering at any time…." Vesper mumbled in a sleep-drunk voice. He may well have actually said such words to someone, once. Though they were probably half-buried in screaming, and not well made out. "I must not put feeling into it… I am a teacher of unbelievers, not a ruffian who delights in another's pain." At the image rising before his eyes in his half-sleep, the corners of Vesper's mouth curled up in a faint smile. It was the maddening sight of children — willful little stubborn ones who ran riot knowing nothing — insisting that they would chew and swallow stones and dirt in place of food, that they had no need of proper meals or anything else. Is it even possible to win over such little children with logic?… No. A thundering rebuke is needed. Browbeating and cajoling. And first one must give them such a scolding that the tears come spurting out. Care comes after that. Vesper, smiling contentedly, ceased his thoughts. That great chest, broad as a cartwheel, began to rise and fall slowly. Starlight pouring in through the wide-open window shone upon him as he slept in peace.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main7_Short: In the quiet before sleep, an old question rises that the faithful must never ask. Does he punish to save them — or does he simply wish them to suffer?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main7_Title: The Place Where Everything Can Be Seen
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main8_Content_0:
Beneath the sun crossing the very highest point of the sky, as the hour drew infinitely close to noon, every shadow vanished without a trace. In an open-air arena spread with rough, dry sand stood Vesper.
"Do you mean to surrender?"
he asked. Having cast off his usual familiar golden armor, dressed in a light tunic and short breeches, he clicked his tongue at the someone before him.
"That will not let you keep your life. This Trial by Faith will not end so cheaply, either."
The one listening to his words was someone of a scrawny, emaciated build. His waist was thinner than Vesper's thigh, and as for his forearms, with a little exaggeration, Vesper's thick thumb looked the sturdier of the two. If Vesper was a fruit grown full and ripe, the one before him was the husk of an empty grain; if Vesper was a great, raging hornet, the one before him was like a glimpse of the petal of the first wildflower to fall. And that one waved his hand, refusing to take the weapon and armor Vesper had held out to him. On the very eve of a duel, no less.
A Trial by Faith with a captured heretic — a duel that, quite literally, divides life from death — was a custom the Order of the Sacred Flame neither particularly encouraged nor strenuously forbade. It had its uses, too, in that it let heathens swiftly confront their own sin and at last proclaim their conversion to true faith.

"Because I face you bare-bodied and bare-handed, you, such as you are, would match my conditions?"
Vesper struck his chest and scoffed. His gaze swept over the other's body. From head to toe, then from one elbow to the other, the span of a blink was enough.
