Owing to the difference in height, to meet the other's eyes straight on he had to lower his head until the back of his neck nearly ached, and frankly, even if the Trial by Faith were to begin and end this instant, that seemed likely to remain the most physically taxing part of it. That gaunt, sorry body of his — even were it furnished not with a weapon but with a war-chariot drawn by two full-grown chargers, victory would be hard to vouch for.
"There is no need for that. This is a consideration of my own, so put on the armor and take up the weapon."
"That I will not resist… is because it is a meaningless thing to do."
The heathen opened his mouth for the first time. In a hoarse, strengthless voice, yet enunciating clearly, he spoke.
"Meaningless?"
Vesper cocked his head.
"Even formed as I am, against you in sword and armor, bare-bodied I—"
"That is not what I mean, child of El'pyros."
A vein rose at the temple of the colossus listening. This insolent cur — what was he saying just now of a member of the Order?

"At the end of this Trial by Faith, the loser's — no, my — answer may change however it will, and by it the rightness or wrongness of the matter may seem, for the moment, to be decided."
The heathen went on, wetting his parched lips.
"But for all that, what changes is only the answer; the thought in my head will never change."
His arm — an arm that looked as though it would snap clean off like a toothpick — pointed at Vesper.
"You, now, look sturdy by nature, but ordinary folk like us suffer pain and sickness for any number of reasons. And each time, we undergo a change of heart and bearing that astonishes even ourselves — not a change of the thought in our heads."
In fact, from the way that arm could not properly hold its point at Vesper and kept dangling and wavering, it seemed it might already be broken. His time spent in the Order's keeping appeared to have been none too comfortable.
"On a day when the head feels as though it will split, on a day when sharp coughs come tearing through the back, on a day when the limbs ache so that taking a single step is hard… if one were to single out only such moments in a person's life and pelt them with questions about reason and conviction, that person could become a heaven-defying apostate, or just as readily a devout believer. Both furnished with perfectly persuasive forms of answer."
"And you delayed the inevitable to spin out such a long-winded speech?"
Insolently, Vesper seized the whole of the wrist that had been leveled at him and twisted it. The joints and the bones turned over meekly, with hardly any resistance. It felt like kneading an underripe vegetable.
{IMAGE}

"Aagh…!"
"Well, then."
Vesper asked.
"Even so, does that thought of yours — that 'thought that the thought in my head will never change' — not change?"
"It does not, change."
Gasping for breath, his eyes hazing and burning, the heathen strove still to go on speaking.
"Rath, er, this very act… what is happening now — that it is not the deciding of a thought's rightness or wrongness — is what I mean."
Along the arm bent in the wrong direction, the heathen's other arm clutched at his own forearm. And still, unable to master the pain, his whole body trembled and shook. His head soon dropped low. Then it lifted again. And so he looked straight into Vesper's two eyes.
"It is proof that, depending on who inflicts the pain and who has no choice but to endure it, only the answer changes."
"But does not the answer stand for that person's thought?"
Vesper asked, gazing up at the sky. He meant to reckon the movement of the sun.
"How much longer is needed at this rate? How much further must the shadows lengthen?"
Without slackening the force that twisted the wrist, gripping it tight like a rein that checks the idle wandering of a word, he went on asking.

"The you of that moment will be denouncing at the top of your voice every conviction and thought you have held all this while. You will even deny the you of now, and praise to your mouth's drying the true radiance you have just then awakened to."
"The answer, yes, it becomes so, however you like, it changes."
said the heathen, his face gone white.
"But for all that, it is a mimicry babbled by this frail spirit unable to overcome pain. To please the other, it will gather up any words it does not mean. The thought in the head — however much the me of that moment plays at confession and repentance — this thought, here, now, in this head, will not change."
"And what is that thought?"
"That a world of dreams exists."
The heathen, gritting his teeth, met his gaze once more — for some reason with the air of a last time.
"And so to your Order's imperfect power, which cannot reach that place, I must not offer up my faith—"
Vesper watched a single thread of blood trickle down from the heathen's tight-clenched lips.
"—even if, at the end of cruel torture, I should truly, truly come to want to, that is no more than a blunder the me of that moment commits, unable to bear the pain."
The heathen curled up the corners of his quivering mouth. He smiled. He was trying to.
"That fact alone, that thought alone, will never, ever change."
Vesper put strength into his grip. There came the sound of bone breaking.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main8_Short: Under a noon sun that erases every shadow, a frail heretic refuses both weapon and recantation. If pain can change any answer, can it ever touch the thought beneath it?
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Main8_Title: The Place Where Nothing Can Be Seen
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Short0_Content: The Order of the Sacred Flame charged Vesper with selecting warriors for a secret knightly order. Before the assembled candidates, he demonstrated by scooping up boiling oil with his bare hands. From these fingertips, reenacting the very trials and agony he had once endured, no words were needed beyond one truth: faith must come before life itself.
ui.TravelerStory_Vesper_Short1_Content: An armored hand gently stroked the young beast. This touch, tender only before things that were not human, had lingered within him since the moment he first encountered the outside world as a child. Yet Vesper never called it innocence. He simply reminded himself that it was awe for El'pyros, the creator of all things.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main1_Content_0: Through the gaps between countless worlds, a single Foreign Matter drifted. It had not, from the very first, recognized itself as Foreign Matter. It was only that it had, as yet, no world of its own — no story to fill one. Just as no one, glimpsing a small black speck whirling on the wind, wonders precisely what substance it is or what history it carries, so the Foreign Matter, too, became simply Foreign Matter. A thing that came from outside the worlds, longing to settle somewhere, yet each time drained its cup of defeat and set out again upon its journey. Through the gaps between infinite worlds, a single Foreign Matter drifted. It knew its own insufficiency. And so it suffered always from hunger — not a hunger to be soothed by the workings of the gut, but a craving to be reborn more complete in the realms of the abstract and the metaphysical. To create something new, something its own, was beyond its strength. So the Foreign Matter went on wandering between world and world. Yet every world already had its old master who had long since seized its laws for himself — a keeper, the owner of its story, present without exception. There was a world of geometry made of points and lines alone; a world of number theory whose parts were infinite yet whose whole was finite; a world of time, where anticipation hardened into remembrance and the flutter of the heart left longing in its wake. Through the seams between such worlds the Foreign Matter drifted, busy without a moment to breathe. And in a gap between endless worlds, the Foreign Matter found it at last — a world left masterless, abandoned. It gazed upon the scene before it, lost for words. It was a place with no left or right, no up or down, no front or back, no floor or ceiling, no inside or outside of anything. A sense of space born not from something being there but from nothing being there — a boundless backdrop where anything at all might happen. And across it, all manner of natural things moved in harmony, each according to its own principle. Great lands born of earth and stone clumped together; deep lands born of flowing things gathered together — water, oil, air; round, burning flames that held those lands in their keeping; the bands of cloud those flames formed as they ranged in rows; and, draping those strands of cloud about themselves like the warp and weft of a garment, the many-armed whirlpools that roared. In such a world of natural things the Foreign Matter cried out for joy. There was no voice to soothe these creations, no cold glare to fix upon an intruder. "Found at last — my world!" the Foreign Matter cried. "I have come, the master of you natural things left abandoned without a master!" Looking down upon its subjects ranged out in countless number — its people, and above all its toys — the Foreign Matter smacked its lips. It dithered over what to lay its hands on first, then at last managed to choose one. It was one of the great lands, born of hard matter clumped together. Up close it saw a slightly smaller clod of land circling around it. "Let me see —" With a touch that mingled greed, curiosity, and delight, it stroked the great land and the small clod around it. "— what if I… did this?" Carefully the Foreign Matter took hold of the small clod. Its fingertips met that round surface and slid a little. Left alone, the clod seemed about to slip from its grasp along its original path, so it soon blocked the way not with fingers but with a fully spread palm. For a while the cold, hard clod pressed a hollow into the Foreign Matter's palm — and then it lost its driving force. No longer able to insist upon its old orbit, it began, naturally, to plunge toward the great land beneath it. That is, it would have — had the Foreign Matter's grip not crushed it to pieces in a single squeeze. Seeing the fragments of the small clod scatter in every direction, the Foreign Matter laughed. It laughed until its mouth split, until its belly tingled, until the rims of its eyes were swollen raw. It watched the surface of the nearest great land suffer terribly. The hard parts turned soft, the soft parts hardened; the high places sank and the low places, conversely, surged up. What had been cold came to a roiling boil, and what had blazed hot cooled to ice. That much change, I forced into being! This is my doing! The Foreign Matter's eyes clouded white with excitement. And this was only one small clod, so far. "How pitiful, that not a soul should be here to behold you in all your teeming multitudes." On the other hand, that little experiment had confirmed it once more. This was a world with no master. Merely a graveyard of abandoned natural things — a stage achingly empty, waiting for an actor to come and trample it underfoot at last. "Rejoice! Your actor has just arrived!" The next great land to become the Foreign Matter's target was shoved feebly aside. The orbit it had traced in a neat ellipse began to bend without end. What would happen next? Perhaps it would collide with another great land, or break free of its burning flame altogether and become an utter orphan… Sweating with anticipation as it read the fortune of the change it had wrought, the Foreign Matter's gaze drifted, all at once, elsewhere. The great lands beside the great land, the deeper lands beyond them, the greater burning flame beyond those, the other flames beside it… ranged out, it seemed, without end. With such a stage before it, was there any need to fix upon a single great land, a single story? "Now I am the story of this place." The Foreign Matter burst out laughing. Then it flung both arms high. "The one and only master here!"
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main1_Content_1:
*

And so time passed.
A century, ten thousand years, a million years — there is an established unit of time called the eon, a span of a billion years that almost no one ever uses, that few so much as know of, and that much time passed.
Boredom was, of course, bound to set in.
"How dreadfully dull this is to look upon!"
the Foreign Matter declared in a voice of feigned solemnity. Was the same old story about to play out yet again, like the hundreds of burning flames and thousands of great and deep lands that had passed beneath its hand? This time, however, it was different. It had to be different. The Foreign Matter meant to make a result far more thrilling and far more irreversible than any story so far.
"As the master of this place, I have decided… to do this!"
It seized the largest, most luscious of the nearby burning flames — the one that therefore held the most lands in its train. And it hurled the thing outright. Not shoving, not blocking, not breaking, but flinging away the entire system gathered around that flame, root and branch. Its destination was another luscious flame's system. That vast, vast distance closed helplessly, and in an instant the moment of collision drew near. The Foreign Matter approached, breath coming in gasps.
The explosion was rapturous.
Since it was the clash of flame against flame — fluid against fluid, the foremost, one might say, of all flowing things — the spectacle was dazzling beyond compare. Centered on the point where they met, a warped, crown-shaped wave bloomed wide open, its tips swallowing whole the great and deep lands nearby. And then the baptism of flame, surging up to scores, to hundreds of times that height, carved a jagged scar deep into the very backdrop of the world — like a signature its master leaves behind. Watching the great and deep lands tremble and reel and brawl among themselves now that they had lost their center, watching them tilt and lurch while the small clods, fallen likewise into panic, served as carrier pigeons spreading that chaos this way and that, the Foreign Matter rediscovered its first joy. For a good while it clutched its belly and laughed — loud enough, to use an awkward turn of phrase, to send the world packing.
The laughter, however, stopped as abruptly as it had begun.

"Is this all?"
the Foreign Matter spat out, as if displeased.
"This is the whole of the story you have to offer up to me, the master of this place?"
Having done it once, it grew bolder still. The Foreign Matter seized another burning flame and did the same. The collision of flame against flame repeated. Perhaps because there was nothing left to hold it back this time, a roar and an explosion greater than the last, a longer and uglier mark, was left upon this world. But for an artist's signature, lost as he was in his creation, to number only two in all the world — for his first masterworks, the very first steps of his career, to come to only two pieces — would that not be a disgrace to his dignity?
The Foreign Matter began to torment everything in sight, mercilessly.
Small clod against small clod, great land and deep land, deep land against deep land, flame against flame — the orbits of their mutual embrace warped and twisted as if gone mad. Every one of them floundered and struck and was struck, was squeezed and swallowed and sent tumbling, throwing off sparks. And those sparks were reflected, just so, in the Foreign Matter's two eyes.
"More, more!"
The burning flames it threw, and threw again.
"More!"
The processions of flame began to scatter. In the midst of the emptied clouds, the traces of this world felt more vivid than ever before. The things that had served their newly arrived master with all their devotion were now — to the Foreign Matter's utter, supreme satisfaction — afraid. They were clutching at the trouser-hems of the very thing that had once found no foothold in any world, begging for mercy. They were prostrate before its all-powerful might, pleading and groveling!
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main1_Content_2:
"This is enough."
The Foreign Matter did not think so. It was not enough yet.
"Perhaps I should stop now."
The Foreign Matter most decidedly did not think so. It could play on, more gleefully, more destructively. And yet its body would not move.
"You would do well to learn the full majesty of my person… why won't it move?"
The rampage ended with no warning at all. It stopped. To the Foreign Matter's own senses, however, it had been stopped. It could not stretch an arm toward another flame. It could not kick out a leg to strike a nearby deep land. It could not turn its head. Even the eyeballs in their sockets were nailed toward one single point.
"What… is this?"
The Foreign Matter strained with all its might, but nothing changed. It could not take any form even slightly other than the one it was caught in now. It cannot move. It must not move — as surely as it is right and proper that great and deep lands should orbit flames, and flames orbit one another.
Some unknowable power lay coiled in this place.
"I'm — I'm just tired."
The Foreign Matter tried not to be aware of its own crumpled mouth.
"I used my strength all at once, that's all. It'll, it'll pass soon —"
"Who are you?"
A voice came, all at once.

"And — and who are you, then?"
The Foreign Matter was a little surprised at how quickly it had regained its composure. Once, it had feared it might revert to its old self — a mere small black speck drifting between world and world — and flee with its tail tucked. But not now. It was not its former self. It was the master of a world, the owner of a whole and complete story!
"I am the master of this place, the actor upon its empty stage. And you, voice — what are you?"
"By whose leave do you dare lay false claim to being my master?"
What sort of non-answer was this? It had said it was the master of this place — who had said anything about being its master…? In that instant the Foreign Matter's thoughts snapped off violently. Immobile though its two eyes were, they were enough to convey the appalling realization that had just dawned. Its slack jaw let out a soundless groan — what if the very impression it had formed on first facing this place, the assumption that this was a world of natural things abandoned without a master, had been a false premise from the start?
"How should this world — eternal and undying, boundless and everlasting — serve any master other than the one whose name it bears?"
What if the very manner in which all things ran their natural course — the natural things made of great and deep lands and flames, and all the motions between them — were the will of someone? What if there had been a master ruling this world from the very beginning, and the Foreign Matter had simply failed to notice, bound up as it was in the most minute and trifling fraction of that vast world? What if a speck of dust, infinitely small against a world made of thousands of needles and the thousands of threads strung through them, had strutted about on top of it and deluded itself: "There is no one here!"?
In the midst of thousands of needles spinning a story from thousands of threads, was there any reason to spare a thought for a single mote of dust dulling a single needle's tip? Of course there was not. Until a moment ago.
Until that mote of dust dared to go skipping across the tips of several needles and begin its rampage.

"Ngh, nngh…."
Frightened now, the Foreign Matter tried to pull itself free. It could not. For that was now the new law of this world. It tried to resist, wielding the power with which it had tormented the great and deep lands and the flames. It could not. One stronger than me, one quicker than me, one cleverer than me — resistance is something you offer against such as those. To declare that you will resist a world and the laws of a world was to say the very same thing as proclaiming that you would murder the morning, force the sea to its knees, and seize and cage the wind and the rain.
"I am at once the stage, and the actor, and the law, and the story, and its master."
"I — I am the master of this —"
"This place is Yubar —"
The master of the world revealed itself. Before the light of a true star, the Foreign Matter's two eyes were stained pitch-black with terror.
"— and I am Yubar."
With all starlight and all darkness, the Foreign Matter's sentence was passed.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main1_Short: A wanderer crowns himself lord of an empty heaven and bends the stars to his whim — until a voice asks the one question a god should never have to answer: by whose leave?
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main2_Content_0:
Yubar's world — Yubar himself, who takes the world as his very being — raised the conductor's baton. For an instant a pure-white flash was drawn like a chalk mark against the backdrop of the cosmos, but it soon subsided. For in a performance, what should shine is not the color in which the conductor's fingertips dance, but the feast of sound that rings out through them.
Yubar closed his eyes and cleared his voice. The air around him warped with tension and excitement.
"Are you ready?"
Countless stars answered. It was not, however, an answer of the kind one can see with the eyes or hear with the ears. This world was a world of stars, and at the same time it was Yubar's world. Yubar was this world, and Yubar was therefore all the stars, and he already "dwelt" within the thoughts of those stars. Yubar spoke, and the stars answered… it was a process of exchanging not words but sentiments and notions, impressions and sensations and feelings. To render it in pen and ink, merely describing the answer of all the stars would take an age — but for Yubar it required almost no time at all. He lifted, ever so slightly, the baton perched upon his fingertip.
And so the performance began.

How can one express a song that takes the Milky Way for its score and the endless stars that embroider it for its notes? That Yubar and the knowledge of his world had never studied acoustics or harmony was at once a hindrance and an advantage. For even if the performance was, objectively, a mess, one does not need much in order to hear that melody and feel something. Just as one need not gird oneself in painstaking preparation to feel the release of sinking one's whole body into water, so it was with the performance of Yubar and his world. He shut his eyes tight and lost himself in the music, oblivious to the passage of time.
The music had meshed and turned as perfectly as the facets of a finely polished crystal and the play of iridescence glinting through their seams — and yet, little by little, it began to go awry.
"Perhaps it grows dull, staying always in the one place."
Yubar laughed to hear the grumbling complaints of a few stars that kept breaking in mid-performance. The further a note was from the score's beginning and end — and especially the more neighboring notes it had around it — the quicker it was to whine. Lodged in the middle of the piece, hemmed in by other chords and structures and passages, left no room for any reinterpretation, a mere prisoner of the one fitting rhythm: there was, admittedly, no special reason that should be entertaining either.
"If you were to swap your places as you pleased, would the harmony of the cluster, the balance of the galactic arm, not break?… And the tuning of the piece besides."

To this the notes had nothing to say. Partly it was that Yubar had soothed them with such generosity, but above all, for a single star to venture any opinion on a cluster of a million such stars — or on the staggering score of a galaxy, a million such clusters gathered again, and on the laws that define it — was a hard thing to do. And so the notes began to vent their nowhere-bound grievances against the loftier tier far above them upon the other star-notes right before and behind and beside them. The sound would ring out better if you weren't next to me, they said; it's because you make that sound in front of me that my own part gets buried, they said… Wherever the interstellar winds carrying such views crossed, fierce sparks appeared. Waves of heated argument, surpassing even the collisions of any particles, bloomed and faded and bloomed again without cease. The sight had long since degenerated into an unseemly brawl among the stars.
"Now, now."
Yubar made his voice stern, for show.
"No fighting, the lot of you."
The notes' discord, however, did not easily subside. He set the baton down for a moment and pressed a hand to his brow. He had no intention of truly losing his temper, nor of taking one side over another to force the conflict to quiet — yet even so, was there nowhere some convenient method that could resolve each and every grievance the notes held… or was there?
And conversely, why should there not be?
Yubar halted the performance and silently snapped his fingers. Then he narrowed the focus through which he beheld the world — small, very small. He passed beyond the tier of the Milky Way, the score; beyond the tier of the cluster that is the bands and planes of stars; beyond, even, the tier of the stars now bickering in the thick of it. What Yubar stopped to observe were the various masses those stars held in their keeping. Made of earth and stone, of water and oil, such things were far smaller than the stars — yet they too held within them the potential for many sounds. And this, though from the Milky Way's vantage — the score's vantage — they were no more than the trifling ink-blots flicked from the tip of a zinc-plate pen as it dabs down a single star-note.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main2_Content_1:
Yubar chose the surface of one land and tapped it lightly. A heavy, far-spreading sound leapt forth in discontinuous bursts: this was a percussion instrument. Yubar chose another land and rubbed its surface with care. A sound at once delicate and deep continued, unbroken, as a continuous spectrum: this was a string instrument. When he breathed upon the surface of yet another land, a scale — likewise unbroken but far lighter and ever-changing, shifting with the shape of the mouth and the texture of the surface — flowed forth: this was a wind instrument. And to think that all those possibilities had been shut up within a single note, the smallest and most fleeting basic unit upon the score! Yubar's eyes flashed like the final moment of a star at full ripeness.
"All of you, stop your fighting!"
It was rare indeed for his will to take shape with an exclamation point attached. And so the stars, too, at once fell silent at Yubar's word and straightened their posture — not out of reproach and the fear that follows it, but as a sign of their reverence for him.
"When you could be a chord, why must you remain a single note?"
What could this mean? The stars glanced at one another, trying to fathom Yubar's meaning.
"When you could be a phrase, why remain a single chord; when you could be a movement, why only a single phrase; and further, when all of you together could be an orchestra complete in every part, why should I force you to remain a mere speck upon the score that is the Milky Way?"

Yubar rubbed and blew upon and tapped the nearby lands all at once, and drew forth, on the spot, a single melody. It was not especially well made — but for that very reason it was a melody that would sit oddly with nothing that came after it, one that, fastened to any accompaniment or lyric, could draw out the harmony in fitting measure while still keeping its own resonance. And all of this took no more than the performance of a single star and the lands attached to it! Seeing it, the stars looked up into Yubar's face with eyes full of expectation. It was the birth of star-orchestras with no further reason to settle for the role of mere notes.
"Well, what are you waiting for?"
His palm spread wide open, and the baton vanished from sight. Not that it had suddenly disappeared somewhere — it had divided. Into countless small fragments of inspiration and brilliance. To the million clusters a single galaxy holds, to the million stars each cluster holds and the several clods of land each of those holds in turn, Yubar's power was given, without exception. The power to judge what music is beautiful and what is not, what note harmonizes with another and what does not, and accordingly to choose for oneself a single music and perform it.
"Begin."
And so the ensemble of the stars went on.

If the earlier song was a stream of water, this one was a waterfall; if the earlier scale was a gentle breeze, this one was a storm. For a moment Yubar forgot even his own station as god and as the world itself, and surrendered his whole body, drifting aimlessly. Both a listener steeped in the orchestra's performance and himself a part of that orchestra — spinning the melody, plucking and tapping and blowing the instruments — he attained a state of selflessness, of egolessness, that fairly carried him beyond himself.
"Even so, you will soon grow weary of it."
said Yubar. The star-notes had become a single orchestra now, but how long would that last? About the time a single star is born and closes its eyes, stars would begin to appear, grumbling that this too was a bother, that they were sick of it. And once that happened, would they have no choice but to become helpless prisoners of an eternal tedium, unable to find anything more to do? Was such a future the cold conclusion that awaited Yubar and Yubar's world?
A boisterous burst of laughter rang out.
"As if!"
The stars, the galaxy, the world, Yubar — all cried out with one voice.
"When there is work to do in such overflowing abundance."
said Yubar. He took countless stars and galaxies for his orchestra and his phonograph, and recorded a performance without end. Said Yubar. He took countless stars and galaxies for his brush and his canvas, and painted a landscape that never ran dry. Said Yubar. He took countless stars and galaxies for his warp and weft, and for the patterns of colored thread woven across them, and let the ridges and furrows of a surging fabric trail down like waves of five hues. Said Yubar. He took countless stars and galaxies for foundation and timber, and raised up structures that climbed higher without end. As conductor and performer and painter and tailor and architect — Yubar and his world, each within his own eternal story, so declared:
"This, my world, is eternal and complete."
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main2_Short: He gives every star the freedom to become its own song. But what does a maker do when even eternity learns to grow bored?
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main3_Content_0:
"And who might you be?"
said Yubar, conductor of all starlight and galaxies.
"I am called Polaris."
"Color, curvature, motion… in a celestial body, what distinguishes one from another is property and function. A name is of no importance."
Dismissing the stranger's words, he drew his own hand up to eye level and studied it. It had unmistakably the shape of a human hand, yet the claws at its tips were the narrow, sharp claws of a feline; and the palm, too, but for the plump bare pads, was covered without a gap in sleek fur. Seen one way it was an unnatural form, yet no one in the world — or rather, the world itself — thought so. For the world was Yubar, and Yubar was the world's sole agent and sole interpreter.
"Well, since you seem to be leaving my stars in peace, I shall call you a guest."
Polaris gazed at him quietly. Before his looks or his build, it was the proportions of his body, the perspective of it, that utterly shattered common sense. He was near enough to meet her gaze. Yet at the same time his two outstretched arms rested on an armrest woven of burning flames, his sleek, slender legs upon a footstool made of great and deep lands. She could not even tell whether she stood before him, whether she had bowed in courtesy, or whether she floated somewhere, forced into the same line of sight. Was this the lot of a mortal granted audience with a god?
Even if that god were no more than a being inside a fairy-tale book?
"What matters is the fact that, in my one whole world, a being such as you has never been, nor could ever be…."
Yubar ended, without much meaning, the act he had begun without much thought. Taking his eyes from his own claws, he looked at the stranger before him, the being who had named herself Polaris. He wanted to know whether she was simply sparing her words, or whether she was truly preparing to say something of importance. And so he set himself to know it. For all things in this world could keep no secret before Yubar. Yet he could not know. The feel of her was different again from the earlier Foreign Matter. This "Polaris" seemed to have come already with a story of her own — and above all, from a whole and complete world that gave that story its support.
His curiosity roused, Yubar cocked his head and waited for the rest of her words.
{IMAGE}

"And what if your entire world were nothing more than something held inside a fairy-tale book?"
Polaris had braced herself for the storm that might follow those words. This god of a fairy tale, who called himself Yubar, might fly into a rage, might marshal all his power to attack — though that would amount, in the end, to a scribble trying to erase the eraser — or might refuse to hear another word and banish her clean out of the world. The last case was the most troublesome, and so she had prepared every manner of countermeasure. Yubar, however, rashly attempted none of them. Instead he began to think.
He thought, very deeply.
"Inside a fairy-tale book — you mean to say, a fiction?"
Yubar asked.
"That this is, at best, a reflection on water; a star's afterimage, bent as it forms; mere static in the galaxy's dark? My world? My power? My… everything?"
"You may regard it so, if you wish."
Polaris answered with a deep bow.
"What a delightful point of view, in truth!"
Yubar snapped his fingers. A hand that mimicked the structure of a human hand, yet kept whole the feline's fluffy fur and soft grip, so that no crisp "snap" sounded when flesh struck flesh. It was an odd sight, but again, to Yubar — from the world's standpoint — there was nothing incongruous about it.
However the finger-snap turned out, it was a delightful moment for Yubar. The claim that "you and your world are inside a fairy-tale book" was far too vague to brush off with instant indignation or dismissal, and was therefore intriguing. A claim anyone could make — and for that very reason, one that laid the burden of proof all the more heavily upon the one who made it. A double-edged sword.
"For so witty a notion, you carry yourself with no little grandeur. Have you any grounds to back it?"
"Yes. Here it is."
Without hesitation, Polaris drew something out and set it down. An object small enough to fit in one hand was moving, ever so slightly.
"It is something that does not exist here — not in you, nor in your world."
Yubar opened his eyes wide and gazed at it.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main3_Content_1: A small brown tuft of fur. That was the first thought that came to him. Without thinking, Yubar looked down at his own body. It resembled his own — the white pelt that gleamed with the sheen of reflected light — but it was more disordered, more ever-changing. And so, above all… it brimmed with a sense of liveliness. What that was, he did not know. Before long, as time passed, he could make out the parts of that tuft of fur — its alien corners, the places that kept moving and the places fixed without any change. Yubar stepped down from the throne of stars and Milky Way and drew near. It was a something shaped like a teardrop. Its features were gathered toward the pointed end, and the tip of its nose, especially, kept twitching. The body, with four legs running downward, was — by what harmony he could not say — slightly warmer than its surroundings. Did it have some mechanism akin to a burning flame? Behind it a long tail trailed. "Well, well…." When the beast vast as the sky thrust its face suddenly forward, the frightened mouse scrabbled backward in a panic. Polaris's wrist, however, was the limit of the room granted it. With its retreat cut off, the creature, valiant beyond measure, mustered against Yubar the greatest threat it could manage. It opened and shut its jaw, clacking its teeth in a sharp "snap." Yubar's brow and his two ears pricked sharply up. "Hush, hush now…." Polaris covered its back with her hands cupped like a bowl, soothing it. Its breath, shallow and quick as if it might suffocate, and its hammering, pit-a-pat heartbeat, began little by little to slow and grow still. Stroking the mouse, Polaris raised her gaze, and it met Yubar's — who, having at last shrunk his frame, could now be perceived as a single person. "It is 'life.'" "A most simple and crude structure." Yubar declared. Then he supplemented the declaration. "With evidence so slight as this, it is not enough to assert that I am a being of fiction." "Is that so?" The mouse surely could not understand human speech, yet as those words fell, it huddled into Polaris's palm, somehow looking a little crestfallen. "A structure that takes for its core the thing that defines its own making, then draws surrounding matter to itself to shape itself? Such a form is one I could demonstrate here and now, with ease to spare." Yubar crooked his fingertips. With effort trifling next to the shaping of constellations, the possibilities of various "life" flickered past before his eyes. Among them were things that, instead of breathing air, swam through the insides of flowing matter; things far larger and more massive than this "mouse"; things whose forelimbs gave up their feet in exchange for light, broad fur and could lift their bodies into the empty air — in short, all manner of fantastical lives. And so Yubar's world and its story began once more to ripen. A place where something that could not exist in this world wandered about as an everyday thing; he was on the very brink of destroying the argument that his world was a mere product of fancy, and that the outside which made it was the real — had it not been for a single remark from Polaris. "But have you not already seen this life?" Yubar heard that riddling remark and grasped its hidden meaning almost at once. And so he tipped his head back and let out a hearty laugh. He felt as though he had fallen into a trap — and at the same time, he was uncontrollably delighted. For was it not so? After seeing the mouse, everything he produced — however original, however seemingly brilliant — he could no longer claim had existed in his world from the start, or that he had known of it. After seeing the mouse, anything larger or smaller, faster or slower, cleverer or duller, could only be something conceived with the mouse fixed as its eternal, unchanging point of reference. And even were he to insist stubbornly otherwise, he had no way to prove it himself. Ending his laughter, Yubar stroked his chin and fell into thought.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main3_Content_2:
"A god inside a fairy-tale book… I?"
Polaris, and — for some reason, having nothing better to do, a single mouse lingering in idle vacancy — gazed intently at such a fictional god. A moment later Yubar, who had been glancing at them, broke into a grin.
"I have understood you well."
At this juncture, to abruptly believe "I am a being of fiction!" was impossible. On the contrary, that itself would be a leap. What was worth noting was rather this: that something which had never been in his world, and someone who had "entered" carrying it from somewhere, had appeared. And had he not, just now, tasted a stinging defeat in his contest with that someone? It was a contest not of power against power, but of wit and wisdom. The cunning that had logically pinned him helpless by presenting such simple, slight evidence must surely have come from somewhere Yubar did not know — somewhere nearly as whole as Yubar's own world, and perhaps more richly varied still.
"At the least, I must grant that there exists some category encompassing the outside of this world. And that you came from there."
Polaris bowed her head. The mouse, with no further reason to be out, went meekly back into the pack. Whether the mouse, too, offered a courteous farewell, there would now forever be no way to confirm.
"Very well, you who came from some greater somewhere that encompasses my world."
said Yubar, having shrunk his frame to a fitting size. Polaris felt that she was, somehow, now looking down upon him rather than up.
"Is that all you wished to say? Or is this merely the groundwork for a body of text yet to come?"
"I wish to show you the place from which you — the descriptions that compose you — have come."
It was a singular turn of phrase.

"The 'descriptions,' you say?"
"Your hair, your fur, the look in your eyes, your neck and shoulders, your arms, your hands… what if they did not simply come to be so as a matter of course?"
said Polaris, watching Yubar prick his ears in curiosity.
"Your body is made of forms and properties modeled after some life — like the one you saw just now — or some part of such a life. I wish to lead you to the world where those descriptions dwell, to the world beyond the world that made you and your boundless power possible."
"A most fantastic and perfectly risk-free, gentle promise!"
Polaris tensed her body. Yubar's words, delighting with feigned childlike innocence, had a bone in them. Not a hard bone, perhaps, but cartilage at least lay hidden within.
"'The world that made my boundless power possible,' you say…."
He twirled a lock of his fine hair round and round, lost in thought. Then, all of a sudden, he opened his mouth.
"If my power originates within this world, does that mean that the moment I step out, what remains is no longer the god that is me, but only the me that is a being who merely thinks and feels something?"
"You may regard it so, if you wish… but is it not a journey worth taking all the same?"
Polaris widened her eyes and posed the question back to him instead.
"To know what sort of place that great world is — the one that bears the weight of all these little imaginings strung beneath it, this world among them — and which of its imaginings shaped you and this world of yours: I should think that yearning, more than anything, must be burning in you now."
Yubar laughed again. Her retorts were so smooth and unflappable that he had no mind even to grow angry. Above all, it struck him to the quick. For a god is not a being who guesses, or supposes, or feigns ignorance. A god is a being who is satisfied only by plunging in himself, digging it all up, finding it all out.
For if there is a world a god does not yet know, then he must, by rights, come to know that too.
"If you have made up your mind, follow me."
beckoned Polaris — she who is known to many as the Guide.
"I will show you what lies beyond all the names and rules you have known: the world of the Rapids."
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main3_Short: A stranger offers a god a single, devastating thought: what if your whole universe is only a page in someone else's book? And what waits beyond the cover?
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main4_Content_0:
"It's about time I tired of this, you'd think —"
said Yubar, drinking the Rapids in to the full. He halted where he stood and drew a deep breath. He opened his eyes wide as saucers and gathered the whole scenery of the world within them. The air of the Rapids, the look of the Rapids, the smell of the Rapids, the sound of the Rapids… outside his own world, the shape of the true world — he etched it into memory for who-knows-how-many-th time. Then, slowly, he scooped up a handful of earth in his bare hand.
And he put it in his mouth.
Polaris, the first time she saw it, had recoiled and told him to stop — but it had been the very first thing he did upon coming out into this world, so what was to be done? In the world of stars he had, very occasionally, "eaten" Star Sweets, but that had been no true taste or food, only the impression of one. To be told that this new use for the tongue, found only after coming out into the Rapids, must be reserved for the proper moment and the proper object alone — was that not too cruel a sentence?
"— still fresh as ever."
Yubar spat out the wet earth he had been chewing. Even in the task of scraping out the gritty grains left in his mouth he could find a satisfaction and pleasure of its own. He stretched both arms out wide and gazed up at the star-strewn sky. Whenever he did so, a wondrous feeling came over him — enough to make him forget what he had set out to do, where he had been going, even that he had been retracing his path in reverse.
"Small a world as this may be, to behold it as so small a self is truly fascinating."
Small stars, and a small world that hung them out across the sky. Once Yubar had roamed the cosmos in fellowship with such stars, and so at first he had struggled even to understand the fact that he was now fixed fast upon some surface. What had he looked at then, and what had he thought?
Yubar mulled over the time just after he had left his own world behind and entered the Rapids with Polaris.

"The world of dreams, however, is gravely incomplete."
Polaris had gone on prattling about something behind him, but the Yubar of that time had had his mind elsewhere. To some degree he had ignored her on purpose. All the while he had been wholly absorbed in examining this new world from every angle. It was around then that he first chewed the earth, and that Polaris, aghast, had wrestled him off it. But there was no help for it.
The alien taste of something felt for the very first time was that addictive.
"Those — are those, then, the stars I once saw from far, far away?"
Yubar craned his neck until it nearly broke, gazing up at the sky.
"Far, so far… how far away are they?"
"I mean to save this incomplete world."
Polaris, for her part, was tirelessly pressing some point of her own.
"And how small a thing am I?"
"Through the power of the gold that lies in reality, I will give this place its form and its nature —"
"Might you be quiet for a moment?"
Yubar spread out a hand still thickly caked with earth and cut her words short. Did he then fall silent at once? Or did he go on exchanging a word here and there afterward? The Yubar of now could not remember. In any case, that she meant to save this world — that much was certain. The specific method?
"Either I didn't listen, or I forgot it… what did I say then?"
"Would you strip away from me, who was a god, a joy never once granted me in all my time?"
Yes, that was it. He had said that. The past Yubar who cut Polaris's words short.

"And what is it I am stripping away?"
She, tenacious as ever, would not meekly back down either.
"Please, hear me. This world —"
"From a state of being ignorant of nothing, I now stand at the starting line of an absolute and perfect ignorance, knowing not a single thing."
In truth — though he himself did not know it — at that point Polaris had already given up any thought of conversing. Not because Yubar's tone or manner was firm, but because of the state of him, looking all but out of his wits — on account of the wet, saliva-reeking earth that streamed down his chin with every word, soaking his chest and the front of his clothes.
What use was there talking to a man so deeply absorbed, when he wouldn't hear a word of it even with the back of his ear?
"To feel, for the first time in all my existence, the joy of coaxing and soothing that ignorance bit by bit and cultivating it into knowledge — and you would do the wretched deed of stealing that joy away? So let us meet and speak of it again, someday, later on."
The Yubar of that time wheeled about with a wave of his hand. As though shooing off some bothersome insect.
"For a while yet I shall be far too busy learning of this world to spare a moment for it."
What had happened after that? He had spent his time exploring the Rapids, feeling the Rapids, coming to know the Rapids. He could not say how many days and nights it had been, but in that time he had met various people and learned things he had not known. There were even pleasures greater than putting cold earth in his mouth. He had come to know a food called "sweets," much like the Star Sweets he used to enjoy back in his world. He had put them in a satchel and was nibbling them out little by little, until — ah!
He had dropped that satchel somewhere along the way. He had been retracing his path to recover it.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main4_Content_1:
"This is surely the place I passed through before…."
Yubar tilted his head. The familiar thickets and rocks, the familiar hills and trees…. And yet swarming in the midst of that scenery were unfamiliar parts that had not been there before.
"I see folk I've not seen before. You there!"
Yubar stepped lightly, daintily, into the throng of strangers.
"You wouldn't happen to have seen a satchel about so big, would you?"
The strangers gave no answer at all. Their whole bodies were shrouded in a pitch-black aura, their forms hard even to make out — shy, perhaps, that they should be. Yubar did not give up, and kept addressing them. He did not shrink from clapping his hands, tapping a shoulder, waving an arm to draw their gaze. It was a sociability that the old Yubar — Yubar the eternal, immortal god — could never have dreamed of.
The Hunters of the Rapids, meanwhile, were a little flustered among themselves.
Yubar gave off, as was only natural, almost none of the scent of gold for which they were mad — for his origin, differing only in tier, shared in the end the same lineage as the fictional world from which the Rapids was derived. And so there was no cause for them to bare their aggression outright; yet to have someone approach them so freely, and address them no less, was a thing they had never met in all their born days.
"A taciturn lot, you are… I'm quite certain I dropped it here."
Yubar put a hand to his waist and let out a small sigh. By now he stood in the very midst of the teeming swarm of Hunters. In a silence so overwhelming that even the sound of leaves turning red would have rung loud as thunder, the gazes and feelers of swooningly many Hunters all trained upon Yubar's every move. While the crystals of galaxy and starlight — sensing the strange currents near their master — alone flashed and gave off warning, the one most concerned, Yubar himself, shut his eyes and let out a long yawn.

"No help for it. I'll just have to find it myself — I say, you there."
His hand came to rest on the nearest Hunter.
"If you'd just step aside a moment, I'll have a look where you're sitting and be quick about —"
The Hunter vanished without a trace. So it appeared, at least — but in truth Yubar had, in his own way, moved it elsewhere. The star-power he had reconstructed after descending into the Rapids was still unstable, and above all, beyond compare feebler than the true god's power he remembered.
Yet to the Rapids and its products, it seemed still recklessly strong.
"Ha-ha, I've made a blunder."
Yubar rubbed the back of his head sheepishly — but the rest of the swarm had no further reason to wait and see. The Hunters, in the forms of all manner of beasts and monsters, drew back, the fur along their spines bristling thick. Baring livid fangs and pincers and upper jaws, they began to make a grim, hissing sound. In the eyes that had watched one of their own vanish, helpless, a fire blazed up.
"I meant to set him down just beside you. My apologies."
Yubar stretched out one hand and pointed somewhere, without confidence.
"If you go about five days in this direction, you should meet him again —"
A Hunter with sinews bulging more than a span high — a thing better called a monstrosity than a beast — lunged at Yubar, all out of patience. Fortunately, starlight condensed into a gentle cone, and the galactic crystals draped over its top like armor, served as a shield. Faced with the inexplicable situation of a barrier with neither weight nor the sensation of biting into anything, yet past which it could go no further, the Hunter snorted in bewilderment.
"Ah, well met."
Yubar thrust his face up just the same on the far side of the transparent shield and smiled at the Hunter.
"Yubar is my name. Now, after this, are we to clasp hands and shake them, or bow our heads, or what?"
"KUAAARGH!"
It was not language enough to warrant quotation marks, but from Yubar's standpoint it was perceived as such. A forepaw of monstrous size was swung, but the shield of starlight did not so much as stir. The galactic crystal even turned the force back upon the attacker — so it was plain as day how furious the Hunter must have been.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main4_Content_2:
"KUAAARGH!"
"I haven't yet learned that manner of speech, you see. If you'd care to teach —"
Yubar's gaze drifted absently toward the bare ground. The spot where the one who had greeted him had been standing.
"— me, then, ah… eh?"
There lay a satchel, crushed flat. Beneath the sole of the very one locked in a contest of strength with the starlight.
{IMAGE}
"L-look at this!"
Yubar, flustered enough to stammer, bent down. To the other Hunters, of course, this was at once an instinctive signal. That the enemy had turned his back to them and lowered his guard — his very body, no less.
"You've been standing on it this whole time! It very nearly —"
He could not finish. He pitched forward, flat. To the one on the receiving end it was a shock great enough to pop the eyes from their sockets and make him bite his tongue — yet even that was, in truth, thanks to the star-throng that desperately shielded their master. For the attacking Hunter had thrown the full weight of its body upon him, meaning outright to kill.
"Ah."
Feeling a strange taste on his tongue, Yubar let out a lament. For an instant, but he felt it. That the situation had gone awry the very moment he was loosening the satchel's mouth; that the last few "sweets," fallen so onto the bare ground, had been mashed by his own falling body — not merely mashed, but smashed to utter bits and pulped together with the earth.

"Ah, ah."
He braced his hands and lifted his chest from the ground. Crumbs of grain went scattering down. The tastiest part, the thing called "honey," had already become one body with the sticky clods of earth. His eyes raked swiftly over the satchel, but there was nothing left inside.
"Th-this was the last of it."
said Yubar.
"The food most like my Star Sweets —"
The crystals of star and galaxy circling round Yubar trembled with an ever-clearer light. They grew nearly invisible, all but transparent. Unlike what the Hunters had rashly concluded as they began to roar, it was not that the power was being lost. It was growing that much thinner, that much keener, that much hotter. So hot that the trail of its heat was hard to follow with the naked eye.
"Is this, then, your greeting to me?"
said Yubar. The shields made of crystallized light formed thicker, faster, in ever greater number, becoming a net with narrow eyes and mesh. And so it caught the swarm of Hunters like a school of fish.
"Then receive, in turn, my hospitality as well."
A blinding light swallowed the whole place. No roar, no scream, no explosion — nothing. A light simply came into being, and was gone.
And with it, all those teeming Hunters.
As the light subsided, Yubar's two hands came wavering up over the rim of the great crater left in the ground.

"Was that too much?"
Groaning, he hauled his body up onto the surface. His two arms — slender as fresh shoots, never once put to hard labor — shook and trembled. His whole body was covered in earth. Yubar flipped himself over and lay back against the ground, gasping for breath. His face, beaded with thick drops of sweat, burned hot. Fur soaked with sweat clung limp along the contours of his body. His throat heaved as if dancing. His flank, his shoulder, the inside of his upper arm ached and pulled taut. From his parched mouth a strange smell began to rise.
And yet none of it was the least bit unpleasant.
"What new experiences these are."
he said.
"How much there is I still do not know, how much I have yet to meet anew!"
He raised a clenched fist. The stars of the sky, ten thousand leagues away, felt so very paltry. Here it might be no more than a trick of perspective, but for the Yubar of old it had truly been so. And here, too, it would soon become so. If only he could truly find the source of dreams and its boundless power.
"Wait… Polaris?"
What was it she had said? That the world was unstable, that she therefore meant to save it… Did that mean the Rapids might suddenly vanish before his eyes before it had laid bare to him all its own origins? Yubar grew abruptly uneasy.
"Had I known, I might have listened a little better…."
Through the words that had passed by in no particular order, and through his talks with the various folk he had met in the Rapids, he had learned that Polaris had revealed herself not to him alone but before many others, and had saved them. Among certain dream products there even seemed to be those who served her for that very reason.
"Next time I meet such folk, I must ask them."
said Yubar, rising to his feet.
"What, precisely, and by what means, Polaris has resolved to set right."
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main4_Short: A god learns to taste the dirt of a smaller world and delights in every misstep — but how long can such gentle wonder go unanswered before something bares its teeth?
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main5_Content_0:
As he wandered somewhere in the Rapids, Yubar met Polaris again.
Where, exactly, in the Rapids was he wandering? He was simply wandering somewhere. Of all the antique, ever-shifting, dazzling sceneries of the Rapids, it was just some place in the Rapids, nothing especially singular or excellent or distinctive. What was Polaris doing there? She was simply standing about — at least, to Yubar's eye, she did not seem to be doing anything. Was she killing time? Sunk in solitary contemplation? She looked somehow downcast — had something happened?
Setting aside all such one-sided interpretations, Yubar thought that, at the very least, since they had met, they might exchange a word of greeting.
"It's been a while. Have you been well?"
Polaris merely turned her head, brusque, to look toward where the words had come from.
"…Ah."
Her eyelids closed very slowly, then returned to their place.
"It's you."
Her two eyes flicked over Yubar's bare hands and his chest. Then, with a jerk of her chin, she asked:
"Still going about eating dirt?"
"I'm trying to quit… have you come to finish your explanation?"
Yubar asked Polaris, whose brusque expression simply would not soften.
"What?"
"That time — you were about to lay out your explanation, of saving the world, of some method or other, and I stopped you, did I not?"
"…While dribbling dirt down your chin all the while."
Yubar watched for a while as Polaris suddenly burst into laughter at her own words. Even with her mouth opened wide in laughter, she looked neither full nor unburdened by it. Though he was no master at reading the relations between one person and another, his first one-sided interpretations were growing more and more plausible.

"Is something the matter?"
"It's hardly been any time at all — I can't very well say I've suddenly grown curious about it now."
Polaris said cynically.
"You didn't hear me out then either, did you… Just go. Once you've seen the Rapids till you're sick of it, then perhaps some curiosity will stir."
"And what do you suppose I have been doing, wandering about all this while?"
Yubar asked.
"I met those who know you, and heard their tales. I came to know what you have done, and what you mean to do hereafter, and why."
To learn of the Rapids while picking out and skipping over only the knowledge of its Guide — was such a thing even possible? Nor was it a secret that had to be dug out with any great difficulty. The products of dreams need gold. Gold, however, is fundamentally a substance of reality. Therefore, if reality and dream are merged into a single world, there will be no more dream products suffering for want of the power of gold — three sentences were more than enough to sum up the whole of Polaris's Plan.
That did not mean it was an easy thing to do, of course.
"Merge reality and dream, and bestow reality's gold upon the products of this place. Is that right?"
"And what do you think of that work?"
At Polaris's question, Yubar fell briefly into thought.
"Is it that you cannot tell whether the work is the right choice — or that you are not certain you can see it through?"
To answer a question with a question was not a commendable thing to do. Still less commendable when the returned question summoned a silence longer and more painful than the original. Yet she who heard it only let her head drop quietly. It was the gesture of one struck to the quick, at the very point she had been brooding over within.
"This is the right thing to do, and therefore a thing that must be done."
Yet that look in her eyes did not cloud in the slightest.
"To save the suffering folk of dreams, it is a thing I must push through without wavering."
"Then you lean nearer to doubting whether you can see the work through."
Was Polaris's idle worry resolved so simply as that? It had only just now come to light.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main5_Content_1:
{IMAGE}
"…It's a bit awkward for the one who dragged you out of that world to say so, but you were a god. One who thought, and did, a great many things."
"I'm still in the midst of being a god, I'd say?"
A barbed remark, slipping out from beneath the playful tone.
"Well, isn't that all to the good?"
Polaris hollowed her lips and waved the matter off.
"Even granting you're a god, surely not everything in your world came to pass the same way — without effort, on a whim. So you must have had such experience —"
she went on.
"— some work that needed a plan laid before it was begun, that took no small toil, that had to have its missteps set right afterward. And could you, by any chance… know it before you did it?"
The two of them locked eyes.
"Whether it was a thing I could do, or whether it was not?"
"That is a worry with no solution."
Yubar's answer came back so lucid it was almost hollow.
"One caught in such a worry can only remain forever not a god, but a worshipper."
"Are you saying I mean to become a god?"
"To save a whole world and every creature within it, without exception — whose work is that, if not a god's?"
To save ten people is a teacher's work; a hundred, a thousand, are the work of a general and a king, respectively. But to save ten thousand, a hundred thousand, and beyond that the one world that is the Rapids and every living and lifeless thing, every object and backdrop, every subject and notion that has its origin in it — that is no task a mortal clad in any office can shoulder. It can only be the work of a god.
"If you try and fail to the very end, that is your answer; and if you somehow find something, that too is your answer — no?"
Yubar shook his head from side to side, drolly.
"If I, this small Yubar, dragged down from the pantheon of the fairy-tale book by your own hand, may presume to add a few words."
Hearing those words, edged as they seemed, Polaris snorted a laugh and shook her head. Watching that somewhat absurd sight, Yubar too nodded and smiled. A stranger who saw it might have thought that one of the two was offering an apology for something, and the other, feigning reluctance, was accepting it.

"The beasts look up to humankind and seek answers. Those humans, in turn, look up to the gods and pose their questions."
said Yubar.
"But whom does a god look up to…? He cannot. A god must be the final, irreversible full stop to all his own doubts and worries."
Polaris gazed at him in silence.
"If you have succeeded in pushing through to the very end, then it was the right thing, and it will go on being the right thing. If someone barred the way midway and you were thwarted, then it was wrong — and was a thing doomed to go wrong from the start."
"What sort of forced logic is that?"
"Do you know some other way to carry oneself like a god? I'll grant you —"
Anticipating, perhaps, a fairly sharp rebuttal at so irreverent an implication, Yubar spread both hands.
"— I am no expert myself either. I was a god from the very beginning, and never once doubted such a role. But if there were a fitting method to become godlike — to become, indeed, a god — and if it were, as you'd have it, a sensible, reasonable procedure one could follow without resorting to any forced logic at all… then would the something one could thereby become really be a god?"
He went on.
"What sort of being is a god? A universal, logical being, conforming to everyone's reason? The symbol of some body, that could win a majority's signed assent, persuade the rest, and at last be issued a unanimous 'certificate of godhood' — is it merely that I have not yet glimpsed such a possibility?"
Polaris bit her lip. That one who had never been a god, and another who had been a god inside a fairy-tale book, should be discussing godhood, the very nature of what makes a god! Was it not a sight beyond merely laughable, sad even.
"Hard as it is even to press on to the very tail end of the path I've chosen, hard as it is even to keep my eyes fixed unwavering ahead — would you have me glance backward and slow my steps besides? Begin to take stock of your own capacity before any truly draining work has even arisen, and the road you must walk only grows the more treacherous. So — the words have come round a long way, but in answer to your question: yes. There is one!"
Yubar raised a finger for emphasis.
"There is a general method by which, before doing a thing, one can judge whether or not one is able to do it."
"What? But…."
Polaris looked confused.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main5_Content_2: "Just now you were saying the very opposite, all this while —" "It is to actually go and do the thing." Sometimes it is the most plainly exposed contradiction that is hardest to catch at a glance. Yubar watched Polaris's brow, which had been smooth in incomprehension, slowly knit. As if the strength had gone out of her, she let out a long breath. "What sort of forced logic is —" But what had he just said about gods and forced logic? If a god cannot resort to forced logic, then how is it a god, and how could the responsibility of saving an entire world be laid upon any being other than a god? She closed her mouth. Unconvinced she might be, but she realized that voicing such grievances back at him would do no good at all. And that, more than anything, was what pleased Yubar to see. "You — I see you're quite the celebrated Guide here in the Rapids…." Yubar grinned. "As a god, though, you're only a greenhorn yet." "Strong words from a dirt-eating god in a fairy-tale book." "And who was it pinning down that very god to pour out her troubles?" "Troubles? Who said anything about pouring out troubles?" Polaris gave a light rebuke and turned away. She gazed for a while at the scenery of the Rapids spread before her, then twisted her head round as if she had just remembered Yubar was there. "Now that I think of it — what is your own opinion?" "Of what?" "My plan, to merge dream and reality. How does it sound to you?" It was a simple question, yet at the same time it was the very first one she had thrown out — the one that had been smoothed over, slipped past by opening an entirely different topic. Yubar held off his answer for a long while. "I am neither the Guide of this place nor its god, only a single Traveler. There is much I have yet to learn." he said. "I am in no position to pass any judgment on a plan you have built up as the culmination of your every experience and conviction — not yet." "There you go evading again." The laughter that trailed Polaris's words — this time it was Yubar's turn, the other way round, to feel the bone within them. "…You won't abandon it because I object, and my work won't change because I raise both hands in favor — so it isn't an answer worth pressing for right this moment, it seems." "My thoughts exactly." Polaris turned her head once more toward the faint, far reaches of the Rapids. Yubar quietly gazed at her back. Anew, the day they first met came to him — and the impressions of when, having descended into the Rapids, he first faced the true world beyond his own. Though in truth what I most wish to ask you is something else entirely. Yubar thought. How complete a world is can only be known from outside that world. Only after coming out into the Rapids could Yubar see how monotonous and unbalanced his own universe inside the fairy-tale book had been. A world with flames and great lands and deep lands of every kind, so many one could never escape them, and yet across whose surfaces not a single echo of life ever resounded… While dwelling within it, those things had been invisible to him. They were so utterly a matter of course that there had been no cause for such a strange perception — closer to a metaphysical sense of indebtedness — to form at all. And this place, then? "If someone were to ask whether this place is not merely another story outside the story, and whether you are no more than another Yubar within it — could you, Polaris, give an answer?" Yubar murmured low. Just as he himself had been, before he knew the truth — what if Polaris, too, were simply a Polaris whose own Polaris had not yet appeared? If so, then was she not merely dreaming of her own complete world and a plan that 'might' be complete within it? "Are you not, like the past me, simply being deceived — failing to see something, yet not yet knowing that you are?" Yubar gazed intently down at his own hand — or rather, at something close to a 'cat's forepaw,' as the knowledge he had gathered in the Rapids would have it. That she sought to borrow power out of doubt not in her plan but in her own want of strength would, in that respect too, become a weakness. Setting aside whether the plan itself was right or wrong, was it not a structure all too apt to let those with wholly different intentions — those even harboring malice — pretend to serve her while lining their own pockets? What if, just then, there were someone scheming in the shadows to corrupt the voice of the renowned Guide Polaris, to spread an altogether different song of terror and division — working not for the Guide Polaris but to accomplish their own twisted ends? Could Polaris herself ever know it? "You have no need to hear my answer — not now, and not hereafter." murmured Yubar, watching Polaris exchange a farewell and vanish. "There are problems heaped before you far weightier than borrowing the likes of my hand; and once you have looked them squarely in the face and found your own answers, then you will have no further need of help from a god in a storybook."
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main5_Short: Stripped of everything he knew, he finds an unfamiliar joy in knowing nothing at all. But who would dare call ignorance a gift — and what was he too distracted to hear?
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main6_Content_0: "And this makes the…." Yubar stopped and bent down a few fingers to count, then gave it up. "Perhaps I should have tied a knot faithfully each day from the very first… in any case, I've spent a fair many nights by now." Now he speaks of spending the night quite as a matter of habit, but originally even that had been wondrous enough to make the fur stand up all over his body. That the light of the nearest star, crossing the land, made the difference between brighter and darker times, and that these are called day and night — even that had been a strange fact to the Yubar of old. However dark it grew on every side, he had no notion that it was the end, or some halt or pause, of a day, of anything. And so he had pressed on, staggering, forcing his way through the dark, only to learn when morning came that he had wandered utterly off course in the night, and would go searching about for the landmarks he had known. It had been a nuisance then, but mulling it over now, those were enjoyable trials and errors. These days he knew how to read the constellations, the shapes in which the trees had grown, the marks left by flowing water, so even in the dead of night he had no fear of losing his way. Not that there was any reason, in any case, to hurry his steps through the pitch-dark — except to mimic the sleep of living creatures. "And yet, the more intimately I come to know the Rapids and the things within it, the more our conversation keeps coming back to me." Yubar gazed up at the night sky and mulled over his meeting with Polaris. There is a most contradictory property to this thing called thought: once it is cast into the mind, it becomes impossible to tell where or how the thought first arose — like the gait of a horse with a broom tied to its tail. Was it because of this thing Polaris said? Or because of that? Yubar thought hard, but each time, only further questions — offshoots and outskirts, byways and tangents and bystanders straying from the original thought — kept springing up endlessly, so he soon gave up. But today was different. Yubar could tell why he kept thinking of Polaris. It had nothing to do with any word Polaris, or anyone among them, had said. It was, on the contrary, because of the word he had never managed to say. "Everything in this Rapids is, in the end, connected to reality, directly or indirectly. And so, the more I see, the more I cannot help growing curious about all the stories of reality." said Yubar. "The tales of reality that other Travelers and folk of dreams pass on to me by hearsay, picked up here and there — its customs and conventions, its rites, its festivals, its institutions… such things have become, more than anything, a great fascination to me." He gestured unconsciously toward the stars. He wanted to point out which among them was the second-nearest to this land. Only after waiting a moment did he realize — for perhaps the millionth time since descending into the Rapids — that the cosmos here does not respond at once to his slightest gesture. Old habits are hard to shake. he thought ruefully. "Speaking of stars — do you know this?" He went on with his talk as though Polaris were right beside him. "The folk of reality, you see — the star nearest to them, they call the sun. And they hold a grand festival in its honor, I hear. The leaders of that festival, and their close ones, claim besides that they wear the voice of that star. How charming… but this you surely already know, all of it?" There could hardly be only that one thing he wished to know about reality. "And in another land, you see, there are those who help all the various compounds dug up by tilling the earth's surface to recover their pure essence. The homeland, they say, of artisans and artists who are masters at refining things — making what glitters glitter the more, what is hard harder still — into works of art." Yubar wet his lips with his tongue and rolled his eyes about. It was the manner of one who, leaning on another's words, tries to paint before his eyes a scene he has never beheld. "In their land, they say, there stand row upon row of structures so grand they can be faintly seen even from beyond the star. And within them — though the relation of parent and child be renewed any number of times (forgive the clumsy phrasing; I still do not fully understand how two grown things come together to make a small thing resembling themselves) — there are heaps upon heaps of objects revered unchanged. And what of when I heard there is a gathering of scholars who store every secret they have uncovered within seven towers?" A soft, downy hand clutched at Yubar's chest. As if warm mineral water were welling up little by little, the sound of his heartbeat came pulsing, throb by throb, through his palm. "I could not stop my heart from racing. Are the secrets I myself have uncovered already all there too? The things I do not yet know — or, the other way round, might I dare to add to that place something they do not yet know? … If ever I go to reality, I resolved firmly, I would by some means enter those seven towers and meet their keepers." And then the voice that had gone on and on broke off, all at once.
ui.TravelerStory_Yubar_Main6_Content_1: "…To you, all these things I have babbled in my excitement are surely just so much that boils down to a word or two?" He let out a laugh mingled with the sound of the wind. "'Ah, that is such-and-such of some place.', 'That is so-and-so's whatnot.'… you would finish the whole explanation with the likes of that, wouldn't you? Not I. I still see not the cover of the book but each separate moment within its pages — the forms and the reasons, and above all, the stories. And so I wish to see it with my own eyes. To plunge in myself, to collide with it and feel it." Without realizing it, Yubar folded his arms and then unfolded them. It was one of those gestures that even those born clothed in a body let slip without thinking, unable to explain it. "You asked me once what I thought of your plan itself, did you not?" There you go evading again. That was what Polaris had said, hearing Yubar's answer that time. Her face had been smiling, but the words struck to the quick. Looking back now, the Yubar of that time had indeed been evading — harping tirelessly, at the head and tail of every sentence, on not yet, not yet. "I hesitated so because — there, again! — because I had not yet found my own answer." A single question hovered about Yubar like a ghost. From the day he first beheld Polaris, and on after he confirmed the existence of the Rapids, it had pursued him without cease. The more he learned how different the world of the Rapids was from the cosmos he had known, the more fiercely it raged. What does it precisely mean, that I am a being of fiction? Does that one word erase the meaning of all my past and all my future? Or, conversely, does that one word merely trouble the mind of whoever hears it, while in itself bearing no substantial meaning at all? "Is it a thing one can wave off with: I am a god inside a fairy-tale book?" said Yubar. "What if the outside of my story is no more than another story? And another Polaris, come from outside the story outside my story — the one who would enlighten you who enlightened me — must I likewise wait for her to enlighten you and me both at a single stroke?" Outside the story, outside the story outside the… Yubar felt dizzy and pressed a hand to his brow. It was like gazing into the whirlpool of a galactic arm. Even should the vast hole bored through its center swallow everything and return it all to nothing, the doubt would not vanish. "In the midst of this, does it have any meaning at all for me — who can claim to know nothing — to stand here delivering sermons this way and that about your possibly-incomplete plan, of which I may likewise know nothing?" He fell silent, growing faint at the thought. The question was vast. Too vast. A question so vast that even had he held it in the days when he was the whole and complete god of a world, he would have had, at some point, no choice but to set it down. The words too — story outside the story, being of fiction, false god in a storybook — felt newly so. The more so for having jostled, since coming to the Rapids, among things one can surely see and touch, hear and smell. "Even for me, once a god… no, still striving to be one, it is too vast." "But now I know." That confident voice sounded just like another person's. Yubar spread his hand and laid it against the night sky. The thickly glittering stars showed their unchanging presence.
